HYPNEROTOMACHIA POLIPHILI
The Strife of Love in a Dream

Francesco Colonna, Venice: Aldus Manutius, 1499

A NEW ENGLISH TRANSLATION
========================================================================

This file is the complete text of the translation made for the Emblems in 3D
project: chapters XVII to XXXVIII, Book II, and the epitaphs - that is, the
entire remainder of the book from the point where Robert Dallington's 1592
English (the only prior public-domain translation) stops, on page 193, to the
Aldine colophon on page 467.

Dallington covers the first half; it is not reproduced here.

CHAPTER XVII
------------------------------------------------------------------------

[p. 193]

*(This page is the seam. Robert Dallington's 1592 English — the only prior public-domain
translation — stops within it, at the word* Mustulento *below. Everything from that word to the
end of the book is here rendered into English for the first time. The whole page is given, so the
join can be checked.)*

On the next side, I saw, of wondrous carving, a Damsel, virginal in aspect, indicating a matronal
majesty in the figment, with the utmost praise of the artificer. Crowned with corn-ears, with an
elegant downflow of hair and nymphal habit, holding in the right a stuffed plenty of ripe grain,
and in the other holding three stalks with bearded ears, and at the feet a bound little bundle of
ears lying, with this subscription:

> **FLAVAE MESSI · S.** — "To the golden harvest. Sacred."

On the third face was a Divine simulacrum, nude, with the aspect — with wondrous manner and art
expressed — of an infant crowned with clusters of grapes, all laughing with lasciviousness; a
vine-branch clustered with grapes he held in the left, and in the other a full plenty of grapes,
out of the lips with the fronds and tendrils pendent; at the feet of which stood a wool-bearing
he-goat, with this writing carved:

> **MUSTULENTO AUTUMNO · S.** — "To the must-laden autumn. Sacred."

*(— Dallington's translation ends here. What follows is ours.)*

The last part had a regal image of conspicuous carving, ruddy in aspect and rigid, holding in the
left a sceptre, gazing toward the sky — in the dark, turbulent and stormy air — and with the other
touching the hail-clouds. Behind, likewise, the rainy and cloud-bearing air. Clad in a pelt-
covering over the nude, shod with antique sandals, and subscribed with this title:

> **HYEMI AEOLIAE · S.** — "To Aeolian winter. Sacred."

---

## Notes

**Confidence: high.** This is the join between Dallington (1592) and this translation. The page
carries the four Seasons as carved figures on an altar: Spring (on the preceding, Dallington-
covered page), **Summer** (Ceres, *Flavae Messi*), **Autumn** (the infant Bacchus, *Mustulento
Autumno*), and **Winter** (a sceptred, pelt-clad king, *Hyemi Aeoliae*). The Latin tags are read
straight from the woodcut. All secure.

- **The exact seam.** Dallington's *Strife of Loue in a Dreame* (London, 1592) breaks off inside
  this page, at *Mustulento*. His readers never had Winter, nor anything after — the temple of
  Venus, the polyandrion, all of Cythera, the awakening, and the whole of Book II. This page is
  where the four-century gap in the English Hypnerotomachia begins, and where this translation
  picks it up. (See [translation/NOTES.md](translation/NOTES.md).)
- **The four Seasons as dedications.** Each figure is an altar-face inscribed "S." (*sacrum*,
  "sacred/dedicated"): the harvest-maiden Ceres, the grape-crowned infant of the *mustum* (new
  wine), the storm-king of Aeolian (windy) winter. A tidy antique personification-set — the kind
  of seasonal quartet the world could carry on an altar.
- **the marble chosen for its veining** — the next page (194) notes the sculptor picked stone
  *veined with black* to render Winter's stormy sky: material chosen to depict, not merely to
  carry, the image. A characteristic Colonna touch, and the first sentence past the seam.

[p. 194]

For this noble figment the outstanding artificer had shrewdly chosen the marble, which — beyond its
whiteness — was veined (in the requisite place) with black, to express the tenebrous, unlit and
nebulous air, with falling hail. Upon the flat of the said venerable Altar, rigidly rigorous, stood
forth the rude simulacrum of the garden-guardian (Priapus), with all his decent and appropriated
insignia. Which mysterious Altar a cupola'd little canopy covered, affirmed and sustained upon four
poles fixed in the ground. Which poles were diligently invested with fruited and flowered foliage,
and the top all covered with manifold flowers; and between each pole, at the rim of the opening, or
gap, of the canopy, hung, fixed, a burning lamp; and, in circuit, ornately, gold foils, by the
fresh and spring-bearing breezes inconstantly vexed, and sounding with metallic little rattles.

At which simulacrum, with the utmost religion and ancient rural and pastoral rite, certain little
flasks, or glass ampullae, with the foaming gore of the immolated Ass, and with warm milk, and
scintillating unmixed Wine, scattering, they broke; and with fruits, flowers, fronds, feast, and
jewels they libated. Now, behind this glorious Triumph, they conducted, with antique and sylvan
ceremony, the little old Janus ensnared, of ropes and tresses twisted of manifold flowers, singing
songs rurally — Talassian, Hymeneal, and Fescennine — and rustic instruments, with supreme joy and
glory, celebratedly exulting, and with solemn applause dancing, and female voices high-sounding.
For which thing, no less pleasure and delight, with stupor, did such solemn rites and celebrated
feasts here invade me, than the admiration of the preceding triumphs.

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The altar of Priapus under a flower-wreathed, lamp-hung canopy, and the
**rustic rite** performed at it — libations of ass's blood, warm milk and wine, and old **Janus led
bound in flower-ropes** amid Talassian, Hymeneal and Fescennine songs. All secure; the rite is a
learned reconstruction of Roman country religion (Priapus, the sacrifice of the ass, the marriage-
and-harvest songs).

- **The sacrifice of the ass to Priapus.** Ovid (*Fasti* I, VI) tells why the ass is sacrificed to
  Priapus (its braying once foiled his lust); Colonna stages exactly that rite, with the "foaming
  gore of the immolated ass," milk and wine. The passage is a miniature antiquarian essay on rural
  cult — the register that fills the second half of the book.
- **Janus led bound in flowers** — the two-faced god of beginnings, garlanded and led as in a
  triumph, to Fescennine (ribald wedding), Talassian (Roman marriage-cry) and Hymeneal songs: a
  fertility-and-marriage procession. It rhymes forward with Cupid's triumph (ch. XXII), where the
  lovers too are "led bound in flowers."
- **the canopy with wind-rattled gold foils and lamps** — the shrine is hung with gold leaf that
  clatters in the breeze and lamps at each corner: the same wind-animated, lamp-lit ornament as the
  later shrines. A buildable little baldachin.
- **the marble veined to depict the storm** (from p. 193) — restated: the sculptor's stone is chosen
  so its natural black veining renders Winter's clouds. Art collaborating with the material's own
  markings.

[p. 196]

*(Page 195 is a blank leaf — a full-page woodcut with no text — and is not counted.)*

Then, from here, both of us somewhat progressed, with inexcogitable solace, and proceeding further,
I beheld again, at the clear and fresh founts of the gracious and grassy meadows and shady groves,
the cascade-Napaeae dancing, and the pleasant Naiads playing, and the marine Nereids singing —
clad, some, in the skin of the sea-calf (not harmed by the wrath of supreme Jove), with great bark-
vessels of *estur* in hand stuffed with fruits and flowers, gathered from the gravelly shores, and
with diverse solaces idly making festival. Many were, in their hands, bearers of green Thyrses,
which at the summit were compacted of orange-flowers, with soft fronds, and of Egyptian roses,
yellow and Persian, and of Narcissus-flowers, with handfuls of crimson flowers, and odorous of
*amuletum*; with sylvan Pan the Arcadian, and the demigod sylvan hill-dwellers, and the Dryads, and
many others, and Zephyr with his beloved Chloris — to whom he had conceded the power over the
beautiful flowers — and many active and singing Shepherds, in their songs expert to contend, and
armed with their crooks, praised together, jubilating and applauding, with serious games and jests,
with most-ancient instruments of straw and of reed, and with trumpeting Tibiae of bark, of *scytala*
form, of a strange sound, the amorous and omnipotent Jove — festively glorifying — and the holy
country-life, and making most-devout the Floralian feasts.

For which thing, how much voluptuous pleasure I felt, I leave to judge to whoever in his cogitation
could feign it. Therefore, copiously stuffed with incredible joy, with my most-pleasing companion,
traversing, we continued our happy itinerary and amorous walk. Whence, some time, the eyes from
their sweet prison and binding — and almost proscription — somewhat removing, Lo! looking above the
tender and greenest tops of the wanton trees, I saw a lofty Pterygium (winged pinnacle), above,
appearing to me of a round fastigium (gable), esteeming it to be little distant from the whispering
shore, toward which she, facetious, was leading me. And in which the gliding and sloping little
rivers, that circled the valley, terminated; and from the feet of the most-ornate hills and little
mountains — part grassy, part wooded — ran, with most-swift water, in clearest little channels with
a grassy and sandy bed, one leaping down to a side. And then again, beyond the said Pinnacle, I saw a
superb and eminent cupola, appearing to me covered with livid lead. Which at the summit had a cyma in
octagonal form with columns, and above another cupola, and then eight quadrangular piers, covered by
a single top, in balustered figure, upon which stood forth a stylus with a most-round Triangle fixed,
especially splendent with golden brightness. Whence very pleasingly offered itself to me such a
showing, by which I was not —

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The turn, within **chapter XVII**, from the four triumphs to the temple: the water-nymphs (Napaeae, Naiads,
Nereids), Pan, the Dryads, and **Zephyr with Chloris** making a Floralian festival by the shore; then
Poliphilo first sees, above the trees, the **great lead-domed temple** with its octagonal lantern and
gold triangle-finial — the Temple of Venus Physizoa, which he reaches on p. 197. All secure.

- **The Temple of Venus.** Still within chapter XVII, after the four seasonal triumphs the narrative turns
  to the round temple of *Venus Physizoa* ("life-giving Venus"), a major architectural ekphrasis (its
  geometry begins on p. 197). This is the first great building of Book I's later half, and — like the
  Cythera theatre — a buildable structure described in the book's own dimensions.
- **the domed silhouette, from a distance.** Colonna gives the temple's profile as first glimpsed: a
  winged pinnacle, a round gable, a lead-covered cupola, an octagonal columned lantern, a second
  cupola, eight piers, and a gold triangle on a spire. A precise skyline for the world to raise.
- **Zephyr and Chloris** — the west wind and the flower-nymph he made Flora (Ovid, *Fasti* V); their
  presence makes the shore-festival a *Floralia*. The flower-and-fertility key of the whole book
  continues, now attending the approach to Venus's temple.
- **"the eyes from their sweet prison"** — Poliphilo's gaze, bound to Polia (the recurring image),
  lifts just long enough to see the temple: even sightseeing is a release from the captivity of love.

[p. 197]

— mediocrely moved by ardent desire, to behold that more nearly and perfectly, suspecting reasonably
there to be a great and antique structure; insomuch that, for this, I almost wished to pray my benign
Guide that she conduct me to it — although toward the place we were all the while traversing. But
within myself, castigating such desire, I said: "Alas, I dare not obtain that thing for which, with a
thorny goad and with sedulous vehement impulse, I am solicited — and especially that thing so warmly
desired, which I firmly judge that, obtaining it, I could make myself content above whatever lover.
Therefore, repressing and suffocating, and vainly damning such inconsiderate conceit, not demanding
henceforth of so long a torment help, with the diurnal pasture of heartfelt sighs — why, then, ought
I to ask of this, to me not so opportune (a thing)? Alas, active heart, shared and not wholly mine —
how willingly dost thou follow the rapacious hawk of thy living?" — which, wrapping itself in these
wanton snares and fecund cogitations, caused, exciting in the inflamed breast, a continual palpitating,
as the tear-weeping Pheasant, down from the fronds, impelled to flight by the cruel Falcon, its sad
heart beats it.

And so, by these such amorous corollaries frequently agitated, proceeding somewhat beyond our moderate
pace, with my Venerable Nymph, eloquently confabulating, and of the marvellous things clearly seen by
divine grace affably conferring, with mellifluous eloquence, we arrived finally, a little distant from
the re-beaten shore, washed by the pleasant waves of the restless sea. In this place of most-pleasant
site, we found, of the building-art, a most-ornate, most-excellently-made and antique temple, of
antiquarian workmanship and of the greatest cost, sumptuously skilfully-made, and consecrated to the
physizoic (life-giving) Venus.

This sacred Temple, then, by architectonic art constructed round, and within the quadrangular figure
in the evened Area shrewdly worked out — and as much as the diametral line found, so much did it render
its height; and in the circle contained in the area, a squaring is noted. From one side of which, upon
the diametral line toward the circumference, such space (was) divided into five partitions, and toward
the centre a sixth supplied. From which, having then circled another circular figure, the learned
Architect had raised this egregious structure and superb building — as to the principal parts, with the
commodulation, dimension, and of all the compass and content he had been able (to make) — and the
thickness of the walls and of the exterior Piers, and between one circuit and the other (that is,
between the principal band and the columnation, or Peristyle), the free vaulting. From the centre to
the circumference, then, in ten radii, or partitions, the lines deduced, where —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Arrival at the **round Temple of Venus Physizoa**, and the beginning of its
**geometric construction** — a circle inscribed in a square, height equal to diameter, the radius
divided 5 (+1), a second circle struck, and ten radial divisions carrying the peristyle and vaulting.
All secure; the geometry is a genuine architect's setting-out, of a piece with the Cythera plans.

- **The temple's generative geometry.** Colonna gives the setting-out as a real design problem: a
  domed rotunda whose height equals its diameter, laid inside a square, its radius stepped into
  sixths, a concentric ring struck for the ambulatory, and **ten radial divisions** organising piers,
  peristyle and vaults. This is the same "describe it so it can be built" method as the island-plans
  (pp. 311, 325) — the temple is a buildable rotunda, and the world could raise it to these rules.
- **Venus Physizoa — "life-giving Venus."** The temple is consecrated to Venus as the generative
  principle of nature (Greek *physizoos*, "life-producing"), not the erotic Venus of Cythera: the
  cosmic, fertile goddess. It stands on the shore at the end of the valley, between the pastoral
  Floralia (p. 196) and the sea.
- **Poliphilo's self-castigation** — the interior monologue that opens the page continues the
  fidelity-thread: he checks his own "inconsiderate desire," refusing to ask Polia for what he most
  wants, and rebukes his "shared, not wholly mine" heart. The pheasant-and-falcon simile (his beating
  heart) recurs from the pelican of p. 287.
- The architectural description of the temple (dome, columns, doors, ornament) fills the pages
  following, the way the theatre filled the end of ch. XXII.

[p. 198]

— cut the circular interstice, he ordained ten arches, resting upon serpentine columns; and, opposite
the solid support, between one encompassing arch and the other, of a facial breadth of two feet, of the
inner circular band, there resided promptly a hewn and polished Corinthian column, of a height as much
as the Ionic of nine diameters (excepting the capitals), of burnished Porphyry — which carried, with the
bronze capital, to the straight architrave, carried round with the frieze and cornice, led up to the
solid of the fastigium of the inflected architrave, or Arch.

Which architrave, frieze, and cornice, at the order of the live (stone), or of the firm, of the
Corinthian, stood forth with as much projection as the perpendicular line of the aforesaid Porphyry
asked — with base and capitals of fine metal caustically gilt and translucent, with elegant *enthesis*,
or swelling. This order, then, of projection was regularly observed throughout all the Porphyry
(columns), balanced and paired, which had to overstand the requisite little wall of the columnation. But
the illustrious Architect, to give the Area a freer expedition, made the intercolumniation passable.

Whence the inflected architraves, with their horns, rested upon the Ophite (serpentine) columns, turned
and lathe-round, illustrable with friction, the due little slab, or plinth, set upon the capital to give
it a solid footing, and not aerial, through the lids insinuated of the said capitals. And under the base
was reserved a half-altar which had to be the little wall, upon which half-altars the bases of all the
Ophite (columns) firmly resided.

The Corinthian (columns) footed upon a sub-column, or truly a sub-base, of the form of a half-Tube, here
and there, with the half-Altars becomingly joined. Which was worked out from two squarings found from the
diameter of the lowest thickness of the Corinthian; there remained a *sesquialter* (one-and-a-half) for
the rest, to little-waves, Tori, Gulets, Knots, and Cymas, or the like lineaments, above and below,
conveniently dispensed, decently conjoined, with the free bases assigned above.

Each Arch stood elegantly decorated of its keystone, with little boys, and alternately of little barks
with flowered foliage. And every triangle (spandrel) specularly shone with a round jasper of varied
colour, its setting egregiously circled, of little-waved foliage translucently gilt.

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The temple's inner elevation: **ten arches on serpentine columns**, with
**porphyry Corinthian columns** (nine diameters) between them carrying gilt-bronze capitals and a full
entablature; the columns footed on half-altar sub-bases; and each arch keyed with putti-and-foliage
keystones, each spandrel set with a round gilt jasper. All secure; a Vitruvian order-description of a
domed rotunda's inner ring.

- **The order of the rotunda.** A ring of ten arches on green serpentine columns, paired with red
  porphyry Corinthian columns (gilt-bronze capitals and bases), the intercolumniations left open "to give
  the Area a freer expedition" — a spacious, open-arcaded interior. The green-and-red stone scheme is the
  same as the Cythera theatre-gate (p. 347); the world's temple can use it.
- **jasper roundels in the spandrels.** Every arch-spandrel carries a round gilt-framed jasper disc of
  varied colour — a rhythmic polychrome accent along the arcade. A concrete, renderable ornament.
- **the tenfold division.** The "ten arches / ten columns" realise the ten radial divisions set out on
  p. 197: the temple's whole plan is governed by the decad, as Cythera was by the number seven.
- **Vitruvian vocabulary throughout** — *enthesis* (entasis), *sesquialter* proportion, tori and cymas,
  "the order of projection regularly observed": Colonna writes as an architect, and the description is a
  genuine (if ornate) setting-out. Rendered with the technical terms kept.

[p. 199]

In the pier of the Arches, opposite, behind the Corinthian, a third of a fluted quadrangular (pilaster)
stood forth, with the base upon the pavement, standing in the face of another (in the band under the
arch that divided the vaults, fixed) wholly similar. The interval of these, from the one to the other,
the radii drawn to the circumstance made, set upon the line of the outermost Piers. Upon the semi-
capitals of which went round a circum-ligation of gracious workmanship.

The half-Tubes and half-Altars were of bright Alabaster, with curving ropes, or bundles, of manifold
fronds and fruits — of *lacterii* (spurges), of medlars, and stalks of Poppy, growing heavy in their
middle descent, of wavering shoots ensnared, suspended and knotted in certain rings comelily adorned.

Under that circum-ligation a little above narrated, between one and the other striated half-quadrangular
(pilaster), in the primary wall was a quadrangular window of one square and a half, as is required in
antiquarian temples. The opening, or lighting, of which artfully occupied a mirror-like, or diaphanous,
plate of *sogobrina* stone, not fearing old age. Whence, in sum, eight windows there were — because one
part the door of the temple occupied, and, directly opposite the Pronaos in front, another part (the
door, with the golden valves, of the rear chapel, or the sacred Adytum, the description of which will,
in another place, be more fittingly treated).

Over against the above-recited quadrangular columns, fixed in the first mural circuit, the piers
projected outside, worked out from the wall of as much thickness as that of the wall — to which their
breadth the lines of the radii of the division, from the centre to the circumference, gave. Which
breadth divided: one portion was for the breadth of the pilaster; the other portion, again deduced into
a twin partition (one here and one there, the other attributed to the collateral Pier), were for an
arching in the solid of the wall, or vaulted, between one pilaster and the other. Of which Piers the
projection, or outlet, divided by a third, usurped the prominence of the vault from the plane of the
scarped wall; and the two thirds the Piers stood forth, in a solid arched wall-and-Piers. This exquisite
observance the elegant Architects praised, so as not to give the wall a rude thickness so great that the
windows should accuse themselves obtuse (deep-set), with conspicuous respect of the rude and superfluous
solid; and for exterior adornment, which vaults in a ring turned themselves, conjoined most-excellently
one to the other with the same thickness, with due binding, from the Piers, carried round upon the wall,
throughout beautifully girt. Not otherwise, between one and the other contrasting arch, opportunely it
stood.

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The temple's wall-structure: fluted pilasters answering the columns, alabaster
half-altar sub-bases with fruit-and-poppy festoons, **eight windows** glazed with translucent *sogobrina*
stone (two bays taken by the door and the rear sanctuary), and the outer piers whose thickness is
governed by the radial lines and lightened with wall-arches. All secure; a lucid (if dense) account of a
buttressed, thin-walled rotunda.

- **Eight windows and the axis.** The ten wall-bays hold eight windows plus the entrance door and, on the
  opposite axis, the door of the **rear sanctuary (the Adytum)** — whose description is deferred ("in
  another place… more fittingly"). This fixes the temple's plan: a central axis from door to hidden
  sanctuary, eight windows lighting the ring. The Adytum is the temple's secret heart (like Cythera's
  fountain), promised for later.
- **translucent stone glazing** — the windows are closed not with glass but with sheets of *sogobrina*, a
  diaphanous stone "not fearing old age": alabaster-like translucent panes. The whole interior is lit
  through stone, a soft mineral glow. A distinctive rendering cue (cf. the alabaster theatre, p. 350).
- **the wall lightened by arches** — Colonna praises the architects for hollowing the thick wall with
  relieving arches so the windows are not buried in "rude and superfluous solid": a real structural
  refinement (a thin, arcaded drum), not mere ornament. The temple is engineered, not just decorated.
- **poppy-and-medlar festoons** — the alabaster sub-bases carry garlands of spurge, medlar and poppy-heads:
  fertility-and-sleep plants fit for a temple of generative Venus. The ornament carries meaning.

[p. 200]

In this intervalled void, between one Pillar and the other — or between the jaws of these arches just-
said — upon the left mural plane, excavated was the window. Which vault, as much as it was distant from
the Pier, so much it circled under the first outer cornice, encompassing the first roof. Ten Piers, or
bones, of the building there were, and as many arches in the solid, with the exterior wall — excepting
the face where, set fast, resided the chapel (sacello).

The said cornice, embracing the round sacello, joined it with the temple. Beyond this binding ascended
its roof, which was a blind cupola, distinct and free of the greater one by itself.

Let us return, then, now, to the interstitial binding above the circum-columnation, or Peristyle — of
the straight architrave, fascia and cornice, stretched perpendicularly above the Porphyry columns —
where there were born, for each stretch of the binding, little half-columns of quadrature, striated, of
egregious Ophite. Upon the semi-capital of which went round a cornice of conspicuous lineament, from
which the convex of the lofty cupola began its beginning above.

Between one and the other of the half-quadrangular (pilasters) just described, I saw a proportioned
window, timely situated, and of a plate of Bononia (Bologna) of Gaul, opaque, constituted in a field
gilt, of artful Mosaic. Which spaces, with commensurate distribution and equal partition, I beheld most-
admiredly depicted, of wormwork tessellation: the property of each Month of the year, with its effect;
and above, the Zodiac occurring, with the Sun operating; and, to that of the Moon, the phases — and she
is called, among the monthly (states), the new little crescent, the halved, and the pre-swollen (full) —
and her circuit, by which the months are included. And the windings of the investigating Sun, the
solstices and the winter-turns, circling; and of night and of day the vicissitude; and the quadrifarious
commotion of the seasons; and the nature of the fixed and wandering stars, with their efficacy. I
suspected that such art was here ordained by the most-noble mathematician Petosiris, or by Necepso. The
inspection of which things (was) enough to draw the inspector, with excessive solace, to a choice and
wondrous speculation — not without egregious spectacle, and elegant fiction, and comely distribution of
figures, with defined painting of colouring and shadings, by which the commodulation of the bodies and
requisite lights, to complacency representing themselves with most-worthy expression of the effects, with
laudable and joyous show to the senses of the soul. A work, without doubt, worthy of pondering, as much
as ever one could contemplate. Then, in one division, the content of the meaning of the aforesaid works,
of antiquarian letters, was elegantly inscribed. The spaces interposed between the half-quadrangulars
were hedged round with bands, carved of comely workmanship.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The completion of the wall (ten piers, ten arches, the round sacello with its
own **blind cupola** joined to the temple), and — the page's real subject — the **upper windows glazed
with mosaic depicting the twelve Months, the Zodiac, the Sun and Moon's phases, the solstices, and the
seasons**: a full calendar-astronomy programme in the clerestory, ascribed to the Egyptian astrologers
Petosiris and Nechepso. All secure.

- **The temple's clerestory is a calendar.** The upper windows are gilt-ground mosaic panels, one per
  bay, showing each month with its labour, its zodiac sign, the Sun's course, the Moon's phases, the
  solstices and the four seasons — a complete cosmological cycle ringing the drum, captioned in "antique
  letters." For a temple of *Venus Physizoa* (generative nature), a zodiac-and-months programme is exactly
  right: the goddess of natural generation under the wheel of the year. A ready decorative programme for
  the world's temple drum.
- **Petosiris and Nechepso** — the legendary Egyptian king-and-priest authors of Hellenistic astrology;
  invoking them signals the windows as serious astronomical iconography, not mere ornament. Colonna's
  antiquarian sourcing again (cf. Macrobius for Serapis, p. 344).
- **the double dome** — the round rear sacello has its own "blind cupola," distinct from the temple's
  great dome: a subsidiary domed sanctuary attached to the rotunda. This is the Adytum promised on p. 199,
  the temple's inner holy place.
- **"Bologna glass"** — *lamina de Bononia*, a translucent/opaque plate used as the mosaic ground: a
  real early-modern material reference, grounding the fantasy in known craft.

[p. 201]

The remaining walls of the temple, with manifold and various-form Emblemature, were laboriously
incrusted of precious marbles — as best the much-knowing Architect, imagining, could often apply to so
great a magnificence of structure; nor, perhaps, was such made for Ammon. Above the order of the
Corinthians, of most-perfect sculpture, the eloquent Apollo resided, lyring. And above each of the
others, in circuit, upon a fit Altar, of the whole entire, a Muse of *pilates* stone — at the opportune
gestures and office, with the utmost praise of the Statuary most-exquisitely carved — set above the
aforesaid, above, of the encompassing binding.

The huge cupola showed the greatest token, rather of divine operation than of human ostentation. But if
human, not without stupor and accusation of the ambition of so much attempted of the founder's-art by
human wit — for, considering so great a vastness, in one sole and solid casting and pour of metal (as I
judged), I remained most-highly marvelling and hallucinated, damning it almost to impossibility.
Nonetheless, this such Bronze-work was all of Vine springing out of most-beautiful vases, of the bronze
material, standing at the perpendicular and order of the columnation — diffusing the branches, vine-
shoots, or twigs, and Tendrils, dizzily entangling themselves, with most-pleasing conjugation, in
observance of the formation of the convex of the said cupola, one with the other with decent density;
with leaves, clusters, little infants climbing and plucking, little Birds fluttering, Lizards creeping,
in emulation of nature, most-excellently worked out, and all the rest passable (open).

The described works (were) so directly conducted, that, proportioned, in the area they artfully appeared
as much as the natural. Of most-perfect gold, all shiningly gilt. The openings — that is, the void of the
foliation, fruits, and animals — most-fittingly presented themselves stopped with crystalline plates, of
diverse colouring tinged, like translucent gems.

To the congruity of the structure opportune is the integrity of the harmony; for every girdable inner
binding demands the outer girdle. The external piers continued the *areobate* footing, with the three
uneven steps, binding all the base of the temple — as much librated from the area as the inner pavement
was raised — above the *areobates*, or *stylobates*, or Scabelli, in place of a Base: an ornament, with
Tori, Alvei, Fasciae, Gulets, and quarter-circles circling round, and again round the sacello becomingly
circled. Its lowest projection received (worn) from the human foot; and above, the Pilasters. Which, in
the interstice, were pierced through, or tubed, and perforated — that is, the guttering, or compluvium of

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The temple's walls (incrusted in emblematic precious-marble panels), its
sculpture programme (**Apollo lyre-playing over the Corinthians, a Muse over each other column**), and its
crowning marvel — **the great cupola cast as a single bronze vine**, its foliage, clusters, climbing
putti, birds and lizards gilt, and its openings glazed with coloured crystal like gems. All secure; the
vine-dome is one of the book's supreme architectural inventions.

- **The bronze vine-dome.** The whole cupola is a single colossal bronze casting in the form of a living
  vine growing from vases at the column-tops, its shoots woven into the dome's curve, populated with
  grape-plucking infants, birds and lizards, gilt all over, and its interstices filled with coloured
  crystal that glows like gems. Poliphilo cannot believe it was cast in one pour. This is a spectacular,
  buildable centerpiece — a golden vine-lattice dome glowing with coloured light — for the world's temple.
- **Apollo and the nine Muses.** The statue-programme crowns the columns: Apollo lyring over the
  Corinthians, a Muse (in appropriate gesture) over each of the other columns. A temple of Venus crowned by
  the god of harmony and the Muses — generation under the sign of music and art. A ready statuary set.
- **the areobate base and its engineering** — the outer piers stand on a three-stepped stylobate, and the
  pilasters are hollowed as *downpipes* ("tubed… the compluvium of precipitate waters"): the temple's rain
  drains through its own columns to a cistern (detailed pp. 202–203). Colonna designs the plumbing.
- **"nor perhaps was such made for Ammon"** — the surpassing-topos: not even the temple of Zeus Ammon
  (Siwa) had such marble-work. The habitual heaping of famous buildings to be exceeded.

[p. 202]

— engulfed, of excellent jointing, one conjoined in the tongued (socket) of the other. For in open-air
buildings, stairs, compluvium, or gutters, ought not to be placed: first, for the peril of the slip;
second, he who makes water next to his own feet destroys, and befouls his footwear. Therefore such
inconvenience ought to be fled. The uncovered guttering, by inundating water, excavates the area — and
more enormously, if a resistance of subjacent stone opposes — so that the water climbs so much the more
to the footing and walls, as it defends itself from the drops, from the resulting drips.

Not without grave injury, damage and loss (and, by the ventilating impetus, the water pours through the
walls, rendering them then putrid and earthy, and through the windows leaking, exhausted and vanished
every rendering): by the sprinkling of which, there grows in the joints herbage — cotyledon, or cymbalaria,
maidenhair, digitello, pellitory, and polypody — and, ready to produce little shrubs and wild figs, a mural
ruin, with populous and reviving fibres, or roots, rendering the walls inconstant and rift.

Let us return. The band of the first wall derived its height to the level of the summit, of the thickness
of the inflected Architraves, or Arches, above the columnation, and those of the vaulting, from the wall,
opposite the Corinthian column. Above the surface of which wall — that is, of the binding of the circum-led
cornice — was a little channel excavated. Near the lip of which, toward the temple, terminated the scaled
slope of the bronze and gilt roof. The topmost of which summit, above the curved (dome), evenly began,
opposite the sublime line of the cornice, of the Frieze and inner Architrave. In the said little channel,
above the wall, in the flat of the cornice excavated, the waters that by rain ran down the sloped roof were
poured into the receivers of the Piers. And by this way the rivulets of the conceived rain guttered,
precipitating to the bottom; and by hidden pipes, or subterranean passages, flowed into the Cistern. Which
had a Devourer (overflow-drain), by which the superfluous of the waters went out, and sufficiently for the
sacred things remained.

**Confidence: medium.** A largely **engineering** page: the temple's rainwater system (roof-channel →

  cistern — not a dream-vision facade. The world can treat it as constructable.

**Confidence: medium.** The junction where **dome meets pier**: the gilt scaled roof (surpassing the

- **The dome-to-pier detail, fully worked.** Colonna resolves the hardest architectural joint — where the
  round dome lands on the piers — with relieving arches, a cornice that both crowns and drains, and a
  scrolled cartouche masking the transition. The dome's rainwater runs off through this cornice into the
  piers (continuing p. 202's system). Buildable to the last moulding.
- **statue-niches on the piers** — each pilaster-face carries a niche (*solium*) with "a most-noble statue,
  with manifold acts": another rank of statuary (below the Muses of p. 201), lining the interior with
  figures. The temple is populated with sculpture at every level.
- **the volute drawn with compasses** — the page ends with an actual step-by-step compass method for
  striking the scroll's spiral (continued p. 204). Colonna hands the reader the draughtsman's technique, as
  he handed the setting-out geometry on p. 197: the book teaches how to *make* the building, not just how it
  looks.
- **surpassing the Capitol and the Pantheon** — the two most famous gilt/domed Roman roofs (Catulus gilded
  the Capitoline temple; the Pantheon's dome was the standard of engineering); Venus's temple exceeds both.

Of the height treating: it is not completable to have only concluded this universal rule — that a round
temple raises itself as much as is its diameter. But it concurs, regularly, to find the height of the
binding above the peristyle (that is, of the topmost line of the cornice): for, the line deduced from the
centre to the circumference of the first circuit, so much presents that height. Then, all the diameter
divided into six divisions, four of those rectified will likewise give the last surface of the upper
binding.

The rule of the descent of the roof ought not to be neglected: one takes the intercapace from wall to
wall, where the ridge-slip ought to be placed, and reduced into two perfect squarings as much as they can
come; and, the diagonal extended, cutting the line, discriminating the two squares — thence, beautifully,
the slope is exacted.

Universally, the Symmetry of this wondrous fabric, by the outstanding Architect elegantly disposed, with
consentaneous bindings, inner and outer, congruous. Much more diffusely the regulation could, to all
conveniences, to the corollaries of the solid, be manifested — and, by those figures of the area, to find
the Height of walls, which here stood straight, as best one could do without obliquity, or straightness,

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The **inextinguishable-fire candelabra** on the pilaster-tops (shell-mouthed,
festoon-hung, each with a hollow bronze eagle), the gilt-mosaic soffit, and then the **proportional rules
of the temple** (round temple: height = diameter; entablature-height by dividing the diameter in six and
rectifying four; roof-slope by the diagonal of two squares). All secure; the rules are a genuine
architect's method.

- **The eternal flames.** Each pilaster is crowned by a brass candelabrum with a shell-shaped mouth
  holding an "inextinguishable fire" that neither wind nor rain can quench — a ring of eternal flames
  around the temple's exterior. A striking, renderable feature: the world's temple can carry perpetual
  fire-bowls on its piers.
- **the hollow bronze eagles** — each candelabrum's festoon is centred on a cast eagle "showing the
  perfection of the natural," hollow and ballasted: the same casting-virtuosity as the vine-dome (p. 201).
- **the temple's proportional canon, stated.** Colonna gives the design rules explicitly: (1) a round
  temple's height equals its diameter; (2) the entablature height is found from the radius and a six-part
  division; (3) the roof-pitch from the diagonal of a double square. These are exactly the kind of ratios
  the world's temple should be built to — Colonna hands them over.
- **"O unhappy times" (leads into p. 206)** — the passage tips toward the famous lament that the moderns
  have forgotten antique architecture; the theory here is polemical as well as practical.

**Confidence: medium.** The famous **lament for lost architecture** ("O unhappy times… how is so beautiful

- **The manifesto for antique architecture.** The page opens with the Hypnerotomachia's most-quoted
  cultural lament — that Colonna's own age has forgotten the ancients' mastery of the orders and of marble-
  polishing (*xesturgy*). It is the theoretical heart of the whole temple-ekphrasis: the building is an
  argument that classical architecture must be recovered. Worth surfacing as the book's architectural creed.
- **The centre of the temple: well, Medusa, hanging lamp.** At the exact centre is the cistern's well-head,

- **"in default only of the spirit"** — the carved nymphs lack only breath to be alive: the standard topos

of such liquor the four upper (lamps) burned. Where reflected the vague colourings of the precious stones,
in the greater lamp, and the greater in those, with inconstant splendour vacillating throughout all the
Sacred Temple. And by the mirror-sheen of the most-terse marbles — such an Iris the Sun, after the rain,
does not paint in the air. But above all, a marvellous thing this represented itself to the sight: for the
sculptor-artificer had perspicuously excavated, in circuit, upon the corpulence of the crystalline lamp, of

excavated, but of raised work, and so-made expressed, that the intent of my eyes, away from so delectable an
object, from the accompanying Nymph, they violated (drew off).

through the marble temple "like an Iris"; and the crystal is carved in relief with a **battle of putti
riding dolphins** that seems alive. All secure.

- **"Burning water, five times distilled."** *Aqua ardens* (distilled spirit/alcohol) reiterated five times
  through the still is the fuel: Colonna specifies rectified spirit, so the crystal sphere glows steady and
  blinding "as the Sun." A precise, period-accurate technical detail (early distillation), and a lighting
  cue — a brilliant central globe of white fire ringed by four coloured gem-lights.
- **the temple lit like a rainbow.** The five lamps' lights cross and reflect in the polished marble,
  filling the temple with shifting colour "such as the Sun does not paint after rain." The world's temple
  interior can be lit exactly so: one blazing white core, four jewel-colours, all thrown across mirror-stone.
- **the dolphin-riding putti** — the crystal globe is carved with a living-seeming relief of infants racing
  dolphins (a marine-love motif, fit for sea-born Venus), so vivid it pulls Poliphilo's eyes even from
  Polia. The lamp is both light and sculpture.
- **the flicker animates the carving** (p. 209) — the vacillating flame makes the dolphin-relief seem to
  move: Colonna notes the optical effect of firelight on carved crystal. A rendering idea (animated caustics).

[p. 209]

— violated. And the vacillation of the light seemed to give motion to the sculpture.

Finally, for the absolution of this marvellous structure of Temple, it remains to say briefly that it was
compacted of quadrates of Augustan stone in part, and part of the above-narrated marble, in perfect
jointing, without iron and timber, with more subtle investigation of sculpture than ever in our century
could be done, nor imagined — nor such did they construct for Apis, the Samnitic-Egyptian God.

Under the bases of the little Pilasters, or quadrangulars — which was the lowest and continuous binding, in
the first band, or wall; and the upper girdle likewise, with the encompassing capitals — went round, in the
most-even pavement, a strip, or band, of finest Porphyry, as much as was the projection of its square, and
contiguous, almost without dispute, another of Ophite. Under the sub-base of the columns was circled, as
much as its thickness, a strip of Porphyry, with two collateral of hardest serpentine, with the order of
the Peristyle in circumduction. The like was seen of the orifice of the cistern, girt in the pavement — a
strip of Porphyry and another of Ophite.

The remainder of the much-admired pavement, between the well-orifice and the peristyle, was of marvellous
emblemature, of little-minutiae, of little tessellation of fine stones circling themselves, elegantly
included, deduced in partition: ten roundels, a foot in diameter, of their colour and species, the one to
the line of the other. There were two of reddening Jasper, most-pleasingly suffused with various spots; two
of Litharmenon, of little sparks of gold, more minute, disseminated of rutilant atoms; two of green Jasper,
variegated with chalcedonic veins, with reddening and yellow spots; two of Agate, confusedly undulated of
milky threads; two, lastly, of most-limpid Chalcedony. And, by the narrowness of the lines toward the
cistern, likewise the circular figures decreased.

Under the vaulting were, in the floor, an *Asaroton* of wormwork emblems — foliage, animals, and flowers,
tessellated of most-minute little bodies, of stone-cuttings diligently tessellated, depicted, and most-
evenly rubbed smooth, or sculptured. Which art Zenodorus had not, in paving at Pergamon; nor such was the
*lithostroton* at Praeneste, in the shrine of Fortune.

Let us return to the cyma, or Pinnacle, of the magnificent cupola — of the same metallic material, refinedly
gilt, above the heaven of the —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The temple's construction (dry-jointed **Augustan-stone and marble** ashlar, no
iron or wood) and its **pavement**: porphyry-and-ophite banding round the pilasters, columns and well; ten
foot-wide **inlaid roundels** (red jasper, gold-flecked litharmenon, green jasper, agate, chalcedony) radiating

- **The floor, buildable.** The pavement is a radial composition: porphyry/serpentine bands framing the
  peristyle and the central well, ten colour-graded stone roundels stepping inward (shrinking toward the
  cistern), and, under the aisle-vaults, a figured *Asaroton* mosaic (the "unswept floor" type — scattered
  naturalistic motifs). A complete floor-scheme for the world's temple.
- **dry construction "without iron and timber."** The whole temple is mortarless, ironless ashlar (like the
  Cythera theatre, p. 350) — Colonna's ideal of pure stereotomy. The building holds by cutting alone.
- **the Praeneste lithostroton and Zenodorus** — the Nile-mosaic of the temple of Fortuna at Praeneste (the
  most famous Roman floor) and Zenodorus's work at Pergamon: the benchmarks the temple's floor exceeds. The
  surpassing-topos, on pavements (cf. the Cythera pergola-floors, p. 355).
- **back to the pinnacle** — the description now climbs to the cupola's gilt finial (continued p. 210),
  closing the temple's fabric from floor to summit before the rites begin.

[p. 210]

— stupendous cupola, eight fluted and *somphe* (spongy), or hollow, columns egregiously rose, with a
noble footing, drawn apart by an interjected and encompassing fenestration, with little arches between
one and the other, upon the collateral piers overstanding. Above which, with an exigent harmony,
*sesquialter* (3:2) of the height, of composite and lineament, were circum-led the Architrave, Frieze,
and Cornice, with the projections level with the subjacent columns. A scaled cupola resided. Above the
projections, level with the substitute columns, resident, for each I saw a simulacrum of a wind, with
elegant expression of its nature — winged, with the wings outspread, and stretched at the shoulders — on
an unstable Peron, or stylus, artfully fixed to turn; and, at whatever blowing wind, all eight *Petasi*
(wind-hats) investigated, circling, involving themselves — the face they turned toward that opposite to
the blast.

In the aforesaid summit of the just-narrated cupola, again eight little Pilasters, with the height of two
squares, rose straight, with an ewer-vase, with the opening inverted, above them. The ascent, then, of the
whole, with exquisite commensuration, and with an object mathematically proportioned to the inspectors.

Upon the bottom of the ewer-vase (so I interpret it, for its form), roundabout, most-beautifully scored of
melon-scoring, was impressed a stalk of the proper metal, which began from the breadth of the bottom,
moderately slender ascending. And by as much as was found the middle of the vase, the stylus, ascended,
sustained a huge hollow triangle, together with the stylus artfully cast. In the summit of which gaped a
round opening; and in the low, corpulent (part), in four locations, it was bored — conjecturing, I
pondered, the shrewd device of the provident artificer for this: that water let in by rain, or conceived
frost, should not occupy it from its office, and to avoid the weight. Through the upper Opening of the said
sphere, free of the lips, the said stylus, or spindle, passed, sharpened at the tip. From the outlet
upward it was as much as from the bottom of the vase to the sphere.

In this fastigium a bronze moon was fixed, eight-day (crescent), as much as she shows, with the horns to
the sky. In the gulf, or sinus, of which sat an Eagle with outspread wings. Under the moon, on the stylus,
were four solid and firm grapples, in which four little chains of the aforesaid metal were retained, and
with the whole bronze-work cast — to indicate, of the founder-statuary —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The temple's crowning **lantern**: eight hollow fluted columns carrying a scaled
cupola, each column topped by a **weathervane figure of one of the eight winds** (winged, pivoting to face
the blast); and the finial — a stalk carrying a great hollow bronze triangle, a horned bronze **moon**
cradling an **eagle**, and four chains (whose sounding bells are on p. 211). All secure.

- **The eight-wind weathervanes.** The lantern is ringed by eight pivoting winged wind-gods, each turning
  to face the wind that blows — a working weathervane-crown, one per wind of the classical rose. A
  distinctive, buildable finial-ring for the world's temple; it also rhymes with the calendar/zodiac
  windows (p. 200) — the temple measures both the year and the winds.
- **the moon-and-eagle finial.** The very top is a horned crescent moon holding an eagle, on a triangle:
  lunar (Venus/night) and solar/Jovian (eagle) signs crowning the temple of generative Venus, with the
  triangle (the number of generation). A precise, symbolic finial.
- **the hollow triangle bored to drain** — even the finial is engineered: pierced so rain and frost drain
  and do not add weight (continuing the drainage-mindfulness of pp. 202–203). Colonna's practicality
  reaches the summit.
- The founder's virtuosity (casting the whole in one) leads into p. 211's account of casting an unbroken
  chain, and the wind-rung bells.

[p. 211]

— statuary, the large fertility of his wit. Whence one could easily judge that such subtlety the shrewd
founder investigated: to found, or cast, an entire little chain without soldering — making a fit mould,
quadripartitely cut, in the centre made a pervious hole, into which is let the first ring, and then, the
formed parts applying themselves into one — infinitely, one derived from the other, lightly it will be
cast.

The said little chains, upon the middle corpulence of the bronze sphere evenly deriving, each in the
extreme, ensnared with itself, retained an airy (bronze) *Chodon* (bell). Which bells, from their middle
toward their low (rim), had comb-like fissures, within which a little ball of fine steel resulted, to
render enclosed the tinkling sound. These bells were, at exigent proportion, agitated by the blowing winds;
upon the corpulence of the hollow sphere they beat, and rendered their tinkle sharp, harmonised, with mixed
booms of the metallic triangle — a grateful and sweet and great sound, curiously excogitated and thoughtfully
found; and perhaps beyond the sound which, at the summit of the Temple of Jerusalem, the pendent chains with
the bronze vases (made), putting the birds to flight.

Lastly, to conclude, remains a rule for understanding all the dimension of the most-celebrated temple. The

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The founder's *tour de force* — casting an **unbroken bronze chain** in a piece-
mould (the lost-wax/piece-casting method described); the wind-rung **bells** with enclosed steel balls that
ring against the sphere in harmony with the great triangle, "beyond the sound of the Temple of Jerusalem";
and the start of the temple's final dimensioning (the eight-window wall 1½ feet thick). All secure; the
casting-note is a real foundry technique.

- **The wind-organ finial.** The lantern's chains hang bronze bells (steel balls sealed inside) that the
  wind swings against the great hollow triangle: a self-sounding aeolian chime crowning the temple, "sweet
  and great," surpassing the fabled sounding-chains of the Jerusalem Temple. The world's temple could carry
  a wind-rung chime at its lantern — sound as well as light and motion.
- **casting a chain without solder** — Colonna details the foundry trick (a four-part mould with a central
  hole, links cast one into the next): a genuine, admiring note on the caster's art, of a piece with the
  vine-dome (p. 201) and hollow eagles (p. 204). The temple showcases metallurgy at every scale.
- **the temple's three self-animating systems** — winds (weathervanes, p. 210), sound (these bells), and
  light (the crystal lamp, p. 208): the building moves, rings and glows on its own. A rich brief for a
  living, animated temple in the world.
- The final dimensioning (wall and pier thicknesses) is completed on p. 212, which then reaches the **door**.

The door, then, of this holy and stupendous temple offered itself antepagmented (framed), of Doric form
and workmanship, all of finest Jasper. And in the fascia of its sublime (lintel), of Greek majuscule
antiquarian letters of pure gold fixed, this saying stood inscribed:

> **ΚΥΛΟΠΕΡΑ** (KYLOPERA) [?the reading and sense are uncertain; the letters are given as transcribed]

The gilded valves, with most-polished ornament of metal, of which door they were, and of most-beautiful
and pervious (open-work) workmanship — so much the more beautiful, as less could their like be made — of
illustrious brightness, closed with an exterior bolt. Which the Conductress Nymph did not dare to remove,
unless first the Divine Priestess of the said venerable and sacred Temple, with the other frenzied long-
haired and most-comely virgins (which in all were seven), religiously unbolted it. These sacred virgins
most-integrally there ministered, most-officious, in the sacred things, to the Priestess-Sage of the
sacrifices; and to her alone to concede the ingress most-deservedly pertained. Whence the sacred virgins,
having benignly respected us, domestically blandishing, accepted us. And, from my faithful conductress
Nymph the cause of her and of my advent heard, to us all — easy and gracious, with large (open) faces —
with them they made us ascend, by seven porphyry stone steps, to the egregious door, bound with the
encompassing footing of a magnificent and elegant propylaeum.

There we found a noble pause, or little area, of a square of blackest and indomitable stone (such as would
not be found in the Euganean fatherland), even and lucidly rubbed smooth, hedged in most-beautiful
emblemature. Before the holy threshold of the dedicated valves, all inter-excavated (intaglio'd), and in
the excavations intersecting little barks of Cytherean conch, of the most-beautiful intersected lineaments
that ever to human eyes most-pleasantly could present themselves. In this place, all affirming themselves,
and both of us, the sacred Priestess began then to make a prayer. Then, in reverence, the Nymph and I
inclined ourselves. What she said to herself, I certainly ignored — because, my head somewhat bent, without
delay the most-ready and exploratory eyes, to the unseen whiteness and polish of the most-vague feet of the
accompanying Nymph, I carried back. Where, again, a little portion of the glittering right calf was
uncovered; for, moderately, by her act moving, the most-tenuous lappet gave way, removed, laying bare the
whitest whiteness of the snow-making —

And then, incontinently, an enucleated admiration succoured in the warm memory: that, it being natural
that whiteness disgregates (scatters) the visual power, this (whiteness), with so much delectation, drew
and congregated all the seeing into itself — not only not harming it, but, to the utmost solace and
extreme pleasure, that so precious object, viscidly retaining it bound to itself, and taken, occupied it.
Whence, the Sacred Woman's devout prayers to the Gods Forculus and Limentinus, and to the Goddess Cardea,
being sincerely finished, and (all) righting themselves, the beautiful Nymph (I alone persisting, with
eyes fixed on her voluptuous operation) — nor for all that would I ever have moved myself, had not the
most-subtle cloth returned to re-cover the divine delights.

Then, suddenly, by the libation-woman the Bolt removed, those twin valves — not with a strident noise, not
a grave rumble, but an acute and grateful murmur, reflecting through the vaulted temple — hissed sweetly.
And, animadverting this, I recognised (it), by seeing under the extreme part of the ponderous valves, of
the one and the other, a voluble and turned little Cylinder, which, by the axle fixed in the valve, upon a
terse and evened plate of hardest Ophite inverting itself, and by the friction, made a most-acceptable
tinkling.

Beyond this, reasonably I was stupefied that the valves, each by its very self, without any impulse, opened
themselves. Whence, then, all having entered, of a sudden — without looking elsewhere, there affirming
myself — wishing to investigate whether the said valves, so timely and moderately, by a counterweight were
drawn, or by some other instrument: whence I beheld a divine device. For in that part where, one with the
other, the valves met in the tongued closure, from the inner part, was a plate of fine steel soldered upon
the metal, most-terse.

There were then, marvellously, two little Axles of a third (foot) in breadth, of best Indian Magnet (to
which the Diamond does not dissent — of Callistone the lover, to human eyes outstanding, by the *scordeon*
made mortal (weakened)) — singularly opportune to navigators — which showed, of their fit colour, cerulean,
smooth and illustrious, fixed most-polishedly in the thickness of the opening of the marble wall (that is,
in the jambs, contiguous to the antae of the artful door). Then, in this manner, by the violence of the
rapacity of the Magnet, the steel plates were violated (drawn); and consequently, by themselves, the valves,
with temperate slowness, unbolted themselves. An excellent and most-exact work — not only to see, but beyond
measure of subtle device. What improbity (audacity) of an artificer's investigation!

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The **self-opening magnetic door**: the priestess prays to the Roman door-gods
(Forculus, Limentinus, Cardea), the bolt is drawn, and the gilt valves swing open *by themselves* — Poliphilo
investigates and finds **lodestone (Indian magnet) axles set in the jambs** that draw the steel-plated valves
open; the doors also ring softly on serpentine-stone rollers as they turn. All secure; the magnet-door is one
of the book's celebrated marvels.

- **The magnet-door.** Two lodestone blocks in the doorposts pull the steel-faced valves open "with temperate
  slowness," no hand touching them — a genuine (if fantastical) piece of magnetic automation, and one of the
  Hypnerotomachia's most-discussed devices. A striking, animatable feature for the world's temple: doors that
  open themselves as you approach.
- **the door-gods.** The priestess invokes **Forculus** (of the door-leaf), **Limentinus** (of the
  threshold), and **Cardea** (of the hinge) — the minor Roman deities of a doorway, exactly right for opening
  a temple. Colonna's antiquarian precision (from Augustine/Tertullian's lists of these gods).
- **the singing rollers** — the valves turn on serpentine-stone cylinders that make "a most-acceptable
  tinkling": the door sounds as it opens (cf. the wind-bells, p. 211). Even the door is a musical machine.
- **the whiteness "scatters the visual power"** — the page opens with Poliphilo's optics again (cf. p. 208):
  the nymph's white calf ought, by theory, to dazzle and disperse sight, but instead draws it — beauty
  overriding the physics of vision. The erotic and the scientific fused, as ever.

In a tablet of Magnet, to the right of the ingress, was carved, of exquisite antiquarian Latin letters,

**Confidence: high** (the two inscriptions are secure and identified); medium for the surrounding prose. The

- **The two mottoes — the temple's thesis.** Flanking the door: *Trahit sua quemque voluptas* (Virgil, Ecl.

  material pun with the meaning — attraction, literal and erotic, is one thing.
- **the apology to the reader** — Poliphilo confesses he cannot describe the temple fully because Polia/the
  nymph's beauty keeps pulling his attention: the inexpressibility topos turned personal, and a wry admission
  that the love-story overrides the architecture.
- **"we three alone remained"** — the priestess, the nymph and Poliphilo, at the well: the rite of Venus (the

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The **ritual implements** borne in procession by the seven virgins for the rite of

- **The apparatus of the rite.** Colonna itemises the sacred vessels with antiquarian exactness — the
  *secespita* (the priest's iron sacrificial knife), the *praefericulum* (the ritual ewer), the *lepista*

- **the dove-book.** The ritual book is bound in cyan velvet worked into the shape of a **dove** (Venus's

- **the unlit virgin candle.** The candle-bearer carries a pure candle "never yet kindled" — it will be lit
  at the rite's climax (the drawing of sacred fire from the well, ch. XVIII). Its unlit state is deliberate:
  the ceremony's central act is the first kindling.
- **"more expert than the Etruscan discipline"** — the *disciplina Etrusca* was the Romans' benchmark for
  ritual correctness (haruspicy, augury); the virgins surpass it. The surpassing-topos, on liturgy.
- The rite itself (the priestess's actions at the well, the kindling, the drawing of water) follows through
  the remaining pages of the chapter into ch. XVIII.

hair), and conjoined, with a stupendous jewel — of most-shining and full-of-colour Sapphire, the one
consigned to the Nymph; but that of the Priestess, of *Ananchitides* (a divination-stone).

Vested, then, devoutly, over the orifice of the mysterial Cistern, without delay she made me approach there;
whence, having accepted a golden little key, with religious observance she unsealed the bolted Well. Where the
sacrificer, consigning to that Virgin who had carried the Mitre the candid candle, took, venerating, the
Ritual book; and, having opened it, put herself before the high Prophetess. Who began, low, in the Etruscan
tongue, somewhat to read. Then, scrupulously, she took the sanctified Brine, and, with many sacerdotal
signings, with the right hand into the thundering Cistern she poured it. Then she made, from the ardent torch
(of which the Nymph was bearer), the pure candle be kindled.

This done, she made the ardent torch be turned, with the little flame downward, into the middle of the
orifice; and, interrogating the Nymph, said these words: "Daughter, what petition and desire is thine?" She
answered: "Holy Priestess, grace, for this one, I ask — that together we may come to the amorous realm of the
Divine Mother, and drink of this holy fount." And to me likewise she said: "And thou, my son, what askest
thou?" Humbly I answered: "I, most-sacred Lady, not only the efficacious grace of the supernal mother
supplicate, but above all — that she, whom, doubtful, I esteem to be my most-desired Polia, I beseech that by
her, more ambiguous, in so great an amorous torment I be not thus retained." The divine Priestess said to me:
"Apprehend, son, then, now, that kindled torch, from her pure hands, and, holding it thus, with me three times
sincerely, in this manner, thou shalt say:

> 'Just as the water shall extinguish this burnable torch, in the same manner, the fire of love re-kindle her
> stone-made and gelid heart.'"

With the holy rite, and with those proper words which the Hierophant said to me, saying — at whatever
terminated and finish, all the expert priestess-virgins, with venerable ministry, this responsory said: "**So
be it.**" At the last time, the ardent torch, into the frigid Cistern, she made me, with reverence, immerse.

---

## Notes

**Confidence: high.** The **rite of Venus at the well** — the priestess vests herself and Polia (mitre,
veils, sapphire and *ananchitides* jewels), unseals the cistern with a golden key, reads in Etruscan, casts
the brine, kindles the pure candle, and then puts the ritual questions: Polia asks grace to reach "the
amorous realm of the Divine Mother," Poliphilo asks that "she, whom I doubtfully judge to be my Polia," end
his torment. He must quench the torch in the well saying "as the water quenches this fire, so re-kindle her
frozen heart," the virgins answering "So be it." All secure; a fully-staged liturgy with dialogue.

- **The rite, and its meaning.** The ceremony is a marriage-initiation: the lovers are vested as a pair
  (matching veils), and the central act is Poliphilo quenching a torch in the cistern while praying that the
  *fire of love re-kindle Polia's cold heart*. Water quenches fire so that love may kindle it — the paradox
  of the rite. This is the temple-scene the visual-novel and the world can stage directly: the well, the
  torch, the vested lovers, the response "So be it."
- **the first clear naming of Polia as present.** Poliphilo says aloud he "doubtfully judges" the nymph to
  be Polia — the recognition the whole book has been withholding is now at its threshold (resolved on p.
  217–218). The rite is the frame in which the beloved is finally identified.
- **Etruscan and the *ananchitides*** — the priestess reads in "the Etruscan tongue" (the archaic sacred
  language) and wears a stone of *ananchitides* (Pliny's divination-crystal, used in hydromancy): Colonna's
  antiquarian sourcing makes the rite feel genuinely ancient and oracular.
- **"So be it" (Cusì fia)** — the virgins' thrice-repeated responsory: a liturgical refrain the world could
  use as the temple-rite's audible signature.

[p. 217]

Not so soon did I do this holy command, than she, taking the precious hyacinthine *lepista*, and with a
little cord of gold and of crimson and green silk (deputed to such office), infusing it into the cisternal
water, drew out of the blessed water, and, with religion, offered it to the Nymph alone. And she, with prompt
devotion, drank it. Immediately then the hieratic Priestess, with the golden little key, diligently re-shut
the covering of the Cistern; and, somewhat reading over the holy and efficacious prayers and exorcisms, she
enjoined the Nymph to say, three times, these words toward me:

> "May the divine Cytherea hear thee, to thy vow; and, propitiated in me, may she nourish her son."
> Responsory from the virgins: "**So be it.**"

The said ceremonies religiously terminated, the Nymph, in that instant, reverent, at the sandalled feet of
purple re-woven with gold, ornated with manifold gems, of the Priestess, having prostrated herself — of a
sudden she made her rise up, and gave her a holy kiss. And to me then the Nymph, boldly turned, with her comely
presence placid, full of pious semblances, with a sigh come warmly from the base of the inflamed heart, thus
said to me:

"Most-desired and my most-cordial Poliphilo — thy ardent and excessive desire, and thy sedulous and
pertinacious love, from the chaste college has wholly stolen me, and has constrained me to extinguish my
torch. And for this, henceforth — although thou reasonably didst suspect that I was she, notwithstanding that
—

---

## Notes

**Confidence: high.** The rite completes: the priestess draws **blessed water and gives it to Polia alone** to
drink, reseals the well, and has Polia say thrice "may Cytherea nourish her son"; the virgins answer "So be
it." Polia kisses the priestess's feet, is raised and given a holy kiss, and then **turns to Poliphilo and
begins her declaration** — that his love has "stolen her from the chaste college" and made her quench her
torch. All secure; the union begins.

- **Polia drinks; the vow is sealed.** Only Polia drinks the blessed water — she is the one being received
  into "the amorous realm of the Divine Mother." The blessing ("may Cytherea nourish her son") makes Poliphilo
  the goddess's foster-child, the beloved she will nurture. The rite converts private desire into a sanctioned
  bond.
- **"stolen me from the chaste college."** Polia was among the temple's chaste virgins (the "college"); Poliphilo's
  love has drawn her out and made her "extinguish her torch" (surrender her chastity to love). Her declaration —
  the turning-point of the whole first book — begins here and completes on p. 218. This is the reciprocation
  Poliphilo has begged for since the crossing (p. 288).
- **the torch quenched / the torch extinguished** — the rite's quenched torch (p. 216) and Polia's "extinguished
  torch" here are the same image: the cold, chaste flame put out so that love's fire may take its place. Colonna
  binds the liturgy to the emotional event.
- The declaration and the lovers' first kiss (the "pledge," *arra*) are on p. 218 — the emotional climax of
  Book I's later half.

[p. 218]

— until here I had not revealed myself to thee — nonetheless, no small fire has it been to me, to keep it
occult and concealed, and thus so long suppressed. But be that as it may, I am, without doubt, that Polia of
thine whom thou so lovest. Congruous, therefore, it presents itself, that so worthy and so-made a love be not
immune from vicissitude, and from equivalent reciprocation and requital. For which thing, behold me, to thy
inflaming desires, all most-ready! Behold, that I feel the ignited fire, from most-fervent love, throughout
all of me to grow up, and to scintillate! Behold me, the end of thy bitter and frequent sighs! Behold me,
most-delightful Poliphilo, a salubrious and present remedy to thy grave and molesting sorrows! Behold me, to
thy amorous and acerb pains a consort principal, and of the whole partaker! Behold me, with my profuse tears,
to quench thy cordial burning, and, for thee, to die, prompt and most-surrendered!"

And, for the Pledge (*arra*) of all this — "Take (me)!" — (embracing me, straining me) she gave me,
lip-to-lip, a little-biting and sipping kiss, full of divine juice; and, provoked by singular sweetness, from
the starry eyes some few little pearls in the form of little tears (fell); insomuch that, by her blandishing
speech, and by the salivous and most-pleasing kiss, from head to feet all inflamed I was altered, melting
myself into sweetest and amorous tears, and wholly lost myself. And likewise the sacrificing Priestess, with
the others standing by — moved by singular sweetness — could not contain themselves from little tears and
sweet little sighs.

---

## Notes

**Confidence: high.** The **climax of Book I's later half**: Polia reveals herself fully — *"I am, without
doubt, that Polia of thine whom thou so lovest"* — declares her reciprocal love in a rush of "Behold me…"
(*Eccome*) clauses, and seals it with a kiss (the *arra*, love's pledge); Poliphilo dissolves in tears, and
even the priestess and virgins weep for sweetness. All secure; the emotional summit of the temple sequence.

- **Polia's self-revelation and reciprocation.** After a whole book of the beloved withheld and un-named,
  Polia declares herself and returns Poliphilo's love in kind — "so worthy a love (should) not be immune from…
  equivalent reciprocation." Her anaphora of *Eccome* ("Behold me — the end of thy sighs… a present remedy…
  thy consort… ready to die for thee") is the answer to every plaint since the crossing (p. 288) and the
  fulfilment of the fidelity-thread the Cythera chapters kept alive. This is the passage the world's temple-
  station and the visual-novel's romance beat exist to deliver.
- **the *arra*-kiss.** The lovers' first kiss is sealed as a legal *pledge* (arra — earnest-money of a
  contract): love formalised as a betrothal, in the temple, before witnesses. Polia's pearl-tears and
  Poliphilo's dissolution "from head to feet" are the book's most direct emotional writing, its Latinate
  ornament briefly giving way to feeling.
- **the whole company weeps** — the priestess and virgins, moved, weep too: the private union is witnessed and
  blessed. The temple of Venus Physizoa has done its work — desire (Trahit sua quemque voluptas, p. 214)
  brought to sanctioned fruition.
- **Chapter XVII nears its end.** A few pages remain (219–224) before ch. XVIII; the union achieved here is the
  hinge of Poliphilo's story, and the emotional counterpart to Cythera's later triumph.

[p. 219]

Which thing the infecund and fasting tongue would not know how to gather, nor so many fit words to beg,
that I could condignly express even a little of what the enkindled heart made of it, in so sweetest a flame
as, in every part, o'erwove it. I remained, then, like one fallen of the Epilepsy. Ultimately, these
amorous and holy gestures and ceremonial rites — in so singular and choice a sweetness and incredible
delight, by love, expedited — I found myself almost in an unthought experience of dying content.

The Hierophant said: "Let us proceed, Polia, then, to the completory of the inner sacrifices of our
sacral undertaking." Now toward the round and blind Sacello — situated directly opposite the door of the
magnificent temple, and with it artfully joined and contiguous — all, composedly, went. Fabricated of
antiquarian and unwonted make, and noble material.

Which was all of stone, diligently re-squared to the form, of precious **Phengite** marvellously built,
with a cupola'd and round roof, of a single and solid rock of the said stone. Such was not, of such
marvel, the Sacello of the isle of Chennim in Egypt, nor that of the celebrated Sacred (place) of Ravenna.
Which stone, of such miraculous nature, that — not being windowed, but all obtuse (closed), and having only
the golden valves — throughout, clearly, it was illuminated (a secret absorbed by it, hidden from our
cognition, from its parent (the sun)); and therefore thus is it denominated. In this interval, two of those
virgins, unburdened, and by precept gone, carried, with sincere veneration: one, a pair of whitest male
Swans, grateful in the auspices, and a most-ancient little urn with sea-water; and the other, a pair of
candid Turtledoves, by the feet bound together with crimson silk, upon a wicker basket full of vermilion
roses and oyster-shells — and, near the golden valves, upon a sacred and quadrangular *anclabris* (offering-
table) disposed, devout and venerating, let them repose.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The move to the inner rite: Poliphilo near-swooning from sweetness ("like one fallen
of the Epilepsy… dying content"); the priestess leading all to the **round blind Sacello** — the Adytum,
built of self-illuminating **phengite** stone (windowless yet luminous); and the offerings borne for the
inner sacrifice: white swans, sea-water, and turtledoves on a basket of roses and oyster-shells. All secure.

- **The self-lit sanctuary.** The Adytum is a domed rotunda hewn from *phengite* — a translucent stone
  (Pliny: Nero's phengite-lined temple that glowed shut) — so it is fully lit though windowless, "a secret
  hidden from our cognition." A gorgeous, buildable feature: an inner sanctum that glows from its own walls.
  It answers the translucent *sogobrina* windows (p. 199) and the alabaster theatre (p. 350): light through
  stone is the temple's signature.
- **the offerings of Venus.** Swans and turtledoves (Venus's birds), sea-water (the sea-born goddess), roses
  and oyster-shells (her flower and her shell): a precisely Venerean sacrifice-set, laid on an *anclabris*
  (the Roman offering-table). Ready iconography for the world's sanctuary.
- **"like one fallen of the Epilepsy"** — Poliphilo's swoon of sweetness after the union (p. 218): the
  emotional aftermath, rendered in the period's medical simile (the "sacred disease"). The rite's climax has
  physically overcome him.
- **the *completorium*** — the priestess calls the inner rite the "completory" (completion) of the sacrifice:
  the union at the well (chs. XVII) is now sealed by an inner offering in the Adytum (Polia's prayer at the
  gem-altar, pp. 220–221).

[p. 220]

And there, the golden valves unsealed, together they entered. But I affirmed myself upon the holy and
reverend threshold. And with vigilant eyes, immovably fixed on the most-beloved object, respecting, I saw the
admonitress bidding that my Polia — true *myropolis* (perfume-seller/sweet one) — should genuflect upon the
sumptuous pavement, and, with sincere devotion, prostrate herself.

Which pavement was marvellous, all of gems, stony, orbitally composed, with subtle make, with manifold and
elegant knotting politely distinct — a work bonily tessellated, disposed in greening leaves, and flowers, and
little birds, and other animals, according as opportune was the grateful colour of the precious stones,
splendid, shining, with perfect evening — from which, doubled, it re-showed those who had entered.

Upon this, then, my little-bold Polia, having religiously denuded the milky knees, with the utmost elegance
genuflected — more beautiful than ever Mercy saw (knees) dedicated to herself. For which thing I stood
suspensefully attentive, with silent lips. And, so as not to interrupt the holy offerings, and contaminate the
propitiations, and interrupt the solemn prayers, and the mysterious ministry, and perturb the altar-
ceremonies, the wicked sighs, by valid love inflamed, I duly incarcerated.

Now, before a sanctified Altar — in the middle of the little sanctuary laboriously situated, of divine flame
lucent — genuflected, humbly, she stood.
