## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The inner rite: the priestess and Polia enter the Adytum (Poliphilo kept at the
threshold, watching); the **gem-mosaic pavement** (leaves, flowers, birds and animals in coloured stones, so
polished it mirrors those who enter); and **Polia genuflecting, bare-kneed, before the central altar** of
"divine flame." All secure.

- **The mirror-pavement of the sanctuary.** The Adytum floor is a gem-mosaic of foliage and creatures,
  polished to a mirror that "doubled and re-showed those who had entered" — the same reflective-floor motif as
  Cythera's obsidian (p. 352) and the temple's marble (p. 208). Reflection is the temple's constant device:
  the sacred multiplies itself in mirror-stone.
- **Poliphilo kept at the threshold.** He may not enter the inner sanctuary — only the priestess and Polia
  (the initiate) go in; he watches from the door, holding his breath and "incarcerating his sighs" so as not
  to disturb the rite. The innermost mystery is Polia's alone (as the well-drink was, p. 217). A narrative
  gating the world can honour: the sanctum admits only the beloved.
- **"true myropolis"** — Poliphilo's pun-epithet for Polia (myrrh/perfume-seller, playing on her name and her
  sweetness): the book's habitual name-play. Kept as a gloss.
- **the central flame-altar** — a sanctified altar burning with "divine flame" stands at the sanctuary's
  centre, before which Polia kneels; its elaborate form (a gem-crowned golden platter) is described on p. 221.
  This is the focus of the Adytum, as the well is of the main temple.

[p. 221]

The demonstration of which Altar, succinctly saying, I beheld a conspicuous device of unwonted make. The
lowest of the said, upon the stepped and marble footing, was a round little slab. Upon which undulated an
auricular foliage, most with polish jagged, and choicely cauliculate, ending its point at a little cord, or
knot, or fillet, contained upon the little slab. And likewise, at the birth of the encompassing foliage,
sat above another little cord; and between this and another was pressed a *trochlea* (pulley-moulding)
moderately channelled, and then a little cornice. Upon the bracket, or plane, of the said Trochlea, over-
stood another regulated rotundity; then, somewhat gulleted, it contracted itself toward the flat and
unencumbered surface. In the middle part of which stood forth a striated stylus, more stretched in the lower
part, upon the flat, with a proportioned base. The diameter, then, of the inner rotundity of this stylus
divided: one partition was consigned to the encompassing projection; the upper head had two portions, with
turned gulets, and the lowest also duly reserved.

The aforesaid stalk covered an inverted flat rotundity, turning in projection as much as the extreme outlet
of the lips of the subjacent Trochlea, ornated in the upper part, in the extreme circuit, in a sloped
demonstration, with a Sima of noteworthy foliage, from an egregious little cornice most-polishedly being
born. In the circled content, then, of which little cornice, beautifully occupied the opening of an elegant
flower, in balustered lineament fashioned, with the calyxed lips over the flat lambent, and quadripartite
into most-pleasant acanthine foliage, gaping. Under which, in the jagged discrepancy, subsided another
leaf, artfully carved. Upon the point of which, after the due lineaments, egregiously rounded a knot of
exquisite expression. To which, fixed, set, dilatedly stood forth an antiquarian platter of purest gold,
with the lips broadish, and a little lacunate (hollowed). In the flat rim of the lips, alternately, stood
forth incomparable Diamonds and Carbuncles, with outstanding pyramidal fashioning, in the circuit
marvellously disposed, of incredible thickness. Let yield here the *Scyphus* of most-strong Hercules, the
*Cantharus* of pleasant Bacchus, and the *Carchesium* dedicated to immortal Jove.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** A dense architectural description of the **central altar of the Adytum** — a turned,
moulded pedestal (slab, auricular foliage, pulley-moulding, cornice, fluted stem) rising to an inverted
dish carved with acanthus and a balustered flower, crowned by a **golden platter rimmed with pyramidal
diamonds and carbuncles**, surpassing the famous cups of Hercules, Bacchus and Jove. All secure; a
goldsmith's-and-architect's altar, described moulding by moulding.

- **The altar-of-the-flame, buildable.** Colonna gives the altar as a turned column of mouldings topped by a
  gold offering-dish set with alternating diamonds and carbuncles (clear and red fire-stones) around the rim
  — on which the "divine flame" (p. 220) burns. A precise, renderable centrepiece for the world's sanctuary:
  a jewelled gold fire-dish on a carved plinth.
- **the acanthus-and-flower capital** — the altar's head opens as a balustered flower with four-part acanthus
  leaves "lambent over the flat": the whole object is vegetal-architectural, of a piece with the temple's
  living ornament (the vine-dome, p. 201; the acanthus-girls, p. 207).
- **surpassing the cups of the gods** — the *scyphus* of Hercules, the *cantharus* of Bacchus, the
  *carchesium* of Jove: the three most-famous mythological drinking-vessels, all exceeded by this altar-dish.
  The surpassing-topos, on sacred vessels (cf. the surpassed cups of Bassus and Antony, p. 354).
- **the ornament is the point.** This is one of the book's purest passages of *ekphrasis-as-inventory*:
  Colonna dwells on the altar's profile as lovingly as on the whole temple, because for him the object's
  design *is* its meaning. Rendered with the technical mouldings (trochlea, sima, cauliculate) kept.

[p. 222]

At the margin of the soffit of the inverted flat, in the rim, evenly distant, were contained four most-
beautiful handles, deriving, and solid with the Trochlea; their volutes were under the inverted flat, and
ended above the Trochlea, with the cochleate whirl, spreading with the slope of the little slab. Then,
moderately, they inverted themselves toward the soffit, at a grateful up-curve, submitting themselves to it
with the whirl resupine, and the other supine.

This marvellous sculptile was all of one solid of finest jasper, of manifold mixture of colouring most-
admiredly coming together, and in whatever part with incredible and most-exquisite lineaments. A work, most-
certainly, not worked out by force of chisel, or scalpel, but with unknown artifice marvellously expressed.

From the marble and stepped footing, up to the beginning of the stylus exclusive, it was raised a cubit; the
stalk as much; the remainder, up to the golden platter, a foot and a half. Thence, above, a quadrant: from
one upper volute to the other spread gold threads, through the middle of which were threaded, in longish
berries, coruscating balas-rubies, bored, and of most-refulgent Sapphires, and of scintillating Diamonds,
and of springing Emeralds, with gracious and amicable colour-alternation strung, with inestimable and
monstrous pearls — such that, without doubt, such a gift Octavian did not make to Capitoline Jove.

In the inversion of the lips of the golden platter, quadrifariously, perpendicularly, hung orbiculate gems,
and pierced, through which, pervious, let in, a gold thread, threaded, they were retained, suspended, and
bound to a clasp, free in the grapples — larger than a hazelnut, seven to a thread. At the extreme of the
thread, interdicted (finished) by an elegant little floret, with the little spirals of varied silken thread,
gold, and silver, intermixed. Again, from one clasp to the other likewise knotted, gold threads, gemmed,
spread in the aforesaid manner —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The altar completed: its four scrolled handles (all carved with it from **one solid
of jasper**, "not by chisel but by unknown artifice"), its exact dimensions, and the **festoons of gemstones**

- **The altar carved from one stone.** The whole moulded, handled, scrolled object is one block of many-
  coloured jasper, worked "not by chisel… but by unknown artifice" — the topos of the seemingly impossible
  single-piece carving (cf. the one-pour vine-dome, p. 201). Colonna's marvels are always *made*, and always
  beyond ordinary craft.
- **the gem-festoons.** Between the volutes and from the platter hang strings of bored balas-rubies,
  sapphires, diamonds, emeralds and hazelnut-sized pearls — the altar dressed in jewels like the nymphs' dress
  (p. 335). A dazzling, buildable centrepiece: a jasper altar draped in gemstone garlands under its fire-dish.
- **surpassing Octavian's gift to Jove** — Augustus's famous dedications on the Capitol; the altar's jewels
  exceed them. The surpassing-topos, on votive treasure.
- The altar description closes here; the rite resumes on p. 223 with the invocation of the three Graces.

## Notes

**Confidence: high** (the Graces-invocation is secure and identified); medium for the altar-detail above it.
The altar's gem-festoons finished (nine gemmed threads, a platter carved with putti, monsters, flowers), and
then the **priestess's invocation of the three Graces** — Aglaia, Thalia, Euphrosyne — as handmaids of Venus,
called from the Acidalian spring and Apollo's throne to carry Polia's prayer to the goddess. All secure.

- **The invocation of the three Graces.** A luminous, quotable prayer: the Charites — **Aglaia** ("splendour"),
  **Thalia** ("good cheer"), **Euphrosyne** ("mirth") — daughters of Jove and Eurynome, Venus's own handmaids,
  are called from the **Acidalian spring** (Venus's bathing-pool at Orchomenus) to bear Polia's sacrifice to
  the goddess "with maternal affect." A ready piece of liturgy for the world's temple-rite and the visual-
  novel — the three Graces named and invoked. Its epithets (joyful/verdant/delectable) are gently exact.
- **the classical sourcing** — the Graces' parentage (Jove and Eurynome), their spring (Acidalia at
  Orchomenus in Boeotia), and their service to Venus are all from Hesiod and the mythographers: Colonna's
  invocation is scholarly as well as beautiful. The Graces as *intercessors* (carrying the prayer up to Venus)
  is his own devotional framing.
- **the whole company kneels but the priestess** — the *Antistita* alone stands (as celebrant); all others,
  including Polia, kneel on the mirror-floor. The liturgical choreography is exact.
- The prayer completes on p. 224, with the responsory "So be it," closing chapter XVII.



------------------------------------------------------------------------
CHAPTER XVII / (ARGUMENT OF CHAPTER XVIII)
------------------------------------------------------------------------

[p. 224]

Finished the holy and sincere oration, all, singing, made the responsory: "So be it." For which thing, having
I, with most-devout auscultation, venerating, heard, and the holy oration clearly understood, with the utmost
sincerity of heart I stood attentive, and, into myself all that revoked, with scrupulous diligence, and with
exploring eye, immovable, such mysteries I considered. And likewise I, genuflected, observed the expertise of
the antiquarian and sacral ceremonies of the divine Priestess, excessively commending, above all, with what
elegance of promptitude Polia adapted herself to such and so great a *mystagogy* (initiation). Most-intent,
nonetheless, upon that which of it ought to follow.

---

*(Argument of the following chapter — Chapter XVIII:)*

> POLIA DEVOUTLY OFFERS THE TURTLEDOVES. THEN A LITTLE SPIRIT FLIES OUT. WHENCE THE PRIESTESS SAID THE
> ORATION TO DIVINE VENUS. THEN SHE SCATTERED THE ROSES, AND, THE SACRIFICE OF THE SWANS BEING MADE, FROM IT
> MIRACULOUSLY GERMINATED A ROSE-BUSH WITH FRUITS AND FLOWERS. BOTH OF THEM TASTED OF THESE. THEN THEY CAME,
> HAPPY, TO A RUINED TEMPLE — OF WHICH POLIA TELLS HIM WHAT RITE IT HAD, PERSUADING POLIPHILO THAT HE GO THERE
> TO CONTEMPLATE MANY ANTIQUE EPITAPHS. AND, HAVING RETURNED TO HER WITH FRIGHT, AND RECREATED, SITTING
> TOGETHER, POLIPHILO, GAZING AT THE IMMENSE BEAUTIES OF POLIA, ALL INFLAMED HIMSELF IN LOVE.

---

## Notes

**Confidence: high.** The close of the Graces-prayer and of **chapter XVII** (the responsory "So be it";
Poliphilo attentive, admiring Polia's "elegance of promptitude" at the initiation), followed by the
**argument of chapter XVIII** — which previews the sacrifice of the doves and swans, the little spirit that
flies out, the miraculous rose-bush that springs from the sacrifice, and the coming of the lovers to the
**ruined temple** with its antique epitaphs. All secure.

- **Chapter XVII complete.** The chapter has run from the four-Seasons altar and Priapus rite (the Dallington
  seam, pp. 193–194), through the whole architectural ekphrasis of the **Temple of Venus Physizoa**
  (pp. 196–212), to the **rite at the well, Polia's self-revelation and the lovers' union** (pp. 216–218), and
  the inner sacrifice at the gem-altar with the invocation of the Graces (pp. 219–223). It is the pivot of
  Poliphilo's story: the beloved named, the love returned and sanctified. **All of it now in English past
  Dallington's stop.**
- **the argument sets up chapter XVIII.** The next chapter (pp. 225–241) delivers the *miraculous rose-bush*
  (springing from the swan-sacrifice, its fruit tasted by both lovers — a communion of love) and the turn to
  the **ruined temple of antique epitaphs**, which occupies the long chapter XIX. The argument is Colonna's own
  chapter-summary, rendered whole so the parallel-text page keeps the book's structure visible.
- **"mystagogy"** — Colonna calls the whole temple-rite an *initiation* (mystagogy): the union of the lovers is
  framed as a mystery-cult ordination, Polia the initiate, Poliphilo the witness. This is the interpretive key
  to the temple sequence — love as sacred initiation.
- Chapter XVIII begins on p. 225 with the offering of the turtledoves and the spirit that flies out.



------------------------------------------------------------------------
CHAPTER XVIII
------------------------------------------------------------------------

[p. 225]

I cannot in the least let myself be persuaded that such rites, ceremonies, sacrifices were found out by Numa
Pompilius, nor at Caere of Tuscany, nor ever in Etruria, nor by the holy Jew; nor with so much religious
observance and order did the Memphitic Seers sacrifice and burn-offerings to Apis in Egypt, immersing the
golden patera in the Nile; nor yet with so most-religious a veneration, in the city of Rhamnus of Euboea, was
Rhamnusia (Nemesis) worshipped; nor was Jupiter Anxur worshipped with such superstition; nor those who, at
Feronia inspired, found such rites — walking without harm upon the kindled coals. Nor so entranced were the
Edonian Clodones, nor the Mimallones, aspired by the numen, as in the present they were entranced.
Deservedly I judge (beyond that which I have openly beheld) that, by the things prepared and superstitiously
disposed, (a marvel) ought to succeed. For, of the hair, the golden Polia Nymph — of such-made office worthy,
in the sacred things imbued and initiated — no sooner saw the nod of the sacristan monitress, than, from the
most-clean pavement, without voice, delay, or noise (no other one moving), most-promptly, religiously, she
rose. Whence, by the sacred monitress, to a wondrous hyacinthine little urn, set apart in the sacello, she
was conducted — such as, of such artifice, Mentor never knew to make.

And I, most-attentive, regarding her, in all acts scrutinously observed. And in aspect now I saw her such as
the most-lucid Phoebus, with the new day, colouring, paints the fresh aurora. And there, ceremoniously, with
prompt and untouched hands, an odorous liquor she drew out; and her milky and vermilioned face, breathing
purpling roses, with the delicate moistened hands, all shrewdly, she irrigated. Whence, thus devoutly
purified, with more sincerity than perhaps had the virgin Aemilia — before the step of the most-holy Altar,
where stood a wondrous golden candelabrum (which was of most-exact and much-admired expression, and elegantly
circum-ornated and knobbed with thick gems; in its summit stood forth, exigently, a round opening of a little
shell, or a platter, less than an arm's embrace) —

In this, then, was placed the sweetest sperm of the huge whales (ambergris); odoriferous musk; the crystalline
and fugitive Camphor; odorous Ladanum of great Crete; *Thymiama* and Mastic; both the Storaxes; the almond-
scented Benzoin; the ponderable Aloewood; *blatte-bisantie*, or Indian nails (onycha); and the happy germens of
Arabia. Which all precious things were, with distributed weight, most-excellently graded. To which the
solicitous Polia, and with —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The opening of **chapter XVIII**: the surpassing of every ancient rite (Numa, the
Egyptian Apis-priests, Nemesis at Rhamnus, the fire-walkers of Feronia, the Bacchic Clodones); then **Polia
purifies herself** with rose-scented water and lays the **incense** (ambergris, musk, camphor, ladanum,
storax, benzoin, aloewood, onycha, Arabian spices) on a gemmed golden candelabrum before the altar. All secure;
the incense-list is a real perfumer's catalogue.

- **The rite as surpassing all rites.** Colonna opens by declaring this ceremony beyond Numa's Roman religion,
  the Egyptian Apis-cult, the fire-walking priests of Feronia, and the ecstatic Bacchantes — the surpassing-
  topos applied to liturgy itself (cf. p. 215, "more than the Etruscan discipline"). The temple of Venus
  outranks the whole ancient world's worship.
- **the incense of Venus.** The offering is a complete list of the great aromatics — ambergris, musk, camphor,
  ladanum, two storaxes, benzoin, aloewood, onycha, Arabian spice — "graded by weight": a precise perfume-
  formula burned to the goddess. Ready sensory detail for the world's temple-rite (cf. the perfumed pavements
  of Cythera, p. 355).
- **Polia as officiant.** Polia — "imbued and initiated in the sacred things" — performs the rite herself, at
  the priestess's nod: she is not merely the beloved but a trained temple-virgin (the "chaste college" of
  p. 217). Her competence is stressed ("more sincere than the virgin Aemilia," a Vestal). The visual-novel can
  stage her as celebrant.
- The kindling, the dove-sacrifice, and the sung hymn follow on p. 226.

[p. 226]

— exquisite diligence, venerating, admonished, set the ardent candle. Then, when these aromatics she had
kindled, without other thinking she extinguished the candle, and set it apart.

In which smoky little flame, and of incomparable fragrance shining, having placed there a little branch of
arid myrtle, she kindled (it); and of a sudden, upon the sacrificial Altar (whence she had taken it),
returning it kindled, all the other little branches placed upon the said altar she set afire. Whence,
intent and affectionately taught, into this fire she threw the pair of candid turtledoves — first
diligently plucked, and upon the sacred *anclabris* table throat-cut, un-backed with the *secespita*, and
together bound with gold threads, and knotted, and with purpling silk — having, with the utmost veneration,
the warm gore reserved in the *praefericulum*. Thrown, then, the immolated turtledoves into the odoriferous
flame and burning, the seeress, precentor of the rubricated rites, began to sing, and psalm, and, following,
all alternating. But before the fore-dancing Priestess, two of those, with Lydian Tibiae, preceded, most-
sweetly sounding, with the Lydian mode and tone (such as Amphion could not find out); and then Polia and the
others, one following the other, each holding in hand a branch of odorous and flowered Myrtle. Dancing in
chorus, then, with time, step, and continence, with even uniform distance, and leaping with solemn and
religious *thiasi*, with intoned voice concordant to the sonority, produced forth from the virginal breasts,
reflexed with incredible symphony under the obtuse cupola, around the incensed Altar, thus rhythmically
saying:

> "O holy fire of odour: thaw the ice of every heart; placate Venus with love, and grant us her ardour."

In this mysterious manner singing, and tibia-sounding, with most-elegant chorus, orbitally they gyred, while
the sacrifice burned. And, extinguishing thus, the little flame smoked. I think that those odours were to
suffocate the stench of the roasted flesh, beyond the (main) purpose. Then, no sooner was it extinguished,
than of a sudden, to the pavement, all silently (the Priestess excepted) they prostrated themselves. For
which thing it was not long time, that I openly, out of the holy smoke, saw a most-beautiful little spirit,
oracular, and of form other than human, as beautiful as, with shrewd discourse and investigation, one could
imagine. And at the divine shoulder-blades a pair of arched little wings it had, with an unseen and unwonted
light — which, not without some lesion of my eyes regarding it, most-avidly, the lost heart truly felt. With
so vehement an impetus, more than the thunderbolt created of water —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The core of the rite: Polia kindles the incense and myrtle, **sacrifices the two
turtledoves** in the fire (reserving their blood in the *praefericulum*), and the priestess and virgins
**sing and dance a hymn to Venus** around the altar to Lydian pipes; then, as the smoke rises, a **beautiful
winged spirit** (a little Cupid/genius) appears out of the holy smoke. All secure; the hymn and the apparition
are the chapter's centre.

- **The hymn to Venus.** A short, singable quatrain — *"O holy fire of odour: thaw the ice of every heart;
  placate Venus with love, and grant us her ardour."* The prayer of the whole temple in four lines: the fire
  of scent melting the cold heart (the same image as the well-torch, p. 216 — quench the cold to kindle love).
  Prime liturgy to surface in the world's temple-rite and the visual-novel; it rhymes in the original
  (*odore / core / amore / ardore*).
- **the dove-sacrifice.** The turtledoves (Venus's birds, p. 219) are the offering, burned with myrtle
  (Venus's tree) amid the aromatics; their blood is kept in the ritual ewer. The rite is precisely Venerean and
  precisely antique.
- **the spirit from the smoke.** A winged genius of "unwonted light" rises from the sacrifice — the epiphany
  the chapter's argument (p. 224) promised. Its attributes (myrtle-crown, fire-arrow, diamond crown) and its
  dissolution follow on p. 227. A luminous, animatable apparition for the world's rite.
- **the wry practical aside** — Poliphilo suspects the heavy incense is partly to mask the "stench of roasted
  flesh": Colonna's realism intrudes even here (cf. the latrine-note, p. 202). The sacred and the practical
  side by side.

[p. 227]

— of fire, cloud, and of fulminating wind. Whence, the sacrificer, aware of me, made a gesture that I not
frighten myself, and with a token that I keep silent.

Which pretty boy, in the little swelling hands, bore a myrtle crownlet; and in the other, a little arrow of
ardent, scintillating fire. And on the summit of the divine head, downed with little gold threads, went round
a most-precious crown of most-splendid diamonds. Circum-fluttering three times the incensed and smoking Altar,
at the last, uncoerced, he resolved himself, and so dissolved himself in the manner of nebulous smokes in the
air; and from the eyes, infuscated by so much shining refulgence, he took himself, and vanished
incontinently.

Which mystic and divine things, in that guise marvelling, and such-made a portent having I, trembling, seen —
some space in the soul considering — I remained thought-heavy, full of devout horror. And after a little, the
intrepid monitress made all the virgins rise up; and, taking a golden little rod in the purified hands,
ordained that my most-choice Polia — from the ritual book open before her, held by the little priestess,
reading, and according to the rubrical orders — should take of the remaining ashes from the cremated
sacrifice. Which, with singular veneration taken up, in a golden sieve prepared for such ministry, upon the
venerable step of the dedicated Altar, sifting, most-aptly she riddled, with so shrewd a promptitude as if
another had ever, most-devoted, operated (it). Where the most-erudite monitress, the other fingers of the
left hand contracted, made her extend the ring-finger; and in the holy ash she expressed certain characters,
with most-exact diligence, such as, in the pontifical ritual volume exemplar, marvelling, limpidly she painted.

That the most-diligent Polia had done this — the sage monitress made Polia, and all the others, again upon the
precious pavement humbly genuflect; and, most-accurately upon the ritual index marvelling looking, likewise she
too, with the golden little rod, superstitiously, in that same ash, signed some mysterious figures.

For which thing I, stupefied and totally alienated, and made all timid — insomuch that on my head not a hair
remained that was not raised — with the soul much suspended, doubting, thought-heavily, in this solemn and
sacred propitiation, that my ingenuous Polia was not stolen away (like Iphigenia), and some other animal, or
damsel, put in — and of losing, in a moment, all my desired good: whence the heart smitten, and into itself
concluding all the little spirits, without vital vigour almost I found myself. Nay, so strongly it shook me,
as the mobile reeds, wind-blown by the impetuous and wanton breezes; and more tremulous than the wooden
shavings, and with the mind vibrating, more than the thin sedges in the marshes, by forceful winds —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The apparition and its aftermath: the winged spirit (myrtle-crown, **fire-arrow**,
diamond crown — a little Cupid) circles the altar thrice and **dissolves into smoke**; then Polia, at the
priestess's direction, **sifts the sacrificial ash** and traces mysterious characters in it with her ring-
finger, the priestess adding her own signs; Poliphilo, terrified, fears Polia will be **substituted like
Iphigenia** and he will lose her. All secure.

- **The Cupid-epiphany.** The spirit from the smoke is Love itself — crowned in myrtle and diamonds, bearing
  the fire-arrow — who circles the altar three times and melts into the air. The sacrifice has summoned the
  god; his brief appearance blesses the union. A radiant, animatable moment for the world's rite (a winged
  light rising from the altar-smoke and dissolving).
- **the ash-writing.** Polia sifts the ashes and traces "mysterious characters" with her ring-finger (the
  finger of the *vena amoris*, running to the heart), copying the ritual book; the priestess adds her signs.
  A cryptic, occult act — love-magic written in the remains of the sacrifice. Colonna leaves the characters
  undescribed: the mystery is meant to stay sealed.
- **Poliphilo's Iphigenia-terror.** His fear that Polia will be swapped at the last moment "like Iphigenia"
  (snatched by Diana, a deer left in her place) is the chapter's suspense: having just won her (p. 218), he
  dreads losing her to the very rite that sanctifies her. The anxiety drives toward the miracle (the rose-bush)
  that resolves it (pp. 228+).
- **the reed-and-sedge similes** — Poliphilo trembling "like reeds… like marsh-sedges in the wind": the
  book's stock nature-similes for fear (cf. the pheasant-heart, p. 197). His body registers the dread.

[p. 228]

— impulse, vibrate. But, be it as it might, the ever-vigilant eyes from my sacrificing Polia I never
dislocated, but, with suspectful admiration, pertinaciously observed, noting what most-aptly she did, and
together the high Priestess.

Who, the ritual seized, with many signings, and with innate sanctimony, exorcised all those things that to
pious love might be impediment and noxious. And a branch of sanctified rue — presented to her by one of those

face throughout — she asperged all, and all (the virgins), and me. The holy aspersion performed, and then

received from the Priestess, she devoutly opened the well of the cistern. And within, the aforesaid little
branches, and the little feathers of the immolated turtledoves, she immersed, holding the well open and
waiting. Beyond this, she those holy ashes, somewhat reading over most-holy execration, sanctified again.

threads and murex silk bound into a little clump), she gathered up. And, having put them in a palm-sized
little box, with solemn religion, she preceding, and Polia with the others venerating following, to the lip

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The purification-sequence before the great prayer: the priestess **exorcises** all
impediments to love, **asperges** the company with sanctified rue dipped in Polia's rose-water, immerses the
myrtle, rue, dove-feathers and the ash-box in the cistern with sung hymns, then strikes the altar thrice and
begins the **oration to Venus in the vernacular** ("in our tongue"). All secure.

- **The rite gathers into the cistern.** Every element of the sacrifice — branches, feathers, the charactered
  ashes — is immersed in the sacred well (the same cistern where the torch was quenched, p. 216): the water is
  the rite's receiving vessel, love's element. The ash-box "buried" in the water is the sacrifice consigned to
  Venus.
- **the shift to the vernacular.** The earlier readings were in Etruscan (p. 216) and Latin/Greek (the
  mottoes, p. 214); the great prayer to Venus is spoken **"in our tongue" (Italian)** — Colonna marks it as
  the one directly-intelligible utterance, the heart's petition in the living language. It runs pp. 229–231,
  the book's fullest prayer to the goddess.
- **rue and hyssop** — the purifying herbs (rue for aspersion, hyssop for the ash-brush): the *materia* of
  ritual cleansing, precisely chosen. Colonna's liturgy is built from real cult-plants (cf. the incense,
  p. 225).
- The prayer itself begins on p. 229 with the invocation "O most-holy Erothea, pious mother."

"O most-holy and inspired **Erothea**, pious mother, and illustrious, unceasing and valid patroness of the
ardent and holy loves, and of the amorous fires, and of the sweetest conjugations untiring helper. If, to
thy divine numen, from her the invoked graces have arrived — by which grateful and accepted be her excessive
ardours, and her already-vowed heart — render thyself pious and yielding to her poured prayers, full of
affectionate and religious espousals and instant entreaty. And remember the exhortatory and divine
persuasions of Neptune to furious Vulcan, by thee sedulously made, when, from the Mulciberian (Vulcan's)

she feeling (it) — he not refusing, but patient, and meekly inclining himself — that (heart) —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The opening of the **great prayer to Venus** (Erothea): the priestess invokes the
goddess as patroness of "holy loves," recalls Venus's own rescue from Vulcan's net (freed while trapped with
Mars), and presents Polia — separated "from the colds of Diana" (chastity) — as one wholly preparing herself
for love's fires, her heart already "uprooted" by Cupid. All secure; a sustained liturgical invocation.

- **Venus invoked through her own myth.** The prayer's rhetorical strategy is to remind the goddess of her own
  loves: here, the net of Vulcan (*Odyssey* 8 — Venus and Mars caught in Vulcan's invisible net, then freed at
  Neptune's plea). The priestess asks Venus to be as merciful to these lovers as she herself was shown mercy.
  This is the standard hymn-form (*da quia dedisti*), beautifully deployed.
- **"separated from the colds of Diana."** Polia leaves the chastity of Diana (the "chaste college," p. 217)
  for the "warm" service of Venus: the prayer frames the union as a passage from one goddess's service to the
  other's — from cold virginity to fertile love. The temple of *Venus Physizoa* (generative Venus) is exactly
  the place for that transfer.
- **"conserving nature"** — a key phrase: love's fires "conserve nature" (i.e. propagate life). The prayer
  makes explicit the theology of Venus Physizoa — erotic love as the preservation of the natural order, the
  same creed as the door-mottoes (p. 214). The union is sanctioned as natural law.
- The prayer continues on p. 230, recalling Adonis and invoking Venus under her cult-names (Amathuntea,
  Cyprogenia, Autophies).

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The body of the **prayer to Venus**: Polia's heart offered in the altar-fire; the
petition that the lovers "navigate to thy triumphal realm" (Cythera); Venus invoked under her cult-names
(**Amathuntea**, **Autophies** "self-born," **Cyprogenia**), reminded of prayers she heard before (Aeacus,
Pygmalion, Hippomenes) and of **Adonis, whose blood she turned to the rose**. All secure; the theological and
mythological heart of the temple sequence.

- **The prayer looks forward to Cythera.** The priestess asks that the lovers "navigate and cross over, by thy
  potent son, to thy delicious triumphal and glorious realm" — i.e. to **Cythera** (chs. XX–XXIV, already
  translated). This prayer at the Temple of Venus Physizoa is the request that is *granted* in the second half
  of Book I: the crossing to the island and the triumph. The two great Venus-episodes are joined here.
- **Venus's own loves as precedent.** The prayer recalls, in turn, Pygmalion (his ivory bride made flesh),
  Hippomenes (the golden apples), Aeacus (the Myrmidons), and — climactically — **Adonis**, "the boy-shepherd
  beaten by jealous Mars," whose divine blood Venus "scattered in a rosy flower." This last is the myth that
  the *miraculous rose-bush* about to spring from the sacrifice (pp. 231+) enacts: the prayer names the
  precedent for its own answering miracle.
- **the cult-names.** Amathusia (Cyprus), Cyprogenia ("Cyprus-born"), Autophies ("self-generated") — Colonna
  heaps Venus's epithets, each a facet of the generative goddess. *Autophies* especially fits Venus Physizoa:
  the self-born mother of nature.
- **"the young man… an impavid and strenuous Athlete."** The priestess certifies Poliphilo's constancy — he
  has been, "many days now," a steadfast "athlete" of love (the fidelity-thread again). His and Polia's mutual
  vow of service to Venus's laws is the ground of the petition. The prayer completes on p. 231.

[p. 231]

— eternally live with thee in the supernal delights and glorious triumphs."

To this end, all the sacred virgins, with high voice, responded: "**So be it.**"

From the holy orations and pious intervention the holy lips were no sooner occluded, than the praying
Priestess — of the sacred (things) most-expert — took of the odorous roses prepared, and many little barks of
little conches, or marine oysters, and, with the most-clean hands filled, those ceremoniously, above the
altar, in circuit of the fire-holder, she scattered; and, placing (some) in a bark of oyster, of the sea-water
of the little Urn she asperged all the divine Altar.

Then, upon the *anclabris* table, the two swans, throat-cut with the *secespita*, immolating — the blood, with
that of the incensed turtledoves, in the golden *Praefericulum*, with devout ceremonies and affectionate
deprecation, the virgins singing measured Odes, and she low-voiced reading — she committed that the bloodless
and slaughtered swans be cremated in holocaust in the sacristy, in a place disposed for such a deed; and that
the ash, collected in a box, in an opening under the Altar, be thrown.

knees, with an unthinkable din in the air; and in the Temple, with a horrendous roaring, thundering — not

broken thunder should inwardly thunder.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The rite's turning-point: the priestess and Polia wash the sacred blood from their
hands (the water caught in the golden *simpulum*), Polia wipes the blood-characters from the pavement with a
virgin sponge, and the priestess pours **the bloody washing onto the altar-fire** — whereupon smoke leaps up
and **the earth quakes**, the temple thundering "as if a great mass fell from heaven," the golden door-hinges
rumbling. All secure; the theophany's onset.

- **The earthquake as divine answer.** The moment the blood-washing hits the fire, the temple shakes with a
  cataclysmic din — the sign that Venus has heard (the prayer of pp. 229–231 is being answered). Colonna stages
  the miracle with full apparatus: smoke, tremor, thunder, shrieking hinges. A dramatic, stageable beat for
  the world's rite (and the visual-novel's temple climax).
- **the reserved blood consumed, then returned.** Every trace of the sacred blood — on hands and pavement — is
  gathered into the washing-water and poured on the fire: nothing of the sacrifice is wasted or profaned ("no
  other contact was licit"). The rite's scrupulous economy (cf. the cistern-immersions, p. 228) reaches its
  climax as the offering goes wholly into the flame.
- **the door-hinges thunder** — the same golden magnet-valves that opened silently (p. 213) now rumble in the
  quake: the whole building responds to the god's arrival. The temple, which moves, rings and glows on its own

- The smoke resolves into the miraculous rose-bush on p. 233 — the theophany itself.

Whence, full and surrounded by marvellous terror, and fearfully agitated, I invoked, silent, whatever divine

occupied, to the raised altitude of the cupola, with a numerosity of vermilion and rubricating roses
together, and with many round fruits, of wondrous odour fragrant, of colouring candid-and-vermilioned; which
offered themselves more pleasing to the taste than, by chance, are not those which, to the famished mouth of
Tantalus, present themselves. More beautiful were they not, those desired by Eurystheus (the Hesperides'
apples).

Upon this rosy bush, then, appeared three white little doves, with some little birds gregariously fluttering
in the branches; and, festive, they leapt, colluding, and most-sweetly sang. And, by such a portent, the
numen presented — in that guise occulted — of the most-holy Mother, rightly I suspected.

For which thing, the sacrificing Priestess having risen, with matronal decorum — and Polia too, with special
beauty (more than ever to my eyes she appeared gracious), and in her sweet aspect laughing — both, reassuring
me, invited me into the sacrosanct sacello to enter; and, within, calling me before, venerating, of the divine
Altar, between the Priestess and Polia genuflecting me, the Priestess, with veteran ceremony, three of the
miraculous fruits extirpated: the one for herself reserved; of the two, to me one, and to Polia the other,
offering. Those, with revoked religion, and the utmost integrity of heart, together, all three, we tasted.

Now, no sooner did I taste the miraculous and sweetest little apple, than without delay I felt in me refresh
and renew the rude and gross intellect, and the anxious and mourning heart all recreate itself, anointed in
amorous joy — neither more nor less than one who, overwhelmed in the deep sea, and to the bottom immersed with
shut lips, without draught of breath, from above returns, most-avidly taking the fresh and most-pleasant airs,
and vivifies himself. For which thing, incontinently, in me more amorous flames began to burn; and with a more
sweet torment of new qualities of love it appeared to me to be transmuted. And therefore I began evidently to
know, and effectually to feel, what the Venerean graces are, and of how much efficacy they present themselves
to the earth-born, and how great a reward joyously they attain, who — through the delightful realms, intrepidly
soldiering, and in the amorous, pertinacious battles — arrive at them. Ultimately, after the devout and sacred
refection of the fatal fruits, taken without hesitation, that divine germ (bush), vanishing from the eyes,
disappeared. The libant Priestess went out of the holy sacello, and Polia paired with her, and I, and all.

the divine cult — both, having deposed the sacred vestments, and stripped off, with choice veneration, all
those mysterious and pontifical instruments, with domestic and templar obsequies, in the sacristy reverently
they re-deposited.

And there, weighingly, the high Priestess, with special majesty, thus familiarly said to us: "My children, now

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The lovers come to the ruined **Polyandrion** — the seaside tomb-temple: white-marble

- **The Polyandrion, in the book's own words.** A "many-men's" tomb (Greek *polyandrion*) by the sea:
  once a thronged festival-temple, now a ruin of headless columns, holding "many little tomb-pits" of those

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Polia's account of the **ancient rites of the Polyandrion** — the yearly funeral festival
for those who died of love: sacrifices of black sheep to three-bodied Pluto, the *lectisternia*, flames quenched
with roses, ashes given to the mourners and **cast into the sea** ("thus perish whoever caused his lover's death"),
the triple spitting, the sepulchral songs, and the *silicernium* (funeral banquet) among the tombs. All secure; a
dense antiquarian reconstruction of a Roman festival of the dead.

- **The rite of the love-dead.** The Polyandrion's cult is the dark inverse of the Temple of Venus's: where
  Venus's rite sanctifies fulfilled love with a rose-bush and shared fruit (pp. 231–233), the Polyandrion mourns
  love's casualties with black sheep, sea-cast ashes, and a curse on those who caused a lover's death. Both use
  **roses** — there for blessing, here for the graves. The world's polyandrion carries this funerary meaning.
- **"Thus perish whoever causes his lover's death."** The festival's imprecation, cast with the ashes into the
  sea: the Polyandrion is not only a tomb but a tribunal — it curses the cruel beloved whose disdain killed the
  lover. A resonant line for the world/novel's polyandrion (it names the moral stakes of the whole love-quest).
- **the Roman festival apparatus** — *lectisternia* (couches spread for the gods), *silicernium* (the funeral
  meal), the Manes (ancestral spirits), the secular games, the reed-and-ash sea-rite, the triple spitting
  (apotropaic): Colonna reconstructs a complete *Parentalia*-style festival with scholarly precision.
- The priest's formula of dismissal ("Illicet") closes the rite on p. 238.

(Tempe). And there, together thus sitting, among the springing and redolent flowers and roses, in this celestial
effigy, with so much delight the gaping eyes, occupied, fixedly I held; and to so beautiful and rare a make, and
divine image, with all the senses, gazing, most-devoted and applied — and, in me, more pleasant, resulting the
heated vexing impulses, in which the soul, from sweetness liquefied, insane I stood, and all anxious, projected
all and curious to consider, marvelling, by what mode and reason that purpling liquor — at the touch of the
precious flesh of the little swelling wrist of the hand, remaining most-pure milk, for some little space — to its
place returned not. No less, with what artifice, in this most-comely body, the mistress nature had particularly
dispensed, and stuffingly disseminated, all the Arabic fragrance; and how, again, industriously, in her starry
forehead, of gold threads becomingly vine-tendrilled, she had fixed the most-beautiful part of the sky, or the
shining Heraclean (star).

Then, to the comely and slender feet the sight converting, I beheld on them the vermilion shoes violently drawn
on, and, over the ivory instep, moon-wise mouthed and sinuated with a *phytontea* (plant-like) opening, with
little gold rings, and with little cords of cyan silk ensnared, and tightly re-bound — most-apt instruments to
intercalate (bind) the life, and excessively to torment the more the inflamed heart. Then, straightway, the
lascivious regard returned to the straight throat, berried in a circle with oriental pearls — not understanding,
of the one and the other whiteness, the true distinction — of a sudden descended to the glittering breast, and
delightful bosom, where sprouted two round little apples, resistant to the garment, and obstinately repugnant;
nor such, without fail, in the orchard of the Hesperides, did Hercules furtively gather; nor such does Pomona ever
see in her orchard, as these — most-white in the rosy breast, standing immovable, fixed, whiter than the flocked
and lucid snow —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The lovers sit on the shore before the ruin, and the page turns from the Polyandrion to
**Poliphilo's rapt contemplation of Polia** — her whole beauty, the landscape around them (a Tempe-surpassing
vale), and then a head-to-foot inventory (the rose-liquid that turns to milk on her wrist, her Arabic fragrance,
her gold hair, her red laced shoes, her pearl-throat, her breast). All secure; a beauty-ekphrasis in the book's
most sensuous manner.

- **The landscape as locus amoenus.** Between the ruined tomb and the beloved, Colonna sets a perfect pastoral —
  mild air, wooded hills, twin rivers running to the sea, birdsong — "let yield the Thessalian Tempe." The
  Polyandrion's death is framed by life and beauty: the setting refuses to be only funereal. A vivid brief for
  the world's polyandrion surroundings (a green, river-cut shore around the ruin).
- **the portrait resumes.** Poliphilo's gaze runs Polia head to foot (as at the triumph, p. 337, and the boat,
  p. 287): the rose-water that becomes milk on her wrist, her fragrance, her star-set golden hair, her laced
  vermilion shoes ("instruments to torment the heart"), her pearl-throat, her breast "whiter than snow." The
  sensuous inventory the whole book returns to whenever the beloved is still.
- **"instruments to intercalate the life."** Even Polia's shoe-laces are figured as bonds that "bind the life
  and torment the heart" — the recurring conceit of beauty as sweet captivity (cf. the rose-withes, p. 341; the
  hair-snares, p. 333). Desire is always, for Colonna, a willing bondage.
- **the milk-and-rose wrist** — a delicate marvel: rose-water touched to her wrist turns to milk and does not
  run off, so pure is her flesh; Poliphilo puzzles at the "mode and reason" (his optics-mind again, cf. pp. 208,
  213). Beauty posed as a natural wonder to be investigated.

[p. 240]

— in the season of Orion at setting, under the *pissatile* (?) body of the placid monster of Pan. Among which
(beauties), voluptuously, I beheld a delicious little valley, where was the delicate sepulchre of my soul — such
as Mausolus had not, with all his having, collocated. Being, then, I, for this, content — and the lacerated
heart conscious that the eyes, distracting it into whatever of those most-elegant parts, dispensed it moribund —
nonetheless I could not, for this, so much bridle the amorous and inflamed sighs, and so covertly castigate
(them), that I did not concede them their simulated sound to express itself.

By this such-made accident, immediately she too, provoked by the contagious love, and stirred, the lewd regards
most-placidly (special envy to the Sun) into me converted; and throughout I felt an irritating fire, itchingly
diffusing itself, into the lowest and interstitial parts, and even through all the capillary little veins,
seminarily to scatter itself. Whence, in her illustrious and notable features continually to contemplate, a
mellifluous sweetness, and solace, sweetly I heaped up. And there, some time, collided by disordered and
insatiable appetite, and by fiery and importunate stimulus gravely oppressed, with piteous words, full of
suasive and vehement prayer, secretly imploring, I appetited within me the desired kisses, sipping and fluid,
and sweetest, with vibrating (like a viper) and succulent little tongue — imagining to feel the extreme
sweetness of the savoury and little mouth (breathing-hole of odorous air, and mossy spirit, and freshest
breath) — and, feigning to enter into the hidden treasure of Venus, and there, mercurially, to steal the most-
precious jewels of parent nature.

Whence — alas, sighing — by that divine mother surrounded I found myself, and by the flame-bearing son circum-
walled, and by so most-beautiful a figure invaded, all henceforth morbid and infected by such notable
circumstances ornated and comely, and by the golden-fleeced head enticed (that whatever hair offered itself to
me a constricting snare, and chain), and beset by these torturing knots, and by the plenitude of such pleasant
pastures, and of amorous sweetness viscously baited — I could not, with whatever shrewd effort, resist the
accessory and invading ardours, and irritating thoughts; and, in me, the arrow-bearing love, having forced
itself, wholly disposed me — so insupportable a burning (patience overcome) to extinguish — and, spurned every
repugnant reason and mature counsel, in the solitary places, with Herculean audacity, to make assault, and the
divine and untouched Nymph, unbridled, to fore-attempt. But first, with sighing and precatory voice, of pity
impetrable, thus to say:

"Alas, divine-born Polia — in the present, for thee to die, eternal praise I esteem; and death more tolerable
and soft, and more glorious, with these thy delicate and swelling hands, would be to me the last end and demise.
For, the soul circumfused by so many tormenting ardours, ever more savagely quickening themselves, it, languid,
scorching, without intermission and pity they burn — so that never is left me to take a quiet hour, nor peace."

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Poliphilo's desire mounts to a **crisis of temptation**: gazing on Polia, his whole body
afire, "invaded" by her beauty and "ensnared" by her golden hair, he is moved by "arrow-bearing love" to make an
"assault with Herculean audacity" on the "untouched Nymph" — but checks himself, and instead begins a piteous
plea ("for thee to die I esteem eternal praise"). All secure; the psychological turn of the chapter.

- **The temptation, named honestly.** After the sanctified union and the blessing, Poliphilo is nonetheless
  overwhelmed by physical desire — imagining kisses, "entering the hidden treasure of Venus," and even an assault
  on Polia "in the solitary places." Colonna does not pretend the sacred rite has neutered desire; it names the
  crisis plainly. The restraint that follows (p. 241) is the point — the fidelity-thread tested at its sharpest.
- **beauty as snare, again.** Her hair "a constricting snare and chain," her sweetness "viscously baited": the
  recurring image of beauty as a trap (pp. 333, 341, 239) reaches its most dangerous pitch here, because now it
  tempts Poliphilo toward force. The plea that interrupts him is the beginning of his self-mastery.
- **"the delicate sepulchre of my soul"** — even in desire, Poliphilo calls Polia's body the "sepulchre of his
  soul" (surpassing Mausolus's tomb): the Polyandrion's funerary theme bleeds into the love-language. Love and
  death entwined, on the very shore of the tomb of love's victims.
- Poliphilo's restraint, and Polia's soothing, complete the chapter on p. 241.



------------------------------------------------------------------------
CHAPTER XVIII / (ARGUMENT OF CHAPTER XIX)
------------------------------------------------------------------------

[p. 241]

For which thing — by this way wishing to this incentive and frequent stimulus to put a finish — lo, that, of
other most-savage fires, my scarred heart, all from the beginning, to burn candently I felt. "Alas, how wilt
thou do here, Poliphilo? Somewhat cogitate of the violence done to Deianira, and to the chaste Roman
(Lucretia) — badly and unhappily turned out — and of many others. Consider that the omnipotent gods of earthly
loves have received resistance — let alone a lacerated and most-abject man. Revoke into memory that all long
time accrues to him who can wait; and that the fierce lions, again, by continued days, are made gentle, and
each other sylvan and cross animal; and the grain-bearing ant, again, by assiduous journey — however most-tiny —
in the hard flint imprints its trodden (path): let alone that a divine form, hidden in a most-human little body,
ought to take in itself the vestige of fervent love."

And thus, observed, reprobating, I confuted (refuted) so great a harm — the vexing passion taming — hoping to
attain the amorous fruits, and coveted effects, and triumphant contest. In memory questioning the holy orations,
and sacrifices, and libations, and the extinction of the torch — in which divine offices herself, and her
Poliphilo, she had intently and especially commemorated with commendatory entreaties — for so much I thought, by
suffering, a more efficacious reward and requital, and the implored (thing) to attain, than that, with perilous
improbity, to profit my most-bitter languors, and lose thence every hope.

The Nymph Polia, aware of the versicolour (changing) of my face, and its varying — more than the illustrious
*Tripolion*, or *Teucrion*, that three times a day changes the colour of its flower — and seeing me altered, and
solicited certainly by the intimate love (so many warm and frequent sighs), pitifully, with her adulating
regards, timely tempered and delineated (dissolved) the impetuous movements and irruent agitation. And so, and
not otherwise, my soul burning, in these continual flames, and burnable asperity, love stimulated me patiently to
hope — that, as the Arabian phoenix, in the aromatic twigs, in the aspect of the ardent Sun kindled, from the
arid ashes hopes to renew itself.

---

*(Argument of the following chapter — Chapter XIX:)*

> POLIA PERSUADES POLIPHILO THAT HE GO TO SPECULATE THE ANTIQUE EPITAPHS IN THE DESTROYED TEMPLE, WHERE
> POLIPHILO SAW MARVELLOUS THINGS; AND, READING LASTLY THE RAPE OF PROSERPINA, HE DOUBTED, INCAUTIOUSLY, THAT HE
> HAD THEREBY LOST HIS POLIA, AND, FRIGHTENED, RETURNED TO HER. THEN, THE GOD OF LOVE COMING, POLIA INVITES
> POLIPHILO TO ENTER THE LITTLE BOAT; WHICH, CALLING ZEPHYR, THEY NAVIGATED, HAPPY. AND, NAVIGATING, BY THE MARINE
> GODS GREAT VENERATION WAS MADE TO CUPID.

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Poliphilo **masters the temptation**: recalling the disasters of forced love (Deianira,
Lucretia — "the chaste Roman"), the resistance even the gods met, and the maxims of patience (the tamed lion, the
ant wearing the flint), he resolves to win Polia "by suffering" not "by perilous improbity," remembering the
sacrifices and the extinguished torch. Polia, seeing his face change colour "like the *Tripolion*," soothes him,
and his soul burns on "like the phoenix" hoping to be renewed. This ends **chapter XVIII**; the argument previews
**chapter XIX** (the epitaphs, the Rape of Proserpina, and the boat). All secure.

- **Restraint chosen — the fidelity-thread's sharpest test passed.** Against the assault-impulse of p. 240,
  Poliphilo reasons himself back to patience: force ends badly (Deianira's shirt, Lucretia's rape), even gods are
  resisted, and constancy wins in time (the lion tamed, the ant's path worn in stone — the maxim of Polia's own
  "perseverance," p. 289). He will earn Polia "by suffering," honouring the torch he extinguished. This is the
  moral resolution of the whole temptation — love as patient service, not conquest.
- **the phoenix.** His unquenched desire is figured as the phoenix burning to be reborn: love that consumes in
  order to renew (echoing the fruit's "transmutation," p. 234). The chapter ends not with desire ended but with
  desire transfigured into hope.
- **the argument sets up chapter XIX.** The next (and longest) chapter takes Poliphilo *into* the ruined
  Polyandrion to read its **antique epitaphs** of dead lovers — culminating in the **Rape of Proserpina**, which
  so frightens him (fearing Polia lost like Proserpina) that he runs back to her; then the **god of Love** comes,
  and Polia leads him to the boat and the crossing (which chapter XX, already translated, continues). The whole
  Book-I arc now joins up.
- **Chapter XVIII complete.** From the incense-rite and rose-bush miracle (pp. 225–233) to the Polyandrion and
  this temptation-and-restraint: the chapter has carried the lovers from the temple of fulfilled love to the tomb
  of love's victims, and tested Poliphilo's constancy on its very threshold.



------------------------------------------------------------------------
CHAPTER XIX
------------------------------------------------------------------------

[p. 242]

Above all the excogitated and exquisite torments of love not mediocrely beset seeing myself — and to the pre-
chosen and salubrious and present remedy, and my heart-healer, being near — stupefied I marvelled that,
against every natural order, she more morbidly infected me. And whatever her outstanding act, ornate eloquence,
biting regard, from so opportune a health, finding myself near, abdicated me (drove me off); whence ever more
multiplied an exhortable suasion, of wishing, to the provoking commodity (a grateful little gift to ravishers),
not to present myself ungrateful and pusillanimous. Fremishing like a furious and snarling dog, the pursued
beast having reached, in the alpine leaps: so I, neither more nor less, a furious coveter, the very desired prey
here reached, wholly to satisfy myself. Accustomed now to an assiduous and familiar death of love, I did not,
for this, repute the atrocity a passion, that thence might be ensued. And therefore every inconvenience, however
most-damaging, licit it suaded me. Whence my *eutrapela* (witty) Polia, shrewd of the improbe condition of
blind Love, and aware — to mortify so importunate a burning, and somewhat to syncopate it, and, as my singular
preserver, succouring — thus benignly says to me:

"Poliphilo, of all mine most-beloved, I am never unaware that antique works supremely please thee to see. So,
conveniently thou canst, in this interval, while we await lord Cupid, go licitly to see these deserted temples,
collapsed by devouring and obsolete old age — or by fire assumed, or by many years shaken — to thy solace to
behold, and the noble fragments left, of veneration most-worthy, to speculate. And I, in this place sitting,
content, will await thee, watchful, awaiting our lord to come, who must ferry us to the holy and coveted
maternal realm."

Then I, greatly most-avid — with the other most-commendable works seen — also these, most-accurately and
multividuously to contemplate, rose from the happy session, from under the tempered shades of laurel, and of
myrtle, and among tallish cypresses (then, about the place, the honeysuckle painting its odorous flowers, where
a voluble flowering jasmine, with soft shade, opaquely covered us, disseminating over us copiously its whitest
flowers, at that time most-sweetly odorous). Absorbed, without other cogitating, from beside Polia, by those
devious embankments of fastigiate and vast heap and ruin — in the greater part occupied with ground-ivy, and
*terrambula*, and implicated with thorns — solicitous I came. Where, ponderingly, I conjectured this to have
been a magnificent and marvellous temple, of choice and superb structure, according as the proven and
illustrious Nymph had shrewdly vaticinated to me. There, then, it appeared that, in a ring around the round
temple, were —

- **Polia's stratagem.** Knowing "antique works supremely please" Poliphilo, Polia sends him to survey the ruin

## Notes

**Confidence: medium** (the hieroglyph-inventory is a plain description; the interpretations come on p. 244). The
tombs disposed in tribunes around the ruined round temple, then the **great red obelisk** behind it, whose base
carries **hieroglyph-panels** — the first (balance, dog, serpent, ark, sword, crown) and the second (eye, wheat,
scimitar, threshers, globe, rudder, olive-vase, ibises, coins) — which Poliphilo "reads" as Latin mottoes on

- **The obelisk of the Polyandrion.** A red-stone obelisk on a hieroglyph-carved base stands behind the round
  temple — the ruin's central monument, and the direct source for the world's polyandrion obelisk (its notes
  call it "the obelisk of Caesar"; the dedication is read on p. 244). Colonna gives the carvings picture by
  picture, then his humanist "translation" of them.
- **Colonna's hieroglyphics.** These panels are the Hypnerotomachia's famous *invented Egyptian hieroglyphs* —
  rebus-pictures Poliphilo decodes into Latin sentences (pp. 244+). They shaped the Renaissance idea of
  hieroglyphic writing (via Alberti, Valeriano) long before Champollion. The world's polyandrion animating one
  of them (the ant/elephant, p. 244) is faithful to their spirit: the stones *speak*.
- **the tombs in tribunes** — the graves of the love-dead are set in niches (*tribunes*) ringing the temple;
  their epitaphs are read through the chapter. The columns' stones (Numidian, Hymettian, Laconian) date and
  dignify the ruin.
- Poliphilo's readings of the two panels — the Julius Caesar dedication and the ant-and-elephant concord-motto —
  follow on p. 244.

## Notes

**Confidence: high** (the two mottoes are secure — the hieroglyphs are given with Poliphilo's own Latin, and both
are famous). The obelisk-base's two hieroglyph-panels decoded: the first a **dedication to Julius Caesar** by the
Egyptians ("for his clemency and liberality"); the second the celebrated **ant-and-elephant concord-motto** —
*by peace and concord small things grow, by discord the greatest decrease* — read from the caduceus, the ant
growing to an elephant (and elephants shrinking to ants), and the fire-vase and water-shell. All secure.

- **The ant-and-elephant hieroglyph — the world's polyandrion device.** This is the exact source for the
  animated ant/elephant hieroglyph on the world's polyandrion obelisk (`_buildPolyandrion`, `this._hiero`): a
  caduceus flanked by an ant swelling into an elephant (concord, growth) and elephants dwindling to ants
  (discord, decline), with fire and water balanced between. Poliphilo's Latin — *pace ac concordia parvae res
  crescunt, discordia maximae decrescunt* — is the motto the world can carry verbatim. One of the most-copied of
  all the book's hieroglyphs (Erasmus and the emblem-books took it up).
- **the obelisk of Caesar.** The first panel is a hieroglyphic dedication to **Julius Caesar** "ever Augustus,
  governor of the whole world," raised by the Egyptians — hence the world's naming of the monument "the obelisk
  of Caesar." Colonna reads the balance/dog/serpent/sword/crown and the eye/wheat/globe/rudder as this imperial
  encomium (justice, vigilance, world-rule, clemency).
- **hieroglyphics as the book's signature.** Here is the Hypnerotomachia's method in its purest form: pictures
  decoded into Latin sentences. The two mottoes — imperial praise and the concord-maxim — set the obelisk as a
  monument of *good rule and harmony* at the heart of the tomb of love's discord. The Polyandrion's dead died of
  love's *discord*; the obelisk preaches concord over them.
- Both mottoes are prime material for the world/novel's polyandrion (the concord-motto especially, already used).

**Confidence: medium** (the two remaining hieroglyph-panels; the inscription itself is on p. 246). The obelisk's

- **the anchor-and-eagle, the trophy-and-comet** — Colonna's rebus-symbols (an anchor bound = steadfast hope; a

- The frieze-inscription — the Polyandrion's own dedication — follows immediately on p. 246.

> **D · M · S ·**
> **CADAVERIBUS AMORE FURENTIUM**
> **MISERABUNDIS POLYANDRION**
>
> "To the Gods of the Dead (*Dis Manibus Sacrum*). The Polyandrion, for the wretched corpses of those raging

This noble and much-admired fragment, in one solid frust (chunk) — and a little portion of its fastigium, or
frontispiece — still retained itself egregiously delineated. In the triangular plane of which, two figments I saw
carved, and not entire: a decapitated bird (I judged it to be of an Owl), and an antique lamp, all of perfect

> **VITAE LETHIFER NUNTIUS** — "The death-bringing messenger of life."

Come then into the middle part of the temple, somewhat immune and unoccupied of rubble I found it. Where, again,
the consuming time, to one illustrious work of note — all of rubicund porphyry — had only pardoned. Which was
sexangular (hexagonal), with the bases upon a solid stone of Ophite, of the same figure, fixed in the pavement;
and six little columns, distant one from the other six feet, with the Epistyle, Frieze, and Cornice, without any
lineament and sign, but simply terse and pure. Which were, on the exterior, imitating the (hexagonal) form; but
the interstices in a circled figure. Where, upon the flat of the cornice, was born a cupola of a single and solid
rock, marvellous artifice; which thinned at the summit, where a pervious funnel, streaked and mirror-like, covered
a subterranean vacuity, illuminated by a circular opening of egregious grating, impeded (closed) of metal casting.
Which noteworthy ciborium, of the utmost polish, thus I found.

part, because the mournful **Alecto** — sister of the two named, daughters of Acheron and of black Night — she too

themselves in the freezing lake; but, frightened by the horrend fury, they climbed, they too, with the others

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The Hell-mosaic in full: an iron bridge between a **burning lake** (sparks, boiling fire,
sulphur-mountain, steam-vents) and a **frozen lake** (glacial, clay-muddy); **Taenarus's bronze door** guarded by
three-headed **Cerberus**; and the three Furies — **Tisiphone**, **Megaera**, **Alecto** — driving the souls back
and forth between fire and ice so neither the burning may reach the cold nor the frozen the flames. All secure; a
vivid, Dante-adjacent infernal ekphrasis.

- **The contrapasso of lovers.** The mosaic's torment (spelled out on p. 250) is that the fire-damned *long for
  the ice* and the ice-damned *long for the fire*, and the Furies keep each from the relief of its opposite — an
  eternal frustration. It is the punishment of love's two failures: those who burned themselves with love, and
  those who were cold to it. The Polyandrion's dead are judged by this fresco overhead. A powerful, thematically-
  exact ceiling for the world's polyandrion.
- **the classical machinery.** Taenarus (the Peloponnesian cave-mouth of Hades), Cerberus, the three Furies
  (daughters of Acheron and Night), the burning and freezing lakes: Colonna assembles the full ancient underworld,
  painted "feigned shrewdly." The world can render it as a fire-and-ice mosaic with the bridge, the dog, and the
  serpent-haired Furies.
- **the painting as trompe-l'oeil** — Colonna stresses the artifice ("feigned shrewdly," sparks "like atoms in
  the sunbeams"): the fresco's realism is itself the marvel, surpassing Parrhasius (p. 250). The Polyandrion's art
  makes Hell visible.
- The torment's logic and the surpassing of Parrhasius complete on p. 250.

[p. 250]

— it appeared to me, that the souls that were damned to the ardent burning, into the ice desired to migrate; and
those that were adjudicated to the most-torpid lake — much more frigid than the Stygian marsh — excessively desired
to enter, refreshing themselves, into the maledict and heat-bearing flames. But, forced to climb the fallacious
crossing (the candescent pass), by fatal disposition it divided itself in such manner, that the souls proscribed to
the inextinguishable fire fell again into their eternally constituted place. By the like, those that attempted to
evade the inevitable cold, refuged, were, from the bridge, re-submerged into the most-freezing deep. By virtue then
of the divine justice, the transit returned to its pristine being.

Without interval, other dolorous souls attempted this same, successively, with vain and impotent wish, and by no
means could they attain the desired effect. Those most-wretched souls, then, that hastened without quiet to flee,
by furious horror and rabies agitated — the incendious flames — could not, by relieving, come and refresh themselves
in the ice. And those likewise, that gave assiduous heed to fleeing the hardest cold, and entering into the ardent
flames, frustrated of the greatest desire, could not. And this, to those, was inescapable, and a pain unceasing —
ever more desirous, losing every hope. Which so much the more ardent avidity increased, as, upon the bridge, the one
and the other felt — those (of the fire) the reflex of its cold, and those (frozen) the heat — the one with the
other meeting at its term (the bridge's midpoint). And this, in the affect, was the greatest quickening of pain and
of torment. For which thing, with so obstinate an art of colouring, and of simulated gestures and expressed
efforts, I saw such a painting skilfully-made, and exquisitely perfect, as ever could be made and shown. And the
title, indicating, was inscribed: that, in the burning flames, were condemned the souls that, for too much fire of
love, killed their very selves; and, in the horrid ice, were immersed those who, rigid and chilly to Love and
refusing, had obstinately shown themselves.

Finally, with such disposition I beheld this odious, frightful and to-be-avoided Barathrum (pit), that where the
lakes met — that is, the frigorific with the most-ardent — by the contrariety they must make, with eternal
controversy, a terrible thundering; because then, meeting, both immersed themselves in an abrupt precipice, effused
into a dark, vast and most-deep passage and immense abyss. Where the profundity was so artfully feigned by the
artificer, that, by the colouring, those demonstrations feigned (themselves) to be true, and (one seemed) to see a
most-absorbing vortex, with wondrous emulation of the colourings, and of lineal symmetry of prospect, and of the
figures the elegance, and copious invention, and artful designation, and with incredible sharpness — such that
Parrhasius of Ephesus, notable painter, could never first glory himself of a like device.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The **meaning of the Hell-mosaic**, made explicit by its inscription: **the fire punishes
those who killed themselves for too much love; the ice punishes those who were cold and refused Love** — and each
is tormented by longing for the other's element, kept from it by "divine justice," feeling at the bridge's midpoint
the very relief they cannot reach. The two lakes meet in a thundering abyss, painted with a trompe-l'oeil depth
surpassing Parrhasius. All secure; the thematic key of the whole Polyandrion.

- **The two sins against Love — the Polyandrion's judgement.** The fresco names the tomb's whole moral: **excess**
  (self-slaughter for love, the fire) and **frigidity** (cold refusal of love, the ice) are the two damnations,
  each eternally denied its opposite's relief. This is the theology the Polyandrion enforces over its dead, and the
  exact counter-image to the Temple of Venus's sanctioned, measured love. For the world/novel, this is the meaning
  to inscribe over the polyandrion: love neither too hot nor too cold — the mean the whole book (and Polia's
  "perseverance," p. 289) commends.
- **the contrapasso.** The torment is *desire itself*, frustrated: the burning long for ice, the frozen for fire,
  and feel at the bridge the relief forever withheld. Colonna makes Hell a machine of unquenchable longing — an
  image of unfulfilled love raised to eternal punishment. Powerful material for the world's polyandrion ceiling.
- **surpassing Parrhasius.** The great Greek illusionist (of the painted curtain) is exceeded by this fresco's
  feigned abyssal depth: the surpassing-topos, on painting (cf. Apelles/Aristides, p. 287). The Polyandrion's art
  makes its doctrine unbearably vivid.
- **the fire-and-ice abyss** — where the lakes meet they thunder and pour into "an immense abyss" of feigned depth:
  a buildable, dramatic centre for the mosaic. The world could render the whole tribune-vault as this fire/ice Hell.

**Confidence: medium.** The souls of the Hell-mosaic, rendered as "concreted air" (shades made visible), each in a
gesture of its torment — stopping ears, hiding eyes, arms clenched against the cold, blowing smoke of the heat,

- **shades as "concreted air."** Colonna's aesthetic note: the painter can only show incorporeal souls by
  condensing them into visible bodies ("concreted air"), a knowing account of how painting represents the immaterial.
  His interest is always double — the horror *and* the artifice of showing it.
- **the gestures of torment** — ears stopped, eyes hidden, arms hugged against cold, smoke breathed, hands wrung:
  a repertoire of expressive poses. For the world's polyandrion mosaic, these give the figures their attitudes.
- The first **tomb-epitaphs** begin on p. 252 — the graves of individual love-dead, which fill the rest of the

## Notes

**Confidence: high** (the epitaph is secure, read from the woodcut). The first individual **tomb-epitaph**: an
"Altar of the infernal gods" to **Laodia Publia**, who "defrauded her age" (denied her youth), refused Love against
the custom of maidens, and killed herself with the sword — one of the ice-damned (the cold, love-refusing).

- **Laodia Publia — the frigid suicide.** Her epitaph names the second of the Polyandrion's two sins (p. 250): she
  was *cold* to love, "refused, against the custom of maidens, the commands of Love," and, despairing, killed
  herself. Not a martyr of love but a refuser of it — yet buried here among love's dead, and (by the fresco's logic)
  destined for the ice. The Polyandrion holds both kinds. A concrete epitaph the world/novel can carry.
- **the form.** Colonna gives the tombs in authentic Roman epigraphic style — *Ara Deum Infernorum*, *Viator*
  ("traveller," the standard address to the passer-by), the abbreviations (*GLAD. INTERF.*): the epitaphs read like
  real inscriptions, and are among the sources for Renaissance epigraphy. The world's polyandrion can carry these
  verbatim on its tombs.
- **"much gladdened, I departed"** — Poliphilo, absorbed in antiquarian reading, is *cheered* by the tombs: the
  therapy Polia intended (p. 242) is working — the graveyard has cooled his ardour into scholarly delight.
- The next epitaph (to Annira Pucilla) follows on p. 253.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium** (the epitaph's letters are secure; one word, *DIDUS*, is uncertain). A second **tomb-

- **Annira Pucilla — a parents' grief.** Unlike Laodia's suicide-altar (p. 252), this is a family monument: an

- **the epigraphic formulae, continued.** *D · M* (*Dis Manibus*, "to the shades"), *puellae incomparabili*,

  Colonna deploys throughout the Polyandrion. The world's tombs can be lettered from these.
- **the ash-vase.** The stone holds a lidless bronze vase "in which the ashes were stored" — the cinerary urn of the
  cremated (cf. the crypt-furnace, p. 247). Each tomb is a real burial, not a mere marker.
- **hybrid nasturtium** — the shore-and-ruin flora continues (cf. p. 236); life overgrows each grave. Colonna keeps
  the botanical thread even through the epitaphs.

> **MAN(IBUS) CIRCA SEPULCRUM**
> **SATAGERENT ANNUALITER**
> **PERPETUO**
> **REPETUND(UM).**
> **EX T(ESTAMENTO) F(IERI) I(USSIT).**
>
> "To the shades. To my gladiator, by my love — for whom, burned to the utmost, I lay down in death's languor; but
> by his blood (alas, wretched me!), unpurified, I recovered. Leaving a pious monument [to divine Faustus
> Augustus?], that yearly, with the blood of turtledoves amid the sacrifice of the arcane religion, this [torch] be
> dipped, with forty-nine kindled torches; and that the weeping girls be loosed (in mourning), and, for the token
> of so great grief, funeral lamentation — with hair torn and let flowing — redden their breasts and face a whole
> day; and, the shades propitiated, they busy themselves about the sepulchre yearly, in perpetuity to be repeated.
> By her testament she ordered it made." *(Several abbreviations are conjecturally expanded.)*

Then, when I had these two epitaphs accurately perused, and most-pleasingly seen, solicitous, inquiring, turning
the eyes — lo, that I see a **historiated sepulchre**. To which, without tarrying, I went. On the anterior part of
which, fixed, was a little altar, together with such (figures) expressed. Upon the flat of it, of wondrous
artifice, was set a head of a sylvan goat, held by one of the horns by a little old man, with the head of hair, in
the old manner, tormented (dressed), confused; who was clad, over the nude, in a pall thrown back over the right
shoulder, coming under from the left, returning over the right, and at the back pendent; near, he was clothed in
goat-skin — one (skin) in front and the other behind at the back, over the shoulders, the feet of both skins
knotted, and the others hanging between the thighs with the rough hair turned to the flesh; and girt with a torque,
or fillet, made of *tanus*, or black vine, with its leaves.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium** (the epitaph is elaborate and several abbreviations are conjecturally expanded). A remarkable
**foundation-epitaph**: a woman to her dead **gladiator**-lover — she nearly died of love, "recovered by his blood,"
and by her will endowed a **perpetual annual rite** (dove's-blood sacrifice, forty-nine torches, girls loosing their
hair and reddening their breasts in mourning) at his tomb. Then a **historiated Bacchic sepulchre** (a goat-headed
sylvan altar with an old satyr). All secure in outline; some Latin flagged.

- **The gladiator's endowment — a lover's perpetual mourning.** The most elaborate epitaph yet: a *foundation*, by
  testament, of a yearly funeral rite for the beloved gladiator — an antique instance of the endowed anniversary
  (like the Polyandrion's own festival, p. 237). It shows love's grief institutionalised: the mourner buys eternal
  lamentation. A rich model for the world/novel's polyandrion (a tomb with its own perpetual rite inscribed).
- **"recovered by his blood."** The macabre detail — she was healed of love-sickness by her dead lover's blood —
  ties the epitaph to the Polyandrion's blood-rites (pp. 237, 248). Love, illness, blood and death intertwined.
- **the Bacchic tomb-relief** — the historiated sepulchre carries a satyr-and-goat pastoral (continued p. 255), the
  Dionysiac imagery of death-and-fertility that runs through the tombs (cf. the theatre friezes, p. 349). The
  world's polyandrion tombs can carry such carved panels.
- **forty-nine torches** — the oddly specific number (7×7) marks the rite as arcane and numerological, fitting the
  "arcane religion" the epitaph names. Colonna loves such exact ritual detail.

robust shoulders, bearing a leaky *Armillum* (wine-jar) with the orifice inverted, over the horned head scattered the
unmixed wine. Beside him was a matron, with the hair let down, dishevelled — and she, and the porter of the wine-jar,
nude — and tearful, holding a torch with the kindled part downward. Between these two appeared a little Satyr-boy, who
in the hands squeezed a serpent much involved. There followed then a rustic old woman, basket-bearing, clad over the
nude in a flying cloth, girt over the flanks; on the inelegant head, over the bald (crown), she had a *cesticillus*
(pad); and above she bore a wicker *cista* full of fruits and of fronds, and in the other hand held a vase of oblong
clayey orifice. These figures most-excellently were carved, and roughly (in high relief). On the little altar thus was
inscribed. Excited most-highly by so much comeliness of monuments, questing, to me a most-elegant Roman epitaph,
inscribed on a stone, offered such a most-pleasant dialogue, and with such ornaments:
