## Notes

**Confidence: medium** (the *Have… Vale* epitaph is secure). The little tomb-inscription **"Hail, Leria, most-loving
of all, farewell"**; the historiated Bacchic sepulchre described in full — an old satyr piping on twin *tibiae* against
a hollow tree-ivy trunk, a leaping boy, a wine-pourer with a leaky jar, a dishevelled tearful matron with an inverted
torch, a satyr-boy strangling a serpent, and a basket-bearing old woman; and the introduction of the **dialogue-
epitaph** (its text on p. 256). All secure.

- **"Have… Vale" — the shortest, purest epitaph.** *Hail… farewell*, framing "Leria, most-loving of all": the Roman
  tomb-formula of greeting and parting the passer-by, at its most distilled. A perfect, tiny inscription for the
  world's polyandrion (address and dismissal, the traveller greeted and sent on).
- **the Bacchic funeral-relief.** The carved scene — piping satyr, wine poured from an inverted jar, mourning matron
  with a reversed (extinguished) torch, serpent-wrestling boy, fruit-bearing crone — is a Dionysiac *thiasos* of death:
  wine, grief, the snake (renewal), the harvest-basket. The **inverted torch** is the antique sign of a life
  extinguished. A ready carved programme for the world's tombs, iconographically exact.
- **the dialogue-epitaph announced.** Poliphilo, "excited by so much comeliness of monuments," is now fully in the
  antiquarian's delight — the graveyard has become a gallery. The Nevia dialogue-epitaph (p. 256) is the chapter's
  finest inscription.
- **rustic detail** — the crone's *cesticillus* (the pad worn on the head to carry loads) and clay vase: Colonna's
  precise, humble realism even in a funeral relief.

with the calves, and little covered with drapes. All the rest was, by the unsated and voracious time, consumed, and by

## Notes

**Confidence: high** (the dialogue-epitaph is secure and famous). The chapter's finest inscription: the **dialogue-
epitaph of Nevia the Roman** — a spoken exchange between the passer-by and the dead woman, who "lived without love, and
loving, dies," having wasted away for love of the cruel, refusing **Proculus**, and asks only that her story be told
"through the whole city and world." Then a **mosaic of a matron self-immolating on a pyre**, and a broken tomb-vase.
All secure.

- **Nevia's dialogue-epitaph — the Polyandrion's masterpiece.** A miniature drama in stone: *Viator*, the passer-by,
  is drawn to "make words" with the dead; Nevia answers that she died loving where she was refused (Proculus "spurned
  the gift of love, refused"), and begs only remembrance — "proclaim it through the whole city and world." It is the
  opposite case to Laodia (the frigid, p. 252): Nevia *loved* and was refused, and died of it (one of the fire-damned,
  by the fresco's logic, p. 250). The two epitaphs frame the Polyandrion's two deaths. This dialogue is prime material
  to voice in the world/novel (the traveller and the tomb speaking) — the epitaph literally asks to be read aloud and
  spread.
- **"cruel Proculus."** Nevia curses her refuser by name — the Polyandrion's imprecation (p. 237, "thus perish whoever
  caused his lover's death") given a face. The tomb is a tribunal against the cold beloved.
- **the self-immolating matron.** A second Hell/death image (after the fire-ice fresco): a woman killing herself on a
  burning pyre — the fire-death of excessive love made literal. Buildable as a tribune-mosaic for the world's polyandrion.
- **the dialogue form** — Colonna casts the epitaph as call-and-response (traveller / dead), the classic *sepulchral
  dialogue* of Greek and Roman epigram, here fully dramatised. One of the passages the project's "beautiful and
  appropriate" quotation-standard is made for.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** A broken vase-inscription (illegible), then a **destroyed tribune** whose mosaic shows a
**shipwreck-romance** in fragments — a man afflicting a girl, a shipwreck, a youth swimming to shore carrying a girl,
a lion, the two rowing a boat; the story is spelled out in a **Greek epigram** on a bronze tablet, which moved
Poliphilo to tears and which he renders "as best I could" into Latin (the full text is on p. 258). All secure.

- **The mosaic and its epigram.** The fragmentary painting (man, shipwreck, rescue-swim, lion, boat) is a picture-
  narrative whose story the Greek epigram tells in full: the tragedy of **Leontia and Lollius** (p. 258). Colonna
  pairs image and text — the ruin shows the tale twice, in paint and in letters. A rich programme for a world's
  polyandrion tribune (a shipwreck-mosaic with its epitaph).
- **the Greek rendered into Latin.** Poliphilo notes he translates the Greek epigram into Latin "as best I could" —
  a nice mise-en-abyme of *this* translation-project: the reader translating the tomb, as we translate the reader.
  The Latin he gives (p. 258) is one of the book's longest inscriptions, a complete prose romance.
- **moved to tears** — the antiquarian's detachment breaks: this epitaph makes Poliphilo weep and "damn the guilty."
  The Polyandrion's tombs are not mere curiosities but move the reader — the effect the world/novel should aim for.
- The full Leontia-and-Lollius epitaph follows on p. 258.

> **HEUS VIATOR** — *(the epitaph of Leontia and Lollius; Poliphilo's Latin rendering of the Greek)*
>
> "Ho, traveller! Interpose thy hands a little (in prayer), being adjured; and, reading, much-groaning, give kisses
> to the metal, adding: 'Ah, cruel monster of Fortune! They ought to have lived.'
>
> "Leontia, a girl, the chief beloved of Lollius, a freeborn youth — when the intemperance of love pressed (her),
> afflicted with paternal torments, she fled away. Lollius follows; but, amid embracing, taken by pirates, they sell
> them to a certain trafficker. Both captive, they board a ship. When, by night, Lollius suspected Leontia to be
> carried off from him, seizing a sword, he butchers all the sailors. The ship, the sea's savagery arisen, dashed on
> the rocks near land, sinks. They climb a rock. By the impulse of hunger, seizing Leontia, I set her on my shoulders.
> 'Favour, be near, O father Neptune,' saying, 'us and our fortune I commit to thee.' Then, with a dolphin-like effort,
> with my arms I cut the little waves. But Leontia, amid the swimming, speaks: 'Am I a trouble to thee, my life?'
> 'Lighter than a water-skater, Leontia, little heart.' And, oft asking, 'Hast thou strength, my hope, my little
> soul?' 'I say (yes).' Those (words) thou rousest. Soon, embracing (my) neck, she sweetly kisses her bearer, solaces,
> exhorts, gives spirit to the diver. I exult. To the shore at last we come, safe. Unhoped-for, a roaring lion attacks.
> We embrace each other. The lion spares the dying. Terrified by the chance, a little boat cast up on the shore
> together with a rowing-oar, we fugitives board. Each in turn, singing, we row. A day and a night — and a third —
> wandering. Only the sky itself, on every side, lies open. By lethal hunger we are tormented; and, wasting with long
> fasting, we rush into embraces. Leontia saying, 'I pray thee, dost thou perish of hunger?' 'It is enough to be with
> thee, Lollius — I am fed.' But she, sighing: 'My Lollius, dost thou fail?' 'Not at all,' I say, 'in love, but in
> body.' With only vibrating and mutual tongues we fed ourselves sweetly; and, more tightly, with gaping mouths, sweet
> kisses cast, ivy-like we embraced. Both, without turning (breath), we die. By the surges — not (even) raging —
> hither, by the breeze, we are carried; and, wretched, in the estuary-air, bound in those very embraces, among the
> Plutonic shades here we are laid. And whom the piratical rapacity did not retain, nor the leonine maw devour, and
> the sea's immensity refused to take — the narrowness of this little urn here holds them both. This unhappiness I
> wished thee to know. Farewell."

---

## Notes

**Confidence: high** (the epitaph is a continuous, secure Latin narrative). The **epitaph of Leontia and Lollius** —
the longest and most novelistic inscription in the Polyandrion: a complete shipwreck-romance. The lovers flee her
cruel father, are captured and sold by pirates, escape (Lollius killing the crew), are shipwrecked, swim to shore
(Lollius bearing Leontia, praying to Neptune, their tender exchange mid-swim), are spared by a lion, drift three days
in an open boat singing, and finally **die of hunger in each other's arms**, kissing — now both held in "the narrowness
of this little urn." All secure; a masterpiece of the sepulchral-narrative genre.

- **The great romance-epitaph.** This is the Polyandrion's emotional centre — not a curse (Laodia, p. 252) nor a
  refusal (Nevia, p. 256), but *mutual, faithful love destroyed by fortune*: two who loved truly, endured pirates,
  shipwreck and a lion, and died together starving, still kissing. "They ought to have lived." It is the tragic ideal
  against which the whole Polyandrion is measured. Prime material to voice in the world/novel — a complete story in one
  inscription, and deeply moving.
- **the tenderness mid-catastrophe** — the dialogue while swimming ("Am I a trouble to thee?" / "Lighter than a
  water-skater, little heart") and while starving ("It is enough to be with thee — I am fed") is the passage's genius:
  intimacy inside disaster. Colonna's "beautiful and appropriate" writing at its height.
- **"the narrowness of this little urn here holds them both."** What pirates, lion and sea could not take, one small
  urn contains: the epitaph's closing turn, the vastness of their ordeal against the smallness of the grave. A line
  worth surfacing whole.
- **the address to the traveller** — like Nevia's (p. 256), it commands the passer-by to *pray, kiss the stone, and
  grieve*: the epitaph reaches out of the tomb to move the reader, and succeeds (Poliphilo wept, p. 257).

[p. 259]

From here departing, more avidly lustrating through the heaped ruins, I found another **tetragonal altar**, which on
its flat had a base without plinth — that is, a gula (cyma), then a little fascia, and then a torus. Beyond this it
was levelled. On which levelling sat a plinth, or little slab, that from angle to angle made a sinuous (curve), as
one of its square figure incurving little by little; the projection of which angles did not exceed the circumference
of the torus, or torus, subjacent. Upon which abacus-plinth lay a circular (base) of a vase; the circumstance of
which did not pass the outlet of the angles of the subjacent plinth. Which vase dilated itself, in the opening, as
much as was the extreme of the lowest of the underlying gula of the base. The rim, or lip, of which — keeping its
thickness — tended (in) an inflection, into itself inverting. On the altar I saw such an epigram:

> **INFER(IS) D(IIS) DEAB(US)Q(UE).**

> **INTEMPERATO AMORE**
> **PERCITUS PUTILLIAE**

## Notes

**Confidence: high** (the Vibius epitaph is secure). After the Leontia-and-Lollius romance, a plainer **suicide-
epitaph**: **Gaius Vibius**, a youth of 19, killed himself with the sword when Putillia (whom he loved) "was willingly
given over to another" — dead of jealous, "intemperate" love. Then a porphyry fragment with horse-heads and myrtle,
its Ionic-lettered epitaph broken away. All secure.

- **Vibius — love's excess, a young man's suicide.** The counterpart to Nevia (p. 256): where she was refused, Vibius
  was *supplanted* (Putillia gave herself to another), and, "not enduring it," killed himself at nineteen. One of the
  fire-damned (excess of love, p. 250). His precise age — "19 years, 2 months, 9 days; the hours no one knows" — is a
  poignant, authentically Roman touch (the exact lifespan, the unknowable hour). A ready epitaph for the world's tombs.
- **the tally of the Polyandrion's dead.** The chapter is building a taxonomy of love's deaths: Laodia (frigid suicide),
  Nevia (refused, wasted away), Leontia & Lollius (faithful, killed by fortune), Vibius (jealous suicide). Each tomb a
  different way to die of love — the full casualty-list the Polyandrion memorialises. The world/novel can draw its
  polyandrion epitaphs from this range.
- **"the hours, no one knows."** The one thing not recorded is the hour of death — a quietly devastating close: the
  life measured to the day, the moment of dying left blank. Colonna's epigraphic art at its most economical.
- **horse-heads and myrtle** — the porphyry fragment pairs horses (death's swiftness, or the sea-Neptune of the
  shipwreck?) with myrtle (Venus's tree): love and death yoked, the Polyandrion's constant emblem-pairing.

[p. 260]

> **ΤΟΜΟΚΟΥΡΕΙ / ΔΑΡΚΙΑ / ΑΡΤΕΜΕΙΣ / ΛΟΝ…ΧΟ** (TOMOKOUREI · DARKIA · ARTEMEIS · LON…CHO)
> *(A Greek inscription, fragmentary; the reading is uncertain.)*

> **MORI MALUI.**

> **SAT EST.**

> "To the shades. Lyndia, a girl; Thasius, a boy. Here I am. Without (thee) I would not live; to die I preferred. But,

With the greatest delectation and pleasure beholding these noteworthy fragments — avid, still more, searching, to find
other new (things) — thence, then, like an animal questing the ever-more-pleasing pasture, transferring myself through
the embankments of ruins, of huge chunks of columns, and some entire. Of which, wishing to know the proportion, one I
measured, extended on the ground, and from the socle to the contracture (fluting) I found, of its shaft, the tallness
seven diameters of its lowest thickness. There, near, offered itself to me a most-ancient sepulchre, without any
writing, in which, by a fracture, looking in, I saw only the funeral vestments and footwear, petrified. I conjectured
reasonably (it) of the sarcophagus-stone (of such effect) of the Troad of Asia — suspecting (it) of the cadaver of
Darius.

And nearby I saw a noble sepulchre of porphyry, exquisitely carved among sylvan little shrubs, of which offered itself
to me to read an elegant epitaph; and it had the cover in the form of an egregious little temple, scaled scale-wise —
one part of the said, over the ark, remaining, and the other lay cast down on the floor, and inscribed with such an
outstanding title.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium** (the Latin epitaph is secure; the Greek is fragmentary). More tombs: a broken **Greek
inscription**; the tiny paired epitaph of **Lyndia and Thasius** ("without thee I would not live; to die I preferred");
a huge fallen column measured (shaft = 7 diameters); a **body-consuming sarcophagus** (Troad stone) holding petrified
funeral clothes; and a porphyry sepulchre with a temple-shaped lid (its epitaph on p. 261). All secure.

- **Lyndia and Thasius — love-suicide, in miniature.** The shortest romance-epitaph: a girl and a boy, and one voice
  (the survivor, now dead too) saying "without thee I would not live; I chose to die." A love-death of *fidelity* (like
  Leontia & Lollius, p. 258) compressed to five lines. Perfect for the world's polyandrion — brief, buildable, moving.
- **the Troad sarcophagus** — the "flesh-eating stone" (*lapis sarcophagus* of Assos in the Troad, which Pliny says
  consumed bodies in forty days) holding only petrified clothes: Colonna's antiquarian precision, and a grim marvel
  (the stone that ate the corpse but left the shoes). The "cadaver of Darius" comparison places it in imperial legend.
- **the column measured** — Poliphilo the architect pauses even among the tombs to measure a fallen shaft (7:1
  proportion): the antiquarian's habit persists. The ruin is read as architecture and as memorial at once.
- **the temple-lidded sepulchre** — a tomb roofed like a little scaled temple (a *naiskos*): a buildable tomb-type for
  the world's polyandrion, its epitaph (Cornelia Annia) on p. 261.

> **EXORNENT; DERELIQ(UO) IBI EPULENTUR. DO(MUS) D(IVAE) P(ARENTIS)**
> **M(ONUMENTUM). D(EDIT) A(NNIA). EX (SESTERTIIS) LLSX ATQ(UE) T(ESTAMENTO) FACIUNDUM DELEGA(VIT).**
> **VALE, VITA.**
>
> "To the shades. Publia Cornelia Annia — that I might not, in desolate bereavement, survive, wretched, alive — of my own
> will give myself, condemned (to death), into this coffin with my dead husband, loved with incomparable love; with whom
> I lived twenty years without any controversy (quarrel). (I charge) our children and freedmen that yearly, over our
> coffin, they sacrifice to Pluto and to his wife Proserpina and to all the shades, and adorn it with roses; with the
> remainder let them feast there. Annia gave this monument of the divine parent (?); from (a sum of) sesterces she
> ordered it, and by testament, to be made. Farewell, life."

Below again (from here departing), under a corymb-bearing and wandering ivy, pendent from a decayed course of wall, very
dense of frond, a noteworthy *zygastrion* (chest) sat, of a stone like ivory, until then in the greater part still terse
and bright. Within which, curiously looking, through a fissure, or chink, of the flat cover, I saw **two entire cadavers
reserved** (preserved). For which thing rightly I judged this sepulchre (to be) of *chemites* stone. On the front of
which I saw these **Egyptian hieroglyphs** carved; and within, again, many glass ampullae, and many earthenware
(vessels), and some little statues in the archaic Egyptian manner, and an antiquarian lamp of metal artfully made — and
in the soffit of the covering, pendent, that one little chain, ensnared, retaining (it), suspended, burned; and, near the
head of the buried, were two little crowns, which I judged golden, but by time and by the lamp-smoke infuscated. Such was
the interpretation:

---

## Notes

**Confidence: high** (both the Latin epitaph and the hieroglyph-interpretation are secure; some abbreviations expanded). A
widow's self-entombment: **Cornelia Annia**, refusing to outlive her husband of twenty happy years, gives herself into his
coffin and endows a **perpetual rose-and-sacrifice rite**; then a translucent stone chest holding **two preserved bodies**,
gold crowns, a burning lamp and grave-goods, its front carved with **Egyptian hieroglyphs** (decoded on p. 262). All secure.

- **Cornelia Annia — love unto death, chosen.** Unlike the tragedies of fortune, this is a *willed* union in death: a widow
  who "would not survive, wretched," and joins her husband in the grave, endowing an annual rite (Pluto, Proserpina, roses,
  a feast). Her "twenty years without a quarrel" and closing "Farewell, life" make it the Polyandrion's tenderest *conjugal*
  epitaph — faithful love that outlasts death by choice. A model for the world's polyandrion (an endowed double-tomb).
- **the preserved lovers in the ivory chest.** The translucent *chemites* stone (Pliny: a marble that preserved bodies, in
  which Darius was said to lie) lets Poliphilo see **two whole bodies** with gold crowns and a lamp still burning — an intact
  Egyptian-style double burial. A haunting, buildable centrepiece for the world's crypt: a glowing sarcophagus with the
  lovers visible within, a lamp burning over them.
- **the endowed anniversary, again** — like the gladiator-epitaph (p. 254) and the Polyandrion's own festival (p. 237),
  Cornelia founds a perpetual rite. The tombs repeatedly buy remembrance: love's refusal to be forgotten is the chapter's
  undertone.
- The hieroglyph on the chest (a meditation on death joining lovers) is read on p. 262.

[p. 262]

> **DIIS MANIBUS.**
> **MORS, VITAE CONTRARIA ET VELOCISSIMA, CUNCTA CALCAT, SUPPEDITAT, RAPIT, CONSUMIT, DISSOLVIT. MELLIFLUE DUOS,**
> **MUTUO SE STRICTIM ET ARDENTER AMANTES, HIC EXTINCTOS, CONIUNXIT.**
>
> "To the shades. Death — contrary to life, and most swift — treads on all things, tramples, seizes, consumes, dissolves.
> Mellifluously (sweetly) it has here joined two, who mutually, tightly and ardently loved each other, (now) extinguished."

Gladdened, with incredible solace, by so much variety of antiquarian and magnificent works, still, without doubt, my soul
increased (in wishing), insatiably, more lustrating, to investigate other novelties. Whence, even if before, tearful, the
Greek epitaph of the two miserable lovers dead of starvation (Leontia and Lollius) had excited me — much more, again, there
presented itself to me a much-admired but pitiable monument, of two other most-unhappy lovers, standing in a great stone,
with such lineament expressed: a square, by the diagonal raised (set lozenge-wise), contained in itself two little
pilasters, with a little cornice and a half-hemicycle above; between which, from the angles of the little arch, hung a
tablet, on which, reading, I saw such a pitiable epigram.

---

## Notes

**Confidence: high** (the hieroglyph-epitaph is secure). The **Egyptian hieroglyph** on the ivory chest decoded — a
meditation on Death (*"contrary to life and most swift, it treads on all… (yet) sweetly has here joined two who loved each
other ardently, now extinguished"*); then Poliphilo turns to yet another tomb, of "two other most-unhappy lovers" (its
epitaph on p. 263). All secure.

- **"Death… sweetly joined two lovers."** The chest's hieroglyph turns death's terror into a consolation: the same power
  that "treads on all, consumes, dissolves" also *unites* the two lovers forever in one grave. It is the Polyandrion's
  gentlest doctrine — death as the joiner of the faithful (cf. Cornelia Annia, p. 261; Leontia & Lollius's shared urn,
  p. 258). A resonant inscription for the world's crypt of the two preserved bodies.
- **the emotional accumulation.** Poliphilo notes the tombs are affecting him in sequence — the Leontia epitaph made him
  weep, and now "much more" this one. The chapter is a rising curve of pathos, building toward the Rape-of-Proserpina
  relief that finally frightens him back to Polia (pp. 280+). The world/novel can pace its polyandrion as this same
  escalation.
- **the lozenge-set tomb** — a square set diagonally with pilasters and an arched tablet: another buildable tomb-form (cf.
  the temple-lidded sepulchre, p. 260). Colonna varies the monument-types tomb by tomb, a catalogue of funerary
  architecture.
- **death "mellifluously" (melliflue)** — the startling adverb: death acting *sweetly*. Colonna's oxymoron holds the
  Polyandrion's whole paradox — the tomb of love's victims is also, in its own dark way, love's fulfilment (the lovers
  united at last).

[p. 263]

> **O LECTOR INFOELIX** — *(the epitaph of Lopidia and Chrysanthes)*
>
> "O unhappy reader, be present at this monument while it calls thee — and then, afterward, it asks that thou read
> into what human pleasure falls. Here is the ash of two lovers, who, long since, mutually burning insolently with
> itching love, by the wicked, unbridled impulse of pleasure, met in a deserted place among ruined rocks, where by
> chance also stood the broken walls of sacred buildings and rough ruins. There we both were ardently urged to pay
> Venus the desired gifts. Lying back, I, Lopidia, saw a snake, slipped down from on high, threatening. 'Ho! cease
> from what thou hast begun,' I say; 'my Chrysanthes, rise, flee — lo, a serpent about to devour us!' — as I watch it
> hurling itself from the wall. Soon he, terrified, looking up: 'O my Lopidia,' he says, 'I beg thee, go thy way, flee
> thou the road, let me attack the dying dragon.' Scarcely had I risen — alas, sad, wretched me! — when I saw my
> Chrysanthes, my life, entangled to destruction and tightly circled in the snake's coil, now anxiously breathing.
> And suddenly it wounds the throat of my Chrysanthes with biting teeth; then I behold my Chrysanthes being
> suffocated. 'Ah, ah, I perish, unhappy! I feel my Chrysanthes dying!' At once, furious, I rush at the serpent, and,
> a club seized, I hasten to strike; but the serpent twists its wrangling neck, nor by force could I drive off the
> entwined one. Striking at last, incautiously missing, I killed my Chrysanthes, most unhappy. Alas, I am undone!
> What have I done? What shall I do? Shall the serpent and I, so wretched, survive? By no means! But with Herculean
> daring — nay, with a ghostly, snarling fury — with that same club, the blow turned, upon the fallen corpse I strike
> the coiled beast, and kill it. What then, a girl, was I to do — lost and dead? My Chrysanthes and the beast,
> witnesses of my crime, thrown over my shoulders, I carry into the city, watering them again and again with sighs,
> heart-grief and tears. I climb a certain platform in the public forum, and, sighing, I make the matter known. In a
> crowd the citizens run together to the cruel and hateful spectacle; they pity the entangled chance, accuse Fortune,
> damn Venus. I attest my crime, I invoke the infernal powers: 'Therefore,' saying, 'receive me to pay the penalty
> together with my Chrysanthes; now let me transfer all the guilt upon myself.' Then, desperate, in the public sight
> of all, a sword seized, I transfix my breast, and gave my most-wretched self to be buried here, in an eternal tomb,
> with his corpse. Farewell."

---

## Notes

**Confidence: high** (the epitaph is a continuous, secure Latin narrative). The harrowing epitaph of **Lopidia and
Chrysanthes**: two lovers meeting secretly among the ruins to "pay Venus the desired gifts" are surprised by a
serpent; it strangles Chrysanthes, and Lopidia, striking at it with a club, **accidentally kills her own lover**;
she then kills the beast, carries both bodies to the forum, publicly confesses, and stabs herself to be buried with
him. All secure; a small, complete tragedy.

- **The accidental killing — the darkest of the epitaphs.** Where the others die of refusal, jealousy, or fortune,
  Lopidia dies of *guilt*: she killed the man she loved by her own hand, trying to save him. Her public confession
  ("I attest my crime… receive me to pay the penalty with my Chrysanthes"), her transfer of all guilt onto herself,
  and her suicide "in the public sight of all" make it the Polyandrion's most agonised story. A powerful, voiceable
  monologue for the world/novel.
- **the moral frame.** The epitaph opens by asking the reader to "read into what human pleasure falls" — a *memento*
  that illicit pleasure (they met to consummate love secretly in the ruins) brought the catastrophe. The citizens
  "damn Venus": the tomb warns against love's unbridled impulse (cf. the door-mottoes' balance, and the fire-ice
  Hell, p. 250). The Polyandrion moralises even its most sympathetic dead.
- **the serpent among the ruins** — the snake striking from the broken wall while the lovers embrace is a vivid,
  emblematic image (Eden's serpent in a Venus-garden): buildable as a tomb-relief or a novel-scene.
- **direct first-person voice** — like Nevia (p. 256) and Leontia (p. 258), Lopidia speaks in her own voice from the
  grave; the epitaphs are dramatic monologues, not just records. The world/novel can stage them as spoken.

[p. 264]

Having read the compassionate case of the unfortunate lovers of this most-outstanding epigram — from here, again
supremely content, departing, not many paces making — there occurred to me a noble tablet of tetragonal marble, with
somewhat of fastigium (pediment), with two little columns, one to a side; of design immune and unencumbered. And, to
the compass of all the quadrangle, was, as if uprooted (in relief), a foliate crown, or jewel, diligently conducted;
in which I read such an inscription. Which stone lay cast down on the earth, but with the workmanship supine (face up).
Which elegant varieties not a little pleasure, in my soul, joyously accumulated.

More ardently invaded (I) found myself to the investigation of the most-worthy antiquarian works. There presented
itself to me a disrupted **tribune**, with the right wall reserved, in which I saw, with excessive voluptuousness, a
**porphyry sepulchre**, of most-worthy device, and of most-excellent workmanship, and of marvellous cost, and of
incredible artifice of sculpture. Which stood — at the extreme sides raised by two quadrangular little columns (a
third of them worked out, with regulated flutings, upon a footing with the base collocated) — and, perpendicularly
subjacent, was a little altar, with three elegant mourning Nymphs, toward the middle turned, weeping together. By the
like, on the other side, semi-detached from the solid, not without the corollary and requisite lineaments. Above both
the capitals the epistyle, ornate, extended itself. Then, with volutes of most-comely fronds and flowers —

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** After the Lopidia epitaph, a marble tablet with a foliate-crown relief, then the introduction
of a magnificent **porphyry sepulchre** in a surviving tribune — flanked by fluted columns and little altars carved
with **three mourning nymphs** weeping toward the centre, its entablature scrolled with foliage. All secure; this is
the tomb of Artemisia (identified on p. 265).

- **The grandest tomb yet.** Colonna signals this sepulchre as the chapter's architectural climax ("most-worthy
  device… incredible artifice"): a fully-articulated porphyry monument with flanking columns, mourning-nymph altars,
  and a figured entablature. It proves to be the tomb of **Artemisia** and **Mausolus** (p. 265) — the archetypal
  monument of conjugal love, the original "Mausoleum." A prime buildable centerpiece for the world's polyandrion.
- **the mourning nymphs** — three weeping figures on each flanking altar, "turned toward the middle": the tomb stages
  its own grief, sculpture mourning the dead. A ready motif for the world's polyandrion tombs (as on the Venus-temple
  well, p. 206).
- **Poliphilo's antiquarian delight deepens** — "more ardently invaded" by the desire to investigate: the graveyard-
  therapy (p. 242) has fully turned his erotic ardour into scholarly ardour. The tombs now *are* his pleasure.
- The tomb's inscriptions and figures (Artemisia drinking Mausolus's ashes) are read on p. 265.

[p. 265]

— invested, the Frieze resided above, located, covered with a becoming little cornice. Between the one and the other
quadrangular (column), somewhat, a *solium*, or niche, with regulated excavation of fluting, stood forth, level with
the plane, between those quadrangulars. The projection of which made, on the one and the other side of its opening, a
little pilaster, with capitals and base; upon which rose an inflected architrave — so detached from the levelled, or
plane, that there remained, in the interior part (that is, at the lips of the solium), a little tongue (ledge). Level
with the capitals, a wavy binding girt the solium, and above (it) the half-cupola.

Which little pilasters egregiously were ornated of sculpture. Under the little pilasters lay a projecting tallish
little altar, with the ornaments of the overstanding little pilasters. Between the one and the other projection of the
said little altars, or sub-column, I saw a **Greek inscription**, by which I knew this to be the monument of the pious
**Queen of Caria** (Artemisia). Thus it said:

> **ΑΡΤΕΜΙΣΙΔΟΣ ΒΑΣΙΛΙΔΟΣ ΣΠΟΔΩΝ** (ARTEMISIDOS BASILIDOS SPODON) — "The ashes of Queen Artemisia."

With socles, and little crowns, and cymas, and gulets, most-excellently the whole girt and companionable.

On the lower plane of the niche was a plinth of the narrated material, in aspect most-beautifully adorned with
sculpture, upon the flat of which stood fixed four equal-placed lion's claws of gilt metal; which pressed (bore) an
antiquarian little ark, with lineaments of notable expression. Upon the cover was a bench (throne), to the compass of
the covering, feigned covered with silken cloth, with an encompassing fringe.

Sat upon (it) a **Matron-Queen**, with regal cultivation, and majestic vestment, on the breast fibulated over a fitted
garment; which, from the collar down through the breast, and transversely in the girding, went round a little fascia,
and, over the belly, dilated in the form of a *tetraphyllon* (four-leaf), that is, in a figure of four hemicycles; in
which, of Greek majuscules, was thus annotated:

> **ΜΑΥΣΩΛΕΙΟΝ ΑΤΙΜΗΤΟΝ** (MAUSOLEION ATIMETON) — "The priceless Mausoleum."

With the right (hand) she held a **chalice to the mouth, drinking**; and in the other she held a little rod, or
sceptre; with the poured (loose) hair, over the head wreathed with a somewhat-fastigiate crown, tapering to another
crownlet at the nape; from which, becomingly and combed, descended the hair.

Upon the keystone of the arched architrave stood forth an oval figure, flattened, of a height up to under the
projection of the Sima of the cornice; in which I beheld impressed a face of regal majesty, crowned, with prolix beard
and twisted hair. I judged it to be the true simulacrum of the husband (**Mausolus**). Retained, here and there, by two
nude winged little spirits, seated upon the extreme circling of the arched architrave; which, with the other hands
free, the little arm extended, a bronze little cord —

## Notes

**Confidence: high** (the two Greek inscriptions are secure and famous). The **tomb of Artemisia and Mausolus** — the
original Mausoleum: a porphyry niche-monument inscribed *"The ashes of Queen Artemisia"* and *"The priceless
Mausoleum,"* with a seated queen-figure **drinking from a chalice** (Artemisia drinking her husband's ashes), a
lion-clawed ark, and Mausolus's bearded portrait held aloft by winged spirits. All secure; the archetype of the love-
monument.

- **Artemisia drinking the ashes — the emblem of conjugal love.** The queen who, out of grief, *drank the ashes of her
  husband Mausolus* and built him the Mausoleum (one of the Seven Wonders): Colonna sets her tomb at the Polyandrion's
  centre as the supreme image of love faithful beyond death (cf. Cornelia Annia, p. 261). The figure with the chalice
  at her lips is the drinking of the ashes made visible. A powerful, buildable centerpiece for the world's polyandrion.
- **"The priceless Mausoleum."** *Mausoleion atimeton* — the tomb names itself the Mausoleum, the monument so great it
  gave its builder's name to all great tombs. The Polyandrion, a ruin of humble love-graves, holds at its heart the
  grandest tomb of all — love's memorial raised to a Wonder of the World.
- **the drinking queen, the borne portrait** — Artemisia with chalice and sceptre; Mausolus's crowned, bearded face
  held by two winged genii: a complete iconographic group. The world's polyandrion could render this as its principal
  tomb-tableau (the widow drinking, the husband's imago aloft).
- **lion-claw feet, tetraphyllon breastplate** — the precise ornament (gilt lion's-paw ark-feet, the four-lobed breast-
  fascia bearing the inscription): Colonna's exact sculptural detail, buildable to the letter.

[p. 266]

— held pendent, incurved (the bronze cord the winged spirits held). Through which had passed some balusters. And
from the retaining hand, perpendicularly, they held suspended a copper thread, festooned and beaded, all excellently
gilt.

Upon the flat of the crown, somewhat inclined, ascended a plinth, with manifold ornaments. In its flat, in the
middle front, resided a rounding of metal, which, enclosed, had a **blackest stone, also mirror-like**, in which I
saw such writing, of Greek majuscules:

> **ΕΡΩΤΟΣ ΚΑΤΟΠΤΡΟΝ** (EROTOS KATOPTRON) — "The mirror of Love."

The encompassing lip, of metal, a palm in evened breadth, was comelily bossed. On its upper circle stood straight a
perfect **nude image, of gilt metal**, with the right holding a little spear, and in the other an antiquarian
*clypeus* (shield) of egregious lineament carved; on the one and the other side of this rounding — one here and the
other there, with the back propped, sitting upon the flat — two winged boys, toward the projections, held a kindled
torch.

On the slope of the aforenarrated plinth, likewise sitting back-to-back, were two nude and winged infants, upon the
flat of the crown; with the hands in view they retained an apple, and with the inner arms seized a most-ancient
bronze **candelabrum**, most-lucent, gilt, in the form of a vase, by a dolphin handle — which handles were two up-
curved, biting dolphins at a knot, and, with the tail, derived, hooked, over the body of the vase, thinning to the
shell-shaped gap, with two other knots toward the orifice; which, somewhat in circular dilatation, upon the lip, in
order, had fixed four sharp pins, and in the middle one, that exceeded the others, with the foot-stalk between the
shins of the boys.

All this sculpture, founded, sat upon a square Ophite (base) rising from the pavement, nude of lineament, except that
in the middle, carved, I saw a **maritime, or naval, trophy** (I thought, in monument of the victory attained, the
fleet of the Rhodians vanquished): a rostrum, or part of the beaked prow, of a most-ancient ship; in the middle of
which stood forth a trunk, in the branches of which was invested a military cuirass, and, by the brachial outlet, the
branches extended, truncated of tips; to one of the said, hung by the ring, was a shield; on the other, a naval
instrument; under the cuirass, transversely, on the trunk, hung an anchor and a rudder; upon the top of the trunk,
where the collar came out, a crested helmet was most-beautifully set. All which things it is not to be believed were,
without symmetry and greatest artifice, exquisitely, with all the requisite lineaments, expressed, and most-
excellently polished — worthy of noteworthiness and eternal memory. The commensuration of which, whoever knows the
proportion of the *sesquialter* (3:2) will easily conduct it perfect. I suspected that by one (workshop) the sculptors
of the Mausoleum and this (were) perfected.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium** (the *Eros Katoptron* inscription is secure). The completion of the Artemisia tomb: a black
**"Mirror of Love"** (a mirror-stone inscribed *EROTOS KATOPTRON*), a gilt nude with spear and shield, torch-bearing
winged boys, a **dolphin-handled candelabrum**, and a **naval trophy** commemorating a victory over the Rhodian fleet
— all in the same hand as the Mausoleum's sculptors. All secure.

- **"The Mirror of Love."** A black mirror-stone set in the tomb, inscribed *Eros Katoptron* — the mirror in which
  love sees itself (as the obsidian floor of Cythera reflected the fountain, p. 352; the Adytum floor mirrored the
  worshippers, p. 220). Set on Artemisia's tomb, it makes her drinking-of-the-ashes (p. 265) a mirror held up to
  faithful love. A resonant, buildable object for the world's polyandrion.
- **the naval trophy and the Rhodians.** Artemisia (I of Caria, or here conflated) is credited with a sea-victory
  over Rhodes; the tomb carries a *tropaion* of captured ship's-arms (rostrum, cuirass, shield, anchor, rudder,
  helmet on a trunk) — the same trophy-of-arms form as Cupid's triumph (p. 326), here martial. The queen is warrior
  as well as widow.
- **the dolphin candelabrum** — biting dolphins forming the handle of a gilt-bronze lamp-vase: Colonna's marine
  ornament (dolphins recur — the crystal lamp, p. 208; the Aldine device). Buildable to the knot.
- **"the same sculptors as the Mausoleum."** Colonna ties this tomb to the historical Mausoleum's famous sculptors
  (Scopas, Bryaxis, et al.) — placing the Polyandrion's grandest tomb in real art-history. The proportion (3:2) is
  handed over for building.

> **ASPICE, VIATOR** — *(the epitaph of Sertullius and Rancilia)*
>
> "Behold, traveller, (the ashes) of Quintus Sertullius and of my sweet betrothed, the maiden daughter of Gaius
> Rancilia, together; and then afterward read what licentious Fate does. In our very flowering age, when the sharper
> force of love rushed upon us, mutually captured — at length, with father-in-law and mother-in-law consenting — in
> solemn wedding we are joined. But, O unhappy fate! On the first night, when, by the law of importunate pleasure to
> be discharged, we were compelled to extinguish the torch and render our vows to the shades of Venus — alas, in the
> very act, the marital house, collapsing, oppressed us both, most joyful, embraced, with the final sweetness. O
> deadly Sister (Fate)! Nor do I know what I had done (to deserve it). Consider: our longer hour was not then in the
> fates. Dear parents, bewail not our wretched and ghost-marked funerals with mourning nor tears, lest you make them
> more unhappy. But you — live your years longer than ours, best reader, and live your own. (Farewell.)"

---

## Notes

**Confidence: high** (the epitaph is secure). The wedding-night tragedy of **Sertullius and Rancilia**: a couple, wed
with their parents' blessing, are **crushed together in their embrace on their first night** when the marital house
collapses in the very act of love — "most joyful, embraced, with the final sweetness." (The next monument begins on
p. 270.) All secure.

- **Death in the act of love — the cruelest fortune.** Sertullius and Rancilia die not of love's excess or refusal but
  of sheer accident, at the instant of consummation: the house falls "in the very act." It is the Polyandrion's most
  arbitrary tragedy — pure "licentious Fate," love and death made simultaneous. The epitaph's turn from horror to
  gentle blessing ("live your years longer than ours, best reader, and live your own") is deeply moving. Voiceable
  material for the world/novel.
- **"extinguish the torch."** The wedding-night consummation is called "extinguishing the torch" — the same phrase as
  the temple-rite (Polia extinguishing Diana's torch, p. 216, 236): the quenched marriage-torch here becomes literal
  death. Colonna's imagery binds the two temples (Venus's fulfilment, the Polyandrion's ruin) once more.
- **the blessing of the reader** — the epitaph ends not with a curse (Nevia, p. 256) but with a *benediction*: "live
  your own years." The gentlest of the tombs' addresses to the passer-by; the dead wish the living long life. A tender
  counterweight to the chapter's darkness.
- **the coffered turtledove-niche** — a new tomb with a perspectival coffered vault and drinking doves (Venus's birds):
  Colonna's continued variety of buildable tomb-forms.

[p. 270]

Not far distant from this — somewhat moved to little sighs by the preceding unhappy case read — I found another
noteworthy and most-worthy monument, with two fluted little columns, one to a side, semicircle-worked out of the solid
rock, of whitest marble, with little bases and capitals, little architrave, little frieze, little cornices, and little
fastigium; in the three-sided (pediment) of which two whitening turtledoves drank together in a little vase. In the
content between the fluted (columns), of low relief carved, was an arched soffit, evenly distributed into little
coffered squares, where, in each, a cinquefoil occupied, by the optic norm (in perspective), the linings diminishing
with the content (depth). Under which an artful ark somewhat stood forth, fixed with two little doors — in one of
which entered —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** A new **whitest-marble tomb**: fluted flanking columns, a pediment with two **turtledoves
drinking from a vase**, and a coffered vault rendered in optical perspective (the cinquefoil-coffers "diminishing with
the depth"), over an ark with two little doors. All secure; the epitaph itself follows on p. 271.

- **Perspective in the coffering.** Colonna notes the vault's coffers are carved "by the optic norm" — in linear
  perspective, the lines shrinking with depth: a knowing reference to the new science of perspective (Alberti, della
  Francesca), applied to a carved ceiling. The Polyandrion's art is technically up-to-date. A buildable illusionistic
  vault for a world tomb.
- **the drinking turtledoves** — Venus's birds "drinking together" from a vase in the pediment: the emblem of paired,
  faithful love (cf. the doves of pp. 219, 233), fit for a couple's tomb. The epitaph (p. 271) proves it a marriage-
  monument, though a tragic one (a jealous wife's suicide).
- **the ark with two little doors** — a double-tomb (two chambers), its doors the threshold between life and death
  Poliphilo keeps reading. The chapter's tombs increasingly pair the dead; the Polyandrion is a place of couples.

[p. 271]

> **· D · DITI ET PROSER(PINAE) · S ·**
> **· V · F ·**
> **TREBIAE Q(UINTAE),**
> **L(UCII) S(EX?) TREBII FILIAE.**
>
> "Sacred to Dis and Proserpina. (This) monument of love and of piety Aulus Fibustius, her husband, (raised) — with
> whom, with the utmost longing, delightfully she lived one month, three days. She, my wife, most-loving to me, most-
> unhappy, left me tears and eternal mourning. Perturbed by an extreme jealousy — when she suspected that I had lain
> with another woman — her sweetest love converted into fury, with the iron (sword), through the middle of the breast
> driven, she killed herself. Alas, wife — why this? My dear consort, thou oughtest to have removed from thy lover not
> only the deed, but even the suspicion. Farewell freely. But I, uncertain, unhappy and trembling, my life loosed
> (undone), rest.
>
> — THE INEVITABLE STATE OF NATURE THE STEPMOTHER.
> — THE BENIGN EDICT OF NATURE THE MOTHER."

---

## Notes

**Confidence: high** (the epitaph is secure; a few abbreviations conjecturally expanded). A **jealousy-suicide**:
**Trebia Quinta**, wife of Aulus Fibustius for barely a month, killed herself with a sword through the breast on the
mere *suspicion* that her husband had lain with another — "her sweetest love converted into fury." The husband speaks,
grieving and reproaching her; the tomb closes with the paired mottoes on **Nature the stepmother** (death) and
**Nature the mother** (the benign law). All secure.

- **Trebia — love turned to fatal jealousy.** A new variety of love-death: not refusal, excess, fidelity, or accident,
  but *jealousy on a false suspicion*. The husband's reproach — "thou oughtest to have removed from thy lover not only
  the deed but even the suspicion" — is a small marital tragedy, and a warning against jealousy's rashness. His closing
  "I, uncertain, unhappy and trembling… rest" is bleak and human. Voiceable material.
- **the two Natures.** The tomb's twin mottoes state the book's cosmology: **Nature the stepmother** (*noverca*)
  imposes death's "inevitable state"; **Nature the mother** (*mater*) gives the "benign edict" (life, generation). It
  is the Polyandrion's philosophical frame — the same double Nature that Venus Physizoa ("life-giving Nature")
  embodies, here shown with its death-face. A resonant inscribed pair for the world's polyandrion (life and death as
  Nature's two faces).
- **the marriage of one month, three days** — the exact, pitifully short span (like Vibius's "19 years, 2 months, 9
  days," p. 259): Colonna's authentic epigraphic precision, the brevity of the happiness measured against the
  "eternal mourning."
- **the epitaphs' cumulative taxonomy** — refusal (Nevia), fidelity destroyed (Leontia, Sertullius), excess (Vibius),
  guilt (Lopidia), and now jealousy (Trebia): the Polyandrion has catalogued nearly every way love kills. The rising
  pathos builds toward the Rape-of-Proserpina relief that ends Poliphilo's visit (pp. 280+).

[p. 272]

From here, with most-joyful solace, departing — with curious desire most-eager to behold new things — hastening to
a semi-integral tribune, I beheld some exquisite relics of mosaic painting, wormwork-made. In this place I found no
sepulchre; but in the glasswork painting, still, **Proserpina, with Cyane and with the Sirens, gathering flowers near
the burning mountain of Etna**, was perfectly discerned. Where **Pluto, unsealing the fire-rooted crater of the
flame-breathing mountain, voluptuously ravished her to his love**; and Cyane, for not being able to succour her,
piteously weeping. There I found huge stones of the putrescent wall gaping, and grassy through the cracks with aster
and pellitory; which was also entangled and destroyed, as by a wedge fixed of a big root of an aged wild-fig, whose
roots, springing everywhere, creeping, had destroyed the tessellations, and, the coition of the joints deserted,
rendered great looseness of the walls.

Whence I only beheld part of a little river, (that) seemed a vestige of human form transmuted into it (Cyane), of
incredible art feigned, and marvellously expressed — such the like as once, in the shrine of Minerva on the Capitol,
in the tablet was seen the rape of the said (Proserpina), painted by Nicomachus. Where, with the mind applied to such
pleasant regard being — lo, at my back I hear the fall of some tessellations; and, finding myself solitary, in a
deserted and silent place, suddenly somewhat frightened, and, turning back, looking, I saw a gecko, or wall-lizard,
that had been the cause of such ruin.

Therefore no little displeasure invaded me, for not being able to see the whole work integrally, it being in the
greater part demolished. Considering, then, the violent manner in which Proserpina was suddenly seized, a sudden and
sad thought, in the loving heart, fiercely struck me, saying: "Alas, wretched, impudent and unhappy me! O importunate
investigation, and unbridled curiosity of past things, and of broken stones inquiring — to what am I devolved? If, by
my ill misfortune, my most-beautiful Polia were seized from me, and, by neglect of so great a present thing — above
all the treasures of the world most-pleasing — were driven off from me!" And, in a moment, a more bitter blow
transfixed the sad heart, presenting already in the confused mind the piteous and lamentable case: that the fugitive
of the burning fatherland (Aeneas) incautiously lost his beloved Creusa. And much more excessively it disturbed me,
invading, such a terror, remembering that, on the sandy and solitary shores, drawn away from my presence, my most-
loving Polia sat alone.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The chapter's turning-point: a mosaic of the **Rape of Proserpina** (Pluto seizing her by
Etna, Cyane weeping, dissolving into her river) — surpassing Nicomachus's famous painting — is half-destroyed by a
wild-fig root, and, as Poliphilo studies it, **a lizard dislodges some tesserae behind him**, startling him. The
image of Proserpina's abduction seizes his mind: he panics that his Polia, left alone on the shore, may likewise have
been snatched (like Aeneas's lost Creusa). All secure.

- **The Rape of Proserpina — the fear that ends the visit.** The Polyandrion's last and most consequential image: the
  abduction of Proserpina by Pluto (to whom the whole tomb is dedicated, p. 236) makes Poliphilo suddenly terrified
  that Polia, out of his sight, has been carried off. The chapter's antiquarian idyll snaps into dread. This is the
  narrative hinge (the argument, p. 241, foretold it): the epitaphs' cumulative pathos culminates in personal panic.
- **the lizard.** A small, precise touch: a gecko knocking tesserae loose in the silent ruin is what startles him into
  the fear — Colonna grounds the supernatural dread in a tiny natural cause (cf. the owls, p. 247). The world/novel
  can use it as the jump-scare beat that turns the polyandrion visit.
- **Aeneas and Creusa** — the exemplum: the man who, fleeing burning Troy, lost his wife behind him. Poliphilo casts
  himself as Aeneas, Polia as Creusa — his antiquarian "curiosity of past things" (leaving her to read tombs) now
  reads as the negligence that loses the beloved. His self-reproach turns the whole graveyard-therapy against itself.
- **Cyane dissolving into her river** — the water-nymph who tried to stop the abduction and melted into her spring:
  the metamorphosis-motif (cf. Cythera's aviary, p. 310) even in the Hell-mosaic. His flight back to Polia is on p. 273.

[p. 273]

And that thus, to her, the trident-bearing Neptune might not violently do (as to Medusa)! Alas, at this point I
certainly experienced what is the affliction of spirit, and the quality of true lovers — extremely more trembling,
terrified, and stupefied, and finding myself in greater anguish, and into more miserable trepidation deduced, than
when I saw myself almost a putrescible little morsel among the gaping and horrend jaws of the venefic dragon, at the
next-door demise. With so much terror that I could judge (myself), through the priest and the removed simulacrum of
the Pellenean temple, to have every serenity struck from the mind, re-cruding every hour, the more, the formidable
grief in the fluctuating heart.

For which thing, impelled by the coquent cares and urgent anguishes, without any delay, most-swiftly brazen-footed —
leaving so noble an undertaking, and illustrious inquisition, and laudable lustration, and virtuous solace — suddenly,
then, through those windings and infested bushes, and rough shrubs, and through the place made narrow of stones and of
thorns, and through those prolapses of marbles, and formless heap of rudiments and fragments, uneven, scrupulous, and
among caustic nettles and pathless ruins, I hasten, with hostile course, by rough ways and innumerable stumbling-
blocks, with prompt velocity — not esteeming the laceration of my ragged toga, here and there held by thorny fronds,
and all full of burs and down, and thistle-tufts, and goat's-beard, and sowthistle, in some part entangled by the
rapacious seeds of hound's-tongue — firmly holding to have arrived at the newest troubles, and formidable perils, and
ultimate and deadly privation of all my hoped good, to my sweetest and most-precious Polia: not wholly alive, but half-
dead, like an asthmatic drawing the breath (not by other way than if the grave odour of the Babylonian gulf I had
drawn), with the eyes wet with tearful dew, near her, having prostrated myself, spasming, with incredible heart-grief
and swooning, scarce I arrived.

And she, with the soft soul moved, with serene forehead, and propitiated and soothing face — thus lurid and afflicted,
with assiduous pulse in my dolorous breast, with bloodless pallor trembling — miserating, grieving, with amorous pity,
marvelled at it; raising me, pretty, into her sweet embraces; and, with a genuine sweetness, and with a most-tenuous
saffron veil, my dirty face, dewy in most-rich sweat, with amorous obsequy lightly rubbed, dried me — both most-
officious and, with blandishment, sponging me. Whence, the cause and accident of so much bitter and troublous anguish
eagerly inquiring, and most-benignly blandishing me —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Poliphilo's **panic-flight back to Polia**: fearing Neptune might ravish her (as he did
Medusa), more terrified than when the dragon nearly ate him (ch. VII), he crashes back through the thorny ruins (his
toga shredded, burr-covered) and collapses **half-dead at Polia's feet**; she, moved, gently raises him, wipes his
sweat-soaked face with a saffron veil, and asks what has happened. All secure; the reunion.

- **The lover's terror as the "quality of true lovers."** Colonna frames Poliphilo's panic as proof of true love —
  the fear of losing the beloved is worse than mortal danger to oneself ("more terrified than… among the jaws of the
  dragon"). The Polyandrion, meant to *cool* his ardour (p. 242), has instead confirmed its depth: the tombs of the
  love-dead make him dread being one of them. The therapy overshoots into revelation.
- **the toga shredded on the thorns** — a vivid, human detail: the antiquarian who wandered the ruins in delight now
  flees them, robe torn, burr- and thistle-covered. His scholarly composure is stripped as literally as his clothes.
  A stageable beat for the world/novel.
- **Polia's tender care.** She raises him, dries his face with her own veil, and asks the cause — the reciprocal
  tenderness that answers his love (cf. her soothing, pp. 235, 241). The reunion is gentle; his fear was groundless,
  and her presence restores him. Her question sets up his confession and her reassurance (p. 274).
- **"the Babylonian gulf"** — the deadly cave/vapour of Babylon (Pliny's Charonium): Poliphilo's breath as if poisoned.
  The erudite simile even in extremity — his mind is antiquarian to the last.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The reunion and the arrival of Cupid: Polia reassures Poliphilo (kisses, "soon I await the God
of love"; **"suffering is most often the cause of most-noble effects"**), and he recovers; then Polia suddenly
kneels, and **Cupid himself arrives by boat** — naked, unveiled-eyed — steering to the shore. This ends the long
chapter XIX and leads directly into the crossing (chapter XX). All secure.

- **"Suffering is the cause of most-noble effects."** Polia's consolation-maxim — the sister of "perseverance alone
  wears the victor's diadem" (p. 289): love's reward is earned through patient endurance. It resolves the whole
  temptation-and-terror arc of chapters XVIII–XIX (Poliphilo's restraint, p. 241; his panic, p. 272) into a single
  lesson. Prime, quotable material for the world/novel — the moral of the Polyandrion passage.
- **Cupid arrives — the chapter joins the crossing.** The god comes by boat to ferry the lovers to Cythera; his
  arrival here is the seam into **chapter XX** (already translated — the crossing, the *Amor vincit omnia* standard,
  the singing at the oars). The whole of Book I's later half now connects end to end: Temple of Venus → Polyandrion →
  Cupid's boat → Cythera. Poliphilo's "unveiled eyes" of Cupid recur (cf. p. 285).
- **the graveyard-therapy resolved.** Polia sent Poliphilo to the tombs to cool his desire (p. 242); it overshot into
  terror (p. 272); now, reunited and instructed, he recovers into "generous magnanimity." The Polyandrion has done its
  work — desire tempered, fidelity proven, patience learned — just as Cupid arrives to reward it.
- **The Polyandrion visit ends here.** The great sequence of tombs is done; the remaining pages of chapter XIX
  (275–282) cover the **boarding of Cupid's boat and the start of the crossing**, before chapter XX (p. 283) opens with
  the nymphs resting the oars to sing.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The full epiphany of **Cupid** and the start of his speech: his blinding beauty (over-gilt hair,
frightful illuminating eyes, rose cheeks, gold-and-cyan-and-mallow peacock wings), his voice that "recompaginates every
dissolved thing" and wakes the dead, and his address to the kneeling lovers — declaring their **sacrifices and prayers
accepted** by Venus and their "ardent desires" about to be fulfilled. All secure.

- **Cupid the god, seen close.** After the multiform, half-glimpsed Cupid of the boat (p. 285) and the little spirit of
  the smoke (p. 227), here the god appears in full, unbearable to look at — the theophany the whole temple sequence
  earned. His wings' colours (rose, cyan, mallow, gold) and his "frightful illuminating eyes" give a precise, renderable
  divine figure for the world/novel.
- **the voice that wakes the dead.** Cupid's power is described as raising cadavers "from the eternal sepulchres and the
  initial matter," calming the sea, bridling fire: Love as the cosmic force of generation and resurrection — the exact
  counter to the Polyandrion's Hell of the love-dead (p. 250). He comes *out of* the graveyard-visit to raise the lovers
  from its dread. The placement is deliberate: Love answers Death at the tomb's edge.
- **the prayers accepted.** Cupid confirms that the Venus-temple rites (chs. XVII–XVIII) and the lovers' constancy have
  been received, and their desire will now be "efficaciously resolved" — the divine ratification that carries them to
  Cythera. His invitation into the boat completes on p. 276.
- **Psyche preferred** — a small psychological touch: Poliphilo imagines Cupid himself finding Polia more beautiful than
  Psyche. The book's habitual surpassing-topos, here turned on the god's own bride.

with a marvellous exterior daub: not of *palimpissa* (pitch), nor blackened with *zopissa* (ship-pitch), but with a

were of blood-red sandalwood. Beyond measure they rendered the heart exhilarant.

the blades, were of illustrious and snowy ivory, not with radish (bleached), but genuine, pre-shining; and the rowlocks
of gold, and the (oar-)thongs of commixed and twisted silk. These maidens were dressed most-richly, of most-limpid

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Cupid finishes his invitation (only he, as "navarch and ferryman," may carry them to Cythera);
the lovers **board the boat**; and the vessel and its **six rowing-nymphs** are described — an *exeres* (six-oar) coated

- **The boat to Cythera.** Cupid's six-oared vessel, smeared not with tar but with solid perfume and built of scented
  woods, gold-nailed and gemmed, rowed by six nymphs — this is the boat of the crossing (chapter XX, already translated:
  the *Amor vincit omnia* standard, p. 284; the six singing nymphs, p. 285). Here is its full material description: an
  aromatic, jewelled sandalwood skiff. A vivid, buildable ferry for the world's digit-0 sailing.
- **only Cupid may ferry them.** The god insists none can reach "the maternal realm and destined island" without him as
  pilot: Cythera is reachable only under Love's own conduct. A narrative gating the world honours (the crossing is Cupid-

- **the six nymphs — the rowers who will sing.** These are the six *nautical nymphs* who rest the oars and sing in

  six-voice part-song of p. 285. The world's crossing can carry both the boat and its six singer-rowers from these pages.
- **fragrance as material** — the hull *is* perfume (cf. the perfumed pavements of Cythera, p. 355): Colonna builds the
  vessel of scent and precious wood, so it "renders the heart exhilarant." The crossing is sensory before it is musical.

To replicate aptly I would not know that which to me was licentiously conceded, and (I) made partaker, to speculate —
every thing, scatteringly, in the soul revolving, with amorous device, embracing (it), in the memory repeating, in the
mind representing a sweet enjoyment, and sweetly, of so much beauty, a soft pleasure verisimilarly I usurped. Two, then,
of these — **Aselgia** and **Neolea** — were of lascivious adornment, preciously clad, Attalically, of *chamochaino*
cloth wefted with golden weft, and of a warp of cyan silk, such as King Attalus in Asia could not find. Two others,
likewise — **Chlidonia** and **Olvolia** — had the voluptuous Babylonian dress of precious *thalassium* (sea-purple),
with varied texture. The last, **Adea** and **Cypria**, were invested of most-noble *melledarum*, with wormwork and airy
stitching, with most-minute and pervious slashes, manifoldly jagged, in the ground set under with gold foil at the
extreme fringes. And at the joint of the arms was, broadly, an outlet of the proper garment, whence came out the ivory
arms, bared, for ostentation of another whiteness than the milky coagulation, with all the requisite ornaments and
nymphal additions. The fresh and wanton breeze then, according to its motion, now the form of the round, untouched and
hard belly, reflowing, disclosed; and the noteworthy pubis; now the fleshy thighs; some time the trembling buttocks.
Then, on the longish little (feet), the footwear, by force (with a shoe-horn conducted) brought back — such were of cyan
silk, and of greening and Punic colouring, exquisitely tanned; on the vertex of the foot, with a sinuate opening,
moon-shaped, most-polishedly fenced round, with rims and gold buckles politely strapped, and with crepidae and gilt
soccoli; and some with silken little cords, gold-pointed, and alternately, by some, suppressed —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The six rowing-nymphs described in the book's fullest costume-manner: their pearls (surpassing
the one Julius Caesar gave Servilia), flower-wreaths, jewelled collars, and breast-bands, and their **named identities**
in three luxurious pairs — **Aselgia & Neolea** (cloth-of-gold), **Chlidonia & Olvolia** (Babylonian sea-purple),
**Adea & Cypria** (slashed *melledarum* with bared arms) — their sheer wind-revealed dress and silk shoes. All secure.

- **The six nymphs named.** The rowers of the Cythera-boat are individuated — their Greek names carry meaning:
  **Aselgia** ("wantonness"), **Chlidonia** ("luxury/daintiness"), **Cypria** ("of Cyprus," Venus's isle), and their
  companions Neolea, Olvolia, Adea. As with the triumph's masque (pp. 338–340), the crew of Love's boat are
  personifications — the sensuous aspects of Venus's service. The world's crossing can name its six singer-rowers from
  these.
- **the surpassing pearl.** The nymphs' pearls exceed the famous pearl Julius Caesar bought for Servilia (Cato's sister,
  his mistress — Suetonius): the surpassing-topos, on jewels (cf. Cleopatra's pearl-tradition). Colonna's erudition
  even in a costume-list.
- **the wind-revealed dress, once more.** The breeze pressing the sheer cloth to disclose "the round belly… the fleshy
  thighs… the trembling buttocks" is the book's insistent erotic motif (the boating-nymphs, p. 313; the triumph-
  companions, p. 331), here on the boat's crew. The crossing is sensuous throughout, before the singing lifts it (ch. XX).
- **the costume-catalogue as pleasure** — Poliphilo confesses he "usurps a soft pleasure" merely from remembering and
  describing them: the ekphrasis is itself an erotic act. The chapter ends (pp. 278–282) with the boat's departure and
  the sea-gods' homage to Cupid, into the crossing of chapter XX.

[p. 278]

— golden circlets, threaded, strained (them, the shoe-cords). And with others, manifoldly adorned, of wanton and virginal
shrewdness, invented to gratify the senses with laborious voluptuousness. All these things, of special dignity, so
gracious and much-admired offered themselves to our amorous mystery, as, to the ardent flames, the fatness (fuel); and to
Vulcan, the sulphurable matter; and, of the Tartarean pit, the vigilant custody to three-throated Cerberus; and to Megaera
and her sisters, the mortal fright; and the florid youth to amorous Cupid; and to the mother (Venus), the commodious
lurking-places.

Separated, then, from the sandy shore, these divine boat-nymphs beautifully reined the ivory oars in the flat grating, by
the gyrons (oar-loops); and each, with the most-shapely faces toward the nude lord (standing on the prow), with majestic
reverence, joyously turned themselves — and their whitening backs to us. My genius, and Polia, with most-luculent
confabulation, said to me: "My Poliphilo (every other thing postposed and refused), most-beloved — I wish that thou
understand and know, that these six present little maidens are the readiest handmaids of that lord, and opportunely
ministering to his pleasant service."

Sitting, then, these solacing, comely and outstanding little Nymphs upon the sandalwood thwarts, paired, turned toward the
divine lord, and to us the delicate back — the divine helmsman, the smooth wings distended, explicating, having called
with odoriferous breath to himself the sweet zephyr, wind-blowing rendered the holy feathers (more than the ardent
carbuncle to the pre-shining torches, coruscating lightnings), and, the plumate wings filled with flower-bearing air, we
began to abandon the garrulous shores, and to navigate upon the deep and spacious sea, with grateful calm tranquil. And,
of great and fearful veneration, and of singular sweetness and alacrity, my amorous and contumacious heart being stuffed,
and all shakeable, distinctly with my genius I cogitated: what heart so inhuman could ever be found — or one of such
hardness, so vivid and so vigorous, however more rough than the bark of the palm to imagine — that, to such-made beautiful
and concupiscible presences, and divine objects, to all gentleness most-tender and most-soft, and mortified, invalid, and
most-lenient, of a sudden would not have shown itself?

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The boat **departs the shore**: the six nymphs turn to face Cupid on the prow (backs to the
lovers), Polia names them "the readiest handmaids" of the god, and Cupid, spreading his wings and calling the **zephyr**,
sails them out onto the calm deep. Poliphilo reflects that no heart, however hard, could resist such beauty. All secure.

- **Cupid the helmsman, wind in his wings.** The god does not row: he *is* the propulsion — spreading his wings, calling
  the zephyr, and filling them with "flower-bearing air" to drive the boat. The crossing is powered by Love's own wings
  and the spring wind. A vivid, buildable image for the world's ferry (Cupid at the prow, wings as sail).
- **the nymphs as fuel.** Colonna's simile-chain casts the nymphs' beauty as "fuel to the ardent flame" — the necessary
  matter of Love's fire, as sulphur to Vulcan, fright to the Furies. Their sensuousness serves "our amorous mystery": the
  crossing to Cythera is an erotic initiation, its crew its instruments.
- **the six named handmaids** — Polia confirms the six rowers (Aselgia, Cypria, etc., p. 277) are Cupid's *pedissequae*
  (handmaids): the boat is crewed by the aspects of Venus's service, ferrying the initiates. The world's crossing carries
  this meaning.
- Poliphilo's reflection on love's irresistibility continues (p. 279), then the sea-gods come to honour Cupid (p. 280).

[p. 279]

And what imprisoned and extinguished concupiscence — glacial and depraved appetite — that would not here have vigorously
unbroken the tenacious cloisters and biting snares, and most-aptly restored itself to the comely, most-beautiful and
amorous spectacles, and would not have turned itself into flame-bearing Etna? And what Diana would have spurned so benign
fires — (fires) to contaminate the chaste Hippolytus, and make lascivious the most-modest Orithyia? But what must those
have felt, who wholly were apt, near, and uniformly disposed (to love)? I found myself like the little fish born in
boiling water — thence extracted, and in other waters set to boil, it never cooks (again). Beyond, then, stupidly I
beheld that divine little spirit, and, in his over-gilt feathers, some restless little plumules, tender and delicate,
such as are on the immature wings of the young hawk not yet flying from the nest, and, at the dewy winds, tremulous
resulting. O how gracious, and how most-pleasant to the senses, the little golden-crimson feathers presented themselves!
Which golden colour, in some feathers, refulged, and (some) of phoenician colouring; some of glaucous colour, and of
emerald tincture, and of mallow colouring, and of cyan, and (some), more than the icteric little bird, yellow — in a
golden colour most-admiredly coming together, and, with harmonic dispensation, most-decorously, through the divine
wings.

For which thing, all the jewels of fecund nature, distributed there, participatingly, to coruscate, I easily judged —
because they irradiated like mobile and most-tenuous foils of most-pure gold, suspended in the breeze, and, in the clear
sun, wind-blowing, comelily painting the waters of the most-placid colours; then torn (reflected) by the unstable and
crisping little waves, in a great emulating gyre. I beheld also the incomparable beauty of the divine composite of Polia,
from hour to hour ever more delicious and shapely presenting herself. Then I beheld also the most-purged and serene air,
the moderate and placid weather, and the saline cerulean waters — like perspicuous crystal, most-limpid, seen even to the
most-open shallows — and, here and there, many wooded rocks; and, ornated of vernal verdure, the scattered (Sporad)
little isles, thick of leafy greening shrubs, and most-pleasantly shady; and many vague places, from the senses, afar,
lost themselves; and in the flattened (waters), like spots, they appeared. Likewise the frondiferous trees over-shadowed
the littoral little banks, and the greenish reflex, then, in the most-nitid and mirror-like waters, as the proper (thing),
was discerned.

Proceeding, then, our solacing and triumphant navigation — where presided the empire and divine monarchy of potent Love;
where resided that lord who, in extreme sweetness, renders himself austere, and, in austerity, feigns himself so sweetly
sweet, and, in sweetness, so bitter, and, in bitterness, presents himself so pleasant. O happy, therefore, whoever,
navigating, should feel his feathered wings prosperous and favourable! Finding myself, then, thus, between two so pleasing
lords — the one inflamed me, the other consumed me — lo, that the marine gods: **Nereus** with the most-pleasing **Chloris**,

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Poliphilo's reflection on Love's irresistibility (no chastity — Diana's, Hippolytus's, Orithyia's
— could withstand it; he is "the fish born in boiling water"), a rapt study of Cupid's **rainbow wings** (gold, phoenician,
glaucous, emerald, mallow, cyan, yellow, painting the sea), the beauty of Polia and of the crystalline, isle-scattered sea;

- **Love's monarchy over the sea.** The crossing is "the divine monarchy of potent Love" — the god "who in extreme sweetness
  renders himself austere… in bitterness so pleasant": Colonna's chiastic definition of Love's paradox (sweet/bitter,
  austere/pleasant), the theme of the whole voyage. A quotable line for the world/novel.
- **Cupid's wings paint the sea.** The god's feathers, "like foils of pure gold in the sun," cast shifting colour on the
  water, "torn by the crisping waves" — a luminous optical image (Colonna's caustics again, cf. the crystal lamp, p. 208).
  A rendering cue for the world's crossing: rainbow light off Cupid's wings scattering on the sea.
- **the Sporades-idyll** — crystal water to the shallows, green shrubby islets, shaded banks mirrored in the sea: the
  perfect calm passage to Cythera. Buildable as the world's approach seascape.
- **"between two lords, one inflamed, the other consumed me"** — Cupid and (implicitly) Poliphilo's own heart, or Cupid and
  Venus: he is caught between the two powers of love. The marine procession honouring Cupid (p. 280) confirms Love's reign
  over even the sea-gods.

being to me by the gods so benignly and so well communicated, more happy I esteemed myself than the fortunate Polycrates.

- **The whole sea worships Love.** The marine pantheon — Neptune, the Nereids, Tritons, Oceanus, Proteus, Glaucus — comes

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Poliphilo's **rapture at possessing Polia**, in a great surpassing-catalogue (Endymion, Paris,
Jason, Theseus, Antony, Apelles — none gloried in their loves as he in Polia); his surrender of his soul "to both" Cupid
and Polia; his confidence that the *Amor vincit omnia* standard guarantees her love in return; and the beginning of the
meditation on Love's cosmic fire. All secure; the emotional summit of the crossing.

- **The surpassing-catalogue of lovers.** Every famous love — Endymion's moon, Paris's Helen, Jason's Medea, Theseus's
  Ariadne, Antony's Cleopatra, Apelles's Campaspe — is exceeded by Poliphilo's joy in Polia. Colonna's habitual topos, here
  at its fullest, marking the crossing as the fulfilment of the whole quest. The *Amor vincit omnia* standard (p. 284) is
  named as the pledge that seals it.
- **"the disparity of the two, save in divinity."** Poliphilo cannot tell Cupid and Polia apart except that one is a god:
  Polia is all but divine to him. He surrenders his soul to both — to the god's power and the beloved's will. The love-story
  and the theophany merge on the boat.
- **the reciprocation hoped and assured** — he trusts that "no other effect can breathe" from such presence "than ardent
  love," and that Polia can "no more flee." The crossing carries the certainty the temple-rite promised (p. 218): the union
  is now secure, borne by Love's own boat to Love's own island.
- The meditation on Love's fire — which "inflames the universe" — completes on p. 282, ending chapter XIX.

[p. 282]

— and burns; transcends, penetrating the most-solid heavens, and thence, without any diminution, the profundity of the

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The meditation on **Love's cosmic fire** — a flame that penetrates the heavens and the abyss, which
no sea-god can resist, and "in which mortals, dying with supreme sweetness, live"; then the marvel of how it burns unquenched
in Polia's snow-white breast and eyes; and Poliphilo's apostrophes to Cupid ("how sweetly thou nestlest in my soul") and to
Polia's eyes ("O sweetest executioners"), invoking Apuleius's Lucius (longing for the roses) and Psyche's helpers. This ends
**chapter XIX**. All secure.

- **"The fire in which mortals, dying with supreme sweetness, live."** The definition of Love the whole crossing has been
  building to: a paradoxical flame that consumes yet nourishes, that kills sweetly and thereby gives life — the *physizoic*
  fire of Venus (the temple's "life-conserving" love, p. 229), and the exact opposite of the Polyandrion's Hell-fire that
  merely torments (p. 250). Love's fire is generative; death's fire is punitive. The two temples, and the two fires, are now
  joined and distinguished. A key statement for the world/novel.
- **the Apuleian frame closes.** Poliphilo names Lucius (the ass who longed for the roses that would restore him) and
  Psyche's four helpers (ant, reed, eagle, Cupid's prick) — the *Golden Ass* and *Cupid and Psyche* — the classical love-
  romances the whole Hypnerotomachia rewrites. His desire for Polia exceeds even theirs. The book signs its literary ancestry
  as it ends the chapter.
- **"O sweetest executioners."** Polia's eyes are Love's arsenal, girding Cupid's quiver from Poliphilo's own heart-wounds:
  the beloved's beauty is Love's weapon, and the lover its willing victim (the fidelity-as-captivity theme, pp. 341, 240,
  brought to its tenderest pitch). The direct address makes it a spoken love-lyric — voiceable.
- **Chapter XIX complete, and Book I's arc closed.** The whole later half of Book I — Temple of Venus (XVII–XVIII), the
  Polyandrion (XIX) — is now translated, and the narrative flows straight into **chapter XX** (the crossing and the singing
  at the oars, already done) and on to Cythera (XXI–XXIV, done). **All of Book I from the Dallington seam (p. 193) onward is
  now in English**, except chapters not in the earlier work-order. The remaining task is Book II (chs. XXV–XXXVII).

CHAPTERS XIX–XX
