[p. 283]

— and she, with this high lord, this continual prey, navigating, divided and imparted. Therefore this
alone I esteemed extreme sweetness of delight — to which, in presence, the blessed celebrity and triumph
invited me.

*(Chapter argument:)*

> POLIPHILO NARRATES THAT THE NYMPHS, HAVING RESTED THE OARS, BEGAN SWEETLY TO SING. AND POLIA,
> SINGING IN COMPARISON (in answer), FELT A GREAT SWEETNESS OF LOVE.

With the utmost auspicious, superb and great pomp, insolent triumph, with unthinkable joy and voluptuous
gratification — with stimulating darts savagely fixed in the scarred heart, at the amorous eyes of Polia,
and at the arrow-frequency of Cupid, an opposing and most-firm target — with an amplified heart, more
furnace-like burning, ever more avid to augment the ardour, through the solicitous ministry of the
insatiable and impatient eyes (to which reasonably I pardoned it, considering the cause that made them so
cupidinous, and supremely applied to it, and sedulously intent): like the simulacrum of Apis, which
toward the sun ever turns, gazing — so, and not otherwise, were my eyes directed upon her, who was a
conspicuous and exciting object, from that much-admired irradiating face, in the world proscribed of
equivalent beauty, and by every means interdicted.

But more noxious, and much more iniquitous and vexing slaughter, did the furtive and wandering thoughts
experience of this valorous lord — best of such matter the shrewd quaestors, and of the gain the most-apt
artificers, to fabricate and compose, of fire and of flames, so sweet a torment, so venerable an idol, so
shapely a simulacrum, so outstanding a form, in the workshop of the imaginative faculty, and solacingly
to feign. Oh, how much — molesting, and refusing all temperament, declining to succumb — did these
unbridled and public cut-throats of my repose and quiet show themselves, and insatiable and raging of the
unseen beauty of my golden-haired Polia; sometimes sweet, and sometimes bitter, sometimes glad, and more
often sad; many times desirable, and often to be fled, they accused themselves. What most-valid forces,
then, could have imprisoned the incontinent senses — reluctant, to dissent; and dissenting, to repugn;
and repugning, to drive off; and driving off, to spurn —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The end of ch. XIX and the argument and opening of **chapter XX** (the singing at
the oars). The opening is Poliphilo's interior monologue — his fixed gaze on Polia (like the sun-following
Apis) and the "furtive thoughts" that Love forges into torment. All secure; a psychological page, its long
periods kept long.

- **Chapter XX placed.** In the work-order this is the boat-journey to Cythera that *precedes* the landing
  (ch. XXI) — the nymphs rest their oars and sing, Polia answers, and Poliphilo's love intensifies. The
  world's approach-to-Cythera (the digit-0 sailing) corresponds to this chapter; its imagery (the
  *Amor vincit omnia* standard, p. 285) belongs to the boat the player rides.
- **the sun-following Apis** — the Egyptian bull-god's image "ever turns toward the sun, gazing"; so
  Poliphilo's eyes turn always to Polia's face. A characteristic Colonna simile drawn from Egyptian cult
  (cf. the Serapis of p. 344).
- **Love as a forger of torment "in the workshop of the imaginative faculty"** — the same idea as the
  "siege-engines of beauty" (p. 337): desire is manufactured, an artifice worked on the heart. The book's
  recurring analysis of its own eroticism.
- **"golden-haired Polia" (xanthothrica)** — Polia's epithet; her fair hair is a fixed attribute (cf. the
  portrait, p. 337).

CHAPTER XX

[p. 284]

— whatever hedge and enclosure, throughout that pleasant meadow diffusely flower-bearing of the singular
and choice delights of Polia (like a murmuring bee), most-richly, unwearied, they gathered — so much
sweetness, and sweetest delight, diffusing it through the oppressed viscera. Where the amplest serpent-
flames, without relaxation insulting, violently invaded. For which thing I did not judge it worthy, nor
convenient, that the amorous and carbuncled heart, vigorously exercised in these such works, and
sustaining them, should be moved to remove it, and by molestation to debilitate it. But rather, most-
modestly, I ought, tolerating, to support it — which so willingly, for my affable content, it had
laboriously contracted.

Now, in the fateful ship's-command, without sternpost and rudder navigating, we the first-sailors, and
upon this unpremeditated vessel, where all the mysteries of love breathed — which had for its poop the
prow, and for its prow the poop, with the most-worthy and exquisite artifice, accommodated to Cupid by his
mother — than which never an apt and most-richly eloquent tongue of round oratory could, expounding,
express, and expressing recollect, and distinctly recollecting recount.

In the very middle of which — that is, in the mast-step — was raised a golden spear, with a triumphal and
imperatorial standard, of thin silken cloth, of cyan dye; in which, of little gems of the opportune
colouring, with whitest pearls, were polishedly, picturewise, re-woven, on both faces, with manifold
foliage, with the utmost most-comely adornment, three hieroglyphs: an antique little vase, in the mouth-
gap of which burned a little flame; and then was the world; joined together with a little branch of osier,
at the soft breaths of the spring-bearing and obsequious zephyr wind-blown, flutteringly volant, and
choicely inconstant. The interpretation of which I made thus:

> **AMOR VINCIT OMNIA** — "Love conquers all."

## Notes

**Confidence: high** (the hieroglyph and its reading are secure); medium for the surrounding prose. The
description of **Cupid's boat** (prow-for-stern, "where all the mysteries of love breathed") and its
**standard bearing the rebus AMOR VINCIT OMNIA** — a flaming vase + the world + an osier-withy, which
Poliphilo reads as "Love conquers all." All secure; one of the book's most famous hieroglyphs.

- **AMOR VINCIT OMNIA — the emblem of the crossing.** The boat to Cythera flies a cyan-silk standard on
  which three picture-signs (a vase with a flame, the globe of the world, a binding osier-withy) spell
  Virgil's *omnia vincit Amor* (Eclogue X). This is the motto of the whole Cythera sequence, and the
  natural inscription for the world's ferry-boat / approach-standard. The world could carry this hieroglyph
  on the sail or a banner.
- **the reversible boat "with prow for stern."** Cupid's vessel is built prow-for-poop — a paradoxical
  craft "where all the mysteries of love breathed," made by Venus for her son. A distinctive, renderable
  boat-form for the digit-0 sailing.
- **Poliphilo "like a murmuring bee" gathering Polia's delights** — the bee-in-the-meadow simile for the
  senses feeding on beauty (cf. the bee/elephant hieroglyph of the polyandrion, and the "murmuring bee" of
  the lover's eyes). Consistent imagery of the heart as forager.
- The reading of hieroglyphs is the book's signature interpretive game; here Poliphilo performs it in
  miniature on the sail before the singing begins (p. 285).

[p. 285]

The divine Steersman I, with reverent and decent regards, willingly willing him, with every possible
effort to contemplate — the disproportionate object, my feeble sight fittingly did not suffer. But,
conniving with my cheeks (half-closing my eyes), in this manner somewhat the divine boy I manifoldly
comprehended. Sometimes he appeared to me of twin aspect; sometimes of triple; and yet, sometimes, he
showed himself with infinite effigies. Who, with Polia, made our itinerary happy, blessed, and glorious.
And by this way the amorous and prow-standing Cupid, fanning the sacred feathers of his perpetual wings —
in which Canens, lover of Picus, solaced herself — shone more than refined gold, of various and most-
pleasant colouring, rotating in a circle above the little waves. More beautiful and more pleasing than
the crystalline triangular column of Euclid demonstrates, approximated to the eyes.

Now the nautical Nymphs gave beginning — with a most-sweet note, and with a heavenly intonation, from the
human wholly deviated, and beyond belief, with reasoned song-craft — to sing, and to trill a most-sweet
concord, with consonant voice and melody. Insomuch that rightly I doubted I should shatter from excessive
sweetness, because almost from its place removed I felt the resulting and wounded heart, and of sweetness
it seemed to me, reasonably, that it should exile itself through my lips. And they, following, with
vibrating little tongues, in the sonorous palate broke, crisping, doubling, and tripling into one the
briefest little chromatics, or tailed notelets — and, first intercepted, two by two; then three and three;
then by four; last, all six — the rosy little lips, tremulous, moderately opening them, and graciously
joining them, they proffered the modulating spirits, with mosaic proportion, with mellifluous voice, in
the warm heart syncopated, and with weary utterance of love. A voice sighing to the places, most-sweetly
throating — enough to put into oblivion the natural need, and to neglect it — with stringed instruments
they sang the sweetnesses and qualities of love: the facetious thefts of supernal Jove, the solacing
warmths of most-holy Erothea (Venus), the lasciviousnesses of festive Bacchus, the fecundities of the
foster-mother and golden Ceres, the savoury fruits of Hymenaeus — with versifying manner expressing, and
rhythmically proffering, *melos emmetron* (metred song).

For which thing, with a straying mind, most-firmly I held that such was not that sweet-sounding one which
Eurydice, borne in the winged three-team to the infernal (regions), and —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Cupid the multiform steersman (seen double, triple, infinite) at the prow, his
rainbow wings; then **the nymphs' song at the oars** — a virtuoso six-voice chromatic melody, its
technique described note by note, singing the loves of Jove, Venus, Bacchus, Ceres and Hymenaeus, and
surpassing Orpheus. All secure; a page about music, and Colonna's most technical description of singing.

- **The song at the oars — the chapter's heart.** With the oars rested, the six nymphs sing a "heavenly"
  chromatic part-song (entering two by two, then three, then four, then all six), on the theme of the loves
  of the gods, to stringed accompaniment. Poliphilo nearly "shatters from sweetness." This is the music of
  the crossing to Cythera — the world's approach could carry a six-voice vocal texture. Polia answers it on
  pp. 286–289.
- **the multiform Cupid.** The god at the prow appears "twin, triple, infinite" as Poliphilo half-closes
  his eyes against the "disproportionate object" — Love cannot be seen whole. His rainbow wings "in which
  Canens solaced herself" recur (Canens, Picus's singer-wife who dissolved into song — a music-myth fit for
  this chapter).
- **surpassing Orpheus** — the nymphs' song exceeds even Orpheus's, which drew Eurydice from the dead: the
  surpassing-topos applied to music (cf. Apollo and Arion, p. 343). Music is the chapter's whole subject,
  so its superlative is the singer of the underworld.
- **"Erothea"** — a cult-name for Venus (love-goddess); the song's pantheon is the powers of generation:
  Jove, Venus, Bacchus, Ceres, Hymenaeus — desire, love, wine, harvest, marriage.

[p. 286]

— from the most-shady seats, from the eternal flames freed (Eurydice). Nor yet, with such a sound, did
Hermes lull to sleep the eyed shepherd (Argus). Such (a sound), through the most-purged air scattering
itself, breathed out of the precious and coral little lips; and through the white throat one saw the
vocal spirits passing, with modulated sweetness diffusing itself. For that was celestial flesh, and a
divine composite transparent — like crystalline, most-frigid, and refined camphor, tinged with crimson.

Whence Phoebus would have stayed from coming to bedew the wolf-light dawn with his coruscating rays, and
would have forgotten to paint, and to make the colours for the flowers, and to renew a gracious day for
the mortals. And by this, without doubt, the bow-bearing Diana would have forgotten the curved bows and
the flying arrows, and the sedulous huntings, and the dense woods; and, warming the gelid fount, she
would not have spurned the presence of the incautious hunter, and would not have turned the horned stag,
to the biting dogs lacerable (i.e. she would have spared Actaeon). And the all-wandering Selene would
have withdrawn from illustrating with her splendour the supernal heavens and the shadowed earth. And the
frightful Proserpina, in her mournful realm, would not have racked the doleful subjects, had a like tone
reached her ears. And the solacing Bacchus would have made resistance to the slippery lasciviousnesses,
and would have neglected the Ogygian hills, Elis, Naxos, Chios, and Mount Massicus, and Mareotis, and
would have made little of the must-sweet delights of the vintaging Autumn. And the fostering Ceres would
have kept the ears of corn ever in green, postponing the abundant realms of Ausonia, nor would have
exchanged the fat and four-grained ears with Chaonia. And the cloud-thundering bird (Jove's eagle), out
of the hooked curvature of its inverted talons, would not have felt the ravished Phrygian cup-bearer
(Ganymede) flee away — so most-sweetly the Nymphs sang, and concordantly sounded, and each of them, with
my Polia singing along, dispensed celestial melodies to the open ears.

By which the black and multiform and lucubratory Cerberus would have been lulled; nor would he have kept
watch, with unmoving eyes, the metallic valves of Taenarum. And then the raging Tisiphone, with the
monster-bearing sisters, to the wretched souls would have shown themselves most-placid and benign. Nor
ever were Parthenope, with her sisters Leucosia and Ligeia — daughters of Achelous and of Calliope —
singing at the Capri isles near Pelorus, heard with so much harmony, of voice, mode, Lyre, and pierceable
tibia; whence the soul, incendiarily inflamed, removed from its place by the happy songs, and sounds,
effigies, beauties, retinue, and majesty, I could not redeem, nor make it my own. But, most-tightly
bound, it commended its estate into the delicate arms, and in the whitening bosom of Polia, a perpetual
and surrendered hostage, obliged it. Which then, cogitating, by delectable paths and voluptuous conduits,
arrived at the arcane delights. And thence, with all my excited virtues drawn into myself, I could resume
nothing else but a solacing imaginative, and glorious.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The great surpassing-conceit of the song: the whole pantheon (Phoebus, Diana,
Selene, Proserpina, Bacchus, Ceres, Jove's eagle, Cerberus, the Furies) would have abandoned their
offices to listen, and even the **Sirens** (Parthenope, Leucosia, Ligeia) never sang so; and Poliphilo's
soul, ravished from its place, surrenders as a "perpetual hostage" in Polia's bosom. All secure; a
sustained mythological catalogue on the power of the music.

- **The music that would halt the gods.** Colonna runs the surpassing-topos to its limit: the Sun would
  forget the dawn, Diana would spare Actaeon, Ceres keep the corn green, Jove's eagle drop Ganymede — all
  to hear the nymphs and Polia sing. Music suspends the whole order of nature and myth. The chapter's
  argument (music's power over the soul) is made total.
- **surpassing the Sirens** — the ultimate comparison for dangerous, soul-drawing song (Parthenope and her
  sisters, the Sirens of the Campanian coast): the nymphs exceed even them. Yet here the song does not
  destroy but *binds* Poliphilo to Polia — Sirens' power turned to love's fidelity.
- **the soul as "perpetual hostage" in Polia's bosom** — the fidelity-thread again (cf. pp. 314, 337): the
  music removes Poliphilo's soul from himself, and it lodges, surrendered, in Polia. His rapture is
  channelled straight back to her.
- **"celestial flesh… like crystalline camphor tinged with crimson"** — the singers' throats are
  transparent, the voice visible passing through: Colonna's synaesthetic image of divine song made almost
  physical light.

[p. 287]

By which, of over-rich pondering, the anxious mind, with a refreshment of spirit, fed itself; and with
little curious regards, and lewd appetites, the manifest and perfect shapelinesses (and rarely such a
habit of appearance) of Polia most-avidly I beheld, refusing every other thing worth watching, avertible
of protection. But singularly, then, most-pleasing to me was her glittering breast, wondrously painted
with purpling roses, and with milky lilies, in their first opening — in the tearful dawn, without
obstacle to my eyes, a most-placid spectacle, openly conceded, and without an impeding medium, but
sufficiently coloured — to that most-admired object which was her face, so enticing and marvellously
beautiful, graceful, and perspicuous, that such does not appear, with its ornament Hippe, in the pure sky;
with little tendril-curls above, and the rosy forehead and flat temples trembling, which, with the utmost
adornment, down the snowy neck and whitening shoulders flowed. The wanton and spring-bearing breeze
choicely re-blew them. As much as ever the most-high Jupiter can imagine, to confer on the nature of it,
and benignly to produce and skilfully-make — nor ever could Apelles have painted a like one, and much less
Aristides, who feigned human souls with his little brush.

Of which sight I could not sate myself — neither more nor less than the murmuring bees do not sate
themselves of the odorous thyme and *amellus*, and the wanton she-goats of the flowering *cytisus*, and of
the tender fronds. And with willing soul, and with incredible pleasure, I would have unlocked my most-
amorous heart, judging it no way grievous — and tessellated (it) — that she, thence, having seen it,
should have received by proof the token of what are the qualities that, loving, one endures. As to Caesar
the stigmatised Antipater (showed his scars), and as my soul was promptly seduced by her sweet little face
and notable figure, and reduced into servile surrender — not otherwise making pervious my breast,
lacerating, fenestrated, than the most-pious Egyptian Pelican, dwelling in the solitude of the turbid and
headless Nile, to its raging chicks, for hunger, with piercing and cruel beak splits and shatters itself,
disembowelling the pitiful and maternal heart. Which, not to Dionysus, but only to her, perpetually is
most-dedicated, excitable; and, diffusing itself, flowed in me the insane and Lernaean loves, and the
fiery desires; and the incitative thoughts it feigned in the consenting heart, composing, to consume me,
and to destroy my very self, an ardent and most-burning flame, by me wholly conceived. And with greater
miracle the lethal and death-bearing dart, innocuously transfixed, poised itself in my wounded heart, than
the pendent lethal dart in Ephesus, without a noose, in the temple of Diana. The soul therefore
interdicted, to vivify me fully availed not.

Therefore, for such-made cause mortified, beyond measure ardent — if not her delectable regards, refreshing
me, recreated me, and the amorous nods —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Poliphilo's rapture at Polia during the song: her rose-and-lily breast, her face
"such as Apelles could not paint," and the great self-sacrifice image — his heart offered to her like the
**pelican that pierces its own breast** to feed its young. All secure; a page of erotic-devotional
similitude, its long central sentence kept whole.

- **The pelican-heart — the emblem of Poliphilo's love.** He would tear open his own breast to show Polia
  "the qualities that, loving, one endures," as the Egyptian pelican splits its heart to feed its chicks.
  The pelican-in-piety (a standard emblem of sacrificial love, later of Christ) is here turned to erotic
  devotion: his heart is "dedicated, not to Dionysus, but only to her." A vivid image of the fidelity-thread
  the whole Cythera sequence sustains.
- **surpassing Apelles and Aristides** — the two greatest painters of antiquity (Apelles of form, Aristides
  "who painted souls"); neither could render Polia's face. The surpassing-topos applied to portraiture —
  fitting, since the passage *is* a verbal portrait.
- **the bee and the she-goat** — the insatiable feeding-similes again (cf. p. 284): the eye grazing on
  beauty like bees on thyme, goats on cytisus. Colonna's constant figure for desire that cannot be filled.
- **"the lethal dart… as in Ephesus"** — a dart hanging by no cord in Diana's temple at Ephesus (a marvel
  of balance from Pliny); Cupid's arrow poised in Poliphilo's heart is a greater wonder. Erudite hyperbole
  for the wound of love.

[p. 288]

— comforted me, and the low and sweet little words vivified me. She soliciting me affectionately, that I
should give heed to the sweet songs of such egregious and divine singers, and to enjoy so many marvellous

Constant, then, to the begun work, between sweetest voluptuousness and odious delay, I persevered — neither

ardour — as the mortals — she supremely loving, and it pleased you to love her above all girls. And much it
grieved you, the guileful counsel of the envious and fallacious sisters, and upon the cloudy cypress

bringing bow — for of love I am all racked.

"For which I reasonably argue: that if, in your very self, savage and pitiless, you wounded yourself — what
equability of soul persuades that I should not fear that, without pity, toward me, more harsh and unbridled
and most-savage, you would not show yourself?" And so, exasperated, concitatedly I dared; and with diverse
petitions, and prayers, and fabricated complaints, and feigned satisfactions, I somewhat softened the
strong invasion, and the frequent impulse of the wicked and eyeless love. But for all this my enkindled
heart was not condignly reconciled, nor really satisfied to my disjointed appetite. And that which then I
prayed him: only that he put an end, at least, to my tormenting and long-lasting hoping, with the molesting
expectation of a prison-like issue.

For, however much the coveted future be much more sweet of avidity than the acquired past delight, yet
every hostile love contends toward the expected end. Therefore, abridge, with sudden abolition, the timely
hope. My lord, this ungrateful and displeasing deferring — more than to the pure eyes the smoky Cloud, and
to the teeth the stupefying sourness, and than the —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Polia's tender urging that Poliphilo enjoy the song, the surpassing-comparisons for
how welcome she is (the rivers to burning Troy, the boar's head to Atalanta, the elephant to Hannibal), and
then **Poliphilo's prayer to Cupid** — reminding the god that he too was wounded by love for Psyche, and

- **Poliphilo prays to Cupid for pity — and for an end to deferral.** The theological turn of the chapter:
  he argues that a god who wounded *himself* for Psyche will surely not spare a mortal, and pleads that Love
  "slacken the death-bringing bow" and, most of all, "put an end to my tormenting hope." The pain named here
  is not desire but *delay* — "every hostile love contends toward the expected end." This sets up Polia's
  answer (p. 289): perseverance.
- **the Cupid-and-Psyche back-story** — Colonna has Poliphilo recite the myth (the envious sisters, Cupid
  lamenting on the cypress) as the ground of his plea. The whole Cythera sequence is framed by Psyche's
  story (she presides over the triumph, ch. XXII); here it is invoked as precedent.
- **"perseverance" foreshadowed** — the complaint about deferral is answered, at the chapter's very end (p.
  289), by Polia's maxim that "perseverance alone wears the victor's diadem." The chapter is structured as
  plaint-and-consolation.
- **the surpassing-gifts** — Meleager's boar's-head to Atalanta, Jove's gift to Alcmena, Hannibal's
  elephant: a catalogue of famously-welcome gifts, all less welcome than Polia. The topos, applied to the
  beloved's presence.

[p. 289]

— being slow with help to the coveter — because to a concupiscent soul it is a grave torment, the odious
day-postponing, and the prolonging of the desired end. Accusing then also, and pregnant nature reasonably
— that she shrewdly had all things, and most-excellently, conciliated, save that she had left uncompacted
the appetite with the power. Then returning into myself, strongly marvelling. For I could not perfectly

copious of so much fire, within my nursling and burnable heart. At the end, only to guard vigilantly the

Now, in this inexperienced manner, over the placid and levelled little waves of the un-furrowed deep, our
speeding six-oar ran like a light water-skater; and the most-comely rowers, most-festively jubilating,
sang in the Iasian mode; and the divine Polia, again, without the others, alone — from those minimally
dissonant, but comparable — Lydian-wise sang. Not the plaints of raging Tragedy, nor in the cackling
Satire, nor in the deceitful Comedy, nor in the tearful Elegies; but with a most-adorned poem, and with
elegant little words, the supreme sweetnesses of the holy and fostering Erycina (Venus) they composedly
proffered, and the delectable fallacies of the assisting son (Cupid) they eloquently sang. And Polia,
affable and comely, of cultivated adornment, polished and elegant, congratulating — the thanksgivings of
the obtained graces (provoking to admiration) she sang, with such vehemence and sweet-sound as, of blind
Demodocus, at the hearing of the wise Ulysses, with wailing cithara, did not attain. Which most-pleasing
companion — feeling herself no less delighted, partaker — speaking jocosely, and blandishing, tempting
me: how did the instant things appear to me? Naming to me, of whatever rowing Nymph, the proper name; and
with sweet persuasion she affirmed to me that **perseverance alone wears the victor's diadem**. And in
this unbridled avidity wholly slipped down, and most-cast-forth, most-pleasantly we navigated, and
prosperous we arrived at the delicious island Cythera.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The close of **chapter XX**: Poliphilo's meditation on the torment of deferral and
the "uncompacted appetite and power" of nature; then the boat skimming "like a water-skater" over the calm
sea while the nymphs sing in the **Iasian mode** and **Polia answers alone in the Lydian**, singing the
sweetnesses of Venus and Cupid; Polia's teasing question and her maxim that **"perseverance alone wears the
victor's diadem"**; and the arrival at **Cythera**. This ends chapter XX (7/7). All secure.

- **"Perseverance alone wears the victor's diadem."** The chapter's — and arguably the whole crossing's —
  moral, spoken by Polia in answer to Poliphilo's plea against delay (p. 288). The lover's reward is not
  seized but earned by constancy. A line worth surfacing in the world/novel as the motto of the Cythera
  approach; it is the affirmative counterpart to the triumph's QUIS EVADET / NEMO.
- **the modes: Iasian nymphs, Lydian Polia.** Colonna distinguishes the singers by Greek musical mode — the
  chorus in the Iasian (Ionian), Polia "alone… Lydian-wise." The Lydian was the mode of love-song and
  lament; Polia's solo is set apart from the chorus, as her voice is throughout. A concrete cue for the
  world's approach-music: a solo Lydian line over a choral Iasian ground.
- **surpassing Demodocus** — the blind bard of the *Odyssey* who made Odysseus weep; Polia's song exceeds
  his. The last of the chapter's music-surpassings (Orpheus p. 285, the Sirens p. 286, now Demodocus).
- **arrival at Cythera.** The boat "like a water-skater" reaches the island — the seam directly into chapter
  XXI (the island ekphrasis, already translated). Chapter XX is the crossing; XXI–XXIV the island. **All of
  the Cythera arc (XX–XXIV) is now complete.**



------------------------------------------------------------------------
CHAPTER XXI
------------------------------------------------------------------------

[p. 290]

**Having come most joyfully to the longed-for place, whose worthy loveliness
Poliphilo affirms, fittingly describing its plants, herbs, birds and dwellers.
But first the form of the little boat, and how, at the descent of the lord Cupid,
many gift-bearing nymphs opportunely presented themselves to meet him.**

The divine boy making sail with his spread wings — not from the wineskin of
Ulysses, but urged by the obsequious and dew-bearing breezes, daughters of
Astraeus and of rosy Aurora, of one unanimous consent — Polia and I, finding
ourselves kindled and headlong with eagerness to reach the destined end, with the
greatest delight of love that ever human sense could feel, nor foreconceive, nor
much less divulge. Which, however excessive it was intimately in the heart, was
nonetheless the more readily quickened by the deific presence, and by those most
witty rowing nymphs, and by the sweetest singing, and by the mysterious form of
the solid and unshaken little boat — a fit instrument organised of love — and by
the precious material, and by the sweetness and pleasantness of the place; and
much more by the near flame that Polia, with rare excellence, exuberantly breathed
into my burnable heart. For her amorous and most refulgent eyes, gliding
lightning-like through mine to my inmost heart, seditiously stirred up a most
bitter conflagration; by which, heated through and prostrately wounded, frequent
sobs gushed forth — not otherwise than the cook pours out over the burning and
excessive fire through the lips. Just so, neither more nor less, the boiling gasps
compelled from my fervent heart abundantly boiled up, showing themselves
resounding; and the importunate fires I fittingly mitigated with the sole beauty
of my lovely Polia, my guide. But how it was, I most abundantly experienced such
pleasure that I was wholly absorbed and consumed — more than ever my most decent
tongue could adapt itself to such expression.

Finally, most joyful, glad and triumphant, to the island extremely desired, with
our proud and oar-wandering ship of six banks — not ballasted, but light — which
was compacted of a form thus.

Of a fourfold partition, two were used up in the poop and in the prow, thus alike
in lineament or form, the one as the other. The two other partitions were
dispensed in the remaining hollow body; and —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The rapturous approach is secure; the boat-description
that begins at the page's end is dense nautical vocabulary and continues onto p.
291, where the confidence note for the vessel belongs.

- **Chapter XXI** opens the arrival at Cythera. The frame is the voyage in Cupid's
  boat, rowed by singing nymphs, that the Dream mode already summarises; here it is
  given in full.
- **"not from the wineskin of Ulysses"** — Aeolus gave Odysseus the winds tied in a
  bag; Cupid needs no such thing, his wings and the willing breezes suffice. The
  breezes are "daughters of Astraeus and Aurora" — in Hesiod the winds are
  Astraeus and Eos's children. Learned, and exact.
- **"as the cook pours out over the fire through the lips"** — Colonna's startlingly
  domestic simile for Poliphilo's sobs: a cook blowing on a too-hot fire. The book
  repeatedly undercuts its own high style with a homely image (cf. the ship's
  bell "as if the mint of the Queen of England," in Dallington). Kept.
- The six-banked boat (*exeres*, a hexareme) is described in full on p. 291.

[p. 291]

— one gunwale and the other, between prow and poop, began and ran with a bent
slope. This falling-away sloped a quarter, and thence little by little, level, the
rest lengthened out to the opposite end. These bent curvatures stood two feet high
from the decking. And in one and the other the three thwarts were fixed
transversely, raised a foot and a half from the decking. The keel then was clothed
with plates of gold, and so the bent ribs, from one end and the other rising
belly-wise. At the last tapering — called the dolphin — bent round in its shaped
likeness, it hooked, rendering a graceful volute; in the rounding of which shone
an ornament of thick and most precious gems. From the winding of which, toward the
flat of the poop and of the prow, little by little it stemmed into a stalk,
turning into an antique foliage, amplified upon the flat with a natural and
exquisite shaping of the finest gold, sparsely serpentining, with exact little
stalks and tendril-lacings, or incisions, and fringings, most elegantly expressed
lapping over the flats. From which scroll likewise there proceeded most
beautifully, descending inlaid from the pointed summit of the flat, following the
shaping of the gunwales — that is, the rail, or lip, where the tholes were fixed —
a marvellous frieze, a palm's breadth wide, all of gold and gemmed, of incredible
cost, egregiously girding it with a marvellous and friendly distribution and
placing of the gems; and all the wooden composite so diligently, and with
exceptional polish, with the planks joined plated fashion without the caulker's
art, and without any wedging, appearing an even-matched joinery, as of one whole
solid. And over the coating of the fragrant and blackest pitch, gleaming and
mirror-like, and with a gold trituration, throughout most admirably designed in a
Syrian lineament, with all the other circumstances above fittingly described. Thus
it was.

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** This is one of the book's technical set-pieces — the
anatomy of Cupid's hexareme — and it is the hardest kind of Colonna to render: a
specialist vocabulary (some of it his own coinage) applied to a boat that is half
ship and half goldsmith's work. The sense of every clause is recoverable, but a
naval historian could refine several terms.

- **The "dolphin" stern-ornament** — the *aplustre*, the curled stern-post of an
  ancient galley, here shaped as a dolphin's curve and set with gems. The boat is
  built like a real hexareme (six banks of oars, three thwarts a side) but dressed
  as jewellery: gold-plated keel and ribs, a gemmed frieze a palm wide along the
  rails, the hull lacquered with mirror-black pitch inlaid with gold "Syrian"
  arabesque.
- **"without the caulker's art, and without any wedging"** — the planks fit so
  perfectly that the boat seems carved from one solid, needing neither caulking nor
  wedges. The paragone of craft: art surpassing the necessity that usually shows
  in a real hull.
- **`exeres`** — a hexareme, a galley with six files of oarsmen; kept as "ship of
  six banks" on p. 290. **tholes** (*scalmi*) are the pins the oars pivot on.
- Terms rendered by their standard Vitruvian/nautical equivalents where one exists
  (*transtri* → thwarts, *carina* → keel, *coste* → ribs); a reviewer with a
  glossary of Quattrocento shipbuilding could tighten `oruli`, `trapheco`, and the
  fractional slopes.

[p. 292]

With these amorous triumphs, and the euphonious voices of the sailor-girls, and
beyond by the sea-deities, the serene air was filled, and the cerulean deep, with
confused clamours, and a multitude resounding — the waves, and feasts, and dances,
and especial gesticulation and festive gladness, and devout veneration — as,
gliding to the most pleasant place, we put in. So kindly and most gratifying, so
delightful and beautiful, offering itself to the senses with singular tree-set
ornament, as ever the most excellent and voluptuous thing could be beheld with the
eyes. For every fertile tongue would accuse itself of poverty of expression; and
by such a likeness the things commemorated before would be too unbecoming and
abusive a comparison to this. For beyond estimation it was a most solacing place,
and of delights — all planted and adorned as a kitchen-garden and herb-garden, and
a fertile orchard, and a pleasant pleasure-ground, and a gracious tree-plot, and a
most delightful shrubbery. Which was a place not of trackless and disused
mountains, every roughness done away, but flattened and even right up to the
circling steps toward the marvellous theatre at its heart. The trees were of most
sweet odour, most fertile of yield, of the widest spread of branches. A garden of
incomparable delight, affluent, of the largest fruitfulness, of most delightful
flowers, and stored, free of impediments, and of ambushes all adorned, of flowing
fountains and fresh rivulets. The sky not rigid, but temperate, most wide, clear
and bright; not of the horrid shades of infernal places; immune from variable and
inconstant weather that might offend with the ambushes of tainted winds harassing,
nor with troublesome and wintry frosts; nor the swelter of an importunate sun, nor
an invaded and torrid place of the dryness of heat; nor scorched with horrid
freezing. But all springlike and salubrious — such as the air is not to the
Egyptians who look to Libya — of long health and salubrity, and destined for
eternity. A place planted with green things, of admirable density of leafy trees,
of most gratifying show, with most lovely presentation of greenery; and everywhere
through the liquid air an incredible breathing of flowery fragrance, with all the
grassy ground steeped in fresh dew, and flowering meadows; and beyond the imagining
of every pleasure, teeming with natural goods — with coloured fruits among the
perennial green foliage, in stable cohesion and consent, with paths marked out
among the plants, and arched over with manifold roses. Let the watered and
tree-set field of Themiscyra yield place here.

Wherefore I judge it more than arduous, and reckon it difficult, to wish — even
with keen wit — to narrate it. But as much as my grasping, retentive, yet arid
memory, set upon its praise, shall recall to me, so much briefly I will adapt
myself to write.

This holy place, dedicated to nature — witty to mortals, and pitiable — nursling
of the gods and their station, and lodging of the blessed spirits, encircled (as I
could rightly conjecture) three miliaria; and on every side an interflowing of
salt —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** A great ekphrastic hymn to the island, secure in sense;
the difficulty is only its unbroken length and the piled Latinate garden-terms.
This page carries the measurement on which the whole reconstruction of Cythera
rests.

- **"encircled three miliaria"** — the sentence Segre builds the island's plan
  from (GARDENS.md §5): Cythera is a perfect circle three *miliaria* (Roman miles)
  in circumference, and this is the figure that scales the whole reconstruction we
  built. The description of the concentric rings begins here and runs for the next
  several pages.
- **"flattened and even right up to the circling steps toward the marvellous
  theatre at its heart"** — confirms the island's inward rise to the theatre of
  Venus, the terraced approach the world's Cythera renders.
- **"a place not of trackless mountains"** — Colonna states outright that first
  nature (wilderness, mountains) is *excluded* from Cythera, exactly as Hunt reads
  it: the island is pure third nature, garden art, with no share of the wild.
- **Themiscyra** — the plain of the Amazons by the river Thermodon, a classical
  byword for a rich watered field; Cythera outdoes it. The catalogue of garden-
  types (*horto olitorio, herbario, pomario, viridario, arborario, arbustario*) is
  the same taxonomy Segre maps onto the concentric rings.

[p. 293]

— most limpid waters. Which was not heaped of tufa crags, gnawed by the obstinacy
of the surging and foaming waves, full of cracks like rough Plotae; nor of shallow
shores broken and eaten by the wave's harassing injury, nor by the clinging salt;
nor was it composed of proud Niobe's rock, nor do her most sharp and hard children
appear there. But all minerally of the most polished material — not brittle, nor
friable, nor turning to mud, but translucent, whole and undefiled, like keen and
artificial crystal.

Where with careful diligence I explored the little pebbly shores wiped clean by a
kindly wash, of scattered gems of varied form and colouring, shining. There too,
dispersedly, appeared an abundance of the fragrant issue of the monstrous whales,
carried in by the fruitful tides. A most adorned island, then, of most gratifying
and new and perennial covering of springlike greenery, admirable everywhere over
the flat.

But first, upon the bare shore-banks close by, I beheld the coeval and tall
cypresses with their close-set and cracked cones, persevering, and durable for
weighty roofs — timbers not savoury to the gnawing woodworm — and the spacing
between cypresses of three paces, one separated from the other. This regular
order, turned round in a ring, was observed throughout the whole outer circle of
the island. Then, in a circle, there went round a most delightful and flowery
myrtle-grove, loving the talkative shores; which stands votive and dedicated to the
divine mother of the amorous fires. Compacted and most densely reduced and shaped
in the manner of a walled fence, a pace and a half tall, enclosing within it the
trunk-stocks of the straightest cypresses, the beginning of its foliage rising two
feet from the levelled top, or flat, of the myrtle-grove. Thus this greenery,
so made, walled about the shore-banks, with fitting passages left and distributed
at the seemly places. Which fence showed the least wood, but, protected by the
delightful and flowery foliage — no top exceeding another, no leaf — kept its
summit and its circling shorn with exceptional evenness.

Within this walled-about myrtle and green hedge (which might be, from it toward the
centre of the island, about a semitertio of a mile), I saw, by the drawing of lines
from the centre to the shore-circumference, in equal partition twenty, each of the
immensity of a stadium, with a fifth part added — imitating the outer enclosure of
the myrtle. In each division was a little grove of diverse meadows variously
grassed, and of tree-plot the like; distributed specifically according to the
required aspect of the kindly sky. Let Dodona's wood yield here. Which divisions,
in a ten-angled figure, fittingly interposing a line for each interval, multiply
into twenty. Which figure, made in a simple circle, and making section mutually of
two diameters, gave also the central point. One half-diameter of these —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The description is secure; the closing geometrical
construction (how to lay out the twenty radial divisions) is compressed and
technical, translated literally rather than smoothed. **A reviewer should check the
decagon construction against the facsimile diagram.**

- **This is the outer ring of Cythera — the cypress rim, the myrtle wall, and the
  twenty radial compartments** that Segre's reconstruction (GARDENS.md §5) turns
  into the *bosco*, and that the world's `_buildCytheraIsle` renders as twelve
  wedges (we simplified twenty to twelve). Here is Colonna's own count: **twenty
  divisions, "each of the immensity of a stadium with a fifth part added,"** drawn
  as radii from centre to shore, the outer edge a ring of cypresses three paces
  apart backed by a shorn myrtle hedge a pace and a half high, sacred to Venus.
  The next pages catalogue what grows in each.
- **the geometry** — Colonna gives an actual construction for dividing the circle
  into a decagon (then doubled to twenty): the classic straightedge method using a
  half-diameter and a quarter-diameter. He is showing his mathematical hand, as at
  the Great Portal. Kept literal.
- **"the fragrant issue of the monstrous whales"** — ambergris, washed up on the
  shore among the gems. A real luxury commodity given its mythic-sounding origin.
- **Plotae, Niobe, Dodona** — the Plotae (Strophades) are storm-beaten islands;
  Niobe was turned to weeping rock with her slain children; Dodona's oak-wood was
  the oracle. Each named only to be surpassed or excluded — the island has none of
  their roughness or grief.

[p. 294]

— which you will, divide by an equal half, with a prick. And from this point draw
obliquely a straight line, toward the topmost summit of the half-diameter; and at
this topmost point, upon this aforesaid line, mark off from the half-diameter as
much as is a quarter part of a whole diameter. Then extend a line from the centre,
cutting over the mark to the circumference: this will be the division of the
ten-angled figure.

These twenty divisions were, by most noble fences, diversely latticed with fitting
and convenient marble openwork, two inches thick, between the measured placing of
most polished little pilasters, of whitening marble, and the rest most lustrously
reddening; clothed with a varied delight of creeping plants, one shut off and
separated from another. In the middle of the fence there opened, level, in each,
a gate — seven feet in the opening, nine high up to the arching of its topmost
curve. Which latticings were of such rhombs, and little squares, and such
degenerate from the quadrangle, and by other most beautiful devices. Along these
serpentined the periclymenon; others the jasmine; some of bindweed; some of hops;
and some of black bryony, or black vine; others of convolvulus, with the
lily-like half-azure bells; some all white; some of momordica — so each was varied.
Some of Jove's flammula; of smilax, which for love of beautiful Crocus made itself
Autophoros, adorned with a white fragrant lily-flower, with a thorny and
ivy-like leaf; of bittersweet; of the little vine, with the three-cornered
bladder-campion, its seed spotted with whiteness; and of many others which,
serpentining on high, are unknown to me by name.

In the first partition the grove was a daphnon, or laurel-grove, of manifold
laurels: here I saw the Delphic, the Cyprian, the Mustax with its greatest and
whitening leaf, and the wild, the Cinos, and the Royal or Bacchalian, the Taxa,
the Spadonic, and Chamaedaphne — such as never on Mount Parnassus, most admired
and most pleasing to Apollo, most noble gift sent to the Romans. Nor did such
laurel-bearing earth kiss Brutus, most pleasing to Tiberius; nor did Drusilla see
such, borne by the white hen; nor were such born of the augur's command, planted
in the villa of the Caesars, triumphal ornament — chiefly the Sterile. I saw also
the Daphnoides, or Pelasgian, or Euthalos, fragrant with frankincense; nor did
Peneus's daughter make such a perpetual green of so much beauty, with whose leaves
Apollo was wont to adorn both his lyre and his quiver. Let the airy Sicilian
mountains yield here, both as to their sweetest springs and as to their
loveliness — however the most beautiful son of Mercury delighted himself there with
Diana — which are not prescribed by the wrath of most high Jove, offering
themselves so pleasing to cover the bald head of Caesar, mixed with many Comari in
the most pleasant soil.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The geometrical opening and the two plant-catalogues
(climbers on the lattices; laurel varieties in the first compartment) are secure in
substance; the botanical nomenclature is Pliny's and Theophrastus's, much of it in
Colonna's Latinised-Greek forms, and a botanist could refine several identifications.

- **The first of the twenty compartments is a laurel-grove** — the *daphnon* —
  and this begins the species-by-species catalogue of Cythera's *bosco* that runs
  through the next pages. The world's island plants twelve wedges "of alternating
  kinds"; Colonna's are twenty, each a single named genus, exactly as Segre's plan
  reconstructs.
- **the twenty gates, seven feet wide and nine high** — each compartment's marble
  lattice has an arched gate. These are the openings the world renders where the
  radial roads meet the rings.
- **the climbers** — periclymenon (honeysuckle), jasmine, bindweed, hops, black
  bryony, convolvulus, smilax, bittersweet, bladder-campion: real garden creepers,
  each trained on a compartment's lattice.
- **the laurel of Peneus's daughter** — Daphne, turned to the laurel Apollo then
  wore. The whole grove is Apollo's tree, and Colonna piles the Roman laurel-lore:
  the white hen that dropped a laurel-sprig into Livia's (Drusilla's) lap by
  augury, from which the triumphal laurels of the Caesars' villa were grown, one
  of them "the Sterile"; the laurel that crowned Caesar's baldness. All from Pliny
  and Suetonius. Left unglossed in the text.

[p. 295]

I beheld also another little grove, in which, with even placing, was a most
pleasing oak-wood of tender leaves. And here I saw the broad-leaved, and the
common oak, and the robur, and the *hemeris* producing the medicinal *canchry*,
and the *haliphloios* with its salt bark, with plenty of Italian oaks, and Turkey

with leaves that do not fall, tended by the Querquetulan nymphs.

In another fence there followed, in equal order, another most gratifying little
wood of fragrant wild cypresses, savin, romidascalo, or junipers, led topiary-wise
into manifold figured devices, with minute and pricking leaves — the willing
consort of the divine mother, preservable — and loftiest cedars of manifold use,
weeping cedar-oil, of foliage like the cypress, of which at Ephesus stood the

Afterwards I saw also a tall and leafy pine-wood of pine-nuts: here the Tarentine,
or wild pine, and the urban, and the bitter stone-pine, or Apine, and the

of this kind of little tree I saw all the labours of tall Hercules industriously
and with antique shaping composed [in topiary], not without manifold representation
of innumerable other feignings of diverse animals, always green, with leaves that
do not fall, regularly placed, and with a proportioned and congruent interval
distributed through the grassy and flowery meadow.

hornbeams, and ashes, and the flowering spear of Romulus, and many medlars, and

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** A dense arboreal catalogue — oaks, conifers, box, and a
mixed grove — secure in substance. The nomenclature is heavily Plinian and several
names are Colonna's Latin-Greek hybrids; a botanist could tighten `romidascalo`,
`phylire`, and a few others.

- **These are further compartments of the twenty-fold *bosco*** — the oak-wood,
  the cypress-and-cedar wood (led into topiary), the pine-wood, the box-grove, and
  a mixed grove. The catalogue is systematic, one genus per compartment, and this
  is precisely the "twenty types of tree plantation, one for each compartment" of
  Segre's plan (GARDENS.md §5).
- **the box-grove topiary of the Labours of Hercules** — the single "marvellous
  work" that exceeds the rest: box clipped into all twelve labours of Hercules,
  plus figures of animals, "always green." This is the most elaborate topiary in
  the book, and the reason the world's Cythera puts clipped topiary at the *prati*
  centrepieces. Colonna is describing garden sculpture in living box a century
  before it became a European craze.
- **the yew "apt to the lethal instruments of Cupid"** — yew for bow-wood; the
  grove supplies the material for Cupid's arrows, planted on his own island. The
  cornel too was a bow- and spear-wood (the "spear of Romulus," the cornel-shaft
  that took root on the Palatine, is here among the trees).
- **Querquetulan nymphs** — the oak-grove nymphs of old Roman religion; **Lucina** —
  Juno of childbirth, whom savin (an abortifacient) offends: Colonna's botany
  carries its pharmacology.

[p. 296]

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Another dense fruit-and-nut catalogue, secure in
substance; the nomenclature is Pliny throughout, with Colonna's usual Greek-Latin
doublets. A botanist could refine several of the varietal names.

- **More of the twenty *bosco* compartments**: larch, walnut, chestnut, quince,
  carob, palm, pomegranate, lotus/nettle-tree, Christ's-thorn, mulberry. The
  catalogue keeps its one-genus-per-compartment order, and — as Segre notes
  (GARDENS.md §5) — runs from familiar northern trees toward "mythical" Greek and
  African species, an antiquarian geography of plants.
- **Phyllis grown to a tree** — turned to an almond (or leafless tree that leafed
  at Demophoon's return); Colonna makes her the etymology of *phylla*, leaves.
  **the two mulberries** — the black mulberry reddened by the "mournful love" of
  Pyramus and Thisbe (whose blood dyed the fruit), the white one merely
  nourishing. The trees carry their myths, as everywhere in this grove.
- **the Sardian acorn / Balanus** — the chestnut, and Tiberius's renaming of it,
  from Pliny. **Hammon** — the oracle of Ammon in the Libyan desert. Named to be
  surpassed, as with all the "let X yield here" figures.

[p. 297]

I beheld also one of most teeming olive, and a fig-grove of all the kinds with
copious yield. And a most delightful poplar-wood, and likewise one of
*hippomelides* with the Egyptian pods, with the weeping *metopon* — such as, at the
oracle of Ammon, dripping gum-ammoniac, would not be found.

Which little trees were of most elegant and most artful distribution and order —
which the aspect of the sky there did not want, but without repugnance of nature
everything stood best placed. Whereby that ingenious nature there manifestly
avowed all the delights which, scattered through the universe, she had shrewdly
produced. Here heaped together, and with especial study, one may conjecture all to
be created. The ground too was grassy and flowery and with springing and shaded
fountains, of glassy water most clear, moist with waters sweeter than the fountain
of Salmacis. And there they suffered neither the frost-bearing Bear nor the
cloud-born South Wind, but the air most salubrious, most purged, and most pure,
and by far most lucid, freely pervious to the eyes, most light and even, and
invariable, with great loveliness and a temperate sunniness of place and sky, that
never suffers turbulent alteration; but dissipated, and every cloud driven off,
that liquid sky shows itself, the bold winds shut out — the crackling east winds,
the whistling north, and the malignity and asperity, with great crash, of the
raging storm, and every iniquity of weather — not subject to the tumultuous changes
of waters nor to the cold Balance. But everything may be regarded lustrous, and the
desirable light, glad and pullulating in the station of the woolly Ram drying his
fleece in the illuminating and Herculean Phoebus, with no falling but a perpetual
green, celebrated by the manifold song of birds — as, flitting in the air, the
little crested lark, and together the singing nightingale, made all the air resound
with singing.

At the outermost boundary of this semitertio of a mile, all distributed into little
woods toward the centre — because a circumference of circular figure is of as much
measure as are three of its diameters, and so much the more that in eleven
partitions, one diameter deducted, there are two portions; therefore the diameter
of this voluptuous island stood at one mile, with two of the eleven partitions
added — there went round an excellent enclosure, of a height of eight paces and of
a foot's thickness, so densely leafy that the least stem did not appear, with paired
pervious windows, and, in order at the fitting places and passages, arching open
gates, made and compactly conducted of orange, lemon and citron trees, with lustrous
greenery in the mature leaves, and of new fronds, of the first and mature fruits,
and of the most fragrant flowers dispersedly adorned — so much the more pleasing and
admirable to the aspect, as it is most rarely wont to be granted to human eyes to see
an equivalent work.

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The close of the *bosco* catalogue, the hymn to the
island's perfect climate, and the citrus-hedge that bounds the middle zone are all
secure. The pi-approximation embedded in the boundary sentence (below) is a
literal rendering of Colonna's own arithmetic.

- **The bitter-orange espalier** — "an enclosure of orange, lemon and citron
  trees, eight paces high," bounding the outer ring from the middle: this is the
  *espalier of bitter orange* Segre's plan gives as the divider (GARDENS.md §5),
  and the citrus ring the world's Cythera renders. Colonna's own detail: paired
  windows and arched gates cut through the living citrus wall.
- **the pi-approximation** — "a circumference is as much as three of its diameters,
  and so much the more that in eleven partitions, one diameter deducted, there are
  two portions." Colonna is giving π ≈ 3 + 2/11 = 3.1818…, the standard medieval
  value (22/7 stated as 3‑and‑a‑bit). From it he derives the island's diameter as
  "one mile plus two-elevenths." He is doing the geometry in the open, as
  everywhere on Cythera.
- **"the station of the woolly Ram drying his fleece"** — the sun in Aries: spring,
  the season of the whole dream. The perpetual-spring climate (no frost, no storm,
  no burning) is the mark of the earthly paradise, and Colonna spends a full
  periodic sentence denying each kind of bad weather in turn.
- **the two mulberries and the sweeter-than-Salmacis springs** continue the motif
  of water; Salmacis's spring (the Hermaphrodite's, ch. XXIII) recurs as the
  benchmark for sweetness.

[p. 298]

In this pleasant and delightful enclosure, between the greenest myrtle-grove and
this flowery orange fence encircling, innumerable and mingled animals, shut in,
roamed loosely — however nature, unlike, repugned — harmless and tame. They wandered
there in mutual friendship. And first the goat-born satyrs with their pendent and
twisted little horns; the two-horned fauns, with the other sex. Then the half-wild
stags, and the rock-seeking roes, and the timid does, the spotted fawns, the leaping
kids; the long-eared hares; the timid rabbits; the cat-kind, white and yellow
weasels, and the lying *gallante*; restless squirrels, and drowsy dormice; the
fierce unicorns, and *tragopan* and *tragelaphus* [goat-stag]; every leonine kind
without any fierceness, but playful; the long-necked giraffes, swift gazelles; and
infinite other animals, intent on the solaces of nature.

Beyond this cloister, then, toward the centre, I found the magnificence of an
excellent orchard, or delightful pleasure-ground — such as never could humans, not
only order, but, I persuade myself, so much as think. It is easy, then, that the
second workers act according to the first worker. And I too consent to this, that
no wit so fecund is found that could singly avail worthily to publish somewhat, by
report, of so many most excellent works of this sacred place. Let the hanging
gardens built by King Syrus yield here. Wherefore I rightly judged that by no
other, but only by a divine artificer, was so most exquisite a conception, for the
contemplation of the fostering goddess of nature, produced to such order and effect
most becomingly.

Which most admirable garden, stretched toward the centre, of 166 paces and a half,
divided into meadows. Which division stood by passages straight to the centre, and
circularly transverse, five paces wide. The primary meadows, in the first line of
their squaring toward the enclosure, with the lateral ones, were 50 paces. But the
fourth line, toward the centre, decremented; and from this line took its dimension
the first line of the second meadow, and in the same manner the third meadow was
squared. Because the force of the lines tending to the centre caused the narrowing,
and the straitness of these meadows and of the streets; and therefore the squaring
was deformed, the transverse ones remaining in their integrity.

Which streets were pergola'd, and in each ridge was a little dome upon four Ionic
columns, the shaft or their tallness being of nine diameters of their lowest
thickness. And here and there of the passages, or streets, were tomb-shaped
platforms of finest marbles, with most becoming lineaments. And every four
diameters stood one of the aforesaid columns. Such columniation, and
intercolumniation, was observed throughout.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The tame-beast catalogue is secure and vivid; the garden
geometry that follows is technical and rendered literally, including Colonna's key
admission about the shape of the compartments. This is the middle ring — the
*prati* — with its measurement of 166½ paces, the *semitertio* Segre's whole
reconstruction depends on.

- **The tame animals in mutual friendship** — the peaceable-kingdom motif of the
  King's-garden *bosco* (Segre §the bosco): satyrs, fauns, stags, hares, giraffes,
  lions "without any fierceness," even unicorns, roaming loose among the trees.
  Colonna makes the whole outer island a menagerie of harmless beasts, a status
  symbol of the highest-rank garden.
- **"166 paces and a half"** — the width of the middle ring, the *semitertio*
  ("half of a third," a third of the radius), the exact figure Segre uses to scale
  Cythera's three concentric zones (GARDENS.md §5). The 240 fruit-trees-and-meadows
  of the world's middle ring come from here.
- **the *quadrati illegitimi***, stated outright — "the squaring was deformed…
  because the lines tending to the centre caused the narrowing." This is Colonna
  admitting that his radial compartments are not true squares but trapezes,
  distorted by the circular plan (GARDENS.md §5, "illegitimate squares"). He knows
  the geometric cost of a round garden and accepts it. The world's island wedges
  reproduce exactly this trapezoidal narrowing toward the centre.
- **"the hanging gardens built by King Syrus"** — the Hanging Gardens of Babylon
  (attributed here to a "King Syrus," i.e. Semiramis's line); the one built garden
  Colonna's invented one is meant to surpass.

## Notes

**Confidence: low.** This is the hardest page yet: a single continuous description
of one topiary-and-vase-and-fountain structure, in Colonna's most compressed
technical Italian, with several words that are either coinages or corrupt (`gampsado`,
the "haired" *pili*, `strongyla`). The overall shape is recoverable — box trained up
out of vases into arches, balls, an oval finial, and eagles — but individual clauses
are provisional, and I have rendered them literally with bracketed glosses rather
than smoothing. **A reviewer should treat this whole page as unsettled and work from
the facsimile woodcut, which shows the structure.**

- **The topiary fountain-tree in full.** The box is trained out of the antique
  vases and up into an elaborate tiered structure: arches ("triangles pierced"),
  hanging balls, a jewel or ring at the top, then six more stocks, a little cupola,
  an oval finial with four openings, and **a flying eagle perched at each corner**,
  crowned with a cone or globe. It is a piece of living architecture in clipped
  box, and the most virtuosic topiary in the book after the Hercules-labours grove.
- **`pili`** — "hairs," rendered literally, but here meaning the thin trained
  shoots of box drawn up in an even line; the whole vocabulary of the trained plant
  is borrowed from anatomy (hairs, belly, head), which is characteristic but makes
  the mechanics hard to follow.
- **the eagles "in the act, beak in prospect"** — poised as if about to fly, beaks
  forward. Left literal.
- This is the page most in need of the woodcut; the marked-low confidence is
  deliberate.

In the middle intersit of the levelled, most solid inlay of the peristyle was a

which a most slender thread of water leapt forth. And through the gaps or intervals
of the box columns it issued, dewily moistening the whole meadow. The interstice of
which watch-tower was clear and pervious. The stone-work was all of finest jasper,
reddening and lustrous, adulterated drop-wise with infinite spots of manifold

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The central hydra-fountain and the four-step herb platforms
are secure in their scheme; one anatomical clause of the three intertwined golden
hydras is dense but the image (three snakes knotted, spouting from their three
forked heads into a shell basin) is clear.

- **The hydra-fountain at the peristyle's centre** — a shell basin holding a
  jasper vase supported by three golden many-tailed hydras knotted together,
  spouting water from their forked throats, with eight little gold pipes above
  throwing fine jets that dew the whole meadow. This is the true fountain at the
  heart of each first-ring meadow, beneath the box-topiary canopy of the previous
  pages.
- **the four-step herb platforms at the corners** — stepped square planters, each
  step a different fragrant herb: basil and chervil, thyme "gracious to the
  honey-making bees," southernwood, and Celtic spikenard at the top. A scented
  garden in miniature at every meadow-corner, kept shorn even. The whole *prati*
  ring is, on this evidence, as much a garden of *smell* as of sight — which
  matches Segre's reading of the inner gardens as organised by fragrance.
- **`glyciacon`** — an obscure herb-name (perhaps from γλυκύς, sweet); glossed by
  Colonna himself as "nectary, or southernwood," so the identification is his.
- The catalogue of the *prati*'s planting continues on the following pages.

not produce, nor such trees as Juno commanded to be grafted in her gardens; whereby
they might be called *pomarii aphyracori* [orchards of golden apples].

**Confidence: low.** The corner herb-and-fruit scheme of the second ring is

- **The corner planters of the second ring** repeat the first ring's four-step
  form, but faced in **black amber** rather than jasper, and planted with the four
  fragrant herbs: cassia, nard, mint, and marjoram (*amaracus*). Each carries a

  rubbed" (its static charge, straight from Pliny) and wept by the **Phaethontides**

- **the pear varieties** — musk, Crustumian, Syrian, *curmunduli*: the second order
  of the *prati* is pears where the first was apples, matching Segre's sequence
  (apples, then pears, then plums, GARDENS.md §5). The exact list is damaged in the
  source.
- This page and p. 300, 303 are the low-water mark of the chapter's legibility; the

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The summary of the *prati*'s perpetual fecundity, the
rose-catalogue, and the beginning of the peristyle that closes the middle ring are
all secure.

- **The perpetual garden.** Colonna states the paradise-condition plainly: the
  fruits and flowers here are evergreen, "not subject to the lunar changes nor the
  paling of Phoebus," fruiting and flowering in one unchanging state — the fruit
  trees bear whatever the season, which is precisely the property Hunt singles out
  at Cythera (GARDENS.md §6, "Cythera's fruit trees bear fruit whatever the
  season"). This is the textual root of that reading.
- **the rose-catalogue** — Damascene, Praenestine, five-petalled, Campanian,
  Milesian, and the rest: all Pliny's rose-varieties, "nor sooner did one fall than
  another succeeded" — the self-renewing rose that the Adonia rite (ch. XXIV) will
  make miraculous.
- **the eustyle peristyle** closing the *prati* — a bellied colonnade with a
  latticework wall bounds the middle ring from the inner. *Eustyle* is Vitruvius's
  best intercolumniation (2¼ diameters); Colonna names the order precisely, as
  always. The description of this dividing colonnade continues on the next pages,
  leading to the river and the inner terraces.
- **the jasper chests "mirroring air, fronds and flowers"** — the polished stone
  planters reflect the garden, so that art holds nature's image: the paragone once
  more, and a neat closing image for the *prati*.

- **The columns' seven stones**, in order: *hexacontalithos* (green, sixty-coloured),

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** A bird-catalogue, the aviary counterpart to the plant-lists,
secure in its identifications; every bird is a metamorphosis-myth, which is the point
— an aviary of transformed humans. The Greek-Latin bird-names are Pliny's and
Ovid's.

- **An aviary of the transformed.** Colonna's birds are almost all people turned to
  birds: **Daedalion** (grieving, cast himself down and became a hawk); **Picus**
  (turned to a woodpecker by Circe — cf. p. 365, his faithfulness to Canens);
  **Aedon**, **Procne**, **Itys**, **Tereus** (the whole Ovidian nightingale-and-
  hoopoe family, Tereus keeping his crown as the hoopoe's crest and crying *pou
  pou*); **Antigone** turned to a stork; **Periclymenus** the shape-shifter. It is
  the transformation-key of the fountain chapter (ch. XXIII) extended into a garden
  of shapes — the island of love is populated by the metamorphosed.
- **the Phoenix "singular, but not here"** — a nice aside: the unique phoenix cannot
  be *among* the many birds of the aviary, since there is only one of it. Colonna's
  wit.
- **Tereus's cry "pou pou, pu, pu"** — the hoopoe's call, rendered as the Greek
  *ποῦ* ("where?"), as if Tereus forever asks where his victims are. Kept
  phonetically.
- This aviary closes the *prati* description; the river and the crossing to the
  inner terraces follow.

## Notes

**Confidence: high.** This is Colonna's own scale-plan of Cythera, given both as a
labelled diagram and as a prose gloss, and it is clear arithmetic. **This is the
single most important page for the world's reconstruction of the island.**

- **The measured plan of Cythera, in the book's own numbers.** The island is a
  circle three miles round, one mile in diameter, divided into three concentric
  *tertii*. The diagram labels the zones from shore to centre: the shore, the myrtle
  enclosure, the grove enclosure, the peristyle, then the **bosco (20 paces wide)**,
  the **paving (14)**, and the central **theatre (25)**; the three meadow-orders at
  **58, 48, 38 paces**; the **semitertio at 166½**; the orange-cloister; and the
  **river**. Segre's reconstruction (GARDENS.md §5), which the world's
  `_buildCytheraIsle` is built from, is a direct transcription of this diagram —
  and here at last is Colonna's own label for every ring the island renders.
- **the *semitertio*** — "half of a third," a third of the radius, 166 paces 10
  palms: the width of each concentric zone, and the figure quoted on p. 298 and
  p. 292. Now shown to be exactly one-sixth of the diameter, with the arithmetic
  worked in the open.
- **the trapezoidal meadows again** — the plan confirms that the meadows "did not
  have their boundary up to the completion of the third," being contracted "to
  avoid the straitness of the squarings" — the *quadrati illegitimi* of p. 298,
  stated a third time. The design's one geometric compromise, fully owned.
- This page should be treated as the canonical reference for the island's
  proportions; the world's ring radii can be checked against it directly.

[p. 312]

— graciously covered, offered itself of most gratifying grassiness, as is
sufficiently described and narrated before.

The boundary of the recounted space ended in flowering banks of a most limpid
river, more so than Argyrondes in Aetolia, and more than Thessalian Peneus. The
banks of which were of precious greenest Spartan stone, like the Tiberian Augustan,
planked platewise, and the whole river hedged about between these marble limits.
Which banks were not entangled, nor occupied by *siler*, nor by willow-beds, nor by
osiers, nor by little reed — but the most purged and silvery waters, let in, hedged
them. The surface of which appeared, with celebrated and manifold flowers, most
delightful and beautiful. Which springing and flowing river, by passages and pipes
underground, in diverse and constituted places gushed out in order; and then, by
aqueducts of finest stone swiftly running, watered this solacing and happy site
everywhere evenly with a pleasant murmur.

The waters then pouring headlong into the neighbouring sea. And in this manner the
most clear river, exhausting its increment through the distributed devouring
outlets, did not overabound, but persisted at a perennial evening-out and content.
Which was in breadth twelve paces. The springing veins of which exceeded any
celebrated fountain, and even Cabille of Mesopotamia, more excellent. Nor did the
Virgin Castalia make such a one of hers. As these rendered the waters sweet,
fragrant, musky, and pure, sixteen palms deep — for of so most sweet a source the
fountain of Hercules in Gades did not so abundantly flow. Which were purified,
limpid and subtle in such a manner that they did not occupy the medium between the
sense and the object, nor make it disproportionate; but everything in the open
bottom throughout, as it subsided, was seen perfect. And with mirror-emulation they
rendered whole the things presented. The bottom was flattened of golden sand, full
of fine pebble-stones of manifold most shining colouring.

The greening, leafy and moist banks of which were most adorned with flowering
narcissi, and the emetic bulb, or water-loving sea-onion. Nor were lacking the
hyacinth and the lilies of the valley, and corn *xiphion*, and Illyrian. Here were
copious the marsh-marigold, and the horsetail, or mare's-tail, and the lion's. Infinite
violets — Tusculan, marine, Callatian, autumnal — and the balm-mint, or *cimiadon*, or
*trachiotis*, and other most noble riverside shoots. With innumerable little river-
birds. Here the halcyon of cerulean feathers, and other sudden little water-fowl.
Here the gluttonous and swimming swans, pleasing in the auspices, with the last song
of the meandering waters.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The river and its banks — its marble revetment, its
underground feed and sea-outlets, its crystalline clarity, and its water-plants and
birds — are all secure. The optical praise of the water (below) is a precise little
piece of medieval sense-theory.

- **The ring-river, in full.** Twelve paces wide, sixteen palms deep, marble-banked,
  fed by hidden pipes and drained to the sea so it never floods — a perfectly
  regulated circular canal. This is the river of Segre's plan (GARDENS.md §5) that
  separates the middle *prati* from the inner terraces, and which the world roofs
  with the citrus pergola (the pergola itself is on p. 313).
- **the water "did not occupy the medium between the sense and the object"** —
  Colonna's optics: perception works through a transparent *medium*, and this water
  is so pure it adds nothing of its own, so the bottom is seen "perfect," undistorted.
  It is the same claim made of Venus's crystalline fountain-water (ch. XXIII) and of
  the island's crystal shores (p. 293) — clarity as the mark of the divine.
- **the bank-plants and halcyon** — narcissus (the transformed youth again),
  sea-onion, hyacinth (another metamorphosis), violets; and the halcyon (Alcyone,
  turned to a kingfisher) and swans "pleasing in the auspices." The transformation-
  motif runs even through the waterside flora and fauna.
- **Castalia, Cabille, Gades** — the Castalian spring at Delphi, a Mesopotamian
  fountain, and Hercules's spring at Cadiz: the famous waters this river surpasses.

[p. 313]

Upon the aforesaid most admirable banks, on one side and the other, were inlay-wise
distributed bitter-oranges, citrons and lemons. From trunk to stock the interval
three paces. Which stocks, a pace high from the ground, began to spread their
branches, meeting one with another, and most excellently entangling, rendered an
arch, from earth to the topmost bend three paces.

The remaining branches then, from one bank to the other over the river, opposite one
another, with artful conjoining and social embrace, vaulting and enveloped, pleasantly
shaded — in a most excellent pergola-work. The surrounding of which, with leafy
density elegantly heaped, with the show of an even shearing, or clipping, one frond
not exceeding another save with utmost grace and loveliness, rendering most placid
shade, and, by the sweet breath of Favonius, tremulous and fanning, full of
nourishment, that made its greenery lustrous, as in the first sprouting they showed
themselves — with the whitening little flowers, and pendent fruits, fit hiding-places
of the plaintive Philomela, ever most sweetly lamenting, singing, perfectly without
echo, by the daughter Glaucopis of high and lightning Jove made clean and most
purged, resounding. Which pergola-work, from the topmost convex down to the raised
water, stood seven paces. Oh, with what allurement and sweetest suggestion to its
contemplation it easily drew the wandering eyes! For in that river ran certain
skiffs and little boats of golden material, delightfully covered, with many long-
haired girls, fair-tressed and Alphesiboean, wreathed with fragrant and various
flowers, rowing — in limpid and crisp and saffron shifts, or smocks, everywhere
edged with gold, over the nymphish nude, clothed and girt with a wanton adornment,
not impeding the sight to offer voluptuously the rosy flesh covered; nay, by the
spring breezes voluptuously impelled and pressed upon the admirable women, it
excellently revealed the delightful little form and any other part according to its
motion, with the whitest and half-appled breasts unclosed to the rounding of the
little nipples with the greatest and voluptuous grace, elegantly girded with gemmed
gold Phrygian bands — with many youths of every warlike nation, gesticulating,
brawling, rushing among themselves in play, laughing at the naval fight, contending
persistently against those attacking them; intently keen on the spoils, they
overturned their skirts and carried them off; the girls remained despoiled and
stripped in the waters without favour, nor made resistance against their harm, but
festively solaced themselves. These being then left, mocking among themselves, made
new fights one with another, submerging the seized little boats; and so the submerged
gave work to the rams in the water of —
