## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The citrus-pergola over the river and the boating-game of
nymphs and youths are secure; the long sentence describing the girls' wind-pressed
shifts is euphemistic-erotic in the original and rendered at the same level.

- **The citrus pergola over the river.** Bitter-orange, citron and lemon planted on
  both banks three paces apart, their branches trained to arch and meet over the
  water into a continuous fruiting tunnel seven paces high — the *vaulted pergola of
  citrus trees trained into architecture* of Segre's plan (GARDENS.md §5), and
  exactly what the world's Cythera renders as the eight citrus-pergola arches over
  the ring-river. Here is its full description: a shaded, fanning, flowering tunnel,
  the nightingale's covert.
- **the mock naval battle of the boating nymphs** — girls in gold-edged shifts row
  golden skiffs while youths capsize them in a playful water-fight, the girls
  "despoiled and stripped in the waters… but festively solaced themselves." A
  Venus-island erotic game, staged on the ring-river. The world's river is empty of
  them; a future pass could add the boats.
- **"Philomela… by the daughter Glaucopis of Jove made clean"** — the nightingale
  (Philomela, tongueless in myth) here sings "without echo," her voice purified by
  Glaucopis (grey-eyed Athena). The transformation-birds recur even here.
- **Favonius** — the west wind of spring; **Alphesiboean** — an epithet from
  Theocritus for beautiful girls "who bring in many oxen" (as bride-price).

[p. 314]

— to recover and renew the playful battle, with festive and pleasing solace, with
the gracious cheeks laughing girlishly, mingled, and sharp cries leaping and
gesticulating.

Moreover the water was copious with manifold fishes, of form beautiful, and various,
and outstanding, with their scaling of golden and grey-green colour; nature,
reluctant, opposed nothing here, so that they were secure and did not flee timid.
Some of such bigness that, as bearers, they conveniently bore the girls, mounted,
to the solacing battle — embracing with their snowy calves and comely little feet
the scaled and yielding bodies, which without any fishy stink swam softly, and here
and there twisting, and willing to do the women's bidding, one drawing the other.
Heaped together were the white swans, with the voice sent forth with the tears poured
out for beloved Phaethon; and otters and beavers, with other water-animals, all most
joyously beneath the topiary covering made festival to voluptuous delight, without
other pondering — so that nothing arose to cause molestation to their pleasure and
solace, nor anything displeasing to oppose it — a silent desire sprouting again in
my soul. In this happy place I would willingly still, with my goddess Polia, wish to
dwell eternally. But then, every other roving desire extinguished and repudiated,
without delay I fell back to my most firm intent, in the unique love of my most
beloved Polia. Nonetheless I judged this without doubt a thing super-excellent, and
super-delightful, above any delight, above every sweetness of pleasure.

Likewise, in the first circular and wooded enclosure of the groves, creatures of the
one and the other sex, ever within that same hedge, dwelt with those animals
appointed to pleasure. In the greening meadows within the peristyle, by another
turning, I saw innumerable youths and outstanding girls, intent on solaces, on
sounds, and songs, on dances, and delightful conversations, and pure and sincere
embraces, given over to adornment and personal cultivation, to compose muse-songs,
and to various works the studious and devoted damsels — where I judged virtue to be
more affected than any other lascivious pleasure.

Beyond then this most clear and delightful river, with a continuous circling, was a
grassy meadow as great as that which stretches from the peristyle to the river. This
river was passable by symmetrical bridges, built with wondrous and exquisite skill,
delineated of most excellent marble, alternately one of porphyry and the other of
serpentine, shining with splendid brightness, preserving the lineament of the roads
tending toward the middle navel of that mysterious island, verdant with every
fecundity of delights.

After the aforesaid meadow began seven steps, level and pedal in front, circling
continuous; in height they climbed seven feet, and in breadth —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The end of the boating-game (fish that carry the girls,
swans, otters), Poliphilo's moralised recollection of Polia, and then the crossing:

- **The porphyry-and-serpentine bridges over the ring-river.** The roads that run to
  the island's centre cross the river on alternating porphyry / serpentine bridges,
  "preserving the lineament of the roads." Segre's plan carries these radial
  bridges; the world's twenty radial roads could gain them at the river-crossing.
- **the seven-step terraces begin here.** "After the meadow began seven steps… in

  the theatre (GARDENS.md §5), the feature the world's Cythera leaves flat. Pages

  triumphs. This is the material for the deferred terrace pass.
- **Poliphilo turns from the pleasure-island back to Polia** — the recurring moral
  beat: he admits the place is "super-excellent… above every sweetness," then
  "extinguishes every roving desire" and returns to "the unique love of my most
  beloved Polia." Colonna keeps the erotic garden inside a frame of fidelity.
- **swans weeping for Phaethon** — the Heliades, Phaethon's sisters, turned to
  poplars (here conflated with swans); another metamorphosis among the water-fowl.

[p. 315]

— as much, of marble work, one of red streaked *triglia*, and one of blackish stone,
blacker than the chisel could withstand, and of greater hardness than the most
illustrious Paduan of its own nature — without the rubbing of a cylinder, or with fine
powder and soot; excluding the rule of the sextant or the *dodrans* thickness, nor
with a foot-and-a-half's setback, nor two feet, but as is recounted above, and by such
measuring all the rest.

Upon the topmost step of the blackest stone stood forward an encompassing and elegant
little colonnade of *pycnostyle* spacing, its continuity interrupted, or intervalled,
by the rule of the breadth of the bridges, which observe that of the roads. These
excellent bridges were duly roofed by the immaculate pergola over the river; and
although the roads tended directly to the centre, the steps were not on that account
cut through from their whole circling. Then, as just said, above the ascent of the
steps there was, of the little columns, as much opening as the width of the paths
afforded. But the royal way tending straight to the gate of the wondrous circus,
opportunely excluded from the narrowing of the lines toward the centre, stood alone,
even, and uniform in its breadth, and its rise over the steps sloped most conveniently
walkable; and so in this place the stairs were necessarily found discontinuous.

Which pycnostyle, with its doubled little columns, the plinths of the bases — of
which, by an ant-like distribution, one made mutual contact with another at the angles
by a diagonal line, set into the straight faces with successive coupling — between
every two, one of alternated colouring of most shining outstanding jasper, and between
every seven, one square of red, capped with a translucent gilt-bronze sphere; and the
others likewise, bound and girt with a little architrave, frieze, and cornice of the
material and colour of the square one, with most decent lineaments. Above the little
columns' capitals, the interspaces were of chalcedony, six in number, one between two
of green jasper spotted with manifold flecks, with due and companionable distance.

Upon which most pleasant pycnostyle I saw, wantonly running about and pausing,
innumerable peacocks — whitening, red, and some fanned with their own colour, and
others with their much-admired feathers let down — and there, intermixed here and
there, all the species of parrots, with no mediocre adornment and delightful show upon
the said work.

The fronts of the steps were seen carved wonderfully with noble and Assyrian
knotwork; and for its greater relief, the intercarving was gracefully stuffed full of
material, in the red ones azure, and in the black ones with a whitening filling.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The technical description of the terrace-steps (red and black
marble), the pycnostyle colonnade crowning the top step, its doubled jasper and red
columns with gilt-bronze sphere finials, the peacocks and parrots, and the Assyrian
knotwork inlaid on the step-fronts. All secure; the architectural vocabulary
(*pycnostyle*, *dodrans*, plinth) is Vitruvian.

- **The colonnade on the terraces, and how the roads cut them.** The top step of the
  seven-step flight carries a *pycnostyle* (closely-spaced) colonnade of paired
  columns, broken only where the radial bridge-roads pass through. The one straight
  "royal way" to the central theatre-gate keeps a constant width and a walkable ramp;
  the other roads narrow toward the centre, so the steps there go discontinuous. This
  is precisely the ringed-terrace-plus-radial-road geometry of Segre's plan.
- **the gilt-bronze sphere finials and jasper columns** — every seventh column a red
  square topped with a gilt-bronze globe, the rest jasper: a rhythm of 1-in-7, the
  island's sevenfold number again (seven steps, seven stones, seven terraces).
- **peacocks and parrots on the colonnade** — the Juno-bird (peacock) and the
  many-coloured parrot crown the terrace, the aviary continuing up the rings.
- **Assyrian knotwork inlaid red-on-azure / black-on-white** — the interlace band on
  the step-fronts; a concrete pattern the world's terraces could carry as an inlay
  texture (cf. the world's `_knotTexture`).

[p. 316]

From this much-admired colonnade up to the following steps, it was levelled into a
circling marble path, six feet in breadth. Where immediately began another seven steps
to climb, with the aforesaid work, measure, and material, and colouring — and all this
was kept entire in what follows.

Upon the topmost was a box-like excavation, four feet in opening. The hollow of which
was sufficiently deep, and so in those that follow. In which grew a hedge of box, of a
glassy sheen, most pleasingly greening. And, level with the bridges and roads, I beheld
a tower of the said greenery, raised nine feet, and five wide, with an open door
gaping three feet, and six high, and so the following ones.

This first hedge, of three feet's thickness, and six high — and so those that follow —
was seen of densest foliage, and was so disposed of the feathering of its own
tree-growth. Between one tower and the other I saw excellently made a triumph, with
horses drawing a chariot, and preceding the one who triumphs certain sword-bearing
soldiers, and with triumphal spears artfully compacted, varying most beautifully the
works. In another space between towers stood forth a naval Enyo. Between two other
towers, a fleet-battle on land. Between two others, a hunt, and antique fables of love.
With most diligent relief, and most exquisite fashioning. Such an order going round,
varying in its sequences.

Within this first rampart, after an encompassing path — like the lower one, between the
colonnade and the steps, of marvellous tessellation, which offered itself to great
admiration, and an excessively delightful artifice, without doubt to weary all human
sight and sense. Which, at first aspect, I readily judged to be *charaine* carpets laid
out and spread flat upon the level, with all manners of colouring, which for such a
show it fittingly served to express — in the manner of a gracious painting, conducted
into more varied and manifold groupings and figures and signs, with the fit diversity
of colourings, of little pot-herbs, to the required distinction of the feigned work.
Some full of colour, others of dark colouring, some middling; some clearer and gayer,
some leek-green, others of a pale verdure, some less so, and of a somewhat reddish
colouring, with a most pleasant reconciling. The principal figures, containing in
themselves manifold designs, were: between two rhombs, a circle; and a rhomboid
between two circles, alternating continuously in a ring — except in that part where the
ways were providently left to intercalate. Which paths always passed between two
uniform figures.

- **The topiary triumphs — Cythera's living reliefs.** Between the box towers,
  Colonna sets *triumphs shorn in living box*: a triumphal chariot with sword-bearing

  clipped greenery. A future terrace pass could render these as hedge-relief panels
  between the box towers.
- **the box-hedge rampart, in numbers** — hedge three feet thick and six high; towers
  nine feet high, five wide, doorway three by six. Concrete dimensions for the world's
  terrace hedges and their tower-gates.
- **the *charaine*-carpet mosaic of pot-herbs** — the ring between colonnade and steps
  is planted as a living mosaic of coloured herbs (leek-green, pale, reddish) in a
  repeating pattern of rhombs-and-circles, so exact it looks like laid carpets. This
  is the *broderie* parterre in its earliest literary form — the world could carry it
  as a patterned ground-texture on the terrace rings.
- **the sevenfold terraces confirmed** — a second flight of seven steps, "and all this
  kept entire in what follows": the terraces repeat, ring within ring, up to the
  central theatre.

ground-pine, thyme, germander, amethyst and sweet violets, rue, primrose, cyclamen,

- **A planting-plan precise enough to build.** Colonna specifies not only the knot's
  geometry but which herb fills each cell and its colour: marjoram / southernwood /
  ground-pine in the three bands, mountain thyme in the rhomb, germander in its inner
  circle, amethyst violets in the central rose, and so on. This is a literal parterre
  planting-key — the world could render one bed exactly from this page.
- **the hollyhock finials and hyssop spheres** — three-cubit purple hollyhocks rise at the
  diagonal-square centres, box-spheres of hyssop elsewhere: vertical accents punctuating
  the flat knot, "an even law kept in all."
- **the second, nine-square parterre begins** — nine interlocking sub-squares generating
  octagons, the companion pattern that alternates with the first around the ring; its
  planting is given on p. 321.
- This is the densest horticultural page of the whole island; it establishes that Cythera's
  parterres are meant as real, plantable designs, not mere ornament.

[p. 321]

— a rhombic demonstration knotted, with its angles too, and these — both, and the
transverse, and perpendicularly conjoined — and by such mutual commerce, and likewise
these, another octagon within the first they prettily formed, companionably encloistering
the nine squares.

Wherefore all these figurations, joining one with another, under and over and alternating,
rendered graciously an elegant knotwork of manifold figuring. All this square completely
figuring. Which fashionings were lined by plates fixed in the ground, of whitest marble, a
half-*dodrans* their surface thickness, and here and there walling round the simples. Within
which stony enclosure, between the bounds, the little herb-varieties, most evened and thickly,
germinated together to the perfect expression of the figuring; and all this likewise observed
throughout every such composite artfully stood. A show, by Jove, conspicuous, and to the
senses supremely most pleasant.

The pictorial kitchen-garden distribution stood thus: every free square enclosure was
clothed with flowering cyclamen. Its bands, of *myrsinites* (butcher's-broom). The band-bounds
of the others, knotted with the meeting-section, were herbaceous of mountain *polium*. The
four little squares of the crossed section, joined within the square, were all covered with
thyme. The octagons walling round the free squares, with the requisite allotment of little
herbs, stood thus greening: one of *laurentia*. One of tarragon. The third of yarrow. The
fourth of groundsel. The fifth of *diosmo* (buckthorn). The sixth of *terrambula*. The seventh

FOLLOWINGLY, with the kept rule, ascended other seven steps, upon the topmost of which a

— the incense-tree, and the myrtle, which does not germinate in Sabaea, and infinite other

## Notes

**Confidence: high** (for the closing measurement-table, which is arithmetic); medium for the grove
and nymphs above it. This page ends chapter XXI, and its final paragraph is **the canonical radial
breakdown of Cythera from the ring-river to the exact centre** — the companion to p. 311's whole-plan
diagram, and the single most useful page for checking the world's ring radii.

- **The island's radial measure, ring by ring (from the river inward).** The inner semitertio =
  166½ paces, distributed as: **river 12 · meadow-beyond 10 · all seven terrace-flights together 8
  paces 2 feet · path 6 feet · first garden 33 · second garden 27 · third garden 23 · grove 25 ·
  theatre-surround 16 · theatre-to-centre 16.** Together with p. 311 (shore-to-river = the outer
  semitertio) this closes the full one-mile diameter. The world's `_buildCytheraIsle` ring radii
  should be checked directly against these numbers.
- **the aromatic grove and the hidden nymphs** — the innermost planting before the theatre is the
  spice-grove, watered by "sacred founts," where nymphs hide singing "fugitive from sweet Cupid":
  the last, most secret ring before the centre, reserved and shaded. The "newest excepted" nymphs
  who do *not* come out to greet Cupid are the shy initiates — a small narrative touch.
- **the innermost colonnade and the emblematic pavement** — the seventh flight tops out at a
  colonnade (matching the first, by the river) enclosing a *sectile emblem-pavement* of circles,
  triangles, almonds, rhombs and scalene figures: the polychrome-marble floor of the theatre-
  precinct at the island's heart. The theatre of Venus itself opens in ch. XXII.
- **Chapter XXI complete (36/36).** The entire Cythera ekphrasis — shore, meadows, river, terraces,

CHAPTER XXII
------------------------------------------------------------------------

[p. 326]

*(Chapter argument:)*

> HAVING COME OUT FROM THE LITTLE BOAT, TO MEET THEM INFINITE NYMPHS CAME,
> SUPERBLY ARRAYED WITH TROPHIES. POLIPHILO NARRATES ALSO THE MYSTERIOUS
> MANNER IN WHICH THEY OFFERED THE DIVINE INSIGNIA TO CUPID, AND WITH WHAT
> HONORARY PROCESSION, HE BEING SET TO SIT UPON THE TRIUMPHAL VEHICLE; AND
> POLIA AND POLIPHILO, BOTH BOUND, FOLLOWING BEHIND, WITH GREATEST TRIUMPH
> CAME TO THE GATE OF THE MARVELLOUS AMPHITHEATRE — WHICH, BOTH WITHOUT AND
> WITHIN, HE FULLY DESCRIBES.

Sweetly, with a mild breeze breathing zephyr, the comely and golden little wings
of the divine boy softly vibrating, and by his tranquil spirit conveyed, we came to
the ebbing shore. Many and infinite gift-bearing demigoddesses, and notable Nymphs,
of conspicuous beauty, came out with us from the fateful little boat. Straightway, to
meet the divine and winged boy, with a chosen troop, with great apparatus of
ornaments, and of pomps, and sumptuous vestments, with a splendour and cultivation
more than regal, with a most exquisite adornment, especially and solemnly venerating,
of tender and most flourishing little age — most delightfully in pyrrhic dance, with
virginal allurements, and heavenly and illustrious aspect, humbly, and with most
decent attendance, obsequious, all bounteously offered themselves.

And before them all, the sacrificing shrine-bearers, the tower-bearers, and the
jubilant fore-dancers went preceding, with trophies of military ornaments arranged on
gilt spears: with the cuirass of furious Pyroeis; with the other conquered armours;
and with the bow, hanging crosswise, retaining the cuirass; and with the barbed quiver
and the axe bound to the extremities of the bow; and, beneath the cuirass, the
spread-out net; with, set below, the face of a little winged boy, and a twin one; and
an apple affixed to the face, transfixed through the middle by the spear; and at the
summit, the starry helmet.

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The chapter-argument (the whole triumph of Cupid in précis) and
the landing: the nymphs come out with trophies to meet the winged boy, and the first
**trophy of arms** is described piece by piece (cuirass of Pyroeis, bow, quiver, axe,
net, apple, starry helmet, all on a gilt spear). All secure; the trophy-vocabulary is
antique-military.

- **The triumph of Cupid begins.** Chapter XXII is the *triumphal procession* on
  Cythera: the nymphs bear trophies to Cupid, seat him on a triumphal car, and lead the
  whole train — with Polia and Poliphilo bound as captives behind — to the gate of the
  central amphitheatre. This is one of the book's four great Triumphs, and the one that
  frames the world's approach to the theatre of Venus (ch. XXIII).
- **the trophies of arms.** Each nymph bears a *tropaion* — arms hung on a spear in the
  Roman manner. The first carries a cuirass (of "furious Pyroeis," one of the Sun's
  horses, here a figure of martial ardour), bow, quiver, axe, a net, an apple, and a
  starry helmet: the disarmed panoply of Mars, taken by Love. The apple is Venus's.
- **pastophorae, pyrgophorae, antiludiae** — shrine-bearers, tower-bearers, and
  fore-dancers: Colonna's Greek-coined names for the ranks of a sacred procession. The
  triumph is staged as a religious rite, not a military parade.
- The following pages (327–328) itemise the rest of the trophies, several carrying
  emblematic inscriptions (**QUIS EVADET?**, **NEMO**).

[p. 327]

Another was bearing yet another trophy. On the point was a little band of laurel;
beneath it, a pair of wings of blackest eagle, outspread; and then, set below, lay the
face of a most noble boy. There followed, and then, crosswise, two thunderbolts bound
together with little bundles of gold and woven silk, flying; and, likewise bound
crosswise to the spear, a sceptre, holding suspended a superb robe.

A bearer, too, was another, of a trophy: of a helmet, with a buffalo's head; and beneath
it an antique cuirass, with two shields knotted at each brachial outlet; between which
two little bands, one to a side, hung pendent, holding the Cleonean skin, with the
knobbed and gland-knotted, sinewy club.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Two more trophies of arms: the second Jovian (laurel, black-eagle
wings, thunderbolts, sceptre and robe — the disarmed panoply of Jupiter); the third
Herculean (buffalo-headed helmet, cuirass, twin shields, and the Nemean lion-skin with
the knotted club). All secure; the attributes identify the gods whose arms Love has taken.

- **Love disarms the gods.** The trophies are a systematic inventory of surrendered divine
  weapons: Mars's cuirass (p. 326), now **Jupiter's** thunderbolts, sceptre and eagle-
  wings, and **Hercules's** lion-skin and club. Cupid triumphs over the strongest of the
  gods — the *omnia vincit Amor* topos made into a parade of captured arms.
- **the Cleonean skin and knobbed club** — the Nemean lion (killed near Cleonae) and
  Hercules's olive-wood club, his unmistakable attributes; here hung as spoils. Even the
  hero of the twelve labours is disarmed by Love.
- **"a sceptre holding suspended a superb robe"** — the royal insignia (Jupiter's, or a
  king's) reduced to a trophy-ornament: sovereignty itself hung on Love's spear.
- Short page (the woodcut of these trophies takes most of the leaf); the emblematic
  trophies with inscriptions follow on p. 328.

[p. 328]

Next in sequence, one raised a trophy with special polish. On a point passed off the
topmost spear-shaft; descending below it, a covering over a rounding half a sextant
thick, resupine in the manner of a plate, in the middle of which was carved a circled
formula. Which a small vase-stalk suppressed. Then a tablet with this majuscule writing
subjacent:

> **QUIS EVADET?**
> — "Who shall escape?"

To this an apple was set below, and next another rounding, like the upper but smaller.
Walled round by a rim, and superimposed upon a solid, or massy, little dish. From which,
continued, descended a longish baluster, and then a little basin.

Likewise another Nymph carried a spear. On the pointed end was an egg-shaped figure, with
a bossed little rim in a circle, and in the middle a sapphire rounding, imitating the
figure, an inch thick; set under it, a small board, thus with the title:

> **NEMO**
> — "No one."

And between two wings the spear, somewhat balustered, passed through. At the bottom a
little dish followed, as is recounted above.

## Notes

**Confidence: high** (the two inscriptions are read straight from the woodcut; the trophy-
description is secure). Two emblematic trophies bearing the paired mottoes **QUIS EVADET?**
("Who shall escape?") and **NEMO** ("No one") — one of the most famous devices in the whole
book, and one Colonna clearly means to be read as a single sentence.

- **"QUIS EVADET? — NEMO."** Read together across the two trophies: *Who escapes Love? No
  one.* The question and its answer are split between two spears carried in sequence, so the
  procession itself utters the sentence as it passes. This is the emblematic heart of the
  triumph — Love's universal dominion stated as a call-and-response.
- **The device's afterlife.** The *QUIS EVADET* trophy — a candle/vessel guarded by the
  motto — became one of the most-copied images from the 1499 woodcuts. Here its original
  context is restored: it is a trophy in Cupid's triumph, paired with **NEMO**.
- **the sapphire "imitating the figure"** — an egg-shaped sapphire an inch thick set as the
  centre of the NEMO trophy: Colonna's habitual precise gemmology, even on a parade-standard.
- Together with pp. 326–327, five trophies now precede the car; the triumphal vehicle itself
  is described in the pages following.

[p. 329]

Consequent was another most noble trophy, borne aloft. On the high spear-shaft a sphere
stood forth upon a *pyrronium*, between an inflected lunar-crescent of two little wings,
subtly leafed with gold foil, one leaf pressed page-wise upon the other.

The remainder of which, forced into a circling, rendered a crown held by a little band,
through the middle of which the spear, slightly balustered, passed perpendicularly. Under
the crown a little basin, with the bottom of an ewer-vase descending upon the oarage of
two conjoined wings. Then an egg-shaped figure, with a byssus-boss coruscating in the
navel. Fixed under this was a sphere, scored melon-wise, with flying little bundles
opportunely bound in.

Many others, of prolix telling: the standard-shafts of which — some of ebony, others of
red, citrine and white sandalwood, and of whitest ivory, and gilt, and covered with
silver, and of other precious woods. Every thing skilfully fashioned of most tenuous gold,
silver, and of polished material, and formed of green silk, and of every other gracious
colouring, with pleasant flowering. Multiply adorned with gems in the fit places, every
thing harmoniously destined and conspicuously applied, with pendent vertebrae —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Another emblematic trophy (crescent-wings, crown, ewer, byssus-boss,
melon-scored sphere), then a general account of the trophies' precious materials — ebony,
tricolour sandalwood, ivory, gold, silver, silk, gems. All secure; a passage of pure
material inventory.

- **The trophy-standards are luxury objects.** Colonna pauses to say the whole set is made
  of ebony and sandalwood shafts, ivory, gilt and silvered metal, green silk and gems — the
  triumph of Love is also a display of the goldsmith's and joiner's art, "every thing
  harmoniously destined." The world could render the trophy-standards as jewelled poles.
- **the crescent-and-crown trophy** — winged crescent, a crown held by a band, an ewer on
  paired wings, a gemmed egg: another disarmed-panoply device in the series, its meaning left
  to the emblem rather than an inscription.
- **byssus** — sea-silk; a boss of it "coruscating in the navel" of the egg-figure. Colonna's
  taste for rare materials extends to the smallest ornament.
- The next standard (p. 330) carries a winged Cupid treading an apple and the Greek title
  **DORYKTETOI** — "the spear-won."

— or little whorls of precious stones, pierced, through which was drawn a golden filament;

Before all these trophy-bearers ran an outstretched and displayed one: the standard-bearing

winged Cupid, unveiled, in the act of drawing with the bow, treading upon an apple; at the

ewer-vase. And there it was ensnared: the little bands, licking above the interval of the
jewel, burst out flying. Within the content of the circle was a tablet, through the
thickness of which the spear bored, and through a sphere superimposed on the tablet in the
middle of the outer part; and so in its lowest part another, subjacent, penetrated. Likewise
in the abacus-work, on both the left and right side, a little spear-shaft jutted somewhat,
passed through the jewel, and stood forth outside. From the one and the other jutting pendant

orifice, in a balustered opening, bit an egg-shaped figure, with lineaments imitating the
form. With two little apples above the circumference, one to a side, in the middle of the
diameter; at the bottom another sphere. Lastly a golden little knot, with varied texture,
fluttering. On the tablet, on the one and the other face, was, in Greek majuscules, this
title:

> **ΔΟΡΥΚΤΗΤΟΙ** (DORYKTETOI)
> — "The spear-won" (captives taken by the spear).

## Notes

**Confidence: medium** (high for the inscription). The gloved dancers and their gold-thread
work, then the two lead standards of the triumph: the boat's own standard, and the great
**celibar** crowned with a winged, unveiled Cupid drawing his bow and treading an apple,
inscribed on both faces **ΔΟΡΥΚΤΗΤΟΙ** — "the spear-won." All secure; the standard's tiered
ornament is described in exhaustive goldsmith's detail.

- **ΔΟΡΥΚΤΗΤΟΙ — "the spear-won."** The Greek term for captives taken in war as spoils; on
  Cupid's standard it names *us* — Poliphilo and Polia, and all lovers, as Love's prisoners
  of war. It answers the trophies of disarmed gods: they are the arms, we are the captives.
  The world's triumph-standard could carry this Greek title.
- **the lead standard: Cupid drawing the bow, treading the apple.** The image atop the
  *celibar* is the god himself in action — unveiled, shooting, the apple (Venus's fruit)
  underfoot — the emblem the whole procession serves. This is the visual key to the triumph.
- **the gloved dancers** — even the dancers' needle-worked gloves and jewelled arm-bands are
  itemised; the entire train is a single coordinated work of luxury art.
- Psyche, Cupid's divine bride, is presented next (p. 331), leading the file of companions.

[p. 331]

And many others, trapped-out with much polish of various flowers, fronds, and little
fruits, not without the company of gold and silver foil, and infected with every colouring
encaustically, with infinite ornaments and exquisite elegance of polish — proceeding most
joyously, with many other insignia and victory-marks, and with trophy-ornaments of exuviae
and spoils and plunder, conquered by the potent and divine arrow-shooting boy, preceding
with moderate distance of triumphal procession, and with much applause and divine revel-rout,
and with sounds and guttural jubilees of the quiver-bearers.

Then, first, there presented herself his goddess-wife Psyche, in a queenly robe, with a
villous underlay, and shining with crimson gold, of gold texture triple-twilled and wefted,
clad in lucent silk — such as Hermaria and Malicha of Hesperia do not produce. And, in
sequence, the companions in silken robes of discreet and versicolour dye, sumptuously and
genially clad, with superb habits, unwonted and new, most opulently jewelled — such as our
nature interdicts the human wit to make, step-motherly — with crisp pleats wrinkling over
the delicate and most-clean little bodies, and over the virginal hips, at the soft impulse of
the fresh, restless breezes.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The end of the trophy-train, then **Psyche**, Cupid's divine wife,
leading the file of companion-nymphs, whose sumptuous jewelled silk dress — wind-pressed over
the body, gold-scaled breastplates, pearl-stuffed *phrygium* bands over the breast — is
described in the book's characteristic erotic-textile detail. All secure.

- **Psyche appears, as Cupid's queen.** The soul-bride of the *Cupid and Psyche* myth walks at
  the head of the companions in "a queenly robe… crimson gold." Her presence sets the triumph
  under the sign of the reconciled love of Soul and Love — the myth Apuleius tells, and the
  frame for Poliphilo's own initiation.
- **the wind-pressed dress, again.** As with the boating-nymphs (p. 313), Colonna dresses the
  companions in silk so fine the spring breeze reveals the body beneath — "crisp pleats… over
  the virginal hips." The eroticism is consistent and deliberate: Love's triumph is sensuous.
- **the *phrygium* over the breast** — a pearl-stuffed embroidered band spiralling up to the
  breast-band, "such as was never invented in Phrygia": Colonna's habitual surpassing of the
  famous craft, here the Phrygian embroiderers.
- **"Hermaria and Malicha of Hesperia"** — obscure place-names for fine cloth (the western
  lands); their weave cannot match Psyche's robe. The surpassing-topos on textiles.

[p. 332]

— of little emeralds in pellets stood forth. And in leek-green colour, of ardent rubies in

crimson colour, of most-lucent pyramidal diamonds. In amethystine tincture, or Punic (red),
of just and whitest pearls.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** A long costume-ekphrasis: the companion-nymphs' gems matched to their
dress-colours (emerald on green, ruby, sapphire, diamond, pearl), the range of silks (shorn,
villous, cloth-of-gold, twice-dipped Tyrian, cotton), and the jewelled fillets, hairnets,
tiaras and diadems of their headdresses. All secure; a pure inventory of luxury dress, in the
book's most concentrated jeweller's-catalogue manner.

- **Gems keyed to colours.** Colonna matches each stone to its ground: emeralds on green,
  rubies on leek-green, sapphires on saffron, diamonds on crimson, pearls on amethyst/red — a
  colour-theory of jewels. The nymphs are dressed by a rule, not at random.
- **the fabrics** — a full textile catalogue: pile-velvets in three and four grades, brocaded
  cloth-of-gold-and-silver, zoned (banded) gowns cycling gold/cyan/green/silver, oyster-purple,
  twice-dipped Tyrian, and figured cotton. The company is a walking display of the loom's whole
  range.
- **the six-pearl rose** — a recurring head-ornament: six thick pearls set as a rose around a
  central conoid jewel, worn on the fillet over the forehead. A concrete jewel the world could
  model on the triumph's figures.
- This costume-passage runs on through pp. 333–334 (hair, then footwear); it is descriptive
  rather than architectural, but it establishes the visual key of the whole procession: extreme,
  rule-governed luxury.

wicked collars sumptuously begemmed, with more excellent research of adornment, and in

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The coiffure-passage: the companion-nymphs' hairstyles catalogued
exhaustively — braided napes, crown-whirls bound with pearl-tufts, fore-blown locks, pendant
foil darts behind the ears, hair flowing to the calves; reddish, golden and raven shades; then

- **Hair as a designed object.** Each style is a distinct construction: gathered nape-clumps,
  pointed crown-whirls pinned with pearl-tufts, tendril curls over the temples, veils and
  hairpins for the raven-haired. Colonna treats hairdressing as one of the luxury arts of the
  triumph, on a level with the goldsmithing.
- **"little snares baited with the… birdlime of amorous hearts."** The one interpretive line in
  the catalogue: all this ornament is a *trap* — the coiffure is fowler's lime for lovers'
  hearts. It reminds us the triumph is Cupid's, and its beauty is a weapon (cf. QUIS EVADET /
  NEMO, p. 328).
- **Aesacus** — a son of Priam turned to a diving bird (a "blackish plume"); another
  metamorphosis-simile, for the raven hair. The transformation-imagery persists even into a hair-
  colour comparison.
- Footwear completes the costume on p. 334.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The end of the costume-ekphrasis: the sleeves (upper arm to elbow, then a
gold-woven under-sleeve to the hand), laced with gold cords, the sheer cotton chemise puffing out
at the elbow-slashes; and then Poliphilo's first exclamation — that these nymphs are so pleasing
to "the amorous eyes" one would wish only to gaze forever. All secure.

- **The slashed sleeve, precisely.** Arm covered to the elbow, a gold-woven under-sleeve to the
  wrist, laced at the elbow so the "snowy cotton chemise" pulls through the slash in a puff — the
  exact slashed-and-pouffed sleeve of high-Renaissance dress, described at its point of origin. A
  concrete costume detail for the world's figures.
- **"desire… reconciled itself with the will."** The hinge line: the sight of the nymphs makes
  *desire* and *will* agree — the beginning of the meditation that page 337 develops, on beauty as
  the instrument that overcomes the guarded heart. Colonna is setting up the moral turn.
- **"bright-eyed" (elicopidi)** — *helikōpis*, Homer's epithet for beautiful, quick-glancing eyes;
  applied to the nymphs, and next (p. 337) to Polia herself.
- After this the register changes entirely: p. 337 leaves the catalogue for Poliphilo's anxious
  reflection and the start of Polia's portrait.

[p. 337]

With such provocation that to bitter death a man would offer himself, of his own accord and
willing. O contagious artifice! O alluring ministry, O assaulting siege-engines — which any heart,
however sound, most safe, valid and quiet, and free, and resisting, you easily infect, suddenly
subvert and depopulate, without delay prostrate, without respite perturb, totally subjugate, and
without struggle drag away. To lay low, scatteringly, all moderate, incredible and stubborn
continence. These are those true and infallible satellites of laborious Love, with an amplifiable
number of most-monstrous executioners, ambushing the immune, remote and disjoined reflections, and
excluding those inclined to such subjection from being able by any means, nor with a daring spirit,
to prevail — and, by the presented, inevitable and drawing sweetness, with so shrewd and diligent
study ensnaring, and with subtle wit invented so most-exquisite a working, and to so beautiful and
most-shapely a work by fecund nature herself, an artifice found for destroying, and a choice
adjunct and accessory of torment. Alas — which reasonably ought to be feigned, and used, for marble
statues, and not for human and fragile hearts. For even that noble and divine sex, despoiled and
denuded, supremely torments and infects the imperilled, let alone with this voluptuous addition of
pernicious snares devised. But this alone accrues: that they do not consider it enough to perish of
love naturally, without adding so much increased increment of excogitated modes, to conduct the
wretched and soft lovers to the death of heart-grief more easily, and continually to excite little
sparks extremely incendiary, to quicken the amorous and fervid little flames to consumption —
divine objects, to refill and confound the warm breast with bubbling little sighs, and to ferment
the heart to love. Now I would not know how duly to express by what means so great a foundation of
love, stable and sincere, firmly placed in Polia, felt itself somewhat shaken by these inevitable
and ready ambushes and impetuous violences. Alas, then, within myself I silently repeated: O my
dear little beautiful Polia, guard your won prey! For a great peril is the passage through so many
piratical fallacies, and manifest cut-throats, and little ambushing plunderers — which, against
all sincere rectitude, are for their amorous offence commended and laudably approved, and by the
sad, offended ones so much the more desired, and reverently the more sought, and the more sweetly
loved.

Now, on her most-joyous forehead, under two half-circles like threads of subtle silk, and blackest
brows more than shining amber, two arrow-shooting eyes festively shone, more than the most-
irradiating stars resplendent in the most-limpid sky. And in her aspect more beautiful than
incarnate and fresh roses; and the cheeks not rouged, but with a most-pleasing and genuine redness,
than which —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The moral turn of the chapter: Poliphilo's apostrophe to beauty as "the
satellites of Love" — siege-engines that overthrow even the soundest heart — his confession that his

- **Beauty as siege-engine — the chapter's moral core.** After eleven pages of costume-catalogue,
  Colonna turns on it: all this adornment is "contagious artifice," an "assaulting engine" that
  subjugates the free heart. It ought to be used "for marble statues, not for human and fragile
  hearts." This is the book's recurring ambivalence — the erotic marvel is also a danger — stated

- **Polia's portrait begins.** The catalogue's technique is now turned on Polia herself: silk-thread

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The close of Polia's portrait (cheeks like autumn apples, the Sun-and-
mystery-god comparisons), then the pivot: **Psyche crowns Cupid**, and two named nymphs take charge

- **The nymphs are named allegories.** From here the procession is a sequence of personifications,
  each Greek name a concept: **Toxodora** "bow-giver," **Imeria** (Himeros, "longing/desire"),
  **Erototimoris** "love-honouring," **Ennia** (perhaps *ennoia*, "thought"), and (pp. 339–340)
  Velode, Omonia "Concord," Diapraxe "Accomplishment," Typhlote "Blindness," Aschemosyne
  "Shamelessness," Teleste "Initiator." The triumph is a masque of the aspects of Love.
- **Psyche crowns Cupid** — the soul-bride sets the votive crown on Love's head, "finer than Hiero's"
  (Hiero II of Syracuse dedicated a famous gold votive crown — the one of Archimedes' displacement
  problem). The myth of Cupid and Psyche presides over the whole triumph.
- **Imeria takes Polia, Erototimoris takes Poliphilo** — the two lovers are formally received into
  the procession as its honoured captives, each led by a nymph. This is the moment they join Love's
  triumph as *doryktetoi* (p. 330).
- **"apples of Decius"** — an uncertain reading; likely a place/variety name for a red autumn apple.
  The comparison is to Polia's flushed cheeks.

her right she would not consent to let her long hair, taken up, extend over the fleshy and quivering
buttocks, with unashamed petulance, like a wanton huckstress — but indicating a most-obscene

more than the most-filthy Hostius had in himself, gazing in his hollow mirrors.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The core of the allegorical procession: **Phileda** gathers the flowers Ennia
scatters; **Velode** presents the quiver with the two arrows (**silver = love, leaden = aversion** —
Ovid's arrows of Cupid); **Omonia** and **Diapraxe** play with gold and crystal balls; **Typhlote**
(Blindness) offers the blindfold-veil; her wanton damsels **Asynecha** and **Ardelia** dance; and
**Aschemosyne** (Shamelessness) presents herself nude with a golden sphere. All secure; the names are
glossed from Greek and the attributes are standard.

- **The two arrows of Cupid.** Velode's quiver holds the Ovidian pair (*Metamorphoses* I): the golden/
  silver arrow that kindles love, and the leaden arrow, "cold and inauspicious," that repels it. Love
  wields both — desire and aversion are one god's work. A key emblem for the world's Cupid-figure.
- **the blindfold offered by Typhlote.** Here is the origin-moment of blind Cupid: Blindness herself
  hands him the veil to cover his eyes. Colonna stages the god's blindfolding as a rite of the triumph.
- **the personifications, read as a sequence** — Concord and Accomplishment play (the gold ball never
  meets the crystal: harmony kept by avoidance); then Blindness, Heedlessness, and Shamelessness attend
  — the darker aspects of erotic love, unflinchingly named. Colonna does not sanitise the triumph.
- **Aschemosyne's "Tribade insolence"… Hostius' mirrors** — a frank catalogue of shamelessness
  (Hostius Quadra, the notorious voyeur of Seneca who watched himself in magnifying mirrors). The
  passage is deliberately transgressive; rendered at its own level, plainly.

[p. 340]

— little urn, most-excellently expressed, and of antique artifice, and of an audacity insolent for
human workmanship. Its orifice had contorted striations, which striae, or rivulets, ending
moderately in the middle amplitude of the vase, with most-even distribution somewhat dilated. Then
the comely girt-work descended toward the round bottom, the corpulence little by little thinning,
clothed with an inestimable making of celery-leaf foliage, standing forth from the solid with
egregious separation; and, continued from the lips of the orifice toward the down-slope, twisting
themselves into exquisite foliage, two little handles they rendered, with wondrous relief, and with
a little foot.

Out of which broadish orifice, flying and crackling, with a most-pleasing pop, sparks leapt out,
running lucent through the air; which then, extinguished, fell as ashen sparks.

The other companion, **Capnolina** (Smoke-girl), bore a little goatish, or earthen, vase, with a
narrow orifice, raised somewhat high and thinning at the bottom; and above its dilation, under the
handles, it had circularly, with even distance, thirteen most-measured Greek letters diligently
impressed:

> **ΠΑΝΤΑ ΒΑΙΑ ΒΙΟΥ** (PANTA BAIA BIOU)
> — "All the things of life are little [trifling / short-lived]."

With many other ornaments and obliquing little channels. Which, from the letters toward the orifice,
was polished-smooth. Out of which, and through the vent-holes, leapt forth a misty and sweet-smelling
smoke, resolving into nothing through the air.

## Notes

**Confidence: high** (the Greek inscription and its sense are secure); medium for the two vessels'
ornament. The last of the matrons: **Vrachivia** with an emerald urn that shoots sparks that die to
ash, and **Capnolina** ("Smoke-girl") with an earthen vase inscribed **ΠΑΝΤΑ ΒΑΙΑ ΒΙΟΥ** — "all the
things of life are little/fleeting" — from which fragrant smoke rises and dissolves into nothing. All
secure.

- **"PANTA BAIA BIOU" — the memento-mori at the heart of the triumph.** Amid Love's parade of pomp,
  Colonna sets a smoking vase inscribed *all the things of life are trifling and brief*, its incense
  "resolving into nothing through the air," paired with sparks that "fall as ashen sparks." The triumph
  of Love carries its own vanitas: pleasure and life alike are smoke. This is the philosophical answer
  to QUIS EVADET / NEMO (p. 328) — none escapes Love, and none escapes transience. A key inscription
  for the world's triumph.
- **the two smoke-and-spark vessels** — Vrachivia's emerald urn throws sparks that die; Capnolina's
  earthen vase breathes vanishing incense. Together they stage the brevity of all things as a
  perfumed, sparkling spectacle — beauty and mortality in one image, the book's characteristic
  doubleness.
- **the procession's shape** — the named nymphs have presented, in order, bow, flowers, quiver-and-
  arrows, balls, blindfold, the nude sphere, torch, spark-urn, and smoke-vase: the full regalia and
  the full meaning of Love, ending on transience. The triumphal car itself follows.

> *(The inscription on the smoking vase, continued:)*
> **PANTA** [BAIA BIOU]

Received finally the offered mysterious and fateful love-tokens and fitting insignia, the divine
boy set himself to sit upon a golden and antique car, or triumphal vehicle, there prepared — all
of golden plates, an embroidered band a *dodrans* wide going round all the fringes. In which,
sun-like, shone encloistered ostentatious gems of bigness and unthinkable price, and of
imperceptible artifice and rarest invention, divinely disposed, and orderly destined. With two
vehicular wheels having the circumference of gold, and the spokes proceeding from the central
axle, in which the pole lay; and, fixed in the middle, they were fashioned longish, in balustered
figment, of precious stones various of fulgurant colouring.

roses and various flowering. And behind the pompous and divined car of the prize-bearer and greatest
triumphator we were drawn, softly and willingly, by **Synesia** (Understanding), a most-outstanding
Nymph.

facetiously, of a sudden I was reassured. There followed immediately after us the curious Psyche.

**Confidence: medium.** Cupid takes his seat on the golden triumphal car (all gold-plate, jewelled,
two gold-rimmed wheels with balustered spokes); **Poliphilo and Polia are bound as captives** behind

- **The triumphal car of Love.** A gold chariot bordered with a jewelled band, two gold-rimmed wheels
  on balustered spokes of coloured gemstone — the vehicle at the centre of the world's approach to the
  theatre. Colonna describes it as a goldsmith's object, sun-like with encloistered gems.
- **the lovers bound as captives — the emotional climax of the triumph.** Poliphilo and Polia have
  their arms bound behind them with *rose-garlands* and are led behind the car as Love's *doryktetoi*
  (p. 330): captives, but bound in flowers, "softly and willingly." Poliphilo trembles; Polia and the
  nymphs laugh; he is reassured. This is the image the whole procession was building to — willing
  captivity to Love. The world's triumph should show the two bound in roses behind the car.
- **Synesia leads them** — "Understanding" draws the captive lovers: even in bondage to Love, reason
  attends. Colonna's allegory keeps its balance (cf. Synesia's opposite, blind Typhlote, p. 339).
- **Psyche's diamond** — carved (p. 342) with Cupid wounding himself: the chlamys-jewel that turns the
  Cupid-and-Psyche myth back on the god. "Not Pyrgoteles" (Alexander's gem-engraver) but a divine hand
  cut it.

[p. 342]

— Pythian Apollo. In which — not by the noble Pyrgoteles, but rather divinely — was Cupid most-
excellently carved, cruelly lancing himself, and incautious Psyche handling him with the arrow, with

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The carved diamond on Psyche's shoulder (**Cupid wounding himself while Psyche
handles the arrow** — the myth's peripeteia in miniature); Psyche's lamp and gold-wefted chlamys; the

- **The self-wounding Cupid on the gem.** The chlamys-diamond shows Cupid pricked by his own arrow as
  Psyche handles it — the moment in Apuleius when Psyche's lamp-oil and Cupid's own arrow undo him. Love
  wounded by Love, watched by the Soul: the emblem that governs the whole triumph, worn on Psyche's
  shoulder. Colonna makes the god's power recoil on himself.
- **the serpent-drawn car.** Two great winged skinks (lizard-serpents) in gold-and-gem harness draw the
  chariot "not swiftly, but with a temperament of triumphal procession." A concrete, buildable image for
  the world's triumph-car: serpent-draught, jewelled tack, ceremonial slowness.
- **Psyche's lamp** — she bears the kindled lamp of the myth (by which she first saw Cupid), here made a
  triumphal attribute. Her arrow ("her firebrand") and lamp are the two instruments of the story.
- **the procession's ranks, named** — Colonna gives the marching order as a liturgy: pastophorae,
  trophigerae, faceferariae, splendophorae, osmiferae, euosmiae, then the musicians. The triumph is
  organised as a sacred rite (continued p. 343).

vain, striving to express a particle of the sweetest sounds, of the sweetest canticles, of the solemn
and playful dances and feasts, of the divine Nymphs and notable girls, of their singular and
incomparable beauties. Of the excellent and illustrious and most-elegant adornment — enough to
interrupt and amputate gracious life, and to dissipate and distract every hard and obstinate heart —
rejoicing with various and triumphal insignia, and with alacrity —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The musical procession in full: every antique instrument named (pierced tibia,
ivory-beaten drum, twin tibiae "let Marsyas yield," lyre, cithara, sistrum, steel triangle, horn,
trumpet); the flower-and-jewel crowned singer-nymphs surpassing Apollo, the Muses and Arion; and
Poliphilo's closing *inexpressibility topos* — no eloquent tongue could render a particle of it. All
secure; a catalogue of ancient music and the chapter's rhetorical culmination.

- **The orchestra of the triumph.** Colonna assembles the entire classical instrumentarium — reeds
  (tibia, twin auloi), strings (lyre, cithara), percussion (drum, sistrum, triangle, cymbal), brass
  (horn, trumpet) — played by flower-crowned nymphs "in ordered procession." The world's triumph can
  draw its sound-world directly from this list.
- **surpassing Apollo and Arion** — the singers out-sing Apollo before the Muses, and Arion (saved by
  the music-loving dolphin): the surpassing-topos applied to music, as it was to gardens (Alcinous, p.
  317) and textiles (p. 331). Cythera exceeds every classical superlative in turn.
- **the inexpressibility topos** — Poliphilo ends by declaring the scene beyond any tongue: the standard
  close to a great ekphrasis, here marking the summit of the triumph before it reaches the amphitheatre
  gate. The beauty is again named as lethal — "enough to amputate gracious life."
- **the flower-crowns, keyed** — amethyst violets, amaranth, everlasting, cyclamen, melilot, yellow and
  white violets, with gold foil and pearls: a specific garland-recipe for the musician-nymphs.

— gesticulation advancing; and of so sumptuous and superb a triumph, and of so many delights and
pleasantnesses, and immense amplitude of precious riches and greatest opulences — rather divine
than of nature — to my eyes, by the Cytherean grace and cupidine privilege, openly to see, and
clearly and really to behold, especially indulged.

In the last place, immediately, in front, next to the drawing serpents, two aegipans and wanton
satyrs, with goatish beards, with goat-feet and cloven, proceeded. Which lewd ones, joyous, with
little wreaths of flowering *satyrion*, and of flowers of *helenium* and of *cynosorchis* (orchid),
pressing down the unkempt hair over the wrinkled forehead, crowned. Each bore a monster, rudely cut
in wood, and gilt, effigied human, clothed: from the three-heads to the diaphragm only; the rest, in
a square, tapering to the lower part, passed off into a basal gullet-moulding, with a little slab,
with an antique foliage at the arm-site, with an apple at the breast. And in the middle of the
square, in the broadest part, appeared the ithyphallic sign.

Before whom, immediately, preceded a polished Nymph, on whose snowy face the porphyry cheeks
reddened, with the ivy-crowned forehead of corymbs, clad in a segmented pall, quivered here and
there by the soft zephyr-breaths, the lappets of the reflexed bosom; she bore a golden little vase,
rounded in the manner of a nipple, from which, by the narrowest channel, sprinkling milk, she
libated.

Likewise, again, two Nymphs preceding, wreathed the one of leaves of the female Mercury-plant, and
the other of male *Hermopoane*, were bearers: the one, of a whole gilt little boy in the right hand,
and in the other another, mutilated of the head, little arms, and neck. The other, with special
honour and obstinate superstition, bore the simulacrum venerated by the Egyptians, of Serapis. Which
was a head of a lion; to the right jutted a fawning dog's head; and to the left, a head of a rapacious
wolf. Which effigy was all contained and surrounded in a coil of a dragon, emitting fore-sharpened
rays; which dragon, with the head, derived to the right part of the simulacrum, most-excellently
gilt.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The rear guard of the triumph: **satyrs and aegipans** bearing gilt ithyphallic
herm-idols; a nymph **libating milk** from a nipple-shaped vase; and two nymphs bearing gilt boy-idols

- **The Serapis-of-the-three-heads.** Colonna's Serapis — a lion flanked by dog and wolf heads, coiled by
  a rayed serpent — is the exact allegory Macrobius gives (*Saturnalia* I.20): the three heads are present,
  past and future, the beasts of Time; the serpent is eternity. Set at the tail of Love's triumph, it reads
  Love under the sign of Time — the same *memento* as PANTA BAIA BIOU (p. 340). A striking image the world's
  triumph could carry.
- **the satyrs and the ithyphallic herms** — the fertility-底 of the procession: goat-footed satyrs crowned
  in orchids (*satyrion*, *cynosorchis*, "dog's-testicle" — aphrodisiac plants) bearing priapic idols. The
  triumph of Love spans the whole range from Psyche's soul-love to raw generation.
- **the milk-libation** — a nymph pours milk from a breast-shaped vase: a nurture/fertility rite opening the
  rear file, balancing the incense and torches of the front.
- This completes the marshalling of the whole procession; pp. 345–346 bring it, under the roofed rose-way,

- **refusing steel** — the golden marble is so hard it "refuses the tenacious steel": Colonna's insistence

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The amphitheatre's fabric: **diaphanous alabaster walls with gilt-bronze

- **The theatre's elevation, buildable.** Two stacked orders of arcades in alabaster, framed by fluted
  half-columns, entablature of gilt bronze — Colonna describes the standard Roman amphitheatre exterior
  (superposed arcaded orders) but in translucent alabaster and gold. This is the direct architectural
  source for the world's central theatre; the world can raise a two-tier alabaster arcade with a gilt

- **the ram-skull altars with micro-reliefs.** Each half-column stands on a little altar carved with

  satyric sacrifice (nymphs piping at a boiling tripod, satyrs grasping a leaky vase). The theatre is

- **"nor did M. Scaurus"** — M. Aemilius Scaurus built the most extravagant temporary theatre of the
  Roman Republic (58 BC, 3,000 bronze statues); the amphitheatre of Venus surpasses even it. The
  surpassing-topos, applied to theatre-building.
- **the leaky vase the satyr stops** — a recurring erotic-emblem detail (the *futile* vase that cannot
  hold water); here the satyrs stop it while the nymphs tend the fire. The reliefs carry the same
  fertility-and-restraint theme as the whole triumph.

Beyond this first binding followed, ascending in order, a similar order of columns, in every thing
conformable, and in no part discrepant. And although the building-art appetites that superposed columns
ought to be shorter by a quarter than those set below — of which the perpendicular came, without the
altar-work, above the centre of the columns beneath, with the sequence, and the third (order) a fifth
(shorter) — nonetheless in this elegant and symmetrical building this was not observed, but of one
height, the overstanding with the underlying. The third quadrangular ones obeyed in the third order.
These superseated columns had also the encompassing binding, like the subjacent. Beyond this girdle,
the quadrangular ones, or little pilasters, furrowed, rose. And between one and the other, a third of it
emerging from the solid, in the evened intercapace gaped a window — not quadrangular in the temple-
manner, but as is requisite in profane buildings, obliqued, or arched.

Supremely, in a turned orb above the square columns, the royal cornice, without projections, with every
ornament and most-requisite lineament, and with the special due drip-moulding in it, with every harmonic
proportion, went round. Beyond the said, raised, circled a clean and unencumbered band, a pace and a half
high.

All this celebrated, illustrious, superb, and supremely-approved building, of finest Indian alabaster, of
glassy sheen, artfully constructed, most-excellently decorated, and egregiously perfected — without any
smearing of lime-paste, or cement, but with stable cohesion and contracted consent, perfect. Which pre-
shining material was not disdained by staining smoke, nor paling by the anointment of oil smeared on, nor
muddied by the infusion of vermilion wine, but in every part unliable, without any infection, kept in its
superb, luculent brightness.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The upper storeys and the wall's finish: the second and third column-orders (kept,
unusually, at **one height** rather than diminishing), the arched profane windows between fluted pilasters,
the royal cornice, and the whole built of **mortarless Indian alabaster** so pure that smoke, oil and wine
cannot stain it. All secure; the note on column-diminution is a knowing Vitruvian aside.

- **Columns of equal height — a deliberate rule-breaking.** Colonna knows the Vitruvian rule (upper columns
  a quarter shorter than lower) and states that this theatre *breaks* it: every order is the same height, for
  the sake of "elegant and symmetrical" effect. A specific instruction for the world's theatre — stack equal
  orders, not diminishing ones.
- **mortarless alabaster.** The whole cavea is translucent Indian alabaster, dry-jointed ("without lime… with
  stable cohesion"), and stain-proof against smoke, oil and wine. A glowing, seamless, self-cleaning shell —
  the world can render it as a luminous alabaster material with no visible joints.
- **arched windows "in the profane manner"** — Colonna distinguishes sacred (square-headed) from secular
  (arched) fenestration, and gives the theatre arched windows: it is a *profane* building, a place of
  spectacle, not a temple. A precise stylistic cue.
- **the bulls dissolving into foliage** — the frieze-relief's bulls turn, at the panel-ends, into scrolls of
  acanthus: the antique "inhabited scroll," figures growing out of ornament. The theatre's carving is
  continuous, scene flowing into pattern.

[p. 351]

The Area contained, by diameter, 32 paces. The thickness of the composite (the built ring), 8 paces.

The partition of the encompassing colonnade was quadrifariously divided over the circumference. Between
one and the other interjected partition stood, with even discrimination, eight divisions, where the
columns were constituted and set. From which the solid proceeded toward the centre; and, both by the

and another, partitely, the gaps of the openings, corresponding linearly, passable, and inter-void, and
artfully vaulted the porticoes, or fornices — the lines narrowing with wondrous convenience, the straight
and the circling transverse, the altitude reserved, and every rule accessory to the harmony. The

and grandly stupendous. For all the pavement of the space of the middle Area of the enclosed cavea of the

hardness, polished and so lustrous, that I — abstracted upon it, at the first placing of my right foot —
in that instant, into an Abyss inconsiderately (and I, all occupied with love and sweetness, truly
moribund), feared to precipitate. But the facing resistance suddenly restored to me the shaken and
terrified spirits, with the hurt of the deceived foot. In which stone clearly was seen, and perfectly
discerned — as in a placid and calm sea the limpidity —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The theatre's interior climax: the **mosaic soffits historiated with "all the

- **The obsidian mirror-floor — the theatre's central marvel.** The whole Area is a single slab of

opening, with the lips, to an interposed little walkway, five feet wide. Which, encircling, was covered

Beyond then the summit of the inflexure of such pergola, the other order of as many steps followed in
order. The first, lower, began so much higher in the band, or wall, encompassingly at the inner part,
that the sublime incurvature of the pergola did not occupy the seeing of the front of that first step.
Such symmetry was directly observable in the subsequent. Then the fourth gradation of this second order,
and so of the third — like the first — was of walkway, and of pergola, and of uniform commensuration.

The boarded walls, or the sides of the said pergolas in circuit, were of blackish stone of mirror
sheen. The first wall of the lower pergola was boarded of *spartopolia* stone; the second of
*hieratites*; the third, supreme, of *cepionis*. The sheen of which, under the pergolas, simulated an
opening of the serene air, that shone within it, and not a closure.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The theatre's seating explained: the **cavea is built of tiers of hollow flower-

- **The planted theatre — a cavea of flowers.** Colonna's amphitheatre has no ordinary stone seats: each
  "step" is a hollow box (a *capsa*) filled with flowers, tier upon tier, with narrow walkways under
  arched pergolas between the three orders. The audience-slope is a garden. This is a striking, buildable
  idea for the world's theatre: concentric planted tiers under three rings of pergola, not bare benches.
- **the black-mirror gallery walls.** The pergola-galleries are backed by walls of mirror-black stone
  (spartopolia, hieratites, cepionis) so lustrous they "simulate an opening of serene air, not a closure"

  itself in black mirror. A powerful rendering cue: dark reflective surfaces that dissolve the enclosure.
- **the Fountain of Venus named, then deferred.** Colonna announces the "most-holy fount of the divine
  Genetrix" at the exact centre, then postpones it to describe the theatre first — the fountain is the
  subject of ch. XXIII, the world's climax-station. Here it is placed: dead centre of the obsidian mirror.
- The three pergola-pavements (perfumed paste, coral, lapis) are described on p. 355.

The wall which the last pergola girded, set fast, was so much raised that the arching of that pergola did

Of all this discoursed fabric, the interior girdle — that is, the hollow steps — stood made of best
jasper, ponderous, continuous, and oriental, and perhaps Cyprian, of confused colouring, with wavering

continuous circuit, of pure refined Gold, in little waves and gullet-mouldings; and over the cohesions

put to sleep with his (golden) statue. Nor ever was such (gold) dug up, so outstanding, by the
Scythians, from the ants and Griffins.

The topmost trough, or box, led in a channel and filled and stuffed with earth, had planted cypresses,
two and two, one next (but untouching) to the other, the pairing three paces distant. Which, with even
form and justly, with a fitting rule interlacing mutually their summits and fore-joined together, with
egregious conjugation inflected themselves — with such-made connexion that they appeared one and the
same. That is, the point of the fourth (cypress) with the fourth. The two then of the middle: that on the
right coupled with the fourth on the right order; and the left, by the like, joined itself with the
fourth on the left side, alternating, one below and one above, knotting themselves, so much the better as
could not be told. Between one and the other of the inflected, or the leaning-together, of the collateral
cypresses, resided a densest Box, of spheres in order, diminishing with even decrement, fastigiate — that
is, decimated into manifold rounding — so excellently shorn (as with little shears) that not one leaf
showed itself to offend its order. And between the neighbouring and curved cypresses, rose a straightest
stalk of Juniper, in a most-just sphere, topiaried with spring foliage, which adorned the empty triangle
of the cypress-arches. The remainder of the terrace-top abundantly germinated various and exquisite
aromatic little pot-herbs, copious of their odoriferous flowers, as appears designed at the top of the
Theatre.

ordered and allotted, and most-pleasant harmony of variation of the flowering colour — such as, in the dewy
dawn, they present themselves fresh — with all the discoursed miracles, astonished and lifeless I wholly
remained. My internal and external senses occupied, and surrounded with ineffable voluptuousness and
delight — beyond the excessive love, which all the while in my lanced heart strongly burned, and the
unceasing siege of the incomparable beauties of my most-comely Polia, my delight — insomuch that I did not
know in what being I was. Finally, into this most-happy place, and most-blessed site, introduced — of a
sudden the two Nymphs who bound us, there, again, unloosed us from the entangled little wreaths. And the
venerable Psyche, most-honorifically, to her beloved Husband, laughing, restored the little golden arrow.

CHAPTER XXIII OPENS
------------------------------------------------------------------------

[p. 358]

*(the last line of the preceding chapter)* …by which we were brought before the
holy and sacred Cytherean fountain.

---

**Poliphilo describes the marvellous artifice of the Venerean fountain standing
at the centre of the theatre's floor, and how the little curtain was torn away;
and he saw the divine Mother in her majesty, and how she imposed silence upon
the singing nymphs, of whom she assigned three apiece to Polia and to him.
Afterwards Cupid wounded them both, and the goddess sprinkled them with the
water of the fountain, and Poliphilo was clothed again. Last of all, Mars
coming, they obtained leave and departed.**

With the most fitting reverence and the highest honour, the graceful Polia and I
knelt devotedly before the mysterious fountain of the divine mother, and I felt
an imperceptible sweetness spreading through me and troubling me, so that in that
moment I did not know what to do. For what with the delightful place, incredibly
pleasing and beyond all belief lovely in its greenness and spring adornment; and
the little birds coursing through the purest air and chattering as they flew
among the new leaves, most joyfully, to the outward senses; and the hearing of
those most beautiful nymphs singing their melodies together with their unfamiliar
instruments; and the sight of their divine gestures and most modest movements,
which drove me ardently toward the extremity of pleasure; and the careful,
curious weighing of a fabric of such dignity of conception and such elegant
arrangement; and the greedy drinking-in of a fragrance I had never known — by
immortal Jove, I truly did not know to which of my senses I should firmly and
steadily apply the object of my attention, distracted as it was by so many
different delights, by so excessive and happy a solace and voluptuous pleasing;
and I accused myself of not knowing.

And all these beautiful and most sweet things offered me an enticement so much
the more gracious and desirable, in that I knew that Polia — heavenly Polia — was
placidly taking her share of the delight in them.

In this place, then, and marvelling too at the novelty and excellence of this
astonishing fountain.

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The chapter argument is secure. The body is one enormous
periodic sentence — a chain of *per…* clauses hung on "I did not know to which
sense to apply my attention" — and English will not hold a period that long, so
I have broken it with semicolons. The sense is not in doubt; the shape has been
compromised, and a reviewer might well restore more of it than I dared.

- **`Eutrapela`** — Greek εὐτράπελος, "graceful, ready in speech, well-turned."
  Colonna uses it as an epithet for Polia rather than a name. Rendered "the
  graceful Polia."
- **`Uranothia`** — a Colonna coinage from οὐρανός, "heaven." Rendered "heavenly
  Polia," to keep the pattern of him renaming her with a new compound each time
  he looks at her.
- **The chapter argument** is set in full capitals in the original, as the running
  argument of every chapter is. Kept as a bold heading rather than shouted.
- The final sentence is deliberately unfinished: the argument runs straight on
  into the next page's description of the fountain. Left hanging, as the original
  leaves it.
- **`per il purissimo aere discorrendo`** — *discorrere* here in its older sense
  of running or coursing through, not conversing.

CHAPTER XXIII
------------------------------------------------------------------------

[p. 359]

Which fountain, at the very middle of this more-than-human building, was
divinely constructed and set out in this manner.

Of that blackest stone which alone, and entire, made the whole paving — that is,
the floor of the area — there rose at its centre a little wall a foot high,
brought to an excellent polish and furnished with every fitting ornament,
heptagonal on the outside and round within. It had its running cymatium and
socle, its small plinths and its wave-mouldings, wrought and set in due order
beneath the bases; and over the middle point of each angle there was built up a
column swelling in the shaft — that is, bellied — seven of them in all, turned
with the utmost exquisiteness. Two of these stood answering one another,
equally, opposite the entrance, in full view of where we knelt face down.

One of these lathe-turned columns, on the right hand, shone blue with the finest
sapphire; and on the left one glowed spring-green with an emerald of a colour so
surpassing, and more brilliant, than the stones set for eyes in the lion on the
tomb of Hermias the prince. Nor was such a one given by Ptolemy to Lucullus; nor
was that of so great price which the King of Babylon presented to the King of
Egypt; nor were those of the obelisk in the Temple of Jove of such estimation;
nor was the statue in the temple of Hercules at Tyre so great a marvel, as this
one showed itself to be.

Next to this followed a column of turquoise stone, most beautifully coloured a
lovely cerulean, endowed graciously with its virtue; and though it was an opaque
stone, it was nonetheless most brilliant, and shone back like a mirror.

Touching the sapphire column there stood another precious one, opaque also, of a
most delightful colour like melilot, and with a lustre like the translucent
flower of the buttercup. Adjoining this was one of jasper of a glassy colour, and
the other of topaz flashing with a golden colour. The seventh, alone and
singularly, was hexagonal, of the most limpid Indian beryl with an oily sheen,
giving back whatever stood before it reversed.

And this one answered to the midpoint between the first two — because every
figure of an odd number of angles has one angle facing the middle of the interval
between two others. So then: the circle drawn about its half-diameter, an
equilateral triangle set up within it, and then a line from the centre, and in
the middle of that line —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The gem-lore and the column order are secure — Colonna
names each stone plainly and the Plinian comparisons are identifiable. Two
weaker areas: the mouldings of the kerb (*cimasula, socco, arulette,
undiculatione*) are a technical vocabulary I have rendered by their standard
Vitruvian equivalents without being certain Colonna means exactly those members;
and the geometrical construction in the last paragraph is compressed to the
point of obscurity, so I have translated it literally rather than smoothing it
into a proof. **A reviewer should look hardest at the last paragraph.**

- **The seven columns and their stones**, in the order Colonna gives them:
  sapphire (right of the entrance), emerald (left), turquoise, a melilot-coloured
  opaque stone, jasper, topaz, and — alone, and hexagonal rather than round —
  Indian beryl. Colonna does not say the seven are the seven planets.
  **A sixteenth-century reader did.** The annotator called Hand B, working on the
  British Library copy, labelled the heptagonal-fountain woodcut with the
  alchemical sign of a different metal at each of its seven angles, one per
  planet (`hp.db`, `folio_descriptions` y7r, "Fons Heptagonis: The Seven
  Metals"). The planetary reading is therefore not a modern imposition but a
  documented contemporary one, and the Dream Garden follows it on that authority.
- **`enthesiata, overo ventriculata`** — *entasis*, the swelling of a column
  shaft that Vitruvius prescribes so a column does not appear pinched. Colonna
  glosses his own Greek with the plainer Italian, so the translation keeps both:
  "swelling in the shaft — that is, bellied."
- **`petra caeca`** — literally "blind stone," the period term for an opaque
  gem as against a transparent one. Rendered "opaque," with the contrast to the
  transparent stones kept visible.
- **`vatrachio`** — βατράχιον, the buttercup, whose petals have exactly the
  waxy translucency Colonna wants for the stone's lustre.
- **`in contrario gli obiecti reddendo`** — beryl's double refraction, which
  returns an image reversed. He is describing an optical property, not a
  decorative one.
- **The lion on the tomb of Hermias** — Pliny reports a lion monument whose eyes
  were emeralds. Colonna's chain of comparisons here is all Plinian gem-lore; we
  leave the allusions unglossed in the text, as he does.
- The page ends mid-geometrical-construction; it continues on p. 360.

[p. 360]

— drawn upon the adjacent circumference: such is the sevenfold division of the
said circular figure.

In the middle of the shaft of the seventh, the beryl column, on the inner face,
there was marvellously carved out of that same stone — as though wrenched free
of the sculpture — a little Hermaphrodite child, held in a socket. The three
shining columns of the right-hand order had likewise, each of them, an infant
boy caught in a kind of receptacle; and so too on the shaft of each of the
precious columns of the left there hung, set into it, the female sex. And this,
by a mystical artifice, was expressed naturally at the middle of the columns,
with such a scintillation of polish as neither the biting of whetstone nor emery
with licking Tripoli chalk can give.

The bases, the capitals, the Phrygian architrave and the cornice stood out in
the purest gold. The arches, and all the solid between one column and the next,
were of the wrought stone of one of the columns of the surrounding order — that
is, of sapphire toward the emerald, and of emerald toward the turquoise — and so
on in sequence, the whole arcade was marvellously constructed.

At the angles of the crown, above the true central perpendicular of each column
beneath, there stood a small altar, and rising from it projected the image of a
planet with its proper attribute, its size exactly a third of the column below
it, symmetrically, and of the purest gold. On the front face, at the right, sat
scythe-bearing Saturn, and at the left the night-shining Cynthia; and beginning
from the first and going round in order they ended at Selene. Beneath these, in
the frieze running round, chased with the most exquisite artifice, were to be
seen the twelve signs of the zodiac, with their governing impressions and
characters, expressed in outstanding carving.

The crown then of this most marvellous fountain, and its roofing, blazed with an
extraordinary cupola of the finest crystal, veinless, utterly pure and
transparent. Xenocrates saw none such; none like it was found in Cyprus, nor
produced in Asia, nor in Germany — without rust or roughness, without a clouded
speck, no core of salt, nor any hairline flaw to be seen. Nor did Nero shatter
such a one. But pure, surpassing, and unalloyed, it was girdled with a raised
work, in a fitting and even binding of foliage issuing from certain little
monsters, with small boys wonderfully interwoven playing among them; and it was
of excellent bulk and convexity.

At the tapering of its topmost peak was fixed a miraculous show: in a golden and
most cunningly wrought [?setting], a carbuncle flashing lightning on every side,
egg-shaped, and of the thickness of an ostrich's.

On the faces of the little wall of that darkest stone, upon which —
