## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The architecture, the planetary order and the crystal
cupola are secure. Two soft places: `Lovo` in the last paragraph is unresolved
and marked (below), and the sequence of planetary figures does not quite close
— Colonna starts at Saturn and Cynthia and says the round ends at Selene, but
Cynthia and Selene are both the Moon. I have translated what the page says
rather than repairing it. **A reviewer should start with that planetary
sequence.**

- **`in uno aureo et faberrimo Lovo`** — unresolved. Probably *l'ovo*, "the
  egg," which would suit a carbuncle described in the same breath as
  egg-shaped; possibly a corruption of a word for the setting or socket. Marked
  `[?setting]` rather than guessed. **Check against the facsimile.**
- **`di crassitudine strutiocamela`** — *struthiocamelus*, the ostrich. The
  carbuncle is the size of an ostrich egg, which for a gemstone is an absurdity
  Colonna clearly enjoys.
- **The sexual program of the columns** is the alchemical heart of the fountain
  and is stated plainly: infant boys set into the three right-hand columns, the
  female sex into the three left, and a hermaphrodite child in the seventh,
  which stands alone, is hexagonal where the others are round, and faces the
  midpoint between the first two. That is the *coniunctio* — the union of male
  and female in the hermaphrodite — built as architecture, and it is the same
  figure the Atalanta Fugiens draws in Emblem XXXIII.
- **`trabe Phrygio`** — the Phrygian architrave; Colonna uses the ethnic
  adjective for a decorative order rather than for provenance.
- **Xenocrates and Nero** are both from Pliny's chapters on rock crystal: the
  authority on it, and the emperor who smashed two crystal cups in a rage so no
  one else could have them.
- **`emusicatamente`** — literally "musically," used of mosaic or inlaid work;
  the sentence breaks off here and continues on p. 361.

[p. 361]

— the ready columns were raised, there were cut, perfectly excavated, letters of
the most ancient Greek, the shaft being three-quarters of a foot. In the hollows
of these there shone, laid in, words of refined silver. On the front face only
two letters were to be seen, intersected with companion emblems of gold and
elegantly polished; and then following, on the other faces, three and three,
they said this:

> ΩΣΠΕΡ ΣΠΙΝΘΗΡ ΚΗΛΗΘΜΟΣ
>
> *as a spark, so enchantment*

Each face was three feet, and from the golden bases up to the architrave the
height stood at seven feet. Of the artifice of this thing, marvellous and most
highly finished, I judge that its dignity will be more fittingly preserved by my
keeping silent than by my discoursing of it poorly and meagrely.

There, between the sapphire and the emerald column, hung on bent rings with
knotted loops the most beautiful little veiling curtain that fertile nature could
ever have devised to produce as a thing more pleasing to the gods — so beautiful
a weaving, and of such a material, that I should never know how to describe it;
but of a sandalwood colouring, woven with the loveliest flowering, and with four
Greek letters of gold subtly embroidered over it, **ΥΜΗΝ**, stretched out most
becomingly and heavenward. Let the marvellous curtain the Samians sent to Delphi
rightly yield place here. This appeared to my Polia as a most precious treasure,
and gracious; and it was this that veiled and hid the majestic and divine
presence of the venerable mother.

And so, both of us — Polia and I — kneeling face down upon our bending knees, the
divine lord Cupid gave the golden arrow to the nymph Synesia, and shrewdly made
her a sign that she should offer it to Polia, and that Polia with that fearful
arrow should rend and split the most noble curtain. But Polia, as though grieved
at the command for such a cutting and breaking, however subject she was to that
divine authority, seemed unpractised, and refused to consent. The lord in that
same moment, smiling, charged the nymph Synesia that she should hand it to the
nymph Philedia, and that she should then present it to me; and that what the
honeyed and most upright Polia did not dare to do, I — [?spellbound], and most
greedy to look upon the most holy mother — should carry out.

Whereupon no sooner had I taken hold of the divine instrument than, ringed about
with a blind flame and not refusing, but rather with an urgent and headlong
passion, I struck the little curtain. And as it split I saw that Polia was almost
saddened by it; and the emerald column, cracking, seemed as though it must
shatter entirely.

And behold, all at once I plainly see the divine form in the salt fountain,
brought forth out of that venerable majesty from which all beauty deliciously
flowed. Nor sooner had that unlooked-for sight —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The narrative — Polia's refusal, the arrow passing from
Synesia to Philedia to Poliphilo, the tearing, the cracking column, the
revelation — is secure and is the point of the chapter. Three softer places: the
inscription's letter-count does not close (below), `thelithoro` is a coinage I
cannot place and is marked, and `salso fonte` is either a real detail or a slip.
**A reviewer should start with the inscription and with `thelithoro`.**

- **ΩΣΠΕΡ ΣΠΙΝΘΗΡ ΚΗΛΗΘΜΟΣ** — *hōsper spinthēr kēlēthmos*, "as a spark,
  enchantment": the smallest kindling grows to a rapture that holds you
  spellbound. It is the fountain's motto and a fair summary of the whole book.
  **The arithmetic does not close**: two letters on the front face plus three on
  each of six others gives twenty, and the phrase has more. Either a face
  carries more than Colonna says, or the transcription has lost something.
  Translated as given; flagged for the facsimile.
- **`thelithoro`** — a Colonna coinage, probably built on θέλγω, to charm or
  bewitch, and so "charmed" or "spellbound"; possibly instead on θέλω, "willing."
  Marked `[?spellbound]` rather than resolved.
- **`salso fonte`** — "the salt fountain." Venus is sea-born, so salt water in
  her fountain is meaningful rather than careless, and it makes the *fonte* the
  sea in miniature. Kept literal.
- **ΥΜΗΝ** — Hymen, god of marriage, embroidered on the curtain that hides the
  goddess. Colonna says four letters, which is right for ΥΜΗΝ.
- **Synesia and Philedia** — σύνεσις, understanding, and φιληδία, love of
  pleasure. The allegory is exact and worth not flattening: Understanding offers
  the arrow to Polia, who will not tear the veil; Cupid smiles and routes it
  through Love-of-Pleasure to Poliphilo, who will.
- **The curtain the Samians sent to Delphi** — a famous votive hanging; Colonna's
  habitual move of ranking his invention above the best-attested real object.
- **`copellaceo argento`** — cupelled silver, silver refined by cupellation, the
  purest available. The letters are inlaid metal in cut grooves.

[p. 362]

— that divine sight breathed upon my eyes and passed into them, but both of us,
roused by an extreme sweetness and driven and harried by a new pleasure so long
desired, remained together in a devout fear, almost in ecstasy.

And finding myself so, I began with some reason to be afraid, misdoubting the
vision that the son of Aristaeus had in the vale of Gargaphie; and in a moment it
put both wonder and terror into me.

In the midst, the divine Venus stood naked in the clear and most limpid little
waters, up to her ample and divine flanks — waters which gave back the Cytherean
body neither thickened nor doubled nor broken nor foreshortened, but wholly and
simply, so that it was perfectly discerned in them just as it was. And round
about, at the lowest level, there rose a foaming that gave off a fragrance of
musk. With such divinity was that body transparent, with such particular clarity
did that majesty and venerable aspect present itself, as a precious and
coruscating carbuncle flashes in the rays of the sun — with features and a
marvellous composition neither seen nor ever imagined among human kind.

She had — oh, with what loveliness — her golden hair pleasantly and delicately
dressed, neatly curled and crisped above the milky whitening brow with wandering
and restless whorls, which were hindered from spreading out like vine-tendrils;
and from her rosy shoulders they were becomingly kept from falling free by the
most beautiful little waves. The face rosy and snowing. The eyes starry and
luminous, with an amorous and most holy regard. The honeyed cheeks purpled. The
small narrow mouth most purple, of coral — the dwelling and the little estate of
every fragrant bud. The breast more than snowy and treasured up, with two small
swelling paps that resisted every inclination. The body most ivory and smooth.
Divine semblances. Ambrosial — breathing, rather, a spirit of musk.

Her hair then, most beautiful, like the finest golden threads trailing, lay upon
the purest waters, not sinking, but scattered in a gyre and floating out very
long: in that show the rivals of long-haired Phoebus in the clear Olympus,
radiating illuminating rays. And above the twisted little locks, over part of the
loveliest brow, with a dense growth and an airy heaping, they shone out before
her and covered her as with a little shade, down to the small ears. From these
hung two ostentatious pearls, such as the divided Union did not hang for her in
the Pantheon at Rome; nor did the island of Taprobane ever produce their like for
conspicuous whiteness. And a circlet went about her, or rather a plaited band of
vermilion-whitening and pleasant roses, springlike interwoven, and it flashed
with little gems.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** This is a blazon — a head-to-toe catalogue — and the
sense of every clause is clear; the difficulty is that Colonna coins a diminutive
or a compound in nearly every one (*melule gene*, *eburissimamente glabello*,
*torcularei crinuli*), and English has to choose between keeping the strangeness
and keeping the sentence readable. I have kept the strangeness where it carries
meaning and let it go where it was only ornament, which is a judgement another
translator could reasonably make differently. Nothing here is *doubtful*; a good
deal is *debatable*.

- **The son of Aristaeus** is Actaeon, who came upon Diana bathing in the vale of
  Gargaphie and was turned to a stag and torn apart by his own hounds. Poliphilo
  has just torn the veil from a naked goddess with his own hand, and he knows
  exactly what the precedent is. Colonna does not name him, and neither do we —
  the whole force of the allusion is that the reader supplies it.
- **`velitati`** — from *velites*, the skirmishers of a Roman legion: harried,
  skirmished at. Kept, because "driven" alone loses the image of being set upon
  from all sides.
- **the divided Union** — Pliny's story. Cleopatra dissolved one of a famous pair
  of pearls in vinegar; the other was cut in two and hung as earrings on the
  Venus in the Pantheon at Rome. Colonna ranks his goddess's pearls above the
  most famous real ones, as he ranks everything.
- **Taprobane** — Ceylon, the classical byword for pearls.
- **`non crasso, non gemino, non disfracto, non breve`** — a list of the optical
  distortions water *would* impose on a submerged body, each denied in turn. The
  water is so pure that refraction itself is suspended. It is a physicist's
  compliment, and I have kept its four negatives rather than smoothing them.
- **`suboliva uno spumamento`** — the foam is Venus's own attribute (she is
  *Aphrodite*, foam-born), and here it is scented. The detail is doctrinal, not
  decorative.

[p. 363]

And within the inner circuit of the most sacred fountain, clear of the join of
the sumptuous steps, flowering, purple Adonis sprang up among its kindred
leaves, purpling, kept just clear of the water; and on the left side likewise

translucent flesh as nothing other than orient pearls set there. Close by stood
the nymph Peristeria, promptly and even boldly ready, attending with a whole
mind upon the services of Venus.

Likewise outside the fountain, upon the stone floor where Peristeria stood, at

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The tableau is secure — every figure is identifiable —
but the botanical and mythological vocabulary is dense and two renderings are
interpretive: `amnice fronde` taken as "kindred leaves" (from *amnicus*,
river-kin, is also possible: "riverside leaves"), and the syntax of the oyster
and torch sentence, whose subject the page leaves implicit (it is Venus's
attribute pair; assigned to the goddess). **A reviewer should start with the
Adonis sentence.**

- **Adonis at the fountain's rim** — the purple flower is the anemone, sprung
  from Adonis's blood; planting him at Venus's water is the myth made
  horticulture. *Thelygonon* and *arsenogonon* are from Pliny: herbs supposed
  to cause the conception of girls and of boys respectively. At the fountain of
  generation, Colonna plants the two sexes as botany.
- **The Three Graces** — Eurydomene and Eurymone facing, Eurymeduse turned away:
  this is exactly the canonical pose of the ancient Three Graces group, two
  frontal and one from behind — Colonna is describing a statue type his readers
  knew. The names are his own coinages on Greek roots (wide-ruling, wide-
  wandering, wide-guarding).
- **Peristeria** — περιστερά, the dove: the dove-nymph attends the doves.
- **Nyctelius** — an epithet of Dionysus (of the night rites). Bacchus with the
  look of "a pert and striking girl" is the androgynous Dionysus of Hellenistic
  sculpture. His tigers are canonical.
- **The matron on the serpents** is Ceres — wheat crown, and the serpents that
  draw her chariot. **Bacchus and Ceres together at Venus's fountain enact the
  adage *sine Cerere et Baccho friget Venus* — without bread and wine, love
  grows cold.** And the annotator Hand E read precisely this pairing
  alchemically (`hp.db` folio_descriptions c6v): "Bacchus et Ceres id est sol
  [et luna]" — the two donors are Sol and Luna, and their dripping of "potent
  liquor" into the fountain is the feeding of the bath of the chemical wedding.
  The world's Chymica layer should quote this.
- **`orificio papillato`** — a nippled opening: the spheres are breasts in all
  but name, and the liquor is milk in all but name. Kept at the text's own
  level of euphemism.

[p. 364]

— they took care to dip their little rosy feet in the salt fountain; and of
their ready little toes one stood out beyond the rest, the one nearest the
great toe. Then the others, step by step, with graceful measure, sloped down
toward the rounded ankle, diminishing in good order toward the outer edge.

By this divine arrangement, then, the most holy majesty of the goddess sat
voluptuously in the very middle of the fountain; and the part of the divine
body that stood among the waters showed neither more nor less than a ray or
splendour of the sun shining through the most polished crystal.

Kneeling there and devoutly persevering, my mind wavered, gazing beyond all
measure and to excess, unable to look fixedly upon the divine spirit breathing
everywhere. And no less thoughtfully I turned over the cause — by what sweetness
of fortune and faith, by what means and merit, such mysteries were granted me
to see clearly, and with my eyes unfit for such an object. But I judged it to be
only the free will of the immortal gods, and the kind consent and faithful
prayer of Polia. Above all things it displeased me that among so many celestial
and divine persons I alone stood there contemptible and foreign, in worn and
threadbare clothes, unlike them in every way, most abject and most poor; and I
would then most gladly have had some means of covering my deformity — as
Erichthonius had, to hide his viper feet. And so, stupefied in my mind with
incredible wonder, I praised the divine benignity to the utmost, that it had
allowed an earth-born man openly to contemplate the works of the gods and the
treasure of fermenting nature.

Whereupon those illustrious nymphs, who beneath the pergolas rejoiced with their
applause and songs and sweet harmony for the prey that winged and rash Cupid —
keener-sighted than Lynceus and eye-covered Argus — was vigorously ready with
his weapons to take in triumph: after a little hour had been spent by the mother
goddess, and the celestial sounds and songs were broken off a while into
silence, to both of us, with divine eloquence and soothing charm, in a gentle
address, that most holy mouth uttered such sweet-speaking words — words shrewd
and beyond doubt able to lull to sleep the wakeful guardian of the fatal
treasure of Colchis, to call back to a kindly shape Aglauros the daughter of
Cecrops, to restore Daphnis of Ida to human form and to the grateful flock, and

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The narrative frame is secure; the difficulty is a chain
of learned mythological allusions in the description of Venus's eloquence, each
identified below, and one alchemical phrase (`thesoro dilla fermentosa natura`)
that is doctrinally loaded and kept literal. **A reviewer should check the
Colchis / Aglauros / Daphnis / Cadmus series against the Italian word order.**

- **`fermentosa natura`** — "fermenting nature." Fermentation is an alchemical
  operation, and Colonna's phrase treats the fountain-tableau as a chemical
  process on display. Kept literal so the Chymica reading survives.
- **Erichthonius** — born of Hephaestus's seed on the earth, serpent-footed or
  serpent-legged, and hidden away for it. Poliphilo, ashamed of his shabby
  mortal clothes among the gods, reaches for the one mythological figure who
  also needed to hide his lower body.
- **The four things Venus's eloquence could do** are a rhetorical tour: lull the
  sleepless dragon guarding the **Golden Fleece at Colchis** (as Medea's charm
  did); soften **Aglauros**, whom Mercury turned to stone; restore **Daphnis**;
  and call **Cadmus and Hermione** back from the serpent-shape they were given.
  Each is a myth of a charm undoing a transformation — fitting for a speech that
  is about to bind two lovers.
- **Lynceus and Argus** — the keenest-sighted of the Argonauts, and the
  hundred-eyed guardian: Cupid outsees both.
- Venus's speech continues on p. 365.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Venus's speech is long, formal, and syntactically
tangled in the original, and English has to break its periods; the sense is
secure throughout. The nymphs' names are Colonna's Greek coinages for the
virtues each personifies (below), and rendering them as names rather than
translating them is a deliberate choice — as with the sense-nymphs, the reader
is meant to decode them.

- **The two sets of four attendants** are the marriage's counsellors, and their
  names are their offices. On Poliphilo's side: **Enosina** (union), **Monori**,
  **Phrontis** (φροντίς, care/forethought) and her "silent sister" **Critoa**
  (judgement). On Polia's: **Adiacorista** (the undivided), **Pistinia** (πίστις,
  faith), **Sophrosyne** (temperance — the one name a reader will recognise
  outright), and **Edosia** (also a keeper of the third door, above — decorum).
  Together they are the virtues a good marriage is dowered with.
- **Picus and Canens** — Picus, king of Latium, so faithful to his wife Canens
  that he refused Circe and was turned to a woodpecker for it. The model of the
  steadfast husband, and a transformation-myth again, which is this chapter's
  recurring key.
- **the Herculean knot** — the *nodus Herculeus*, the knot that bound a Roman
  bride's girdle, proverbially hard to loose: the emblem of indissoluble
  marriage.
- **the violet gems set "turning" (anterota)** — the stones are mounted to
  revolve in the ring; *anteros* (returned love) may also be punned. Kept as the
  literal mounting.
- Venus's charge continues onto p. 366.

[p. 366]

— famous age she might feel herself, and worthy of memory; indulging her genius
and never defrauding it. Offering herself a yoked sacrifice with sincere and pure
faith toward him, and steadying what would falter, anxiously and carefully and
kindly to receive him, and gratefully, with the most tenacious bond, to embrace
him.

All these divine nymphs, at the command of the sovereign goddess and without
delay, each began lovingly to kiss with open kisses the one committed and
entrusted to her, in close embraces, with many nymphish blandishments and
attractive endearments; and promiscuously eager, and often pressingly embracing
and kissing us, with due and fitting inclination assenting to the divine Mother,
they began assiduously and with especial courtesy to serve the charge committed
to them.

And to the most prompt little son — the holy little words scarcely uttered and
the divine discourse hardly finished — he, with native licence, bold and pitiless
and severe, with the flying golden arrow (not the Gortynian, and drawn not from
the Ityraean bow but the divine one), no sooner had the string's [?loosing] driven
it out with the force of the taut cord than it struck, carried through the middle
of my unwitting heart, and suddenly pierced it; and then, so quickly, dyed with
gore, smoking from the hot blood issuing out of the arrow-wound — a wound not to
be healed by the Cretan dittany shrub — without delay it transfixed also the
heart of my red-haired Polia, and in her throbbing breast, stained with her own
unspotted soul, he took the wounding and bloodied arrow up again, and at once,
washing it in the maternal fountain, laid it back.

Ah me, that straightway I began to feel in the innermost and deepest bowels the
honeyed burning of an exuberant little flame, spread and sown far and wide, and
occupying all of me; and clouded over with amorous ardours I trembled, and my
eyes were darkened. And without pause my kindled breast, opening to itself, drew
her to it more harpy-like and more bitingly than the snaky hair of the polyp,
than the whirlwind swallowing water; and the precious love and the divine and
never-to-be-blotted image of Polia being let in — with its noble, chaste and
sweetest conditions, informing the prepared and lovingly disposed subject where
it remained eternally ruling, that heavenly and unwashable likeness most firmly
imprinted and most beautiful — I remained like dry and parched straw kindled in a
sudden and violent fire, and like the torches of burnable pine, not a hair's
particle preserved that the amorous flame did not penetrate. And it almost seemed
to me that I was fittingly changed into another form, with great wavering and
faintness of the intellect, unable to comprehend it except by that likeness of
Hermaphroditus embracing Salmacis in the living, fresh spring, when he, in the
mingled sex —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The famous wounding is secure and rendered as close to
the pitch of the original as English bears; two textual weak points are flagged.
The passage ends mid-sentence on the Hermaphroditus image — which is the whole
book's central figure — and continues on p. 367.

- **`amthook`** — placeholder. The transcription reads *l'amento*, which is not a
  standard word; likely *l'ammento* or a form for the notch/loosing of the arrow
  from the string (cf. *amentum*, a throwing-strap). Rendered "the string's
  [?loosing]" in sense; **marked and to be checked against the facsimile.**
- **not the Gortynian bow / not the Ityraean** — Gortyn in Crete and Ityraea
  were both bywords for archery. Cupid's bow is neither earthly kind but "the
  divine one." The Cretan **dittany** that cannot heal this wound is the herb
  Virgil's Venus uses to heal Aeneas — so the one remedy that works in epic is
  denied here on purpose.
- **`pyrrothricha` / red-haired Polia** — πυρρόθριξ, flame-haired. A rare
  concrete detail of Polia's appearance, kept.
- **Hermaphroditus and Salmacis** — the nymph Salmacis embraced the boy
  Hermaphroditus in her spring until the gods fused them into one two-sexed body
  (Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV). Poliphilo can describe being pierced by love only
  as *becoming another form* — and reaches, inevitably, for the myth of the
  hermaphrodite. This is the **coniunctio** the whole fountain is built to argue
  (the seven columns' sexual program, p. 360), stated now in the first person:
  the alchemical union is what falling in love feels like from inside. The mark
  the annotators chase through the book lands here.

[p. 367]

— is seen to transform into a single form. Neither more nor less than unhappy
Byblis, feeling her own tears become for her a liquid fountain of the Naiad
nymphs. Dwelling then already in the sweetest flames, no longer alive than dead,
without a living pulse — and by an unimpeded passage, out of the height of
sweetness, I freely let my little spirit exhale, thinking I had been seized by
epilepsy, falling with buckled knee.

The most merciful goddess, suddenly, with her cupped divine palm — having set
down the oyster-shell and closing the spaces of her longish fingers — divinely
drew up the salt waters and, moistening, sprinkled them over us. Not as
indignant Diana rained upon the unlucky hunter, tearing him to a beast for the
dogs, but on the contrary, unhesitating, sprinkling to transmute — gratifying and
embracing the sacred nymphs. And no sooner had she kindly done it, and I was
sprinkled and anointed with the sea-dew, than in me at once the clarified spirits
were stirred and grew more intelligible; and without waiting my burnt and
consumed members reverted to their former state, and I felt myself, without
fail, renewed with worthy qualities. I knew truly that I was renewed in a like
manner to Aeson, nor did my return to myself seem otherwise than when
twice-living Hippolytus was called back to the longed-for light, by Diana's great
prayer, with the herb *glycyside*, to desirable life. And the assigned nymphs
affectionately stripped from me the plebeian robes, and dutifully clothed me anew
in a white and somewhat elegant garment. And being made tranquilly secure of our
amorous and strengthened state, and most delightfully refreshed, consoled, and
moved and anointed with sudden joy and gladness, at once they made us kiss with
new-wine kisses, and with the vibration of the tongue sweetly to kiss and closely
to embrace. And in like manner both of us, the joyful and festive nymphs, in
their sacred college receiving us to the new novitiate and office of fruitful
nature, all sweetly and charmingly kissed.

Whereupon the mother goddess, with most elegant address and placid discourse, and
propitious with a majestic gaze, reasoning, and with divine breath dispensing a
genial balsam — things unlawful to publish, and to vulgar men not to be told —
labouring long to establish and to ferment our kindled loves, and to unite our
hearts as one under her fruitful and sweet laws for a long age, made us
great-souled in stable and equal love. And therefore, ever devoted to offering
and munificently conferring favour and defence against every chance perturbation,
she largely and freely promised; and in such discourse, most gentle, most
charmingly conferring her grace.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The healing-and-renewal sequence is secure; the two
transformation-similes (Aeson, Hippolytus) are identified. The alchemical verb
`fermentare` recurs and is kept literal. The page breaks as Mars arrives.

- **Byblis** — who wept for love of her brother until she dissolved into a
  spring (Ovid). The image continues the run of transformation-myths, and here
  it is the *dissolving* into water that Poliphilo's swoon echoes.
- **`fermentare gli nostri accensi amori`** — "to ferment our kindled loves."
  Venus's act of binding the lovers is named with the alchemical operation for
  the fourth time in this chapter (cf. p. 364, `fermentosa natura`). Colonna is
  insistent, and so is the translation.
- **Aeson** — Jason's aged father, boiled young again by Medea's herbs. **The
  twice-living Hippolytus** (*virbio*, Virbius) — killed, then raised by
  Asclepius at Diana's plea. Both are resurrection-by-herb, matching Poliphilo's
  own revival by the goddess's sea-dew. *glycyside* is the peony, a real
  medicinal in Pliny.
- **The dew that transmutes, not destroys** — Colonna sets Venus's sprinkling
  explicitly against Diana's on Actaeon (again — cf. p. 362): the same act of a
  goddess casting water on a mortal who has seen her, but here it heals and
  clothes rather than turning to a stag. The chapter answers its own earlier
  dread.
- **"things unlawful to publish, to vulgar men not to be told"** — the standard
  formula of the mystery religions (and of alchemical secrecy), marking Venus's
  final instruction as an initiation.

— steps, out of the recesses beneath the first pergola, valiantly making for the

then, only the divine Mother with her son, and with those continually standing

solacing delights — all the attendants withdrawn.

---

## Notes

**Confidence: high.** This is straightforward descriptive prose — the arming of a
divine warrior — and the classical comparisons are all secure. It is Mars,
though the text withholds the name and identifies him only by his splendour and
his coming to Venus; the reader supplies it, as with Actaeon and the rest.

- **The soldier is Mars.** The book's earlier triumph-relief already showed Mars
  before Jupiter with his wound; here the god of war comes disarmed to the
  goddess of love, and the two embrace "not with human blandishments but with
  divine" — the *Mars and Venus* of a hundred paintings, and the moment that
  ends the lovers' audience. That Colonna never names him is the same discretion
  he uses throughout.
- **`argyraspida`** — silver-shielded; the *argyraspides* were an elite corps of
  Alexander's army with silvered shields.
- **the shield Brontes did not make "for the exiled Trojan"** — Brontes is one of
  the Cyclopes who forged Aeneas's arms at Vulcan's forge; Mars's shield outdoes
  even that. **Didymaon** — a legendary armourer named in the *Aeneid*.
- **"the divine Julius did not bring from Britain"** — Caesar was said to have
  dedicated a breastplate of British pearls to Venus Genetrix in her temple;
  Mars's cuirass surpasses it. Colonna's habitual one-upmanship, and it keeps
  Venus's Julian association (cf. the Caesar obelisk in the polyandrion) alive.
- **Lycaon** — here Mars's hound (the name of the wolf-king of Arcadia, apt for a
  war-god's dog).
- The dividing marks close chapter XXIII; XXIV opens on the next page.

CHAPTER XXIV OPENS

[p. 369]

**By the coming of the armed one just recounted, Poliphilo tells how they went
out of the theatre with all the company, and with the other nymphs came to a
sacred fountain; where the nymphs tell of the sepulchre of Adonis, and how the
goddess yearly assembled there to fulfil the holy ceremonies; and, ceasing from
the dance and song, they urged Polia that she should tell her origin and her
falling in love.**

Adorned with new qualities, with my excellent Polia and with our companions,
departing thence from the sacred fountain, we returned out likewise by that same
gate and entrance by which we had come in, where all the nymphs of the sweet
sounds and singing awaited. Who came festively together with us; whereupon I,
stuffed with fruitful love in my kindled and enlarged breast, with every
accessory sweetness, shut out my past sorrows, every troublesome contrary
extinguished, every doubtful thought curbed, no longer now hesitating over Polia,
but as to the sole Augusta of my soul. Sylvia of my heart, and the Ptolemaïs of
my life. Arsacid of my senses, and Myrrha of my love, and of all of me the
mistress and revered Empress — festive and glad, humbly and most devotedly, I
contentedly succumb, with a more intense, sincere and honourable love than pious
Aeneas bore to his dear, beautiful and divine mistress. Having now at last won
her precious love and willing heart, in this amorous contest an Aristaeus.

It came to pass that the merry little throng of nymphs returned to their former
solaces and pleasures, with the celestial harmonies and angelic concord, with
girlish games and solacing jests, and showing themselves briskly full of laughter
at our obtained and consummated desires, gently giving themselves around us in a
sporting round. And through the holy island, by the paths or streets marked out
among the plants of the fruit-bearing orchards, which were green with perennial
and spring —

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The chapter argument and the narrative are secure. The
difficulty is the cascade of learned epithets Poliphilo heaps on Polia — each a
famous lover or beauty, and each identified below; the syntax is a list and
translates plainly, but the allusions are dense.

- **Chapter XXIV** is short (twelve pages) and takes the company from the theatre
  to a second sacred fountain and the tomb of Adonis, ending as the nymphs ask
  Polia to tell her own story — which is Book II. This is the hinge of the whole
  work.
- **Polia's titles** — *Augusta* and *Empress* (imperial); **Sylvia**, **the
  Ptolemaïs**, **Arsacid** (of the Parthian royal house), **Myrrha**: a chain of
  royal and legendary women, some loving, some (Myrrha) tragic, piled up as
  honorifics. Colonna is not being careful about their stories, only their
  grandeur.
- **"than pious Aeneas bore to his… divine mistress"** — Dido, or Venus his
  mother; the epithet *diva* leans toward Venus, keeping the Aeneas/Venus thread
  of the last pages. Left as the text's ambiguity.
- **"in this amorous contest an Aristaeus"** — Aristaeus pursued Eurydice; naming
  himself so, at the moment of winning Polia, is faintly ominous, and it echoes
  the earlier Actaeon (Aristaeus's son) motif. Colonna's mythology is a web, and
  the translation keeps the thread rather than smoothing it.

— foliage, walled about with box like little walls, and with myrtle and juniper,

pleasant fragrance, and their freshest and dewy fragrant leaves disposed.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Descriptive garden prose; secure in sense. Two soft
points: the marble lattice's thickness (`sextante semisso` — a fraction of a foot,
the exact value uncertain, marked) and `Polycarpia` as the name of the garland

- **Polia weaving a garland of her own hair and flowers** — the *Polycarpia*. The
  detail of her uprooting long golden hairs to bind the flowers is one of the
  book's tender-strange moments; kept literal.
- **The banks "not mossy… but Macedonian marble"** — Colonna's habitual figure:

  ferns) only to deny it in favour of the artificial. The paragone again.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** A long ekphrasis of the Adonis fountain's setting, secure
throughout; the measurements are given plainly and the botany is precise. The one
oddity is `xii passi` (twelve paces) for the surrounding measure of a hexagon then
also said to be thirty-six in circumference — the text gives both figures and I
translate both rather than reconcile them, as with the Great Portal's numbers.

- **The hexagonal fountain** — note that this second sacred fountain is
  *hexagonal*, where the theatre's fountain of Venus was heptagonal (the seven
  columns). The change of figure is deliberate: six is the number of the tomb it
  crowns (Adonis, whose story the next page tells), not of the planets.
- **the citrus cloister** — orange, lemon and citron in an "alternating marriage,"
  a ring of fruit trees enclosing the spring: the same trained-citrus architecture
  the Cythera reconstruction gives the river-pergola (GARDENS.md §5). Here it is a
  *claustro*, a cloister, which is what Colonna calls it.
- **the gold pergola with real roses** — the same figure Hunt reads at the fountain
  of Venus (GARDENS.md §7): the structure is gold, the roses are living. Colonna
  repeats it here, which strengthens the case that the enclosure we built for the
  Cythera fountain is right.
- **`centifolie… graecule autumnale`** — the hundred-petalled rose and the "little
  Greek autumn" rose are both real Plinian varieties.

The tessellated pavement was laid level over all the enclosed ground. Which was

with the little cornice, which was a quincunx; which tomb the nymphs said to be of

rose-bushes her divine calf, to succour him who had been beaten by jealous Mars,
with a woeful and indignant face, and with anguish of soul.

This little history was seen perfectly carved on one long side of the sepulchre;
and the son Cupid then gathering the purple blood into an oyster-shell — adding
that that divine gore was laid up in that sepulchre, placed with the ash, with
every holy rite. Whereupon on the front of our entrance to the sepulchre it was
hollowed out in a circle to the size of the square, and then stopped up with the
precious stone jacinth, of a transparent vermilion colour, with great coruscation
of flaming splendour, burning unsteadily by the light set opposite, so that I
could scarcely fix my eyes on it for the wavering.

On the other long side of the sepulchre I saw likewise Adonis, carved with some
shepherd-hunters, among some little shrubs, with dogs and the dead boar, and he
slain by it; and Venus falling sorrowfully weeping into the pitiful embraces of
three half-swooning nymphs, clothed in finest cloth, weeping together with the
goddess; and the son, with a little bundle of roses, I saw wiping the maternal
eyes, tearful with flowing tears.

There, between the one sex and the other, in a garland of myrtle, I saw thus
inscribed: **IMPURA SUAVITAS**. In like manner on the other little history, in
Greek, was thus expressed: **ΑΔΩΝΙΑ**. So exquisitely feigned in sculpture did all
these things present themselves, that I was moved to a sweetness of pity.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The two carved histories on the tomb are secure and
vivid; the measurements of the sepulchre (`pedi quinarii`, `dextante`, the
quincunx cornice) are a technical vocabulary rendered by standard equivalents.

- **The tomb of Adonis**, the goal of chapter XXIV. The two long reliefs tell the
  myth: on one side Venus rushing naked from the fountain and tearing her calf on
  the thorns to reach the dying Adonis, Cupid gathering the blood into an
  oyster-shell (from which the anemone springs — cf. p. 363, Adonis flowering at
  the fountain's rim); on the other, the boar-hunt and Venus mourning in the arms
  of three nymphs. The tomb is thus the origin-story of the flower that grows at
  the fountain of the previous chapter — Colonna closes the loop.
- **the jacinth glowing in the tomb-front** — a red transparent stone set over a
  lamp, so the tomb appears to hold a burning coal: the blood of Adonis kept
  alight. A theatrical relic-effect, and the same glowing-stone trick as the
  Medusa-door's viper eyes (docs/HP_SOURCEBOOK.md §1).
- **IMPURA SUAVITAS** — "impure sweetness," between the sexes, in a myrtle garland
  (Venus's plant): a motto on the double-edge of desire, love as sweetness that is
  not clean — the shadow-side of the *coniunctio* just celebrated. **ΑΔΩΝΙΑ** — the
  Adonia, the festival of mourning for Adonis.
- **`dextante`, `septuncio`, `semiasside`, quincunx** — Roman fractional measures
  (ten-twelfths, seven-twelfths, a half-as, five-twelfths). Colonna measures even
  a tomb in the duodecimal *as*. Rendered as the fractions; a reviewer with the
  facsimile could confirm the exact values.

[p. 373]

— above the fountain. In which was aptly fixed a golden serpent, feigned to creep
out from a hidden cleft of rock, which, with coiled windings of a fitting
thickness, vomited abundantly into the sonorous fountain the clearest water. So
that by this mastery the meaning craftsman had cast the serpent in a globed coil,
to curb the force of the water — which, by a free and straight pipe, would have
scattered beyond the limits of the fountain.

Upon the flat of the aforesaid sepulchre the divine Mother sat, carved as a woman
in childbed — not without utmost astonishment — of a precious three-coloured
sardonyx stone, upon an antique seat, her seat not exceeding the sardine vein; but
with incredible invention and artifice the whole little Cytherean body was of the
milky vein of the onyx, as though unclothed, because only a veiling was left of
the red vein concealing the secret of nature, veiling part of one thigh, and the
rest descending over the flat, passing then up over —

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The cameo-carving conceit is the difficulty: Venus is
carved from a banded three-colour sardonyx so that the layers of the stone
supply the flesh (white onyx vein), the drapery (red vein), and the seat (dark
sardine vein). The description of which vein does what is dense and continues onto
p. 374; the sense is secure but the exact anatomy of the drapery is intricate.

- **The gushing golden serpent** — a fountain-jet dressed as a snake, deliberately
  coiled so the water is throttled and does not overshoot the basin. A working
  hydraulic detail given a mythic skin, entirely characteristic.
- **Venus carved *puerpera***, as a woman who has just given birth — an unusual
  and pointed epithet at the tomb of Adonis: the goddess of love shown in
  childbed over the grave of her dead lover, birth and death in one image. The
  figure is developed further on p. 374 (she is nursing Cupid).
- **the three-coloured sardonyx** — the ancient cameo material, whose natural
  bands a carver exploits to give figures of one colour on a ground of another.
  Colonna imagines a single stone whose layers become flesh, veil and throne — an
  impossible cameo, and his highest praise. The "secret of nature" the red vein
  veils is, at its plainest, the pudenda; the phrase is the standard learned
  euphemism.

[p. 374]

— the left nipple, resisting it. And from the shoulders, turned to the water,
hanging down, it showed — imitating with marvellous sculpture, nonetheless, the
holy members — she embracing and giving suck to Cupid, indicating with the image
the maternal affection, with a gracious colouring of the cheeks of both from the
reddening vein, with her right little hand [?patting]. O most beautiful work,
miraculous to contemplate, wanting only the vital spirit. With the parted brow,
the ringleted hairs over the smooth temples, and at the back of the head gathered
composedly with a little knotted band; the loosed part thence extended down to
the seat, tendril-like. And exactly sculpted the little tresses, with the openwork
whorls egregiously expressed by the labour of the drill, preserved of the
translucent shining sardine vein — such as, of happy Polycrates, enclosed in the
golden horn, was not dedicated by Augustus in the shrine of Concord. The left
little foot she held drawn back to the seat, and the other stretched to the
outer edge or rim of the flat. Which holy foot the nymphs, bowed and fallen
kneeling, and we, kissed with utmost religion. Beneath which little foot, in the
little cornice, there remained a small band of lineament clear; and on this, in
little letters of our own, I saw annotated this distich:

> Non lac saeve puer, lachrymas sed sugis amaras,
>    Reddendas matri, carique Adonis amore.
>
> *Not milk, cruel boy, but bitter tears you suck,*
> *to be given back to your mother, for love of dear Adonis.*

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The completion of the cameo-Venus and the Latin distich
are secure; the couplet is elegant and its sense plain. One gesture-word
(`tatula`, a diminutive verb of touching/patting) is uncertain and marked.

- **Venus nursing Cupid over the tomb** — the statue resolves: the *puerpera*
  Venus of the previous page is shown giving the breast to her son, but the
  couplet turns it: he sucks not milk but the bitter tears she weeps for Adonis.
  The image of maternal love over the lover's grave is pushed to its sharpest
  point — the child of love feeding on grief.
- **the drill-work tresses of translucent sardine vein** — the carver has used the
  clear band of the stone for Venus's hair, drilled into openwork curls. The
  reference is to the famous emerald(?) intaglio of **Polycrates'** ring, which
  Pliny says Augustus dedicated in the temple of Concord in a golden horn:
  Colonna's cameo outshines even that most storied gem.
- **`tatula dextra`** — "with her right [?patting] hand," the gesture of a nursing
  mother; the verb is a Colonna diminutive and its exact force is uncertain.
  Marked for the facsimile.
- The couplet is one of the book's genuine small poems, and being Latin it is
  quotable verbatim; given here with a plain English gloss beneath, as with the
  other 1499 inscriptions.

[p. 375]

Having done and duly performed this honorary and devout ceremony, we went out of
the sacred little pergola. The illustrious nymphs with affable eloquence said to
us: Know that the present place is mysterious, and most celebrated with the
greatest veneration; and every year, anniversarily, on the day before the Kalends
of May, the divine Mother comes here with her beloved son in a divine pomp of
lustration, and with her all we her subjects, of our own accord at her command,
with observed attendance and with proud solemnity, assemble. Come here, then,
with sweet tears and little sighs, she commands us that all the roses of the
pergola — and the lattices too be stripped of them — and over the alabaster
sepulchre, with high-sounding invocation, ritually to strew them, and heapingly to
cover it. Then in the said order and process she first departs. On the following
calendar day the despoiled rose-bushes reflower to the same number of glowing
roses.

And on the Ides another time the goddess, returning in the former manner —

---

## Notes

**Confidence: high.** Plain expository prose — the nymphs explaining the annual
rite of the Adonia — with no obscure vocabulary. The one detail worth a note is
the date, which ties the tomb to the frame of the whole book.

- **"the day before the Kalends of May"** — that is, **the last of April**, the
  eve of May Day. This is the exact date of the whole dream: the book ends
  "1467, on the Kalends of May" (ch. XXXVIII, translation/en/page_465.md), the
  first of May. So the yearly mourning-rite for Adonis at this tomb falls on the
  very eve of the morning Poliphilo wakes. The dream is dated to the Adonia, and
  the reader who holds both dates sees that Poliphilo's whole vision of winning
  and losing a beloved is folded inside the festival of a goddess losing hers.
- **the roses stripped and reflowering "to the same number"** — the miracle of the
  rite: the rose-bushes are stripped bare to cover the tomb and bloom again
  overnight, undiminished. The rose that springs from Adonis's blood (p. 372) is
  renewed each year, death feeding flower — the same cycle the anemone at the
  fountain of Venus makes (p. 363).
- **`pridiano dì delle calende di Magio`** — kept as "the day before the Kalends
  of May" rather than modernised to 30 April, so the Roman-calendar form (which
  matches the book's own colophon) stands.

[p. 376]

— she says that devoutly the heap of roses is removed from the sepulchre, and
within the fountain, with divine applause, all scattered; and, thrown into the
emissary rivulet, thence they are carried away.

After the divine Lady, as is her custom, has washed herself in the fountain and
come out of it, again in commemoration and amorous memorial of the dear and
beloved Adonis, beaten by Mars, with moist eyes she throws herself embracing over
the sepulchre, weeping, her rosy cheeks bedewed with flowing tears; and all we,
with a lamentable piping, piteously weep, because on such a day the divine calf —
of the little foot we kissed — was pricked by the thorns of these roses. And
therefore on that same day the cover of the holy repository is solemnly unsealed
by her and revealed, and with venerable ceremony all we, glad and exulting and
singing — the son having received it, carries the oyster-shell with the divine
gore, and she, the priestess and newest bearer of the bundle of roses unwilted of
their greenness, with serene grace, most festive.

No sooner is the precious liquor drawn out than at once all the whitest roses, as
at present they appear, are re-dyed in purple colour. And in such order, three
times pompously lustrating this fountain, and she alone weeping, her eyes wet,
wipes them with the handful of roses; at the third circling, the sacred things
laid back in their place, all that most celebrated day is solemnly dispensed to
pleasures alone, to dances, sounds and songs, most dedicated. And on such a day
her grace is easily obtained.

Opposite the sepulchre, at the fountain, there were five steps of the bordering
stone, sloping down to the flat bottom — not rough, not gravelly, but of precious
and vermiculate inlaid paving. The channel of the emissary rivulet flowed on,
underground, beyond the lattices, carrying the succeeding water.

The maiden nymphs having domestically and eloquently narrated so memorable and so
curious a mystery, began again to sound, and rhythmically, most sweetly and with
the greatest pleasure, to sing the recounted little histories and the past
happenings. And dancing in a circle about the fountain for a long while, then all
kneeling and seated and interlaced, in such most acceptable pleasantness and most
delightful greenery — I then, particularly stripped and freed of every holding-
back respect, in that unwonted fragrance of my dainty Polia, which still breathed
from her most elegant and cleanly self, and being all perfumed with a recent
exhalation of that fragrant sweetness of her delicate garments dewing balsam — I
placed myself amorously and freely in her lap, eagerly kissing both her milky
hands and that snowy breast, ivory and lustrous shining; and then mutually — not
ungrateful but voluptuously vying — being in her sight, such impulses of love
approved themselves. Whereupon the singers, set out over the most pleasing
greenery —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The completion of the Adonia rite is secure; the closing
turn to the lovers dallying in the grass is one long periodic sentence, broken up
in English, its sense clear.

- **The white roses re-dyed purple by the blood** — the climax of the rite: the
  gore drawn from the tomb turns the freshly-bloomed white roses red, re-enacting
  the origin of the red rose (or anemone) from Adonis's blood every year. The
  fountain's whole meaning is this annual dying-and-reddening, love and death in
  the one flower.
- **"her grace is easily obtained" on that day** — the rite has a practical
  religious payoff: petitions to Venus succeed on the Adonia. Colonna gives his
  invented cult a working liturgical logic.
- The song of the nymphs turns, on the next page, into their request that Polia
  tell her own story — the doorway to Book II.

[p. 377]

— and their melodious instruments, and the singers, the mellifluous voices held
back in their delicious breasts, fell silent.

Whereupon, thus briskly and voluptuously at leisure, with nymphish converse for a
little while, they showed themselves much desirous to learn our state and
condition. And one among the others, named Polyorimene, most witty and pleasing,
said: O Polia, our consort and partner fellow-servant of the goddess we
cultivate, the loveliness of your elegant aspect and your conspicuous and notable
form, and your noble and illustrious virtues and excellent well-mannered mind,
and your especial and incomparable beauty, make us not undeservedly eager to
learn the cause of your happy loves, and the original beginning of your excellent
and generous lineage — which we judge to be notable and sublime and of illustrious
origin. For we have gathered you to be of probity, of wit, and not meanly learned
in letters; distinguished in shrewdness, with especial grace in your virgin
gestures, of exceptional form; of surpassing beauty, with most sweet loveliness,
and most excellent in modesty, and worthy in the highest degree of honour.
Because your most admirable countenance and heavenly likeness, extremely beautiful
and genial, is not wholly earthly, but rather appears in every way, by open
token, to have more of the divine. Therefore tell us — grateful, indeed most
grateful — of the troublesome torments and the impudent disdains, through discord
and unequal disposition, and how at times you feigned yourself deaf, not to hear
the anxious prayers of importunate and passionate lovers; and how, the two not
continually seeing one another, the sad and desiring heart feeds only on a
consoling persuasion, proceeding from composed imagination and delightful
figments, such as they would wish and most greatly desire, vainly satisfying
themselves with sweet little sighs and feigned solace and pleasure. And in such
commendable leisure, intent on the act, our quiet and solacing sitting will not
grow wearisome.

---

## Notes

**Confidence: high.** This is a formal set speech — the nymph Polyorimene's
request that Polia tell her story — and it is clear, courtly and free of the
botanical and mythological thickets of the surrounding pages.

- **The pivot of the whole book.** Polyorimene's speech is the doorway from Book I
  (Poliphilo's dream of the journey) into Book II (Polia's own first-person
  account). She asks for exactly what Book II delivers: Polia's lineage, and the
  story of her cruelty and disdain toward Poliphilo — "how you feigned yourself
  deaf" to a lover's prayers. The nymphs frame Polia's beauty as "not wholly
  earthly… more of the divine," setting her up as the worthy object the second
  book will justify.
- **"the sad and desiring heart feeds only on a consoling persuasion"** — a small,
  precise piece of the book's psychology of unrequited love: the lover sustained
  by imagined satisfactions, "composed imagination and delightful figments." It
  is the theme Book II will dramatise from the woman's side.
- **Polyorimene** — another Colonna coinage (πολυ‑, many; the second element
  perhaps ὄρος/ὁρίζω), left as a name.

[p. 378]

When the nymph, with most gentle courtesy, had finished her kind persuasion and
most acceptable reminder, my golden-haired Polia, ready and most mild, rising with
her festive and most witty images or semblances, and with cheeks flushing and rosy
little lips suffused with an honest and reverent blush, made ready to satisfy in
every way — of a nature prompt to every virtue — and to give effect to the honest
petition. Not, however, that she could first conceal it, or hold it in at all,
that she did not inwardly sigh a little; which sweetest little sigh penetrated,
reflecting, into the depth of mine — nay, of her — heart, by the uniform accord,
as happens to two equally shared and concordant war-trumpets. And each, gazed
upon with a divine gaze, intrepidly, with those playful and flashing eyes fit to
shatter (ah me) adamant into a thousand little fragments — with pious and humble
voice, and with most elegant gestures becomingly revered by every one, she
returned to her solacing seat upon the thyme-grown ground, following the begun
work, seated. With fitting —

---

## Notes

**Confidence: high.** A single flowing sentence of preparation — Polia rising,
blushing, sighing, and settling to begin her tale — clear throughout. The only
interpretive touch is `litui` (war-trumpets) as the figure for two hearts in
accord, kept literal because the image (two instruments tuned alike, one sounding
when the other is struck) is the point.

- **The last beat of Book I.** Polia blushes, sighs once, and sits to begin. The
  chapter has brought Poliphilo from the wounding at the fountain, through the
  tomb of Adonis, to this threshold: the woman is about to speak. Everything to
  this point has been Poliphilo's dream of *her*; from here it is her account of
  *him*.
- **"two equally shared and concordant war-trumpets"** — Colonna's simile for
  sympathetic resonance: strike one tuned instrument and its twin sounds. He uses
  it for the two lovers' hearts, so that Polia's involuntary sigh rings in
  Poliphilo's chest. A precise, slightly martial image for a tender moment —
  characteristic of the book's refusal of easy sweetness.
- **`acrocoma`** — golden/fair-haired at the tips (ἄκρος + κόμη), one more of the
  Greek epithets for Polia's hair (cf. *pyrrothricha*, red-haired, p. 366;
  *abrodieta*, dainty, p. 376). Rendered "golden-haired."

## END OF THE FIRST BOOK OF THE HYPNEROTOMACHIA OF POLIPHILO

---

## Notes

**Confidence: high.** Three lines and the book-division. The Italian colophon
reads *FINIS DEL PRIMO LIBRO DILLA HYPNEROTOMACHIA DI POLIPHILO*.

- **The end of Book I.** With Polia settling to speak, Colonna closes the first
  and longer book — Poliphilo's dream of the journey through the wood, the portal,
  the palace, the doors, the triumphs and the fountain, ending at the tomb of
  Adonis where the woman he has won is about to tell her own side. Everything
  Dallington translated, and everything in this project's chapters XVII–XXIV,
  belongs to Book I.
- **What comes next.** Book II (chapters XXV onward, from p. 381) is Polia's
  first-person narrative: her ancient Trevisan lineage, the plague that made her
  vow herself to Diana, her cruelty to Poliphilo, his death in the temple, and her
  relenting. It is the shorter book and the mirror of the first — "two dreams told
  toward each other," as the awakening (ch. XXXVIII) will call the whole machine.
- **Page 380 is blank** in the source (a leaf-turn before Book II's title page),
  so there is no page_380 in the translation.

CHAPTER XXV (BOOK II BEGINS)
------------------------------------------------------------------------

[p. 381]

*(Chapter argument:)*

> POLIPHILO BEGINS THE SECOND BOOK OF HIS HYPNEROTOMACHIA, IN WHICH POLIA AND HE, CONVERSING, NARRATE BY TURNS
> IN WHAT MANNER AND BY WHAT VARIOUS CHANCE THEIR FALLING-IN-LOVE (CAME ABOUT).
>
> HERE THE DIVINE POLIA NARRATES HER NOBLE AND ANCIENT ORIGIN; AND HOW, BY HER PREDECESSORS, TREVISO WAS BUILT;
> AND OF THE LELIAN GENS (SHE) DESCENDED; AND BY WHAT MODE, UNAWARE AND IGNORANT, HER BELOVED POLIPHILO
> IMPROPERLY FELL IN LOVE WITH HER.

*(Polia speaks:)*

My feeble voice, O gracious and divine Nymphs, will come to your benign audience as discordant and inelegant as
the terrific raucousness of the diving Aesacus to the sweet song of the plaintive Philomela. Nonetheless, wishing
I, with all my slender efforts of the intellect, and with my scanty sufficiency, to satisfy your pleasant petitions,
I shall not desist from (my) power. Which (petitions) — every hesitation set aside — they, more than would elsewhere
be congruous, worthily merit a more copious river of eloquence, with far more rounded elegance and more adorned
polish of pronouncement than in me, by any pact, is found, to attain their gracious affect. But to you, celibate
Nymphs, and to me somewhat — however confusedly and inelegantly stammering — I shall, in some little portion, have
gratified much (enough), when, willing and devout to your desires and demand, I shall present myself rather with a
soul not mediocrely prompt, humble seeming, than with enucleated, terse and comely eloquence pleasing. The ancient,
then, and most-antique genealogy, and lineage, and my fatal love, garrulously I shall begin to weave. Whence,
already being in your venerable conventual sight, and seeing myself sterile and fasting of eloquence — and (before)
so outstanding and divine a company of you, O Nymphs, sedulous handmaids of kindled Cupid, and in so benign and
delightful and sacred a site, of sincere airs and flower-bearing breaths breathed-upon — I, fittingly compelled to
assume a venerable daring, and a tranquil fear of speaking. Then, before all, give pardon, O most-beautiful and most-
blessed Nymphs, to this my babbling, and to the female and earth-born and pusillanimous efforts, if it happen that,
in some part, I incautiously —

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The opening of **Book II** (chapter XXV): its argument (Polia and Poliphilo will now narrate,
by turns, how they fell in love — beginning with Polia's own account), and the start of **Polia's first-person
narration** — a modest *exordium* to the nymphs, disclaiming eloquence, promising to "weave" her ancient lineage and
"fatal love." All secure; the great structural pivot of the whole book.

- **The book turns to Polia's voice.** Book I was Poliphilo's dream, seen through his eyes; Book II is **Polia telling
  her own side** — her family, her cruelty to Poliphilo, her punishment and conversion, her own experience of the love
  the first book showed from outside. It is the earliest sustained *female first-person* narration in the Italian
  romance tradition. The register drops from Poliphilo's dense ekphrasis to a more direct (if still ornate) storytelling
  voice. Nothing in the 3D world depends on Book II, but it completes the translation.
- **the modesty-topos.** Polia opens with the conventional disclaimer of eloquence ("my feeble voice… stammering… female
  and earth-born efforts") before the nymphs — the humility-formula of a speaker, here gendered. Colonna gives his
  heroine a rhetorically self-aware voice.
- **the frame.** Polia narrates *to the nymphs* (the "handmaids of Cupid," at the fountain of ch. XXIII): Book II is her
  testimony within the dream's own setting. Poliphilo is her listener and, at intervals, co-narrator (per the argument).
- **Aesacus and Philomela** — the diving-bird's croak against the nightingale's song: Polia's habitual self-deprecation,
  and the transformation-birds (cf. p. 310) recurring in her very first sentence.

CHAPTER XXV
------------------------------------------------------------------------

[p. 382]

— in my professed haranguing transgress. O sacrosanct fount, in which mysteriously is the disposition of the arcana
and of the treasure of the celestial genetrix, full of assiduous sanctimony and pacate religion — and which, at
present, upon thy flowering banks seats, with so much consolation, and so notable, the demigoddesses; and in which
the most-excellent and contemplable part of her most-beautiful body specularly (in mirror) thou feignest to have —
for which thing thou art most-highly, of obstinate reverence, to be worshipped: for so much, never let (it be) that,
whatever of you I behold, all veiling my piteous eyes, they be not converted into flowing tears — approaching, in my
tranquil mind, to commove (the memory of) the lacerated Dirce, the weeping Byblis, the envied Galatea, the fugitive
Arethusa, and the dolorous Egeria — I return not wholly free of my spirits. Then, with what affect of soul, and what
study, and with what vows is the inelegant tongue invited to such narration? For my first original stock was unhappy,
inasmuch as of it was (one) who, by divine will, justly, into springing fountains and liquid rivers transformed
himself. O deplorable metamorphosis! O unfortunate case, and badly luckless, and miserably grievous! O indissoluble
series of the fates! O inevitable and perpetual order! In such a case, precipitate and adverse, shall I be able to
narrate thee without grave sighs, and dolorous voice, and imperfect, sobbed words — and without irrigation of tears
upon the dry cheeks? As the wandering Ulysses, reciting the miserable ruins of Troy to Alcinous, King of the
Phaeacians, wept — and (why) does it not break my breast, of cordial sighs, in this most-holy place of felicity,
(where such are) denied and interdicted of provocation? And in which place, reasonably, the eyes of tears, and the
breast of sighs, sterilise themselves — and, to so blessed and gratifying an audience, remote and alien — and
especially in this most-sweet and dearest victory, of my most-appreciated Poliphilo.

Marvel not, then, auspicious, most-comely and heaven-dwelling Nymphs, if I, incontinently — both for my feeble
parentage and progeny, and for my first falling-in-love, difficult — some time, sobbing, should interrupt my prolix
sermon; worthy, nonetheless, of tarrying, and of a considered and attentive audit. For, undoubtedly, two marvellous
things you will comprehend: one, first, an unwonted and unheard cruelty and inhuman — nay, swinish ferocity, and
feminine atrocity, beyond belief — arrived at such a happy and amorous exit as, at present, openly you see it. The
other, the greatest and unthinkable love of the whole world, having such a beginning and exordium.

Divine and Cytherean Nymphs: in the time when the verdant and fecund palm, sprung miraculous and prodigious out of
the woollen fillet, in the Vestal flames, from the forehead of Ilia Silvia, over-shadowed, triumphant, the spacious
earth and the immense sea — the Lelian family, most-noble, was amplified into great —

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Polia's tearful preface: an invocation of the **sacred fountain** (the mirror of Venus's beauty,
where the nymphs sit — the fountain of ch. XXIII), her confession that her "first stock" included one metamorphosed into
a river (an "unhappy" origin), and her warning that she will tell **two marvels — her own cruelty (a "swinish ferocity")
and the greatest love in the world** — dating the start to the age of "Ilia Silvia" (Rhea Silvia, mother of Romulus). All
secure; the frame and stakes of Book II.

- **"Two marvels: my cruelty, and the greatest love."** Polia states Book II's theme: her own **cruel refusal** of
  Poliphilo (which will be punished), and the **immense love** it nonetheless produced. Book II is, in part, her
  confession and repentance — the female counterpart to Poliphilo's fidelity. The word she uses of herself — "swinish
  ferocity, feminine atrocity" — is startlingly self-condemning. This is the moral engine of her narrative.
- **the mythic dating.** Polia sets her family's rise in the age of **Rhea Silvia** (Ilia, the Vestal mother of Romulus
  and Remus), tying her lineage to Rome's origins — and, by the palm sprung from the Vestal fire, to the founding of a
  city (Treviso, p. 383). Colonna gives his heroine a legendary Roman ancestry.
- **the fountain as Venus's mirror.** The fount reflects "the most-excellent part of the goddess's body" — the mirror-
  motif again (Eros Katoptron, p. 266; the obsidian, p. 352), here the sacred spring where Polia testifies. Her tears,
  though, must be held back in this "place of felicity" where weeping is "interdicted."
- **the transformation-origin** — an ancestor turned to a river ("O deplorable metamorphosis"): Polia's family carries the
  Ovidian metamorphosis-curse from its root, foreshadowing her own near-transformation. The book's pervasive
  metamorphosis-theme is now given a personal, genealogical form.

[p. 383]

— state and dignification of magistracy, for its things most-excellently done, and its manifold victories strenuously
attained. Nor to you is hidden the reason that magnanimous men, and whatever virtuous action, in the ancient and
imperial city, were condignly stipended (rewarded).

One, then, of this ancient and honoured lineage, descended, named **Lelio Syliro** — by the holy Senate (long is the
most-potent reason) sent as Consul, and designated, into the region and March **Taurisana**, so named from the high
mountain (Tarvisium/Treviso). Thither, again, coming to people (it) — where presided a magnificent and opulent and
most-sumptuous lord and high-dwelling regulus, parent of an only daughter, named **Tito Butanechio** — who gave his
outstanding daughter in solemn and just and untouched wedlock. Marrying, then (by *confarreatio*), alacritously, with
this (girl) endowed of prudence, and a notable maiden of egregious character and matronal gravity — beyond the
conspicuous beauties, and the affluent plenty of the goods of fortune — she, ingenuous and generous, of manifold
virtue and preclear learning, and most-comely, nurtured bounteously in regal delights and paternal good-manners,
called **Trivisia, Calardia, Pia** (her mother named **Rhoa Pia**). She, amply dowered of patrimony by her father, was
given a great part of the tenth region, Venetia — a level fatherland, hedged by lofty and conspicuous peaks of imminent,
notable mountains, of founts, streams, and down-fallings of rivers; wooded, and of harmless animals abundant.

Celebrated, then, most-magnificently — the Herculean knot dissolved — the legitimate Hymeneals; and religiously invoked
holy Cinxia, fulfilling the matrimonial laws, favouring the divine Zygia Lucina — they had most-noble seed, and copious
birth, taking up (bearing) more sons, male and female, alternately. Of which the first-born was **Lelio Maurio**,
surnamed from the dusky colour; the second, **Lelio Halcyoneo**; the third, **L. Tipula**; the fourth, **L. Narbonio**;
the fifth, **L. Musilistre**. In the daughters, nature — seconding the superior virtues — conferred so much beauty and
comeliness, that never, by human conceit, would they be reputed conceived (of mortals). The first was named **Murgania**,
and one **Quintia**; the third, **Septimia**; the fourth, **Alimbrica**; the fifth, **Astorgia**; the sixth, **Melmia**.
Whence, briefly saying, the parents, unmindful of the fecund benefit of the presider over birth (the goddess), and
glorying of the elegant offspring, deemed them born of their own virtue. Alas — who ever the fatal difficulty, and the
inconstant, fallacious and mobile fortune, expedited and unharmed can evade? For to them it befell, by the demerit of so
great a divine gift — not otherwise than to Atalanta and Hippomenes — and, beyond this, comparing themselves improbably
to our Lady Mother, the Cyprian (Venus), genetrix of our arrow-bearing Lord, and, of beauty and dignification,
preferring themselves. O evil and nefarious deed, and temerarious daring! Wherefore, then, when the years of her
infancy began to exceed (grow), the plebeians, and the vulgar, rude and ignoble, and uncultivated people, not otherwise
than thus —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Polia's **genealogy and the founding of Treviso**: her ancestor **Lelio Syliro**, sent as
Consul to the March of **Taurisana** (Treviso), marries **Trivisia Calardia Pia**, dowered with the Venetian
countryside; their eleven children (five named sons, six named daughters) are so beautiful the family **compares them
to Venus** — a hubris (like Atalanta) that will bring divine punishment. All secure; the historical/legendary frame of
Polia's family.

- **The founding of Treviso.** Colonna roots Polia's lineage in the real city of **Treviso** (Tarvisium), named from
  its mountain, settled by the Roman consul Lelio Syliro — tying the dream-romance to an actual North-Italian place.
  This has long fed the theory that the author (the acrostic names "Francesco Colonna") was a Trevisan; the passage is
  the book's strongest geographic anchor. (Nothing in the 3D world uses it, but it grounds Polia.)
- **the hubris that dooms the family.** The Lelii's fatal error: they credit their daughters' god-given beauty to
  "their own virtue" and let the daughters **compare themselves to Venus** — the classic *hybris* (Atalanta,
  Arachne, Niobe) that provokes the goddess. This sets up the plague and the vow to Diana that drive Polia's own
  story (the argument, p. 150 of NOTES: "Polia's plague, her vow to Diana"). The cruelty Polia confessed (p. 382) is
  the fruit of this ancestral pride.
- **the Roman marriage-rite.** *Confarreatio* (the patrician wedding), the "Herculean knot" (the bride's girdle),
  Cinxia and Zygia Lucina (goddesses of the girdle and of marriage/childbirth): Colonna gives Polia's parents an
  authentic Roman nuptial, his antiquarian precision now serving the family-history. The register stays learned even
  in Polia's plainer voice.
- **the eleven children named** — a full family roster (Maurio, Halcyoneo, Tipula, Narbonio, Musilistre; Murgania,
  Quintia, Septimia, Alimbrica, Astorgia, Melmia): Polia situates herself among siblings, giving the narrative a real
  household. Her own name and place in it emerge as the account proceeds.

[p. 384]

— judged that Murgania was Venus herself. Whence, in the suburban places, they constructed a Sacello, in which she,
lurking, at appointed times, ceremoniously showed herself, feigned (as the goddess); and with annual and suppliant
vows, superstitiously, the popular concourse worshipped (her). Thence was born such a name, among the peoples, even
to this day: **Fada Murgania** (the Fay Morgana); and the place still keeps the memorial name **Murganio**.

For which unjust and enormous thing, and cruel human impiety — audacious, avaricious, ambitious, superb, and
nefarious — the gods (who do not suffer mortal offences unpunished, nor permit any insolence to grow up), irascible
that the earth-born should wish, usurping, illicitly to assimilate themselves to the supernal gods — (and to compare
with) the most-holy mother of our tremendous lord (to whom now most-deservedly we serve) — showed themselves a raging
avenger (not otherwise than Juno to Antigone, and the indignant Eriboea to Isis): the impious temple thunder-blasted,
the royal house lightning-struck, reduced to coal, not far distant hence, where by chance she then found herself,
remained an eternal name, **Casa Carbona**; and Murgania (turned) into founts, with all those who in that place found
themselves, converted. And so likewise **Quintia** and **Septimia**, sisters fleeing not far from Murgania, and they
transformed into welling founts. And **Alimbrica**, made ash, not distant from the said, by the terrific lightnings of
the great indigene and lightning-hurling Jove; and all the palace and royal mansion, in that place also built for
pleasure, all converted into coals; and the place was called **Carbuncularia** — thence it leaps forth into a little
river. And **Astorgia**, fugitive, weeping the miserable cases, she too into a little river runs down into her father.
And likewise **Melmia** — their perpetual name they gave to those places, licking in waves, embracing the sweet father
**Lelio Siliro**. And he, transmuted into liquefying matter, augmented by the dear daughters, makes a celebrated river,
of most-purged welling waters, which still in that most-pleasant region, flowing, most-fresh is seen: from his truncated
name, **Sile**, it is named. And his consort (**Calardia**), thunder-struck, weeping the miserable and horrend cases,
transmuted herself into a notable fount, from her surname called the **fountain Calardia**, near the beloved father
**Tito Butanichio**, made into a liquefying river, weeping the hard and cruel lot, mingled with those of his line. And
her mother **Rhoa**, between her husband and her most-beloved brother **Caliano**, flowing, derive into the sweetest
son, Sile.

Nor was any, even of the males, unpunished by the celestial ire and just vengeance. For the second-born, **Lelio
Musilistre**, made into a rivulet of his name, embraces the father, inundating the Altinate peoples. And the other two
younger brothers — innocent, unweaned, teething — the divine retribution somewhat more temperate, they too experienced
metamorphosis: one into a little bird of his name, **Alcyoneo** (clad with regal and incorruptible plumes), and the
other, younger, into the **Tipula** animal (water-strider). Which, dwellers of the father, not immersing themselves,
ever with him stand, fluvial.
