## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The end of **chapter XXVII**: Polia wakes drenched, "more dead than alive," heart hammering; her
nurse comforts her, and Polia tells her the whole vision and the day's events — **but hides Poliphilo's death**, confessing
only that she had been "insipid and foolish to Love"; the nurse, "with senile expertise, suspects the cause," promises to
be her "true remedy" if she obeys, and Polia submits as a "most-following, most-mild, disciplinable" pupil. All secure;
the turn toward counsel and conversion.

- **Polia's half-confession.** Tellingly, she tells the nurse everything *except* that she killed Poliphilo — she admits
  only being "foolish to Love" (*blitea*). Her remorse is still incomplete: she can confess coldness, not yet the death.
  Full remorse for Poliphilo comes later; here she takes the first step, admitting her *sin against Love* (not yet against
  the man). Colonna traces the conversion in exact degrees.
- **the nurse as physician of the soul.** The nurse "suspects the cause" (love denied) and offers herself as "the true
  remedy-maker" if Polia obeys — the wise-counsellor who will, in the next chapter, argue Polia out of her cruelty and
  toward love. Polia's submission ("a most-following, most-mild, disciplinable" pupil) is the first act of her new
  humility — the proud, cruel girl now teachable. The counsel itself fills chapter XXVIII.
- **the first warmth received and returned.** The nurse weeps *with* her, holds her, and Polia yields — the bond of love
  (maternal here) that begins to melt the heart Poliphilo's eros could not. Book II's insight: the cold heart is opened
  first by being *loved* (by the nurse), then learns to love (Poliphilo). Grace before eros.
- **Chapter XXVII complete.** The whirlwind, the vision of Cupid's punishment, the nightmare of the executioners, and
  the nurse's rescue — the terror that breaks Polia — are translated. The nurse's persuasion (ch. XXVIII) turns her toward
  love.

CHAPTER XXVIII
------------------------------------------------------------------------

[p. 409]

"— only, out of so anguished, afflicted, and prodigious a peril, will draw my mind, and the successive life, out of so
much mourning and grief."

*(Chapter argument:)*

> POLIA RECOUNTS BY WHAT MODE THE SAGACIOUS NURSE, BY VARIOUS EXAMPLES AND PARADIGMS, ADMONISHED HER TO AVOID (THE
> GODS') IRE, AND TO EVADE THE THREATS OF THE GODS; AND HOW A WOMAN, DESPERATE FOR INTEMPERATE LOVE, KILLED HERSELF.
> COUNSELLING (POLIA), WITHOUT TARRYING, TO GO TO THE PRIESTESS OF THE HOLY TEMPLE OF THE LADY VENUS, (AS TO) WHAT SHE
> OUGHT, UPON THIS, TO DO — (WHO) WILL BENIGNLY LEND HER FIT AND EFFICACIOUS INSTRUCTION.

Not without supreme fatigue and expended labour, divine and outstanding Nymphs, can one draw a disposed and inclined
soul back from a purpose — most of all (a purpose) made difficult by obstinacy, and by time habituated, and the more
while, from it, one takes some delightful diversion and recompense. And to wish to adapt it to the contrary, and revert
it wholly alienated (from the former), by a fallacious estimation, most-most-difficult it shows itself. And, marvelling
at this, one is not (moved) in the least, if the sense, some time depraved, distorted, and corrupted, is wont to make
things of sweet matter appear ungrateful, unsweet, spurnable, and bitter. And less marvellous it offers itself, most-
outstanding Nymphs, if whiteness, to the sick, impure, and blear eyes, appearing blackish, offends; if things rutilant,
of a livid coating, and the (things) glittering of candour and of splendour shining, spotted, sprinkled with rust,
covered with caligo, suffused with cuttlefish-vomit, and infuscated with atrament (ink), are damned — without doubt, not
by defect of the object, but by the sensual disease. So, and not otherwise, I: since, to the colds of chaste Diana, my
soul and my mind being firmly habituated and professed, and religated and proscribed — grave, then, and much difficult
rendered itself the ingress of ardent Love, acceptable.

To which (Love), as to a cruel enemy, to resist (inexpert of its sweetness), I had opposed a pertinacious, contradictory,
and repugnant Nausea. And, wishing then, probably intent, into the gelid heart the new love to induce, it necessitated,
industriously, to seclude the repugning contradictors. Now the sagacious and versute Nurse, most-intent to wish that hard
and massed —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The opening of **chapter XXVIII** (the nurse's counsel): its argument (the nurse admonishes Polia
by many examples to fear the gods' wrath, tells of a woman who killed herself for love, and counsels her to consult the
priestess of Venus's temple); and Polia's reflection that a soul long "habituated to the colds of Diana" finds Love's
ingress "grave and difficult" — her chastity a "sensual disease" that makes sweet things (love) seem bitter. All secure.

- **The turn of the whole book: Diana → Venus.** Polia diagnoses her own cruelty as a *disease of perception* — like
  sick eyes to which whiteness looks black, her Diana-habituated soul finds Love "bitter" and feels "nausea" at it. Her
  conversion (chs. XXVIII–XXIX) is the *curing* of that sense, the reversal from Diana to Venus that Book I's temple-rite
  completed (she who was "separated from the colds of Diana," p. 229). Here is that separation's beginning, from her side.
- **the nurse as the agent.** The "sagacious and versute Nurse," seeing Polia's "hard, massed" frozen heart, sets out to
  thaw it by counsel — the persuasion that fills this chapter (Cupid's power over gods, the fate of the cruel). She is
  the physician of Polia's diseased sense (as the argument says, she is "the true remedy," p. 408), and will send her to
  Venus's priestess for the cure proper.
- **the argument previews a suicide.** "A woman desperate for intemperate love killed herself" — the nurse will tell a
  cautionary tale (the other extreme, love's excess) to balance the warning against love's refusal. The Polyandrion's
  two damnations (excess and coldness, p. 250) structure the nurse's counsel too.
- The nurse's examples (Cupid's conquests, the punished cruel) fill pp. 410–411.

— gelid (ice) diverting, to impigliate (grasp), that in me for long time had habitually been confected and hardened — as

"We have found — nay, it is even wont to be said — Polia, my sweet little daughter, and my mirror: he who takes counsel

Whence rightly we know the harsh ires visited and used against Ajax Oileus, as contumacious, and to the severe Gods
maledict — and therefore, by celestial lightning, miserably he perished. Likewise, again, the famished companions of
Ulysses perished. And he (Diana) who, for the entreaties of the huntress Diana, revoked Hippolytus from obscure death to
the light of the fostering day. And so many, by this way, have mortally perished, by negligence and little fear of the
divine retributions threatening. The most-impudent **Propoetides**, who despised the holy Venus, into hardest stones were
badly transmuted. And the weaver, the Lydian maiden (**Arachne**), was transformed by Minerva into a spider. And, for
disobedience, again, the shapely **Psyche**, into so many troubles and intolerable labours, perniciously found herself.
No less, too, many other noble girls — to their vowed lovers rural and ferine cruelty using — the supernal vengeance,
upon their malevolent hardness, bitterly, by diverse and terrific cases, an inexorable avenger has shown itself. Beyond
this, it is to be greatly revoked into the mind: how cruel, how unmild, how impious, how violent, how potent in his
Tyranny, the son of the Divine Mother is — so much truly, that, by true and undoubted experience, we have liquidly found
(however hidden it be) that not only the mortal men, but even the divine breasts, he has, vigorously, without any respect
and miseration, acerbly inflaming, wounded. Did not the rain-bringer and sky-clearer **Jupiter**, with difficulty, from his
amorous —"

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The nurse's counsel proper begins: "he who takes counsel cannot perish"; she warns Polia she may
have **offended the gods** by her cruelty, and recites the punished — Ajax Oileus (lightning), Ulysses's men, the
**Propoetides** (turned to stone for scorning Venus), **Arachne** (to a spider), **Psyche** (her labours for
disobedience), and "many girls cruel to their vowed lovers" — then turns to **Cupid's power over even the gods**
(Jupiter). All secure; a catalogue of divine vengeance.

- **The nurse's argument: fear, then love.** She works first by *fear* — the gods punish the cruel and the scornful of
  Venus (the Propoetides, the cruel girls) — completing what the visions began (chs. XXVII). Her list is a compendium of
  the *punished-for-refusing-love* myths, aimed straight at Polia's case. The rhetoric is deliberate: terror softens the
  ground for the positive argument (Love conquers all, even gods — pp. 411).
- **the Propoetides — Polia's mirror.** The Propoetides (who denied Venus's divinity and were turned to stone — Ovid,
  *Met.* X) are the exact type of Polia's family (who compared themselves to Venus, p. 384) and of Polia herself (the
  stone-hearted, p. 396). The nurse names the precedent for the petrification Polia risks (Anaxarete, p. 396). Her
  cruelty is a scorn of Venus, punishable by stone.
- **Cupid wounds the gods.** The pivot to the positive case: if Cupid overpowers Jupiter himself (and Mars, Apollo —
  p. 411), how can Polia, a mortal girl, resist? Resistance is not virtue but folly. This is *Amor vincit omnia* (p. 284)
  turned into a nurse's practical argument. Love is inevitable; better to yield gracefully.
- **Hippolytus** — revived by Diana/Aesculapius: even the chaste hero (Polia's model) is bound up with the gods'
  power over life and death. The nurse subtly undermines Polia's Diana-devotion by showing Diana too serves the larger
  order.

[p. 411]

"— and ardent torches, avail to avoid himself, nor evade unharmed — (Love) having made him personate himself, for the love
of many damsels; and, by that same Cupid, then, the delightful conjoinings he attained? Now let us intermit the other Gods,
and convert our speaking to the furious and belligerent **Mars** — who, continually bearing the impenetrable Lorica, and
hard and fatal armatures, could not, one little bit, prevail against that Archer Cupid, nor protect himself, nor from his
robust breast drive (him) off, nor reluct, and less defend himself from the amorous wounds, nor to the pointed arrows
resist. Then, my little daughter Polia, my little heart — great is his power! And therefore, if he to the supernal, most-
omnipotent (gods) has not pardoned, how believest thou that he does with the terrestrial? — and especially to those who,
for his service, are disposed and apt; and much more to those who, debile, fragile and unarmed, dare, rebelling, vainly to
repugn? — against which continent ones, that flee him, much more irascible, active and laborious, he opposes himself, with
manifold and troublous invasion, and frightful damages. And if he, of his very self, pardoned not, to fall in love with the
beautiful Psyche, how, to others, will he be innocuous?

"Do we not openly know that, in his marvellous quiver, he contains **two dissimilar arrows**? The one figured of fulgorous
gold; the other, of livid and ill-omened lead. The first, of forced and vehement love, most-violently the hearts to
irritant loving kindles; the other, on the contrary, intolerable superbity, and a rabid and prompt hatred exciting,
provokes, and displeasing cruelty. Of which two exercising — that of the amorous burning — the Sycophant **Phoebus**
(Apollo), striking, direly and extremely he smote; and the (women) beloved by him, with the leaden arrow, he wounded —
because he (Apollo), the all-seeing, manifesting, revealed (Venus's adultery with Mars), and, temerarious, wished to
impede the holy loves of the divine Venus. Whence he (Apollo) long grieved of it, in repudiations and denials and ill-
terminating effects; and the like, to all who, subject, under him find themselves — and to none was he (Love) prosperous.

"Whereupon, the more ardent the affected girls (are), the more displeasing they render themselves, atrocious, austere, and,
of him, refusing and fugitive; and this same, to his lineage and progeny. And for so much, many, of every condition, fell
into such reciprocation and vengeance, for wishing inconsiderately to resist him, and his swift darts lightly to contemn.
And therefore, in this acerb night, by dire and truculent image, he has shown it (to thee). Hear, then, my daughter, and
take the digested, sane, and useful counsel: never wish to oppose thyself to that which thou canst not resist, with
equality of power, nor to contrast; nor that which cannot otherwise be, not to flee (i.e. do not flee the inevitable). And,
even, to the weighed and mature counsels, refuse not. For, being of body most-comely and most-whole, and of soul shrewd,
and of tongue —"

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The nurse's argument at its height: **Cupid overpowers even the gods** — Jupiter (made to disguise
himself for love), Mars (his armour useless), Apollo (punished for exposing Venus's adultery); his **two arrows** (golden =
love, leaden = hatred) that he wields as he pleases; therefore Polia, a mortal, must not "resist what she cannot resist"
but yield to love. All secure; the positive case (Love is inevitable and irresistible).

- **The two arrows — the key to Polia's cruelty.** The nurse names the crucial fact: Cupid's **leaden arrow** excites
  "superbity, rabid hatred, and cruelty." Polia's coldness was not her own virtue but Love's *leaden wound* (Apollo's
  punishment) — she was made cruel by the god she scorned. This reframes her guilt: she is a victim of the leaden arrow,
  curable by the golden one. The two arrows (first named at Cupid's quiver, p. 339) here become the mechanism of the whole
  Book-II drama: hatred (lead) to be replaced by love (gold).
- **resist not the irresistible.** The nurse's practical wisdom: "never oppose what you cannot resist… do not flee the
  inevitable." Since Love conquers gods, resistance is folly, not chastity. This is the argument that turns Polia — not
  that love is good, but that refusing it is *impossible and punished*. Prudence, not passion, opens the door; passion
  follows (ch. XXIX).
- **Apollo's punishment** — struck with the golden arrow (to love Daphne) and his beloveds with the leaden (to flee him),
  because he exposed Venus and Mars: even the sun-god is Love's plaything. The surpassing-of-the-gods argument (cf. p. 286)
  turned to counsel.
- The nurse's counsel concludes, and sends Polia to Venus's priestess (pp. 412+).

[p. 412]

"— eloquent, of rarest and memorable beauty, with the face of outstanding and elegant filament by the Greatest Maker
created — thou oughtest somewhat, and most-accurately, to consider, that almost one could preconise (proclaim) him to have,
in thee, celestial beauty singularly shown: a composite without peer. And, beyond all the preclear and incredible beauties
that in thee especially he placed, of two amorous and splendid eyes thy choice and comely forehead he adorned — (such)
that, so adorned, would not appear (even) of the nine stars, with the three more lucent, the crown of Ariadne in the limpid
sky... (nor the) forehead of Taurus of the Hyad sisters. For which most-worthy things, perhaps the Lady Venus, to her holy
Altars, with an arcane summons wills thee; and so much beauty, of a notable polish, is not to be lost, without her amorous
fires, like the fruit-losing willow. Wherefore thy graceful aspect indicates, rather, to be worthy of her warm services,
than of the gelid and unfruitful Diana. Then, perhaps, for this, the divine disposition and fate, of thy girlhood pious
care having, by nocturnal revelation, the prodigious tokens of the Gods, cautious render thee. For easily it could befall
thee, as to many others has intervened — because to the Gods enemies they present themselves, who the outstanding office of
nature (love and generation), in this life, neglect. And for so much, take, briefly, such an example:

"I, already, my dear little daughter, in our city knew an adolescent-girl (it is not many years), most-beautiful — like
thee, generous, and endowed of choice famousness, and of preclear progeny and delicious lineage born and descended, and of
manifold virtue comely; delicate, and, in whatever her work, most-apt and refined, and busy, of exquisite cultivation, and,
to the womanly polish, studious and cultivated, and, with the increment of fortune, in riches and delights grown-up. Whence,
finding herself in the florid age, which to the highest Gods is wont to be grateful — by many suitor-youths frequently she
was requested. But, especially, among whom, one — a peer of elegance, and coequal of gentility, and of virtue outstanding,
and of soul generous, adolescent — with much petition desired her. Whence, after great and large espousals, and importunate
prayers, she never, by any mode, would consent. And, persevering in such ambitious levity, boastful, the florid years, and
the most-potent and beautiful part of the verdant youth — O me, Polia — brief and scanty she consumed, not pondering that
there is no more amiable and coupled thing than the similitude of love of the matched age. And, sole remaining in that
depraved diversion of soul, in the cold and unpartnered beds — finally, beyond the twenty-eight years finding herself, Cupid
(who is not unmindful of injuries done him) —"

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The nurse turns from myth to a **cautionary exemplum** (its point aimed at Polia): first, praise of
Polia's Venus-worthy beauty ("worthy of Venus's warm services, not gelid unfruitful Diana"), then the tale of a beautiful,
high-born girl who **refused all suitors** — including a worthy peer — out of "ambitious levity," wasting her best years in
"cold, unpartnered beds," until at twenty-eight Cupid took his revenge. All secure; the beginning of the negative example.

- **The willow that loses its fruit.** The nurse's governing image for Polia: beauty unused for love is "like the fruit-
  losing willow" — a waste of nature's "outstanding office" (generation). To neglect love is to make oneself "an enemy of
  the gods." This is the *carpe diem* argument (Venus Physizoa's creed, p. 229) turned to persuasion: beauty exists to be
  used in love, and refusing it is both folly and impiety.
- **the exemplum's mirror.** The refusing girl is Polia's double — beautiful, high-born, cruel to a worthy suitor, wasting
  her youth. The nurse holds up Polia's own crime and shows its consequence (Cupid's revenge, pp. 413–414). The tale is a
  prophecy of Polia's fate if she does not repent, and a warning against *both* extremes (cold refusal, then — the twist —
  uncontrollable lust).
- **Ariadne's crown, the Hyades.** Polia's beauty outshines the constellations (Ariadne's crown, the Hyades on Taurus's
  brow): the surpassing-topos, now in the nurse's flattery. Praise softens Polia before the warning.
- Cupid's revenge (the golden arrow, the lust, the loveless marriage) unfolds on pp. 413–414.

[p. 413]

"— irate and implacable, resumed his curved and dolorific bow, and, noxiously, through the middle of the superb breast,
wounded that sylvan and contumacious heart, with a pointed golden dart penetrating to the extreme line; and, the limit
being transgressed, and in her bosom, burning, nestling itself, the most-valid Love, with the blind fires, fervidly began
to re-kindle; and the wound so profound, perilous, atrocious, and various, that, drawn (healed) into a scar salubriously,
it could not (be). And, by the stimulating ardours amorously forced, and under the unwonted bite and bridle, and sedulous
pricking, impatiently vexed, she began, all languishing, to perish — desiring, then, the sweet petitions that the noble
adolescent vainly made — and, to his aspect, no more he appears (i.e. he was gone). And already Love, his convenient
violences licitly using, immodest, in her, beyond thinking, and urging, quickened. And, having made of her re-struck heart
a furnace-like fire — not so much the most-beautiful and elegant youth, but, by her ill misfortune, made venereous, of
whatever condition anyone had been (had she, of special grace, been able to have him), to her ardent and voluptuous desires
and itching concupiscences, without respect, she would have appreciated (him) most-opportune. I judge that, had an Egyptian,
or an Ethiopian, and an exploded (base) man offered himself, she would not have refused him to her demands — let alone (any)
of our patricians.

"Ultimately, the ingenuous Matron — excessively amorously languishing, and, in the acerbities of the reinforced flames,
exaggerated, and by the enticing ardours stimulated, and of itching appetites, and intemperate lasciviousness, incredibly
agitated, and by so much importunate libido irritated (as if in Didyma born) — and the intolerable pressure not sustaining,
in bed, most-sad, sick and infirm, she fell. Whence, like Antiochus, son of Seleucus, of his stepmother beyond measure
enamoured, and by an immortal languor invaded, (who) was detected, by the pulsing touch (of the pulse), by Erasistratus the
physician, to be languishing of love for the stepmother — by such a way, by the shrewd and expert physician clearly
understood that the woman lay languid, of measureless love maniacally suffering; consulting upon it, the stepfather and her
mother, that death might not supervene, found the opportune remedy: to marry her. So that it stood not long time, that there
was found for her a patrician man, of good condition of kindred, and rich — but old, and of precipitate age, and occiduous
senectitude, more than he (being shaven) showed; come almost to the doubtful age; and somewhat the cheeks were pendent, the
eyes ulcerated, the hands tremulous, the breath fetid, the head hiding (because there appeared the back of a scabby dog), and
the habit (of body), in the breast, all drooping; only, anxious, holding the soul to rapacious avarice most-devoted, and, to
the inexplicable Cupidity, supremely intent. And being come —"

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Cupid's revenge on the refusing girl: he strikes her at twenty-eight with the **golden arrow**, and
she burns with uncontrollable, indiscriminate lust (she would take even a base man) — falls sick of it (like Antiochus, whose
love-sickness Erasistratus diagnosed by his pulse); and her parents, to cure her, **marry her to a rich but repulsive old
man**. All secure; the exemplum's grim turn.

- **The two arrows enacted.** The girl who was cold (the leaden wound, or none) is now struck with the **golden arrow** and
  swings to the opposite extreme — indiscriminate lust. The nurse's exemplum dramatises Cupid's power to make cruelty into
  its opposite: the frozen become the incontinent. Both extremes (the Polyandrion's ice and fire, p. 250) are Love's
  punishment for refusing the *measured* love in due season. The lesson for Polia: love now, moderately, or be forced later,
  ruinously.
- **the Antiochus diagnosis.** The nurse cites the famous tale (Antiochus's secret love for his stepmother Stratonice,
  diagnosed by Erasistratus from his racing pulse — Plutarch, Appian): a learned medical exemplum for love-sickness, and the
  precedent for marrying the girl off "as a cure." Colonna's erudition serves the nurse's argument.
- **the repulsive old husband.** The grotesque bridegroom (pendent cheeks, ulcerated eyes, fetid breath, avaricious soul) is
  the antithesis of the "worthy peer" the girl refused: her punishment is to get, too late, the opposite of what she scorned.
  The grotesque portrait (continued p. 414) mirrors the executioners (p. 406) — Book II's ugliness is always the wage of
  refusing beauty's proper use.
- **married as a remedy** — the parents marry her to save her life, but to the worst possible match: the tale turns on the
  irony that late, forced love is a torment, not a cure. The disastrous wedding-night follows (p. 414).

[p. 414]

"— (I suspect the dark, funereal, and deadly pre-announcer was the night-wandering, ill-omened, immense and improbe
Ascalaphus (screech-owl)) — the unhappy Hymen; and pompously celebrated (as is bounteously wont) the tight commerce of
matrimony. And, come the desired night, that the yearning woman so long had concupiscently expected — firmly judging (it) to
be the hour of extinguishing the fiery and venereal appetites, not considering what the husband might be: for she, at that
point, blindly excited of libido, of unbridled desire enveloped, only pressed to the fruit of the delectable conjugio; and,
beyond measure of itching appetiting, and to the libido most-abandoned — the frigid and impotent old man adhering, and set
in the debile arms — inflamed beyond the fit by incontinent and biting concupiscence to sub-enter (be roused), Cupid
irritant, sedulous in amplifying the fire (more than the bellows to the little fire exciting) — she consequuted no other (by
her ill misfortune) save that, by the foaming old man, her comely face and purple mouth, from the salivous lips, was spat
upon and slobbered, as if a snail, running over it, had lined it. Nor with blandishments, nor with venereal and petulant
gesticulation, and caresses, nor endearments, could she ever heat, commove, nor irritate the impotent and sterile, queasy
old man to be roused — the breath of whom seemed an aura of a putrid cloaca, and of a fetulent quagmire. His gaping mouth
held the pallid lips, gapped and crisping, and with a discordant voice; and almost toothless — in the upper palate had
remained but two rotten big-teeth, and cavernous, like Pumice stone; and below, four others, two to a side, quaking, and, in
their site, unstable. The beard hard, like the hairs of a long-eared ass, like pricking briars, abundant and whitening. The
vermilion eyes moist and tearful. The nose *silo* (flat), in its hollows bushy, and gaping, and mucous, and snaily, and ever
snoring — so that all that night it seemed he bellowed with a most-windy wine-skin (bellows). The face foul, and the head
whitening of *morphea* (leprosy); and the cheeks warty; and, over the eyes, the brows turgid. The throat, with hispid skin
like a marsh-tortoise's, deformed and goitred. And the trembling hands, without any vigour. The rest of the body putrid,
morbid, and invalid, and, of its tardigrade, decrepit. And, in moving, the garments exhaled a putor of fetid urine.

"For which thing (my daughter, attend, and lend thy memory to this audition), the most-lascivious woman, of her voluptuous
appetitions totally frustrated, could never (all the scortatory efforts, and of illustrious harlotry, discharged) excite the
prostrated members of the enormous and unvigorated senectitude. Now it befalls that, for a long time, she, by the malevolent
and tedious old man — idle, inert, desidious and craven, more jealous than the barbarian decurion — not being able to
receive, nor consequute, other save beatings (converted into infinite Jealousy), and railing, and garrulous cries, and cold
and languid sloth, and fastidious tedium —"

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The wedding-night disaster: the lust-maddened girl, married to the **repulsive, impotent old man**
(described in extended grotesque detail — toothless, fetid, leprous, urine-smelling), gets only spittle, impotence, beatings
and jealousy from him; her "voluptuous appetites totally frustrated." All secure; the exemplum's punishment complete.

- **The perfect punishment.** The girl who refused a worthy young lover in her prime is condemned to *unquenchable lust*
  chained to an *impotent, disgusting old man* — desire without any possible satisfaction. It is the exact *contrapasso* for
  refusing love in due season: she gets love's fire and none of its fulfilment, forever. The nurse's warning to Polia is
  total — refuse now, and Cupid will make you burn, too late, for what you cannot have.
- **the grotesque as moral.** The old husband's catalogued repulsiveness (like the executioners, p. 406) is Book II's
  signature: ugliness is the wage of misusing beauty. The girl who scorned a beautiful lover ends in a bed of putrescence.
  Colonna makes the moral physical and unforgettable.
- **"attend, and lend thy memory."** The nurse breaks the frame to drive the lesson home to Polia directly: *this is your
  future*. The exemplum is not a digression but a mirror held to Polia's exact case (beauty, refusal, a worthy suitor
  scorned). It is the argument that, with the visions, breaks her.
- **the woman's fate** — the argument (p. 409) said she "killed herself for intemperate love": the tale's end (her suicide)
  is the ultimate warning, completing on p. 415. Both of Book II's love-deaths (Poliphilo's, from cold refusal; this woman's,
  from forced excess) frame Polia between the two errors the whole book warns against.

[p. 415]

"— and deceived of her unbridled desire, she recognised, in herself returned, her unhappy lot, ashamed of her ill
obstinacy. And hard, not so much of the fastidious and nauseated old man and the unfruitful copula, but of the passed-
over and neglected, irrecoverable time, uselessly dispensed, from her infancy up to that hour, supremely grieving —
which she never knew (how), henceforth, that she no more hoped, by any mode and price, to be able to re-have it, nor
re-acquire, with the greatest doloration she contristated herself. And, beyond this, to her ill, was a mortal accessory,
thinking of the other happy and content married-women, and, frequently coming to mind, imagining, of those that lay in
the sweetest embraces of their most-desired lovers, and of the amorous and delectable solaces, and of their consummated
appetites and desires — as she judged, the wanton nature stimulating, and the wicked and scelerate love. She, in herself
finally re-taken, and in ardent envy bursting, and, in the mind sedulously repeating the intolerable and tedious
superbity of the odious old man, and of the dolorous, unconsoled life having grown weary — she set to scratch and claw
the face, and the breast, with the little palms, savaging, to beat; every hope truncated, dissolved into inundating
tears. And the facile eyes, into weepings more bitter than Egeria's converted; no thing grateful, none appetible, every
thing untasteable, save the improbe death — and to desire the accelerated end that Iphis made. Whence, of here, was born
a rabid furor, of her very self a lovesick and most-cruel executioner concrete; she took, secretly, one black day (the
husband of this unaware), a cutting and knifed iron; and, like a conscious malefactress, impotent of her desires, and
every confidence broken, of herself a mortal enemy made — consenting to the furious conceit — she used a horrend and
frightful vengeance: and, crowned with funereal smilax and with fronds of *ostrya* (hornbeam), through the middle of the
sad heart, impiously (the infernal and mournful Furies invoked) — O unheard crime! — all transfixed the noxious iron.

"O wretched and afflicted me — if, in this my little age (which may the supernal (gods) preserve me from), such a
misfortune, as of thee, could befall, for some similar offence, I would die before the time, of grief, and, of sadness,
accelerating the supreme cloister of my life. O me — who would sufficiently avail, then, to this horrid, most-unhappy
and urgent tempest, and miserable demise of the recounted woman — and my calamity, in kind, in amplitude, in weight, and
asperity, ably, then, assimilating, to compare? What (encounters) of shades, of Lemures, of Manes, of Larvae; what
nocturnal apparitions; what of Demons frights, ever more noxious and horrible, could incur upon me — if these dolorous
eyes should see some sinister of thine, and damage? Then, Polia, my daughter, and my sweetest hope: attend, with the
soul erect and united, the inevitable ire of the Gods — either timely, or with tardiness, wont infallibly to make like
vengeance — such as, for her displeasingness, came to Castalia, from Apollo; and, by this same mode, the shapely Medusa —"

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The exemplum's end: the frustrated wife, grieving her **irrecoverable wasted youth** and envying
happy wives, claws herself and **kills herself with a knife** (crowned with funereal smilax, invoking the Furies); the
nurse says she would die of grief if the like befell Polia, and warns her to fear the gods' **inevitable vengeance** (as
struck Castalia, and Medusa). All secure; the cautionary tale complete.

- **The suicide — Book II's second love-death.** The woman kills herself not from love refused (Poliphilo) but from love
  *forced and unfulfilled* — the other extreme. She, like Polia, is "a conscious malefactress" (the exact phrase, pp. 397,
  399), self-slain. The two deaths frame Polia between the errors: too cold (Poliphilo's killer) and too late/too hot (this
  woman). The nurse's warning: choose measured love now, or die of one extreme or the other.
- **the grief for wasted time.** The deepest note: she grieves not the ugly husband but the "irrecoverable time, uselessly
  dispensed" — youth spent in refusal, unrecoverable at any price. This is the *carpe diem* argument's dark heart (love in
  season, for time cannot be re-bought — completed p. 416). Polia, still young, can still choose.
- **the nurse's love for Polia.** She says she would "die before her time" if such befell Polia — the maternal love (cf.
  p. 407) that grounds her counsel. Her warning is not cold doctrine but a mother's fear. The warmth that thaws Polia is,
  again, love received before love given.
- **Castalia and Medusa** — women punished for scorning suitors (Castalia fled Apollo into her spring; Medusa's cruelty
  turned her hair to snakes, p. 416): the myths of petrification/transformation for coldness, Polia's exact risk. The
  nurse's final application follows on p. 416.

[p. 416]

"— who, with so much direness of soul displeasing to the young suitors, and reluctant, then, for her ferine hardness, by
the supernal Gods, the blond hairs (were) made horrible and sinuous vipers; the amorous throng, thenceforth, terrified,
from the snaky head, in flight converted themselves; and she, more rabidly agitated, desiring, affected them — whence she
could not re-have them. And so, making little of the celestial dispositions, and ordained causes (which make, in the
opportune, due, and destined time, the young to fall in love), the mad girls, in this most-appreciated age which thou
(art), no more considering, make to such mysteries a bad resistance, injuring the heavens and the benign nature.
Wherefore it is not to marvel a little, if so miserably, some time, they perish.

"O me, most-beautiful Polia, my most-precious daughter — the time of our life is more to be esteemed, and supremely
appreciated, more than the amplest treasures of Darius, and the riches of Croesus, and the felicity of Polycrates, and
above every thing of the world. And this our life, of little age, more perpetually and swiftly is a-running, and more
fugitive flees, than do the rapid Horses of Phoebus; and more it empties itself out than the most-tenuous evanescent
Bubble. For all this, we ought joyously to adapt the sweet years to facetious Love — opportune, and matured coming.
Because then, into the incommodious old age coming, still shrewdly we wish to feign the youth passed; and for so much we
give heed, intently, to extirpate from the hoary head the white hairs, and to infuscate and draw them to blackness, with
lye of litharge, and quicklime, or with barks of walnut — and to wish, by art, longly to feign and conserve that which the
natural denies: to illustrate the skin, and, painting it, to extend (smooth) it, and to conserve the shrivelled flesh
swelling and fresh. And, beyond measure, we are gnawn, mordantly, in the heart, of continual and unceasing pain, sighing
and weeping the transacted time, delicious, amorous, and solacing; and of the despising of that repudiated age, and of the
rare, much-desired regard, by the refuged youths interdicted — because the age asks parity of similitude. And,
commemorating the lifted (lost) loves and the amiable sweetnesses, and avidly desiring to live more than in the time of
the florid youth (which is not known, then, by remoteness from the end — but, the privation approaching, for this urges the
appetite of living), if possible it were, the years of Nestor, and of Priam, and the years of the Sibyl.

"Then, Polia, my dear little treasure — for as much as thou appreciatest the present life and little florid age, gracious —
O me, take heed, lest, for such a cause, in thee Cupid pre-demonstrate, and, by such a vision and show, presage the
tumefied, and already conceived, ires, perhaps, against thee. Whence, perhaps, to the supernal Gods thou believest, with
superstitious and vain —"

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The nurse's conclusion: **Medusa** turned to snake-hair for scorning suitors (her would-be lovers
fleeing her in horror when at last she wanted them); the *carpe diem* argument in full — **time is the greatest treasure**,
life flees "faster than Phoebus's horses," so "adapt the sweet years to Love in season," for old age brings only vain hair-
dye and unquenchable regret; and the warning that Polia's vision may **presage Cupid's wrath** against her. All secure; the
counsel's climax.

- **The great *carpe diem*.** The nurse's peroration is one of the book's most direct statements of its theme: **love in
  its season, for time cannot be bought back**. Life is briefer than a bubble; old age can only dye its hair and weep for
  the youth it refused; "the age asks parity of similitude" (love your equals in youth, not old men, too late). This is the
  positive creed of Venus Physizoa (generative love, p. 229) as practical wisdom — and the argument that, with the visions,
  finally turns Polia. Quotable, and the moral core of Book II.
- **Medusa — the last mirror.** Medusa, cruel to suitors, is turned to a snake-haired horror whom lovers flee when at last
  she wants them: the exact terminal image of refused love (petrification/transformation, cf. the Propoetides, p. 410;
  Anaxarete, p. 396). Polia, warned, sees her own Medusa-fate. The nurse's every exemplum is a mirror.
- **the vision as omen.** The nurse reads Polia's dream-terrors (chs. XXVII) as Cupid's *presage* of wrath: she must repent
  *now*. This turns the counsel toward action — the visit to Venus's priestess (the argument, p. 409) that begins the cure.
  Chapter XXVIII completes on the threshold of that turn.
- **Chapter XXVIII nears its end.** The nurse's counsel — the mythic warnings, the cautionary tale, the *carpe diem* — is
  the intellectual pivot of Polia's conversion: fear (the visions) plus reason (this counsel) plus, next, the priestess's
  cure. The remaining lines send Polia to Venus. (The chapter runs one line past; the next chapter, XXIX, is the visit.)

"— opinion to supplicate thee (the gods) and please (them). Cautiously animadvert that, to thee, there come not, as to the

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The end of the nurse's counsel (**go to the priestess of Venus, confess, and be cured**) and the
opening of **chapter XXIX** — its argument (Polia begins to fall in love, revives the dead Poliphilo, is driven out by
Diana's nymphs, and finds him at Venus's temple), and the dawn after the night of visions. All secure; the turn to action.

- **The prescribed cure: confession to Venus's priestess.** The nurse's practical counsel: Polia must go to the priestess
  of Venus, "openly confess her contumacy," and receive "salutiferous instruction." This is the therapeutic structure of
  Book II — the cold heart, thawed by fear (the visions) and reason (the counsel), is *cured* by confession and by love.
  It mirrors Book I's temple-rite (the priestess who unites the lovers, ch. XVII): the same Venus-cult, from Polia's side.
- **the argument's whole arc.** Chapter XXIX delivers the conversion in full: Polia falls in love, *raises Poliphilo from
  the dead* by her tears and embrace, is expelled by Diana's nymphs, and is reunited with him at Venus's temple. The dead
  lover revived by the converted beloved is the miracle that answers her crime (his death, p. 395). Book II's climax.
- **Hebe's warning.** The nurse's last exemplum — Hebe, who tripped serving the gods and was replaced by Ganymede — warns
  Polia to approach the gods carefully. Even innocent offence to the divine has consequences; how much more Polia's cruelty.
- The morning breaks, and Polia — alone — feels the first stirring of love (p. 418).

— she, having gone out of the chamber, I remained alone. And there, scrupulously, I re-cogitated, ruminating, the useful
sayings, the warm and weighed admonitions, the manifest and terrible examples — most-excellently having touched that part
which, me contumacious and savage rebel, rightly damned, and, by the celestial ires, keenly to be punished. Whence, those
(ires) I, terrified, desiring, to my power, avoiding, to flee, and free from this scruple to evade — there came to my mind
(ignorant by what celestial care led) the lover **Poliphilo**, whom I knew that, by my impious ferocity, in the sacred
Temple, bitterly, of his gracious life he despoiled himself.

**Love**, then, artful, in this first motion finding somewhat of a little entry of ingress — together with kindled little
sighs, little by little began to penetrate the interdicted place; and, with its first sweet little torches, in the hard and
torpid heart, quietly nestling itself, collocated itself. And already, feeling a pleasant little flame to run and dilate
itself through the cordial parts, and even to the intimate base of my inexpert heart, and to nourish itself, from the
consent beginning — an incentive and sweet desire, to enter, vigorous and intrepid, under the amorous laws of the solacing
Cupid; and no more to wish to present myself an obstacle, nor extraneous, to the amorous darts.

And being now, with prompt deliberation — I thought, ambiguous, of various encounters and dispositions of the various lot,
and manifold ends, interposed, only for this sweet Love; and the industrious and tenacious little memory, for this, in my
mind, up-boiled, the fearful vengeances of Juno representing, which strongly terrified me. Considering, then, of the
dolorous **Phyllis**, when she, for the blind love of the tardy Demophoon, saw her delicate flesh expressly cover with hard
bark and turn woody. And the incontinent and enkindled **Dido** I see simulacred in my mind, who, with the funereal gift of
the son of Anchises (Aeneas), blinded and turned in fury, killed herself. And of the lying **Stheneboea**, for the illustrious
adolescent Bellerophon, to perish. Then accedes **Scylla**, daughter of Nisus, King of the Megarians, with a ferocious soul
impelled by immoderate love of the King of Crete (Minos), shearing the golden hair of her paternal head — she consequuted no
other, wretched, effect than badly to perish. And likewise, of those two ingenuous Egyptians (Lopidia?), I see naught but
the obscure death of their ardent affect. And **Echo**, for the unfruitful son of Cephisus (Narcissus) — what befell her? O
sad and dolorous me — the undue love of **Byblis**, and of the tearful **Dryope**; and the unjust appetence of the weeping
**Myrrha**, which she had of Cinyras. **Nyctimene**, daughter of Nycteus, she, with a scelerate love of the paternal
conjoining ardescent, saw herself then (turned) into a nocturnal bird (owl), enemy of the precious light, and fugitive. Also

- **The frozen heart thaws — at last.** This is the moment the whole book works toward: the "hard and torpid heart" (the

- **love enters through remorse.** Crucially, the flame is kindled by the memory of *the man she killed* — "ignorant by

- **the fear of metamorphosis.** Against the new flame, her learned memory throws up the whole gallery of women destroyed

- Her decision to go revive Poliphilo (and her Anaxarete-fear) completes on p. 419.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Polia's conversion completes: after a last catalogue of love's victims (Smilax, Canens, Acis,
Helen) and a last recoil (her Diana-vow), the **flame surges irresistibly** ("as Nessus's venom through Hercules's body"),
Cupid strikes again, and she turns wholly to the dead Poliphilo — **resolving to go and revive him**, grieving "him, tenderly
loving me, I reputed an enemy," though still terrified of being Anaxarete. All secure; the turning-point achieved.

- **Love wins the inner battle.** Polia's mind swings between the new flame and her fears (the metamorphosis-victims, her
  Diana-vow) until Cupid's second stroke settles it: "with all my soul already suborned of amorous suggestions, to the
  swooned Poliphilo I returned." The conversion is dramatised as a genuine psychomachia — reason, fear, vow, and love
  contending — won at last by love. Colonna gives his heroine a fully interior conversion, not a mere plot-turn.
- **the resolve to revive him.** She resolves "to behold, dead, him whom I would not see alive" — the exact reversal of her
  crime (she watched him die, p. 395; now she seeks his body to restore it). The dead-raising miracle (the argument, p. 417)
  is set in motion by her converted love. Her grief — "him, tenderly loving me, I reputed a mortal foe" — is, finally, true
  remorse for the *man*, not just fear for herself (the completion begun at p. 408).
- **the Nessus simile.** Love spreads through her "as the Lernaean venom through Hercules's body" — love as a consuming
  poison, unstoppable once in the blood. The image (love as Nessus's shirt) is double-edged: her salvation comes as an
  affliction, sweet and burning at once (the book's sweet/bitter paradox, p. 279, now hers).
- **still Anaxarete.** Even converted, she fears she is Anaxarete (the stone-turned cruel maiden, pp. 396, 415) going to her
  victim. The dread of her own guilt persists into the reunion — which the miracle (his revival) will absolve. Chapter XXIX
  continues to the temple.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Polia, converted, hastens to the temple, finds **Poliphilo lying dead, "colder than marble,"** and,
prostrating herself on the body (like Laodamia on the dead Protesilaus), pours out a lament — cursing herself as "the most-
impious of all women," worse than Phaedra, and begging Death to take her too. All secure; the lament over the corpse.

- **Grief where there was none.** The tears Polia refused the dying Poliphilo (p. 396) now flood her over his corpse. Her
  self-condemnation is total — "of all women the most-impious… more than Phaedra against Hippolytus" — and she begs to die
  with him. The frozen heart (p. 419) is now all fire and water: love and remorse together. Her conversion is complete in
  feeling; the miracle of his revival (pp. 421–422) will complete it in fact.
- **Laodamia and Protesilaus.** She casts herself as Laodamia (who died on her dead husband's body / begged the gods to
  restore him briefly): the myth of love reaching across death — and the precedent for the revival that follows. Colonna
  chooses the exemplum that promises the miracle.
- **the reversal, exact.** She now curses "the first light" of her own life and begs Jove's lightning to reduce her to
  ash — the punishments the visions threatened (pp. 401, 384), now *desired* as expiation. She wants to become the love-
  corpse she made. The self-punishing love is the measure of her repentance.
- She feels his faint pulse and begins the revival on p. 421.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Polia's lament peaks (she calls the Furies upon herself, names herself "bitch, perfid, barbarous"
for killing the man who loved her), and then — weeping over him like **Argia over the dead Polynices** — she lays her hand
on his cold breast and **feels a faint pulse re-boil**; embracing him closer, his "fugitive spirits" re-warm. All secure;
the revival begins.

- **The revival by love and tears.** Polia's weeping embrace does what the Furies and the visions could not undo — it
  *revives the dead*. Her hand on his cold breast feels the "deafened pulse re-boil"; her closer embrace re-warms his
  spirits. Love and remorse, poured out over the corpse, raise him. It is the miracle that answers her crime (she watched
  him die, p. 395; now she raises him), and the emotional counterpart to the rose-bush and communion of Book I (the dead
  love made living). The converted beloved is herself the reviving power.
- **Argia over Polynices.** She weeps like Argia (who braved death to mourn and bury her husband Polynices — Statius):
  faithful love over a corpse, the exemplum of devotion reaching the dead. Colonna's chosen parallel for the revival.
- **the reversal completed in the body.** Where she once made him "cold as marble" (p. 420) by her frigidity, her warmth
  now literally re-warms him. The stone/cold imagery that ran through her cruelty (porphyry, marble, ice) is undone by
  the heat of her converted love. The two temperatures of the whole book — Diana's cold, Venus's warmth — meet and resolve
  in her embrace.
- His full waking and first words follow on p. 422.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The miracle completes: Poliphilo **revives fully** in Polia's arms — she kisses him, bares her
breast, and he wakes, meekly saying *"Polia, my sweet Lady, why so wrongfully dost thou make me suffer?"* — and Polia, her
heart bursting with joy, gives him a "must-sweet kiss," the two **entwined like the serpents of the caduceus** (and
Asclepius's staff). All secure; the resolution of Polia's crime and the reunion of the lovers.

- **"Why so wrongfully dost thou make me suffer?" — the revived lover's first word.** Poliphilo wakes not with reproach for
  his death but with the same tender plaint he made alive (ch. XXVI): his love is unchanged by dying. His gentleness meets
  her guilt with grace — she is forgiven by his very reviving. The circle closes: the man she killed for loving her, loves
  her still, revived by her love.
- **the serpent-embrace.** The lovers entwine "like the serpents of the caduceus… and Asclepius's staff" — the emblem of
  *healing* (Asclepius, the divine physician who raised the dead). The image seals the miracle: love is the medicine that
  raised Poliphilo, and the reunion is a healing. It also echoes the Aldine dolphin-and-anchor and the book's serpent-
  imagery (the polyandrion, the caduceus-hieroglyph, p. 244), here redemptive.
- **the two temperatures resolved.** Polia's blood, "constricted by grief and fright," now "loosens the veins" in joy — the
  frozen circulation of her cruelty thawed into warm life, as she thawed his cold body (p. 421). Both lovers are restored
  to life and warmth together. Diana's cold is finally overcome by Venus's fire, in both hearts.
- **the reunion.** This is the meeting Book I showed from the outside (the temple-rite, the union, ch. XVII); Book II now
  gives its true origin — the revival by love. The lovers are joined; what remains (pp. 423+) is Diana's nymphs driving
  them out, and their coming to Venus's temple, where Book I's dream will meet Book II's history.

[p. 423]

Whence, no sooner had he completely re-assumed and refreshed the pristine virtues — in my bosom and in my arms — and
somewhat re-purpled the cheeks, than the Pontiff (Priestess) of the Sacred Temple, with a tumultuary throng of the
obsequent little priestesses and ministers of the holy service (perhaps, my anguishings and tearful lamentations, and the
high and improbe sighs, in the thundering Temple, having heard), came there toward us; and, animadverting (arrived) of the
illicit operations, interdicted in that holy and unpolluted place, gravely offended, with her other ministers, of ire
extumescent — some with rods, and others with branches of young-oak, at us reproving, and gravely threatening, and
beating — dissociated our sweet embracing, perturbing it.

For which thing, then, immodestly I doubted lest to me should befall that which, to the terrific Medusa, the irascent
furor of Minerva befell — when she, in her clean Temple, Neptune amorously knew (lay with). And that which likewise
befell Hippomenes, and the avaricious and swift Atalanta — who, for illicit conjoining, converted themselves into Lions.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The reunion is broken up: **Diana's priestess and nymphs**, hearing the commotion and finding the
lovers embracing in the temple, **drive them apart with rods and oak-branches**, "gravely offended" at the "illicit"
love in the chaste sanctuary; Polia fears being transformed (like Medusa, or Atalanta and Hippomenes turned to lions) for
her temple-desecration. All secure.

- **Diana expels the lovers.** The chastity-cult violently rejects the new love — beating and driving out the pair for
  their embrace in Diana's temple. It dramatises the book's central conflict (Diana vs. Venus) as physical expulsion:
  Polia, having chosen Venus's love, is cast out of Diana's house. The two goddesses cannot share her. This is the
  necessary break — she must leave Diana to belong to Venus (the "separation from the colds of Diana," p. 229, enacted).
- **the transformation-fear, once more.** Polia fears becoming a lion (Atalanta and Hippomenes, who profaned Cybele's
  temple with love) or a gorgon (Medusa, who lay with Neptune in Minerva's temple): the punishment for love in a chaste
  sanctuary. Her whole story has been shadowed by the fear of metamorphosis (her family, p. 384; the visions); here it
  peaks as she is caught in the very act the myths punish. The final vision (pp. 425+) will resolve whether Venus or Diana
  prevails.
- **the irony.** Polia is now punished by Diana for *loving* — the exact reverse of her earlier cruelty (punished, in
  the visions, for *not* loving). Whichever she chooses, a goddess is offended; only Venus's grace (the coming vision, and
  Book I's temple-rite) reconciles it. She is caught between the two, as the crossing was "between two lords" (p. 279).
- The beating, expulsion, and the lovers' parting complete on p. 424.

**Confidence: medium.** Polia is **beaten and banished** from Diana's temple (the nymph Algerea seizing her, Polia

- **From Diana to Poliphilo — the image swapped.** The clearest sign of her conversion: in her chamber, "the image of the
  Goddess Diana offers itself no more… and, introduced the effigy of my Poliphilo, solely of him I pondered." The idol of
  chastity is replaced by the beloved. Polia is now wholly Venus's/love's. The interior transformation the whole book
  worked toward is complete.
- **love triumphs over disgrace.** Beaten, stripped, exiled, publicly shamed — and Polia does not care, "for the enkindled
  love super-abounded." The love that cost Poliphilo his life (and near-cost hers) now outweighs every punishment. The
  fidelity-thread (his, in Book I) is now hers too: love that endures all shame.
- **the love-tokens.** Polia makes a pearl-sewn crimson heart bearing their entwined names in Greek letters, and a chaplet

  love).
- **the vows and parting** — the lovers betroth themselves ("firm and faithful espousal, mutually") and part joyfully:
  the union Book I's temple-rite formalised (p. 218) here has its private origin. Book II is filling in the history behind

**Confidence: medium.** Polia's **total transformation** ("from cold, fervid; from timid, magnanimous… the rigid breast a
little furnace of love; disdainful hatreds into inseparable loves"), her making of love-tokens (the hair-chaplet sent to
Poliphilo), and then a new vision: **Diana's ice-chariot** (drawn by stags, empty quiver, threatening vengeance) pursued by

- **The transformation, stated in full.** Colonna lists the complete reversal: cold→fervid, timid→magnanimous,
  bashful→incautious lover, hatred→inseparable love, the "rigid breast a little furnace of incensed love." This is the
  answer to every image of Polia's coldness (porphyry, marble, ice, wax-on-rock) — all melted into "a furnace." The
  frozen heart the whole book set out to thaw is now fire. Her conversion is complete.
- **Diana vs. Venus — the final vision.** The two goddesses appear in opposed chariots: **Diana in crystalline ice**
  (cold, empty quiver, vengeful) drawn by her stags in *leaden* chains; **Venus in fire** drawn by swans in *golden*
  cords, with Cupid. The whole book's conflict (chastity's cold vs. love's warmth; the leaden arrow vs. the golden,
  p. 411) is staged as a chariot-confrontation. Ice pursued by fire: Diana fleeing before Venus. The vision (its outcome
  on pp. 426–427) confirms which goddess claims Polia — and it is Venus.
- **the love-tokens sent.** Polia sends Poliphilo a chaplet woven of gold and *her own plucked hair* "in sign of perfect
  love" — the hair that was her pride, her family's hubris, and (torn) her grief, now given freely to the beloved. The
  motif resolves: beauty offered in love, not hoarded in cruelty.
- The confrontation of the goddesses and Diana's rebuke conclude on pp. 426–427.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The vision's resolution: **Cupid's flaming torch drives off Diana's ice-chariot**, whose freezing
car "melts and disappears" before Venus's fire — and Polia finds her chamber **strewn with roses and myrtle** (Venus's
tokens), takes it as the goddess's protection, and resolves to follow the nurse's counsel: **to go to Venus's temple** and
reveal her love. All secure; the divine confrontation decided in Venus's favour.

- **Fire melts ice — Venus wins Polia.** The chariot-duel ends decisively: Venus's fire liquefies and dissolves Diana's
  ice. The whole book's conflict (chastity's cold vs. love's warmth) is settled — Polia belongs to Venus. The roses and
  myrtle that fill her room are Venus's claim-tokens (her flower and tree), and Polia reads them as the goddess "fighting
  for her, most invincibly." The frozen votary of Diana is now under Venus's banner.
- **the decision to go to Venus's temple.** Polia resolves to complete the nurse's prescription (p. 417): go to Venus's
  priestess and "reveal the occulted burning." This is the act that leads directly into Book I — the temple of Venus where
  the priestess unites the lovers (ch. XVII). Book II is about to rejoin Book I's dream at the seam.
- **love as a thistle "combing" the heart.** Her burning love "carminates" (cards/combs, like wool through thistles) her
  heart — the same tearing-pest imagery Poliphilo used of his love (the moth, the caterpillar, p. 393), now hers. The two
  lovers' torments finally match: she suffers as he did. The symmetry the whole double-narration builds toward.
- The coming to the priestess, Polia's confession, and the reunion complete on p. 427.

more peace and sincere concord than the Geryones lived together. Scarce made the irrevocable espousals, than the Sacred
Priestess called Poliphilo into her presence.

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The close of **chapter XXIX** and the seam into Book I: Polia comes to Venus's temple (finding
Poliphilo already there, praying to be restored), **confesses her whole cruelty** to the priestess ("more dire than a
Tigress, more deaf than a stopped Asp… of pity naked"), repents, is struck by Poliphilo's loving gaze, and **vows herself
Venus's worshipper and Poliphilo's, never to refuse him** — whereupon the priestess **calls Poliphilo forward**. All
secure; Book II rejoins Book I.

- **The seam: Book II meets Book I.** This scene — Polia at Venus's temple, confessing to the priestess, vowing herself to
  love, the priestess calling Poliphilo forward — is the *same* temple-rite Book I gave from Poliphilo's side (ch. XVII,
  the priestess who unites the lovers, pp. 216–218). Book II has told the whole history behind that moment: Polia's
  lineage, cruelty, punishment, and conversion, ending exactly where Book I's dream showed the union. The two books now
  interlock. (In the world's terms, this is the origin of the union the Venus-temple station depicts.)
- **the confession — full remorse at last.** Polia names all her cruelty without excuse ("of pity naked, of compassion
  unmoved… hostile hatred toward my Poliphilo") and repents — the complete confession her whole narration built toward
  (from "swinish ferocity," p. 382, to here). Her conversion is now moral as well as emotional: she owns the crime and
  renounces it.
- **the vow of obedient love.** She vows to be "Venus's veracious worshipper… never to refuse Poliphilo… graciously
  yielding" — the exact reversal of her refusal (ch. XXVI). Her betrothal-vow completes the union Book I sealed. The proud,
  cruel maiden is now the devoted lover.
- **Poliphilo's gaze as arrow.** His loving look strikes her heart "like a swift arrow from a drawn bow" — she now receives
  the wound she once dealt. The lovers are at last mutually pierced. Chapter XXIX ends on the threshold of their formal
  reunion before the priestess — where Book I's temple-scene takes over.

*(Chapter argument:)*

> POLIA HAVING ACCUSED HERSELF, BEFORE THE TEMPLE-PRIESTESS, OF HER TRANSACTED IMPIETY — AND (SHOWN) THAT, AT
> PRESENT, ALL WAS SUFFUSED OF ARDENT LOVE — DEMONSTRATING POLIPHILO STANDING BY, THE RELIGIOUS MATRON CALLED HIM TO
> HER. WHO, SUPPLICATING (FOR) THE STABILITY OF BOTH IN ONE RATIFIED PURPOSE — POLIA, FROM IMPATIENT LOVE STRENGTHENED
> IN HER, INTERRUPTED THE RESPONSE.

Appearing, sedulous, without delay, to the venerable Priestess, Poliphilo, expeditely, and with devout inclination,
presented himself there being; and I, with affectionate and thundering sighs (which, in the vaulted Temple sounding —
lo — to our hidden ears the emulous (echo) sent them back), and with the eyes only on him fixed — then, nude and
divested of every cold hardness, but most-mild and meek and outstanding, I laid open to him the gaping opening of my
enkindled heart; and, of his enticing and festive and intent eyes, I most-often imprecated (invoked) a fated domicile
and delicious lodging. And I, as desirous, courteously made it (my heart) only of that worthy and meritorious Lord — an
adjunct, and, together, to possess all my life, and my very self, to what he arbitrarily should will. Who, to me, then,
so much the more grateful presented himself, as, more, before, hateful and displeasing I had held him — a more gracious
and most-efficacious remedy to my ardent love opportunely offering himself, and much more salutary (than) — to the
navigators, upon the estuous sea with the rainy sky — appear the lucid stars of Castor and his brother Gemini, on the
right part of the Charioteer above Orion collocated, and even the desired and secure ports.

Whence, in the last degree of love wounded, I beheld him immovably to take (in), with a gracious intuition; and this was
a sweet congeries and heap of invasive fire in my breast — and my soul, thereby, from every other solicitude excluded:
only him it pleased (me); only him, most-pleasing, it desired; only him, a solace, offered itself; and, to my
insatiable and desirous regards, a delectable object — from the vacation of which impatient, and, of avidity,
stimulated, and, by an immodest appetite impelled, and, by such amorous gratifications, taken and possessed, that
almost externated (beside myself), and in ecstasy, immovable, I beheld him — whence, already beyond measure unbridled
being my eyes — and, because I felt and experienced what thing was the new love, I, miserating, reasonably, to those
(his eyes) pardoned their scrutatory importunity. But Poliphilo, who —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** **Poliphilo's plea to the priestess** begins: encouraged by Polia's changed aspect, he asks the
priestess of Venus — "the ultimate refuge… true remedy-maker," who exists "to re-unite discordant lovers into one will"
— to intercede with Venus so the two be bound "one sole bond." All secure; his petition for the union.

- **The priestess as the uniter of lovers.** Poliphilo names her office exactly: she serves Venus "to re-unite the inept
  and discordant souls, into one will and consent, the lovers." This is the very function Book I showed her perform (the
  well-rite that joined the lovers, ch. XVII, pp. 216–218). Book II gives Poliphilo's own petition that set that rite in
  motion. The two accounts of the same priestess dovetail.
- **the plea's structure.** Poliphilo asks the priestess to *pray to Venus on their behalf* (completed p. 430): that Cupid
  wound Polia's stony heart so she love him, making two hearts one. It is the request the whole dream-quest of Book I
  answers (the union at Cythera, the Fountain of Venus). His confidence ("I am come… because thou alone art able") frames
  the priestess as the lovers' advocate before the goddess.
- **love as inequality to be equalised.** Poliphilo diagnoses the lovers' trouble as "inequality" — he wounded, she not
  (Cupid's "lictorial lancing" fell only on him). The priestess is asked to *equalise* the love (make Polia love as he
  loves). This is Book II's insight in his mouth: love must be mutual to be whole, and the temple's rite makes it so.
- His full petition (Venus commanding Cupid to strike Polia) completes on p. 430.

will and her mind, unequal from mine, and more separated from mine (O me!) than Ossa from Olympus. For I so extremely love
her, that never have I found myself mine, but ever all hers. A just thing it is that, as I am all hers, and a humble
servant, she, uniformly, be all mine, venerable lady, and totally possessress. Then thou, excellent sacrificer — being
sole and chief, in whose sentence consists and depends the power to commune (us) under this amorous Yoke, and, with the
utmost expertise, to master and discipline those who, wholly, with sincere and pure heart, are addicted to this holy
service, of the most-holy and mysterious flames perpetually to serve — that now, if I find not myself deceived, I believe,
and (hope) that this ingenuous and comely, and of singular virtue preclear light, and of beauty celestial splendour, with
me (in this place convened) consents to such services to be received and re-numbered (enrolled)."

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Poliphilo's petition in full: he asks the priestess to pray Venus to **command Cupid to strike
Polia's stony heart** with the dart, so she love him and the two become "one" — to "make coequal this displeasing
dissimilitude"; he professes total love ("never have I found myself mine, but ever all hers"), and hopes Polia now
consents to be "enrolled" in Venus's service. All secure; the plea for the union completed.

- **"Two hearts coming into one."** Poliphilo's whole prayer is for *equality* of love — that Polia be struck as he was
  struck, so their "dissimilitude" (he burning, she cold) be made "coequal." This is the union the temple exists to
  effect (and Book I's rite performed): not his conquest of her, but the equalising of two into one. His "never found
  myself mine, but all hers" is the self-surrender that love, made mutual, will requite ("she be all mine").
- **the dramatic irony.** Poliphilo, not knowing Polia has *already* converted (chs. XXIX — her side, which he did not
  witness), prays for what has already happened: Cupid has already struck her stony heart (p. 419). The double narration
  gives the reader what the character lacks — we know Polia is already his. His plea is answered before he finishes it,
  which is why Polia "interrupts the response" (argument, p. 428) — she can no longer contain the love he is praying for
  her to feel. A neat structural payoff of the two-books design.
- **"Ossa from Olympus."** Their wills were once as far apart as the piled mountains of the Giants — a learned image for
  the "dissimilitude" now being closed. Colonna's erudition serves the emotional reconciliation.
- **the priestess's office, restated** — she alone can "commune them under the amorous yoke" and enrol them in "the
  service of the mysterious flames": the temple-rite of Book I (the joining at the well). Poliphilo's petition sets up the
  scene Book I dramatised. Polia's interruption (her overflowing love) follows on p. 431, closing the loop.

[p. 431]

Already the eloquent and inflamed Poliphilo fell silent from his sweet and most-accepted narration, with most-pleasant
and sweet little words; and that most-sweet mouth soothed my soul. And, taken and circum-obsessed by his mellifluous
tongue, in me I felt not the soul, but, among the rosy lips transmigrated, delightfully to enjoy I experienced. Whose
semblances fully satisfied my most-avid eyes — more grateful than offered itself, to the scelerate Stheneboea, the son of
the king of Ephyra (Bellerophon) — and all consenting, bound, and, to his meritorious petitions, duly most-prepared. By
which supreme sweetness, universally by me circumfused, it constrained me — by superfluous love already invaded — to
fulfil (it); and, by the henceforth not-simulated pity that, at present, of him I had, all commoved to satisfy — my heart
being not, of his most-wretched life, oblivious — in me so rabidly kindled, that I no more availed, one little bit, the
importunate and vehement flame to conceal, nor suppress. Wherefore it would duly, opportunely, have been (if I, by such a
way and going, had not conceded it an exit) without doubt (a cause) to burst. And, interrupting the sacrificer's (the
priestess's) response, I, first, imperterrite and incontinent, gave a most-gaping place to the flying torches, most-mild;
and, in such a manner, to the lover Poliphilo, inflamed, I said:

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The end of **chapter XXX**: Poliphilo's plea done, Polia — "taken by his mellifluous tongue," her
soul "transmigrated among his rosy lips," her love so kindled she "would burst" if she could not release it —
**interrupts the priestess's response** to answer Poliphilo directly. All secure; the overflow of her love.

- **Love that cannot wait.** Polia's love so overflows that she cuts off the priestess before she can rule, unable to
  contain it — the argument's "impatient love strengthened in her interrupted the response" (p. 428). Her eagerness is the
  exact opposite of her former frozen silence (she refused Poliphilo one word, p. 396; now she cannot stop her love from
  speaking). The reversal is total and dramatised in the very structure (interruption).
- **"my soul transmigrated among his lips."** Her soul leaves her and lives in Poliphilo's mouth as he speaks — the
  mutual self-loss of love (he "never found himself mine but all hers," p. 430; she now "feels not the soul in me"). The
  two selves dissolve into each other: the "two hearts coming into one" Poliphilo prayed for, already accomplished in her.
- **the answer preempts the priestess.** Polia's declaration (pp. 432–433) answers Poliphilo's petition before the
  priestess can — Venus's grace working through Polia's own overflowing love. Her speech and the kiss-pledge follow, the
  climax of Book II's reunion.
- Chapter XXXI opens with Polia's declaration of love.

"Equally, I know not, with what remuneration, most-loving my Poliphilo — save with sincere faith, and with veracious and
ardent love, and with sweet and choice pity, conveniently supplying (it) — to recompense the cruel injury inflicted (on
thee); with equal vicissitude, and with no less pity, remunerated, of the Hyades. For, no less does thy honest petition
commove and provoke me, than thy presence, for me languishing — from hour to hour successively, judging thereby, without
fail most-certain, to be the effect. Not otherwise tormenting appearing to me than Hector, slain, dragged through the
flying dust, with great runnels of fuming blood, and with the blond hair cruented, and with the face besmeared and
dusty, before the tear-bearing eyes of the dolorous and most-beloved Andromache. O my heart! O sole my good! O sweet
hope! — thy tormented and transfixed heart being saddened, by my ferocity of soul perverse, savage, dire and impious,
and, of error deceived, so protracted a time embittered — drawing the woeful life in unceasing weepings and plaints —
and, at present, full and nautically stuffed of tribulous insults of love, to my tear-weeping eyes represented. And, to
wish to follow the greatness of thy noble and worthy soul, and, of excellence of love fervidly adorned — which now shall
not find deaf and inane audience — for this, in a little hour, thou shalt see put a mode, and salubrious end, to thy
griefs. For, a blind desire having, licitly, domesticated itself, from thy edacious eyes, of my heart, in the most-prompt
breast — I too find myself not immune, nor void, but, participant, I commune with thy ills. For which thing, I intend not
to spare my life (which lies in thy arbitrament and will), and my florid and unhurt girlhood, to thy ardent desires and
gracious vows to defer (yield). And, not using now that which, before, I reasonably ought (i.e. not persisting in my
refusal), I could easily incur the inevitable ires of my lord Cupid — where —"

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** **Polia's answering declaration of love** (chapter XXXI): she will repay the cruelty she did him
"with sincere faith and ardent love"; his suffering (like Hector dragged before Andromache) moves her; she now "communes
with his ills," will not spare "my life… my florid girlhood" to his desires, and would herself "incur Cupid's ire" if she
refused. All secure; her formal reciprocation.

- **The reciprocation — love returned in kind.** Polia answers Poliphilo's petition (that she be made to love him) with her
  own declaration: she loves him, will yield "my life, my girlhood" to him, and repays "the cruel injury" she did with
  "equal vicissitude." The "dissimilitude" he asked the priestess to equalise (p. 430) she now equalises herself — the two
  loves made coequal, two hearts one. Book II's reunion is complete in her words.
- **Hector and Andromache.** She figures Poliphilo's love-tormented state as Hector's corpse dragged before the weeping
  Andromache — casting herself as the grieving wife watching her beloved destroyed. The image of a wife mourning a
  slaughtered husband is her acknowledgement that she *killed* him (chs. XXVI, XXIX); her love is inseparable from her
  remorse.
- **fear turned to love's servant.** She notes she would now "incur Cupid's ire" if she *refused* — the same god whose
  wrath the visions threatened for her cruelty now compels her love. The conversion is sealed: Cupid's power, once her
  terror, is now her ally. Refusing love, not loving, is the punishable sin.
- Her vow and the kiss-pledge complete the declaration on pp. 433+.

"— with every solemn and ratified faith and most-firm loyalty, I have disposed myself, with thee, wholly amorously to

ominously shown me, threatening (his) part.

"But thou, who so festively and perpetually, to the furious torches, and to this angarious weight of that enormous Cupid,

for such-like resistance and flight, would not have clad himself of fluttering plumes, had he, to Circe, consentaneous
rendered himself. By such-like fugacities, many have experienced what it is, to the grateful loves, to be a flee-er and
refusing. And beyond —"

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Polia's declaration continues: she vows, "with ratified faith and firm loyalty, wholly amorously
to live" with Poliphilo, giving him her "inviolate florid person"; she calls him her "presidium, triumphal Bulla,
Asylum, treasure above all jewels," and — fearing to become one of the punished cruel (Eurydice, Daphne, Hesperie,
Arethusa, Picus, all destroyed for refusing love) — commits wholly. All secure; her vow of love, sealed with exempla.

- **The vow of loving service.** Polia gives Poliphilo everything — "all the soul, all the heart, all my power" — and
  her "inviolate florid person." The refusal of ch. XXVI is completely reversed: she who would not "extinguish her
  torch" now offers herself wholly. The union the temple exists to make is here consummated in her vow. Her endearments
  ("my little soul, my Asylum, my treasure") are the love-language she once refused him, now lavished.
- **the exempla of the punished refusers.** Her fear-catalogue (Eurydice bitten fleeing Aristaeus; Daphne turned to
  laurel fleeing Apollo; Hesperie snakebit fleeing; Arethusa turned to a spring fleeing Alpheus; Picus turned to a
  woodpecker refusing Circe) is the mirror of the nurse's counsel (ch. XXVIII) and the visions (ch. XXVII) — all the
  transformed-for-refusing-love. Polia now reads them as warnings *to herself*, and chooses love to avoid their fate. The
  transformation-theme, her lifelong terror, is resolved by yielding.
- **love as refuge, not conquest.** She calls Poliphilo her "Asylum, most-safe, whither securely I take refuge" — love as
  sanctuary, the opposite of the "cruel enemy" she once resisted (p. 409). The reversal of her whole relation to Love is
  complete: what she fled is now her refuge.
- The kiss-pledge (the *arra*) and the priestess's response complete the chapter (pp. 434–435).

"— this, as much as, with acrity of wit, I can conjecture — the warm and stelliferous heavens, the spacious and fruit-
bearing and fostering earth, and the wave-sounding sea, the potent son of the Divine Venus, with Dominion strenuously
possesses; penetrable wherever he wills, without opposing contraposition. Nor do I believe that studded cuirass, nor
triple-twilled Lorica, nor steel helm, nor shield-defence — however fatal they were — could resist, nor spurn, nor

torve Heart, however rigid, however reluctant, however most-fugitive and pertinacious, and however of asperity imbricate,

"I would doubt, then, lest, with such malefic arrows irate (against so much softness of soul), most-intemperate,
bacchant, and against me of every safeguard unarmed, he should draw (shoot), and then, never, for weeping, nor for

feel a mordant appetite of this Poliphilo — most-pious Lady (I suddenly began) — after that, to my piteous eyes, the

most-charming speeches, and sweet laments, arrived — perfused of amorous ardour, I have shattered my heart through the
middle.

"No otherwise glad and gracious to him, and pleasing rendering myself, than Atalanta to Hippomenes, and the pleasant

(sparing, not lacerating). Then return, alacritous and festive and most-jocund, my Poliphilo, my joy, my gladness, my
