## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Polia completes her declaration — Cupid's power penetrates all (no armour resists him), so she
dares not refuse; and, moved by Poliphilo's grief, she "shattered her heart through the middle" for love, welcoming him
("my joy, my hope, my Refuge, my most-ardent love") and promising his torments will vanish "like fog in the wind" — and
**gives him the kiss, the *arra*** (pledge) of her love. All secure; the seal of the reunion.

- **The kiss-pledge — the union sealed.** Polia gives Poliphilo "this amorous kiss, for a pledge (*arra*) of my inflamed
  heart" — the same legal love-pledge Book I sealed (the *arra*-kiss, p. 218). Book II now shows its true origin, from
  her side: the kiss that betroths the lovers, given freely by the once-cruel Polia. The two accounts of the betrothal
  kiss meet exactly.
- **love's total reversal, in her endearments.** "My joy, my gladness, my solace, my hope, my Refuge, my most-ardent
  love" — the litany of love-names lavished on the man she once dragged out by the feet (p. 397). The "return, alacritous
  and jocund" undoes the death she caused: she summons him back to life and joy. Her promise that his torments will
  "vanish like fog in the wind" answers his years of suffering (chs. XXVI).
- **Cupid's universal dominion, restated.** Polia's argument (no cuirass, no shield resists Love's arrow) echoes the
  nurse's (p. 411) and the boat-standard's *Amor vincit omnia* (p. 284): Love conquers all, so she yields. The book's
  motto, now in her own mouth as the reason for her surrender.
- The kiss, the priestess's response, and Poliphilo's turn to narrate follow (pp. 435–436).

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The **kiss** is exchanged (tongue-bite and all), and the **priestess**, moved to tears with the
watching nymphs, gives her response: since the lovers are "already, of love, mutually kindled… composed and unanimous,"
she need not intervene — **Love has united them himself**; but, delighted, she asks **Poliphilo to recount** how he fell in
love and how Polia refused him. All secure; the priestess blesses the union and prompts the next narration.

- **"Love has conciled you himself."** The priestess's verdict: the lovers have done the work of union themselves (through
  Polia's conversion and Poliphilo's constancy), so she need not "interpose." Love "who moves all like things" has joined
  them. This is the theological seal on the reunion — grace has already acted; the priestess only witnesses and blesses.
  Book I's rite (where she *does* actively unite them at the well) and Book II's (where she finds them already joined)
  are two facets of the same event: the outward rite and the inward reality.
- **the priestess weeps.** She and the nymphs are "moved to tears" by the lovers' kiss — the same weeping-for-sweetness
  as the temple company in Book I (p. 218). The witnesses' tears bless the union both times.
- **the prompt for Poliphilo's tale.** The priestess asks him to tell "how thou wast lancinated, and she refused so
  sweet an act" — cueing Poliphilo's own narration (chs. XXXII+), the male complement to Polia's story (chs. XXV–XXIX).
  Book II now gives *his* version of the courtship: the festival, the letter, his suffering. The two lovers narrate by
  turns, as the book's opening argument promised (p. 381).
- Poliphilo's narration, praising perseverance, opens on p. 436.

CHAPTER XXXII

[p. 436]

— pleases (me)." Having probably finished her grave words, the charming Priestess — Poliphilo, all alacritous and content,

*(Chapter argument:)*

> POLIPHILO LAUDS PERSEVERANCE, OBEYING THE COMMAND OF THE PRIESTESS. INTERMITTING (RESUMING) THE PARTS TOLD OF HIS
> FALLING-IN-LOVE, HE NARRATES ALSO HOW HE SAW HER AT A FEAST IN THE TEMPLE, WHERE, OF LOVE SUPREMELY AGITATED, HE THEN
> MORE GRIEVED OF HIS DEPARTURE. WHENCE HE MANIFESTS HIS TORMENT BY THE INVENTION OF SENDING HER AN EPISTLE (LETTER).

"Reverend and holy Priestess: Virtue is, in the arduous and funereal fatigues, and turbulent incommodities, and ungrateful
expense — the knowing to conserve oneself, and, with suasible hope, to the distempered soul, a bridle and temperature, with
probity and shrewd mode, to put; and not, impatient and inconsulate, to precipitate and fall, but, suffering,
perseveringly, to present oneself to the undertaking — however most-strait and difficult it be — and, to the voluble and
obstinate lot, and to its mockeries, and insidious versutia, with dissimulation to cede. Because not with fortitude (force),
but with virtue and wit, one conquers — as Bellerophon, persevering, succeeded to glory. Because, to all the stipends and
prices, the strenuous soldier prefers the glory.

"Wishing, then, I, legitimately, the honour (which is the due and expected prize of my amorous Agon) to consequute — firmly,
valorous, I disposed myself to endure (as an) object at which the violent Cupid might make, of me, a despicable, opprobrious
inconstancy. Judging it dementia and levity to be, timid and vecordious, to accede to the battle; and no thing to present
itself more valid than the fortitude of the soul; and no mediocre shame and verecundity persuading me — to the soldier
befalling that, in the begun contest, he turn tail and show the shoulders. But above all, never, to the militant, does it
appertain to despair, and, in the initiated battle, to defect (fail) — because it is better not to begin, than, having begun,
to leave the undertaking. For, if I err not, it seems to me that one cannot truly be called happy, if he has not somewhat
sustained his opposite (adversity) — because thence is born insolence, is generated confidence, from which proceeds the
unhappy exit, as to Polycrates. And therefore the perfection of the touchstone-trial is so much the better felt, by its
contrary, as, upon the index Battus, clearly is comprehended."

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The priestess's blessing done, **Poliphilo begins his narration** (chapter XXXII) with a **praise
of perseverance**: virtue is to endure the "arduous fatigues" of love without despairing, "not with force but with wit and
perseverance one conquers" (like Bellerophon); the good soldier never turns tail, for "it is better not to begin than,
having begun, to leave the undertaking." All secure; the theme of the whole book stated.

- **The praise of perseverance — the book's moral, from his side.** Poliphilo's constancy through Polia's cruelty
  (chs. XXVI) is here made explicit doctrine: *love is won by perseverance, not force*. It is the male complement to
  Polia's maxim "perseverance alone wears the victor's diadem" (p. 289) and the nurse's counsel — and the argument's
  heading names it. This is the value the whole Hypnerotomachia commends, and the through-line of both books: Poliphilo
  endures, Polia converts, and the union rewards perseverance. Prime thematic material for the world/novel.
- **love as an *Agon*.** Poliphilo casts his courtship as a *contest* (Agon) he must not abandon — "the soldier never
  turns tail." Love is a trial of endurance, its prize (the "honour," Polia) won only by not despairing. The imagery
  (soldier, touchstone, Bellerophon) frames constancy as heroism. His whole suffering (chs. XXVI, retold now from his
  view) is the Agon he won by persevering.
- **Book II's structure completes.** Polia told her story (childhood → cruelty → conversion, chs. XXV–XXIX); now Poliphilo
  tells his (the festival, the letter, his torment, chs. XXXII+), as the argument (p. 381) promised — the lovers narrating
  by turns. The remaining chapters are his courtship-account, filling in the human history behind Book I's dream.
- **"the touchstone felt by its contrary."** Happiness (and love) is proved by adversity, as gold is tested on the
  touchstone: Poliphilo's suffering *validated* his love. The book's consolation — trials are the making of true love.

[p. 437]

"Beyond this, holy Lady — if Polia, egregious girl, here present (whose unvisited beauties the celestial spirits would
easily contaminate), without fatigue, expense, and bitterness of heart, and imperilling of the amiable life, had drawn (me)
to my ardent desire — by immortal Jove, likewise, similarly, I could, without those (torments), lightly leave her. But who
has no repugnance (opposition), a glorious palm acquires not, nor (he) who persists not at it. Because neither glory, nor
triumph, nor any good, can be consequuted without industrious fatigue; then fatigue is cause of good, and perseverance
births it, with its Companions. And for this, a more precious thing it is (and so it is held) which troublously one
acquires, than the (thing) fittingly attained. Lucius Siccius Dentatus, therefore, of his fortitude would not be dignified
of praise and memory, had the scars, drawn-over, of his wounds, at the back been seen — because, to the degenerate
soldiers, easy presents itself the wounding from behind; but, to the strong resistant, appertains only the wounding in
front (facing the foe).

"For which thing, Love — in my contaminated, infected, and most-defiled heart (of its morbid qualities) being, unbecomingly,
risen an invader — used a more burning displeasingness than the meridional Aethon of Phoebus uses to the fresh little
flowers and soft plants and herbs; which, immoderately, it burns more than the insatiable Vulcan (fire of) Etna. For which
cause, tightly being, of such an effect, haltered, infinite accidents, and various accessories, and manifold peril, with
evident danger, showed my pitiless, collapsed, and infirm fortune against me, wrongfully mocking. Of which pernicious and
deadly cases, at present, in some part, obeying thy vow (wish), I shall begin briefly to narrate.

"Notable Priestess, and most-outstanding Lady: after that my lethal languors are quieted and somewhat settled — hastening
to satisfy thy benign precepts, more with my pleasant words than with tearful sobs, I would touch that part where I am
allotted so most-preclear a love (being silent of that which already is said) — (which) more fervid and active, wholly,
constrained me. Now, me, in thy venerable and choice, and Polia's gracious, presence, happy reputing, I shall take a modest
daring; since, with a most-humane face, thou showest thyself not to be aggrieved of this audition.

"Phoebus being risen, to re-sup the fresh tears of the weeping Aurora, with the refreshed and golden rays — every star of
the orient put to flight — illuminated, with his Eoan (dawn-light), our hemisphere, disterminated from the horizon; and,
the laborific day made, the lazy quiet dispelled, and the ponderous earth —"

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Poliphilo continues his narration: hard-won love is the more precious (no palm without struggle;
Siccius Dentatus's honourable front-scars); Love invaded his heart "more burning than Etna," bringing "manifold peril";
and he begins the tale proper — at dawn, he came to Diana's temple (the festival where he first saw Polia, p. 438). All
secure; the frame of his courtship-account.

- **Perseverance, restated: love earned is love valued.** Poliphilo's thesis — "a thing troublously acquired is more
  precious than one fittingly attained"; "no palm without repugnance." His suffering *made* his love valuable; had Polia
  yielded easily, he "could lightly have left her." The book's moral (perseverance, p. 436) deepened: the trial is not
  incidental but constitutive of true love. The world/novel's whole quest-structure rests on this.
- **the front-scars of Siccius Dentatus.** The Roman soldier honoured because his wounds were all in *front* (facing the
  enemy, never fleeing): Poliphilo's emblem of honourable endurance. His love-wounds, borne facing the trial, are his
  honour. Love as valorous combat, once more (the Agon, p. 436).
- **the tale begins at dawn.** Colonna opens Poliphilo's narrative with the ornate dawn-formula (Phoebus drying Aurora's
  tears) — the epic gesture for "one morning." His story of falling in love (the temple festival) starts on p. 438. This
  is *his* version of the first sight Polia gave from her side (her window, p. 386); here it is the temple.
- **love as fire hotter than Etna.** Standard, but the register is his: Love "invaded" his heart, burning "more than
  Vulcan's Etna." His passion is stated at full pitch before the narrative shows its origin.

[p. 438]

— of new verdure re-vested, and whatever animal, glad, to the work of effectrice nature intent — I arrived at the sacred
Temple of chaste Diana (this one, no more hoping to re-see). In which she (Polia), and many other noble and outstanding
girls, festive, with solemn rites and celebrated offices, in that fostering day, hymning, celebrated. And, as the wood
already once having been in the fire, then, re-putting it (in), more quickly re-kindles than would that which never felt
flame — like the returning, upon the imprint, to its (former) form — not otherwise, of her being aware, quietly beholding
her, and recounted (recognised) among all those (like a Goddess eminent among her Nymphs), more outstanding, and more most-
adorned of most-comely beauties (multiplied by great desire), more ornate and elegant, to me manifestly offered itself her
angelic form; with the eyes more beautiful and lucid than the clear Sun, rutilant, by which all the place coruscated, with
the other singular virtues troop-wise stuffed. Whence, of most-sweet ardour excited, I reiterated, from head to feet and
throughout, stupid (stunned), to re-inflame myself, incandescent. And then the provoked flames, and the amorous lightnings,
from her serene forehead and placid face, and from the novelty of the admirable beauty, to proceed, I recognised. And, as
Pandora-Ceres, first, in the fertile earths, by the hooked ploughshare subverted, the yielding crops disseminated, and
Melissus, King of the Cretans, first, to the highest Gods religiously sacrificed — so I, first, to her vowed and offered my
soul and my heart. And so, first, she, in the tender heart (by the pricking arrows ploughed) sowed the amorous burnings — a
more noxious and mortal sowing than Jason scattered, and worse than Annona (famine). Suddenly I, prone to the swift and
sudden rapine, more tender than, to the ardent fire, the whitening and liquable wax (disposed then to receive the impressed
images) — whence, by diuturnal and continued ardour, my heart become a flagrant little furnace — in my mind I disposed her
eternally to love, as excessively I love. Her comely and honest presence — auxiliary, and an excellent and celestial
irroration, and remediable relief, to my burnable and fragile heart, I esteemed, and a salutary refuge. While, with
scrutatory and applied regard, I beheld, indefatigable, the divine work, with the eyes to the delicate and elegant face
ever inhering — where Cupid, foster-child, in me the frequent thunderbolts jaculating, solicits — the aspect of which face,
more ornate appearing than the amplest heaven (perspicuous, liquid, serene, and most-purged air interposed, of most-lucid
stars most-ornate seen), in which two of the more lucent illustrated, converted into two festive eyes, pre-fulgent, and, of
two most-tenuous and arched brows overstanding, blackest, decorated — in which so much —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Poliphilo's account of **falling in love at the temple**: at a festival in Diana's temple he sees
Polia among the virgins "like a Goddess among her Nymphs," and — "like wood once burned that re-kindles faster" — is
inflamed anew, his heart "a little furnace," resolving to "love her eternally"; he praises her sun-bright eyes and starry
face. All secure; his version of the coup de foudre.

- **His side of the first love.** Where Polia gave the first sight from her window (p. 386), Poliphilo gives it at the
  temple festival — his heart "ploughed by Cupid's arrows," his soul "vowed and offered" to her. The two accounts of the
  falling-in-love complement each other (as the book's frame promised, p. 381): her vanity-at-the-window and his
  worship-at-the-temple are the two faces of the one event.
- **wax and fire — the loving heart.** He is "more tender than wax to fire, disposed to receive the impressed images":
  Polia's beauty stamps itself on his soft heart. It is the exact inverse of Polia's *stony* heart (porphyry, marble):
  his heart is wax, hers stone. The two temperaments the whole book contrasts, here in his own image.
- **"a salutary refuge."** He calls Polia's presence "a salutary refuge" for his burning heart — the same word (*refuge*)
  Polia used of him (p. 433). The lovers each name the other their refuge: the symmetry of mutual love, retrospectively
  complete.
- **the beauty-ekphrasis.** His praise of Polia (sun-eyes, starry face, arched brows) resumes the beauty-inventory of
  Book I (the triumph, p. 337) — now motivated as the memory of first love. It continues on p. 439 (her teeth, breath,
  hair).

[p. 439]

"— (was) enticement, and incitement of love, and so-much singular beauty, as the most-workmanlike Jove could ever imagine
to put in them; and, in the residual formal and specious figment, put on her every perfect diligence — (such) that
Phianor, in the effigy of Neptune (nature's imitator), knew not, nor could, to paint. Which breathes a similitude of
purpling roses, commingled among milky and whitening lilies. And among the most-purple lips breathed a *Myropolium*
(perfumery), and Emporium of wondrous fragrance, in a little apothecary of whitest Ivory (in most-tiny teeth orderly
disposed) hedged. The head most-blond — (such that) not so is the Baetican straw matured — more beautiful to the eye than
if she had of the little river Gracis tasted. Which all things, chiefly, in her manifestly (beyond the notable occultation)
seeing — not only content, but certainly, above whatever lover, most-happy I would appreciate myself, if she should give me
her most-precious affect — with the soul, to her volitant, secretly saying: 'O highest Gods — thus, could I aptly reduce and
violate her to my inflamed desires, as Acontius reduced Cydippe (deceived by the deceitful apple), or with commodious
fortune, as the fierce Achilles conquered the most-gentle Deidamia — or by another way!' And how much the more most-intent I
stood, in immense delightment and most-jocund delight — and no other really than a celestial demonstration I seemed
presentially to enjoy — and, clearly seeing her, and, now laughing, and now mannerly speaking, some time toward me directing
her starry and most-pleasing eyes (accompanied with two vermilion roses, suffused of honesty and of elegance); and now,
expert and aptly to the sacred instituted and imposed offices ministering, with Nymphal gestures, with entire and devout
intent, and with matronal gravity; and some time, to the ears arriving that voice which, arousing, invited my soul to the
exit, and to the repudiation of its dear conjunct (its body) — all my spirits commoved themselves to me, feeling myself all
to be covered and surrounded of an inexpert sweetness — insomuch that the soul, neglecting its natural domicile, ever thus,
with Lady Polia, at pleasant feasts, it would, moribund, have persevered. Thence, then, I recognised the impetuous insult
to the amorous fire, and, of this, its quickening, by her, to contemplate. Nor, of this, knew I to redeem, with valid
forces of wit, the insanable eyes from the sweet allurement — of my heart, by the most-shapely face pedicated (led captive).
But, sighing, tacit, with most-firm purpose, I said: 'Of this notable Nymph, for certain, am I wholly. In her most-white
breast consists all my flattering hope, and in it I have reposited and —'"

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Poliphilo's beauty-praise completes (Polia's rose-and-lily face, her ivory teeth in a fragrant
mouth, her blond hair), and he recounts falling wholly in love — wishing to win her (as Acontius won Cydippe by the
inscribed apple, or Achilles Deidamia), watching her minister at the rites, his soul so captivated it "would have died
persevering at the feast," and resolving "of this notable Nymph I am wholly (hers)." All secure; his coup de foudre
complete.

- **His surrender — "I am wholly hers."** Poliphilo's vow ("of this Nymph I am wholly… in her breast all my hope") is the
  exact counterpart to Polia's "I am wholly his" (chs. XXXI). Both lovers, in their own narrations, surrender totally to
  the other. The mutual self-gift the union requires is spoken twice, from both sides — Book II's deepest structural
  point.
- **Acontius and Cydippe.** Poliphilo wishes to win Polia "as Acontius reduced Cydippe" — the lover who tricked his beloved
  into an unbreakable vow by an inscribed apple (Ovid, *Heroides* 20–21). This is the mythic seed of his *letter-writing*
  (the argument, p. 436: "the invention of sending her an epistle"): like Acontius, he will woo by writing. The exemplum
  cues the courtship-by-letters that follows.
- **the soul that would die at the feast.** So captivated is Poliphilo that his soul "neglects its natural domicile" and
  would "die persevering" gazing at Polia — the ecstatic self-loss of love (cf. Polia's soul "transmigrated among his
  lips," p. 431). Both lovers describe the same dissolution of self into the beloved.
- **the beauty-ekphrasis motivated.** The inventory of Polia's beauty (roses-and-lilies, ivory teeth, blond hair) is here
  the *cause* of love, not mere ornament — the book's habitual beauty-catalogue given narrative function. Poliphilo's
  suffering and letter follow (pp. 440+).

[p. 440]

"— intruded all my good. This one, decently, I revere, and her, above all, I honorifice and worship — neither more nor less
than the Athenians their Pallas, and the Thebans the pleasant Bacchus, and the Indians Dionysus, the Romans Liber, and the
Arabians Adonis, the Ephesians Diana, and the Paphians the most-holy Venus, and, by the Tyrians, Hercules, and, by the
Aricians, the *fascelis* Diana. And this one, indefatigable, I follow — as the Heliotrope, Clymene, mutated into a flower,
revoluble gyres, following the aspect of her beloved Phoebus (Sun). And thus I, with amorous sect (devotion), hers wish to
be — ever with this same state of mind, nor, for terror, nor for delightment, ever wavering; but with affectionate
performance, to her vows most-humbly wish to succumb, like the timid partridge in the taloned claws of the rapacious Eagle.
Nor other image, nor simulacrum, nor shrine, in the intimate of my heart affixable — nor painted, nor carved — do I hold.
And, by this one, I hope to restore myself, and amorously to live glad — esteeming (it) a greater adornment than, to kings,
the Diadem, the Paludamentum to Emperors, to Pontiffs the Galerus, and the Lituus to Augurs. And, Polia dominating,
Poliphilo — this shall be my praise, glory, honorification, and sublimity — offering myself, in her amorous surrender, thus
vanquished, and thus prostrated: hoping, unanimous, to permeate to the triumphal realms, and to the delectable state, of
the Divine Cytherean (Venus)."

Standing, then, variously rapt, demented, and absorbed, in these feigned, so delicious cogitations and ponderings, and
fruition of such an image, from hour to hour, and from point to point, the adventitious and blind wounds, in the consenting
soul glowing, fecundated themselves; and (Cupid) received, and, of me, usurped wholly the jurisdiction, Tyranny, and licit
power. To all such affectionate mystery, this only supremely I desired: 'O me, could I open to her and discover my soul, and
indicate my intrinsic desires — with the Socratic affect, of fenestrating the breast, and of showing her the percussion of
the amorous wound, and the immoderate love that I bear her; and tell her of my pressing snare, and of the urgent flame, by
which, liquefied, the heart consumes itself; and show her the dissipation of the amorous life; and tell her, with piteous
and mild words, and groaning laments, the ultimate (extremity) that, in loving her, I sustain.' And thus, with the mind
erratic, cross, pathless, and vague, of intemperate ardour supremely I languished — and now sighing, and now glad; now
placid, quiet, and tranquil; some time indignant, without hope, hesitant, and discontent. That little Sacred and celebrated
day, with these commingled and inverse accessories, I consumed — briefest, for more than one atom of time esteemed, and
more than an instant moment."

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Poliphilo's rapture: he vows to **worship Polia** as the nations worship their gods, following her
"like the heliotrope the sun," her image "the only shrine in his heart," her love "a greater adornment than a king's
diadem"; and he longs to **open his breast** ("the Socratic affect") to show her his love-wound. All secure; the height of
his devotion, on the festival day.

- **Love as sole religion.** Poliphilo's devotion is cast as *worship* — Polia is his Pallas, his Venus, the "only shrine
  in my heart, no other image affixable." His love is monotheistic idolatry of the beloved. It answers Polia's own turn
  (she replaced Diana's image with his, p. 424): each lover makes the other the sole object of worship. The Diana-vs-Venus
  frame resolved in love's own cult.
- **the Socratic breast-window.** He wishes he could "fenestrate his breast" (open a window in his chest) to show Polia his
  wounded heart — the tale (from Momus) of the wish for a window in the breast to reveal the true heart. His love's
  frustration is that he cannot *show* it; the letter (pp. 443+) is his substitute — writing as the window to the heart.
- **the heliotrope.** He follows Polia "as the heliotrope (Clytie/Clymene) turns to the sun": the flower-of-faithful-
  following, and a transformation-image (Clytie turned to the heliotrope for love of the Sun) — the metamorphosis-theme
  turned, for once, to constancy rather than punishment. His love is the faithful turning the whole book commends.
- **the day "briefer than an atom."** Time flies in love's rapture — the festival day "consumed, briefer than an instant."
  The lover's altered time (cf. Poliphilo's day-that-is-a-year of longing, p. 386). His grief at its ending follows (p. 441).

[p. 441]

"And already the rubicund Sun, and beardless, at the extreme parts of Hesperia, the future serenity indicating — from the
sacred oracle, the delicate and ingenuous and promiscuous (mixed) women took leave and departure; and, to the solemn
offices and ceremonial observances (not as the Egyptians to Isis and Osiris, with wailing; nor as the barbarians, with
cymbal-, drum-, and pipe-strepitus; but as the Greeks, with choral dances, with melodious songs, and Latin consecrations of
little maidens, with devotion, and with the utmost alacrity performed) they made an end. Whence, from my unfed eyes and
vacillating senses, her choice and non-human image separated and disjoined, I found myself decocted and burnt of vehement
love, and to crackle like burnt Salt; and, with the eyes stupefied of the illustrious beauties, and of the brightness and
genial polish of her charming form — of there, I, again, with (eyes) frequently to salute her, and, within myself, saying
to her: 'Farewell, farewell, little robber and thievish (one) of my every good' — and secretly 'farewell' replicating,
frequently, with that little of heart which she, in her departure, permitted to remain in me (feeling myself to be ravished
and carried off, with her, my soul) — I made, I too, most-hardly, and sobbing, departure; her milky and whitening breast
made, of me, spoils, a high Trophy, and delicious repository.

"Not by other way (alas me), with the eyes desirously following her, than the beloved Protesilaus the ardent Laodamia,
pained, beheld his departing — and, more wretched, not discerning him, fell upon the shore, moribund, weeping, of mortal

crags, the rigid mountains of Murex, the sylvan shrubs of Prinus, and the most-harsh shores, the curvings of the banks, of
the knotty waves and irruent, wave-sounding floods. As now, wretched me, relinquished by my re-found delight, by my unique
good, and most-efficacious remedy, in so much tear-weeping anguish and harsh torment — with a re-kindling of more ferocious
love, and thus laden of every grief? And, of this, I feel myself to agonise, because the relief of my anguishes,
singularly, beholding her, I felt. I persuade not myself, then, that thou, O unfortunate Io, in thy clear father Inachus,
thus afflicted sawest thyself, with the mutated form, and with the once-blond tresses made noxious and rigid horns, and the
human voice, thundering, to bellow, and the verdant meadows become an unwonted —"

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The festival ends and Polia departs; Poliphilo, "burnt of love, crackling like burnt salt,"
follows her with his eyes and bids her a secret "farewell, little robber of my good," feeling his soul "ravished away with
her." He laments his loss like **Laodamia over the departing Protesilaus, Ariadne on Naxos, and Io transformed**. All
secure; his grief at parting.

- **Parting as bereavement.** Poliphilo's grief at Polia merely *leaving the festival* is as extreme as a widow's
  (Laodamia), an abandoned lover's (Ariadne), a transformed victim's (Io) — his soul "carried off with her," his heart
  left behind as her "trophy and repository." The lover's separation-agony (cf. his day-is-a-year, p. 386) at full pitch.
  The parallels are all women mourning lost love, casting Poliphilo in the bereaved-beloved role.
- **"little robber of my every good."** His tender-reproachful farewell — Polia the "thievish one" who steals his heart
  and soul as she goes. The Petrarchan *dolce nemica* (sweet enemy, cf. p. 392) in a gentler key: she robs him, and he
  loves her for it.
- **the Greek vs. barbarian rites.** A learned aside distinguishing the Greek manner of worship (choral, melodious,
  devout) from the Egyptian (wailing) and barbarian (clashing cymbals): Colonna's antiquarian taste, and a note that
  Diana's temple keeps the *decorous* Greek rite. Even in grief his mind classifies.
- **Io, the transformed.** He invokes Io (turned to a heifer, her blond hair to horns, her voice to lowing): the
  metamorphosis-theme again, here as the image of loss and disfigurement. His grief-catalogue completes on p. 442, with
  Perillus's bull. Poliphilo's love-torment matches Polia's (chs. XXVI) — the two sufferings mirror each other.

[p. 442]

"— aliment (grass)? I remained no less lamentful, disconsolate, and bewildered — for the commuted pleasures into gravest
penalities — from my eyes, of tears rainy, that preclear light detracted and taken. By which, precipitately, I gave entry,
and gaping ingress, to that holy and golden arrow (not in the least repugning, but humbly, prone, bending myself — like a
slack and tormentable willow-wand, torquing myself, and more pliable than the Amerine willow twisted into a band) — I

torch which, most-efficacious, served to my obscure cogitations. O splendid light of my blind mind! Lady of the life!
Mistress of my will! Queen of the Heart! Empress-Goddess of my soul! — which, from whatever part besieged and circum-
impelled, began gravely to alter itself within the burnt breast; and, by this cause enkindled, and throughout estuated,
burning, a more sweet lowing to the gaping mouth sent back, with dolorous little sighs, from the dire torment — than the

not so much does humanity rejoice and gesticulate, using its delightments, as it grieves then, and contristates itself
more, of the privation of those.

"But, for all this, grave I esteemed not, for such-made a girl, to consume myself, nor frequently to die; but, to every

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Poliphilo's love-torment at its height: bereft of Polia's "light," his soul "burns in the furnaced
breast like Perillus in the bronze bull," and, "most-prompt to every supplice," he yet turns to bitter **imprecation** —
cursing Polia's cruelty and begging the gods that, if he dies, she too be denied when she begs for death. All secure; his
anguish and its dark turn.

- **The bronze bull of Perillus.** Poliphilo's burning soul is Perillus roasting in his own bronze bull (the torture-device
  he built for the tyrant Phalaris, first tried on himself): the maker destroyed by his own art — an image of the lover
  consumed by the love he "gave entry to." His self-inflicted torment, learnedly figured.
- **the willow that yields to the arrow.** He "gave gaping ingress to the golden arrow… bending like a willow-wand": his
  heart, unlike Polia's stone, *welcomed* love's wound (the wax/willow to her marble/porphyry). His susceptibility is the
  exact inverse of her hardness — the two temperaments the whole book contrasts.
- **the imprecation — and its dramatic irony.** Poliphilo curses Polia, praying that if he dies she be denied even the
  death she begs for. The reader knows this is *exactly what will happen* to her (the visions, her longing to die,
  chs. XXVII, and her later grief) — his curse is answered. But we also know it *converts* her, not destroys her. The
  double narration lets his bitter prayer land as both justice and, unwittingly, the means of her salvation. A dark
  structural payoff.
- **love's grief exceeds its joy.** His maxim — "humanity grieves the privation of pleasures more than it rejoices in
  them" — is the book's melancholy note: love's loss outweighs its having. It frames the whole courtship-torment. His
  resolve (to endure "every supplice") is the perseverance the chapter praises (p. 436), tested to its limit.
- The chapter completes (p. 443) with Poliphilo's decision to write the letter.

[p. 443]

"— glorious death, miserably living, she acquire not.' Alas me — suddenly, in me the reason reciprocated (returning), all
these absurd curses, imprecated against my Polia, into me I re-torqued (turned back): 'Hey, Poliphilo — against thy good,
adverse thy soul, against thy heart, and adverse thy hope, art thou daringly, temerariously, to blaspheme? And that
sacrary of every virtue (like Herostratus, burning the temple), cursing, nefariously to invade?' I damned, then, the
amorous rage that of furor inflamed me, and that so demented me, praying the Gods, afterward, for her, all the contrary,
and all into benediction re-voking.

"Now, no more appreciating dying than thus living, I disposed myself to find a quite able and honest device, to give her
notice henceforth of my molesting and insupportable languors, and to confer to her my eternal conceit — thinking rightly
that there is no thing so hard, concreted in the human heart, that, with the little fire of love, softens not, is
conquered, and tamed; and (that) the round Ball, apt to roll, stable persists — but who gives it the impulse, knows the
office of its circled form. By such argument I cogitated to write to her, and to tempt (test) what might be the soul of so
noble and ingenuous a Nymph — a marvellous composite of every virtue and outstandingness, but, to me, a diuturnal contest,
and turbid sedition, assiduous anxieties, and continual grief, a familiar death without privation (deprivation), by the
privation of a thing so elegant, desirable, and beloved. And, of this, such an opinion persuaded me not, that in her other
should be found —"

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The end of **chapter XXXII**: Poliphilo, reason returning, **repents his curse** ("against thy own
good, thy soul, thy hope, dost thou blaspheme?") and revokes it into blessing; then, "no more appreciating death than
life," he resolves to **write to Polia** — trusting no heart is so hard that "love's little fire cannot soften it." All
secure; the decision to write the letter.

- **Curse revoked — love over spite.** Poliphilo turns his imprecation (p. 442) back on himself and "revokes all into
  benediction": his love masters his bitterness. He will not truly wish Polia harm — the constancy of his love holds even
  against her cruelty. This is the perseverance the chapter praises (p. 436), now moral: he blesses where he could curse.
- **"no heart so hard that love's fire cannot soften it."** Poliphilo's hopeful maxim — the very thing Book II proves,
  Polia's stony heart finally thawed (p. 419). His faith that the letter can move even her hard heart is vindicated by the
  whole plot. The "round ball that rolls once given the impulse" is his image: her heart needs only the right push
  (his letter, then Cupid's arrow) to yield.
- **the letter as the "device."** Unable to open his breast (the Socratic window, p. 440), Poliphilo chooses *writing* as
  the way to "give her notice of his languors" — the epistle that the argument named (p. 436). Chapter XXXIII is the letter
  itself, a set-piece courtly love-letter.
- **Herostratus** — who burned the temple of Diana at Ephesus for fame: Poliphilo fears his curse "invaded the sacrary of
  virtue (Polia)" like that arson. The learned self-reproach. Even his repentance is figured antiquarian.

[p. 444]

"— than similar propriety, genteel manner, and ductile humanity." For which thing, cautiously, I made to be given her the

*(Chapter argument:)*

> THE FIRST EPISTLE, WHICH POLIPHILO NARRATES HAVING WRITTEN TO HIS POLIA; AND SHE, NOT MOVING IN THE LEAST, HE SENT HER
> THE SECOND.

*(Poliphilo's first letter to Polia:)*

"Most-avid, and supremely most-cupidinous, to reveal somewhat the not-mediocre flame of the impatient Heart — which, for thy
preclear and singular love, greatly and validly inflamed, languishing, consumes itself — O, of veneration preclear, and
most-worthy Nymph, unique in earth of beauty, marvellous and perfect exemplar: with these — not little words, but profuse
and unimpeded little tears — blotting the present papyrus, I have taken this tolerable and honest daring (not temerarious,
but, beyond belief, strongly impelled by the continual stimulus, and by the molesting assiduity of infest love), to reveal
and declare my incredible passion, and sincere affection, which I, for thee, and to thee, bear — my sweet good, and my
sweet hope, and sole refrigerium of my unknown afflictions, and, by thee, unthought languors. To whom, with piteous voice,
and reverent words, and humble prayer, my estate, in peril, I recommend; and, of my arrow-shot and wound-dealt heart,
supplicating succour, to moderate the disordered burning.

"O Polia, divine light, and my venerable Goddess — insurd not thyself, I pray, now, to my opportune mendicables (beggings),
and (things) besought, with the face lowered, a deprecator, of most-warm love fervescent; thee I call, thee I invoke — that
thou hasten, timely, salubrious aid, efficacious comfort, necessary relief. Wherefore, my heart being, with the rapacious
hooks of thy stelliferous eyes, from my breast divulsed (torn), is originated the cause of this my inept and inelegant
writing — by me confused, and by love disposed. And, already in the preterite days, I would have attempted the like; but
never have I been able to find a mode so convenient and arcane. Then, for such respect, this my tormenting torment,
tacitly, I restrained, deferring. For, at present — since no more slow and suspended (was) my desire, intruded and
encloistered, I could not bridle it. For the violence of my love thus wills, and my depraved lot, to this my found mode, and
sweetest exordium, urges me, draws me — O egregious Nymph, and, of whoever ever was, most-beautiful. Then attend, and
commove thyself, pious; present thyself benign; render thyself, with placation, unible, to so much benevolence —"

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Poliphilo's decision made, he sends the letter — and **chapter XXXIII gives the first love-letter**
in full: an *avowal-and-plea* (he reveals his "incredible passion," calls Polia "divine light, my venerable Goddess, sole
refrigerium," his heart "torn out by the hooks of her eyes," and begs her to "commove herself, pious… present herself
benign"). All secure; a set-piece courtly love-epistle. *(The argument notes she was unmoved, and a second letter followed,
pp. 448+.)*

- **The love-letter as genre.** Chapter XXXIII is a formal *epistola amatoria* — the courtly love-letter, a recognised
  Renaissance genre (Boccaccio's, the *ars dictaminis*). Colonna gives Poliphilo's suit its written form: avowal, praise,
  self-abasement, and plea for mercy. It is the substitute for the "Socratic breast-window" (p. 440) — writing opens the
  heart that could not be shown. A distinct register within Book II (direct address, no narrative frame).
- **the heart torn out by the eyes' hooks.** His governing image: Polia's "stelliferous eyes" have "hooks" that tore his
  heart from his breast — the beloved's gaze as a grappling-hook (cf. the eyes-as-arrows, p. 427). Her beauty is the wound
  and the cause of his writing.
- **the plea unanswered.** The argument tells us in advance that this letter *fails* — Polia "not moving in the least"
  (her cruelty, chs. XXVI, now shown receiving his letters). His perseverance (writing again, the second letter) is the
  chapter's point: love that keeps writing though unanswered. The world/novel's persistence-theme.
- The letter's plea completes on p. 445.

[p. 445]

"— affection and love, beyond every cogitation — to this mystery a necessary preserver — because now, more than the usual,
this my blind fire, refusing more to stay suppressed and covered, I have licitly attributed to it this exit and breathing-
hole, manifesting how much is the improbity and insolence of the intense love — not convenient, more from hour to hour, but
greatly and sufficiently passionate, to transfix my heart and pierce through, and to reveal, solicitously, the secret
martyrdom which I, thee loving, support; and no more to occult so many my diuturnal and unceasing pains — which, willingly,
for thy venerated love embittered, I repute, with integrity of soul, a laudable action to tolerate; most-greatly holding it
firm, that thou art of nature most-humane and softenable, noble and magnanimous, and of customs approved, in aspect most-
mild, and of wit perspicuous, and of urbanity elegant, munificent and liberal, preclear of every virtue.

"All these particular and amplest gifts, to thee communicated by the high heavens — with that innate fluency, and
conspicuous and luculent speaking, and divine aspects, and attractive semblances, with the form beyond humanity outstanding,
with decorous polish specious and noteworthy — draw me to translate the soul, and the heart, and the life, into thy
whitening bosom. They draw me, venerating, insatiably to gaze, and then, insensate, leave me. Then, more subtly those
considering, I satisfy my hoping, to consequute my desired desire — otherwise, so many choice and sublime conditions would
be hallucinated (deluded), offending, of ingratitude, the benignity of the gracious artificer (God).

"Most-comely Polia, then, may it please thee now, to these my first speeches and anxious writing, to offer thyself, with
serene forehead, and to give not-doubtful faith, that I bear thee the greatest and most-singular love that ever, in the
world, a lover to a woman bore. And therefore excite thy benign audition to these just and honest petitions — that I only
ask thy pleasant and precious love; which, beyond the ornament, will be solace and conservation of my fugitive living, and,
to my acerb anguishes, moderation, and profitable lenitive. And, while I shall live, another never shall I be able to love,
without fail, than thee — with venerable service, and subject, to succumb, as to my sole Divine lord (thee) — whose
unthinkable outstandingness of beauties has transported me to this perilous pass, that I know not to imagine by what mode I,
wholly in thee, am alive, and in me, wholly dead — ignorant of the animadversion (attention) of my wretched life.

"For the health of which, from nowhere know I to find help, save both day and night, and at whatever hour, of thee sweetly
to think; and, thinking, to feign a most-apt remedy — which, at present, more necessitates than ever; otherwise, invalid and
infirm to resist the amplification of so much —"

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Poliphilo's first letter continues to its plea: he asks Polia (whom he trusts "most-humane, noble,
magnanimous") to give "not-doubtful faith" that he bears "the greatest love that ever a lover bore a woman," asking only
"thy precious love"; he vows to love none but her while he lives, "wholly in thee alive, and in me wholly dead." All
secure; the letter's petition.

- **"Wholly in thee alive, in me wholly dead."** The letter's central paradox — his life is in Polia, not himself (the
  self-loss of love, cf. "never found myself mine but all hers," p. 430). His whole being is transferred to her "whitening
  bosom." This is the mutual self-gift stated in the letter's own voice — and, ironically, prophetic: he will *literally*
  die of this love (chs. XXVI) and live again in her (ch. XXIX).
- **the flattery-plea.** He praises Polia's virtues (humane, magnanimous, mild) precisely to *make* her so — arguing that
  her heavenly gifts would be "hallucinated" (wasted, ungrateful to God) if she refused love (the *carpe diem* / use-your-
  gifts argument, the nurse's too, p. 412). The letter is rhetoric aimed at softening the stone heart he hopes love can melt
  (p. 443). It fails (she is unmoved), which is the point: rhetoric alone cannot; only the visions and grace convert her.
- **asks "only thy love."** He asks nothing but her love — "the greatest and most-singular love that ever a lover bore." The
  letter is a pure suit, humble and total. Its failure (Polia unmoved) drives the second letter and the whole tragic
  courtship. Poliphilo's persistence in writing though unanswered is the perseverance the book commends.
- The letter concludes on p. 446 (still ch. XXXIII), and a second follows.

[p. 446]

"— continual flame, will succeed the rapacious and deadly lot. For which thing, one of these (fates), by every way, it will
behove me, from thee, to accept — if, to (my) health, benign and mild, henceforth thou present thyself: Behold me, felicity
present! Behold me, a triumphant victory attained! Behold me, a crown of love won! Behold me, full content! And if, by
chance (which I persuade not myself), the contrary thou shouldst do: Behold me, troublous, miserable, and discontent. The
one (way), both of us satisfied; the other, discontent — with (thee), then, vainly repenting of it. Consent not, for so much,
Polia, Nymphal adornment, and my most-loving, to incur into this infamous note: that thou consent to my soul-slaughter —
because thy sublime condition repugns and discrepates from impiety. Nonetheless, I offer thee the oblate and immolated soul,
and the slaughtered heart — of both which, licit (as Lady), and to thy liking, dispose. For, in perpetuity, affectionately,
both alive and dead, thine I am. Farewell."

Believing, Sacred Matron, that the Damsel, to my amorous words somewhat duly commoved, would assent — no otherwise than the
called Corydon, by Battus, succoured to his grief — but by no other mode I dispersed vainly my writing and speaking than to a
marble-born statue. And so much fruit, then, made my speeches, as wind-eggs (unfertile eggs). And therefore, reasonably
considering that the first blow does not split the tree — with Herculean audacity (which Love in me breathed), and by the
found way, commodiously, of writing —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The **end of the first letter** (Poliphilo lays out the two fates — her mercy = his triumph, her
refusal = his ruin — and offers "the oblate and immolated soul, both alive and dead thine I am. Farewell"); then **Polia,
unmoved** ("to a marble-born statue I spoke, my words like wind-eggs"), and Poliphilo's resolve to write a second ("the
first blow does not split the tree"). All secure; the letter's close and its failure.

- **"Both alive and dead, thine I am."** The letter's sign-off — total self-surrender, prophetic of his literal death and
  revival (chs. XXVI, XXIX). He offers Polia "the immolated soul, the slaughtered heart" to dispose of at will; she will,
  in fact, slaughter them (his death) and then dispose them back to life (his revival). The letter foretells the plot.
- **the marble statue.** Polia receives the letter unmoved — "to a marble-born statue I spoke, my words like unfertile
  wind-eggs." Her stony heart (porphyry, p. 389) is proof against rhetoric: the letter cannot melt what only grace will.
  Colonna's point — persuasion fails where the heart is stone; the visions and Cupid's arrow (not the letters) convert her.
- **"the first blow does not split the tree."** Poliphilo's perseverance-maxim (cf. the "round ball needs an impulse,"
  p. 443): one letter failing, he writes again — the constancy the whole chapter praises. His love keeps writing into
  silence. The second letter follows.
- **the two fates offered.** He frames her choice starkly — mercy (his triumph) or refusal (his death and her vain
  repentance). She chooses refusal, and *does* vainly repent (chs. XXVII–XXIX): the letter's warning comes true. The
  double narration makes his prophecy the plot's spine.

[p. 447]

— a few days thence, this second little epistle — sedulous and intently superseding to my health — I sent to tell her:

*(Poliphilo's second letter to Polia:)*

"If less were my harsh torment than thy accustomed cruelty, most-beautiful Nymph and Polia — a slaughterer of virtue —
to my long afflictions, with blandishing hope, it would persuade me to patience. But clearly, now, I recognise (by my
depraved and unpropitious Star) thy crude savagery and ferocity, whatever my incendious martyrdom to overcome and beyond
surpass. Then, what avails, what boots it, to Love, to increase and increment, every hour, to my already-consumed little
heart, so sweet a fire, if ever more atrocious and frigescent thou show thyself, more than rigid ice, and thy breast more
frigorific than are Dirce and Nomè, founts, and more than the Salamander, cold, which, with (its) contact, extinguishes
the fire? To my ancillary and servile patience, and to my notified vows and indicated affect — so much the more kindled,
as the more the contrary opposes itself, of thy displeasingness — nonetheless, I cannot unbind the amorous and solid chain,
which, under so soft and pressing a yoke, angariously (oppressively) holds me. Nay, the more I re-kick, so much the more I
implicate myself, taken and captive in this amorous fish-trap (Nassa), like a little fly involved in the inextricable work
of Arachne (a spider's web). And thus, tightly re-bound, and enslaved and captive, not valid nor apt for flight,
constrained am I, that I, bending, incline myself to thee — because in thee alone consists my precious liberty, and my every
necessary good.

"Whence, if thou openly understandest, my Lady, so sincere and consummate affection, and so much voluntary subjection, and
so active and laborious love — why, then, wilt thou not accept so freely these things given to thee (with all my life
offered), which, in thy delicate hands, ambivalent, hangs? Alas, sweetest and beautiful little Polia — succour, I pray thee,
and leave and concede to penetrate, a little, these my (not superb, not arrogant) but devout words, into thy heart; and
arouse in thee somewhat of compassion; receive the warm sighs; auscult my domestic and familiar laments; recognise the
cordial benevolence; attend to so faithful and meek a subject. For, avidly (visibly), I die, I consume myself, of thy
immoderate love — insomuch that all the world could not retract me, nor remove me (more firm than Milo), from (this): that I,
above every other most-precious thing, excessively love, worship, and revere thee, and that I, bowed, adore thee — O effigied
and true simulacrum of a Goddess before my eyes, and to my sight, publicly, so conspicuous and notable represented — in which
most-limpidly I see depicted all my health, and expressed all my peace, delight and content."

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Poliphilo's **second letter**: he now recognises Polia's "crude savagery" (her breast "colder than
ice, than the salamander that quenches fire"), yet cannot "unbind the amorous chain" — the more he struggles, the more he
is "caught in love's fish-trap, like a fly in a spider's web"; he begs her to "let these devout words penetrate thy heart"
and "arouse somewhat of compassion," worshipping her as "a true simulacrum of a Goddess." All secure; the second, more
desperate plea.

- **Love as inescapable trap.** The second letter's image: the harder Poliphilo struggles against love, the more he is
  "caught in the fish-trap, like a fly in Arachne's web." His captivity to love (the recurring theme, pp. 240, 341) is
  now total and acknowledged — he cannot flee even Polia's cruelty. This is the perseverance of love as *bondage*: not
  chosen constancy but inability to leave.
- **the salamander-cold heart.** Polia's breast "colder than the salamander that quenches fire with its touch" — the
  perfect antithesis to his fire. The whole book's fire/ice contrast (Venus's warmth vs Diana's cold, the Hell-fresco,
  p. 250) is compressed into the lovers' two hearts: his flame, her salamander-cold. Only her conversion (fire winning,
  p. 426) resolves it.
- **the beloved as goddess-image.** He worships Polia as "a true simulacrum of a Goddess before my eyes" — the idolatry
  of love (cf. "the only shrine in my heart," p. 440). She is his religion; his letter is a prayer. Its failure (she
  unmoved) shows even worship cannot move the stony heart — grace must.
- The second letter concludes on p. 448, and the argument turns to the death-and-revival (from his side).

[p. 448]

"Now, my hope — deny not to me, wholly thine, who thus piteously supplicate pity, and, to my urgent fire, a temperament —
that, without that, to live I know not, nor can; and, if I could, I would not. Because securely I hope, in that angelic
semblance, in those most-modest and ornate customs, in that graceful and illustrious aspect, (to find) help some time —
which, without doubt, is a special and preclear token that the supernal Jupiter, with exquisite and supreme diligence, has
skilfully-made thee, a miraculous ostentation, of all excellent beauties polished; which, without doubt, of all the
beautiful damsels of the world, transcend, outstanding, and, in thee alone, complexively (all together) perfect. For which
thing, in the least I doubt not that, again, that same Artificer — who so much good, and celestial gifts, in thee has feigned
and carved, benignly, of his similitude — I hold, then, a certain opinion, that likewise some fragment of clemency, in thy
human heart, he has, by every mode, collocated; and has not created thee among the Hyperborean Griffins, nor of mother
Niobe, nor of the sylvan and rough father Apulus, nor generated of the cruel Thracian Diomedes, nor of the furious Orestes,
nor of the malign Phaedra — but of most-humane parents, and, perhaps, beyond-worldly. And this is that which, chiefly,
conserves and sustains me, in so much fervour rosy and fluid. Otherwise, the carbuncled heart, and the soul, indignant,
would, henceforth, have fled. Succour, then, auxiliary and health-bringing (one) — for I supplicate not the insolent desire
of Midas, nor that of Pygmalion, but that, propitiated, thou lend favour; subvene to the need; show thyself pious; placate
thy ire; settle the soul; tranquillise the mind; mollify thy heart; embrace the amorous affect. Rule (as Lady) him who
wishes, thy most-faithful servant, eternally serving, to serve thee. Farewell."

*(Chapter argument — Chapter XXXIV:)*

> POLIPHILO CONTINUES HIS DOLOROUS HISTORY; AND HOW, POLIA NOT COMMOVING HERSELF FOR THE TWO EPISTLES, HE SENT HER THE
> THIRD; AND THERE, SHE STILL ENDURING MORE IN HER CRUELTY, BY CHANCE POLIPHILO FOUND HER ALONE, PRAYING, IN THE TEMPLE OF
> DIANA — WHERE HE DIED. THEN, IN HER SWEET EMBRACES, HE RESUSCITATED.

"Lady most-whole in the sacred (things), and Divine Priestess: since, of my dolorous, unpolished and inelegant narrating,
to thy holy and benign sight, up to now, it has not irked (thee) — henceforth, drawing to the end my prolix haranguing, I
shall follow briefly. Daring —"

---

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The **end of the second letter** (Poliphilo hopes Polia's beauty proves her born "of most-humane
parents, not of Niobe or Diomedes," and begs her to "mollify thy heart, embrace the amorous affect… rule thy faithful
servant"); then the **argument of chapter XXXIV** (the third letter, and — from Poliphilo's side — his **death in Diana's
temple and revival in Polia's embrace**), and the start of his final narration. All secure. Book II is about to retell,
from his view, the death-and-revival Polia narrated (chs. XXVI, XXIX).

- **"Some fragment of clemency."** Poliphilo argues from Polia's *beauty* to her presumed *mercy*: God, who made her so
  fair, must have "collocated some fragment of clemency in her human heart" — she cannot be born of cruel stock (Niobe,
  Diomedes, Phaedra). It is the letter's last hope, and a poignant misjudgement: her heart *is* stone (till grace melts
  it). The argument-from-beauty-to-kindness fails, because beauty and cruelty coexisted in her (her family's hubris,
  p. 384) until she was converted.
- **the two failed letters.** Both letters (chs. XXXIII) leave Polia "not commoving herself" (argument). Poliphilo's
  perseverance in writing is heroic but futile — rhetoric cannot convert. The third letter (ch. XXXIV) will also fail, and
  only his *death* and her *visions* accomplish what words could not. The book's insight: love is won by grace and
  suffering, not eloquence.
- **the convergence.** Chapter XXXIV retells the temple death-and-revival (Polia's chs. XXVI, XXIX) from Poliphilo's side —
  the two narrations meeting at the same event, the structural climax of the two-books design. His account of dying and
  waking in her arms completes the mutual telling.
- **"drawing to the end my prolix haranguing."** Poliphilo signals the narration is nearly done — Book II approaches its
  close (the reunion, the priestess's blessing, and — after XXXVIII, the awakening — the end of the dream).

"— complacenting thee (in) that which, loving, unpremeditatedly befalls, most of the times, (to) whoever intensely loves.

*(Poliphilo's third letter to Polia:)*

"Sooner would I consume my tongue, ingenuous and most-noble adolescent-girl, than ever it could somewhat, upon the candid
papyrus, express how toilsome, how grave, how acerb is my bitter pain — which, day and night, in the languishing heart,
re-doubled, increases without intermission — seeing thee thus deaf and displeasing. And only because I recognise, too,
thee not to be content, and satiated, still, of my grave torments (no less, in the least — nay, excessively greater — than
those which, not much time (ago), twice I have sweetly written thee). But, since the fallacious, the forced, the savage,
and dolorific Love, with the impious fortune and my adversative star, necessarily constrain me, to thee, voluntary, to
handmaid and serve — O Nymph, above the human grasp, of wondrous beauty, and, of conspicuous and elegant filament, most-
admired; but, above all and whatever other, I dare say, excessively pitiless and cruel, like a sylvan and untamed beast,
more than the most-immense and famished Lion of Androcles, rigid and displeasing. Which things belie the human seed, and
that thy meek and divine simulacrum, of thy comely aspect pre-shining, and of that celestial and rare make, denigrate —
of humanity naked, and rebelling to the amorous little fires of Cytherea, and to the divine Empire of the shrewd Nature a
spurner. For, a juridical cause, and odious experience, alluring me, transport (me), (that I ought) to speak of so much
appreciable time vainly consumed... amorously afflicting thee, and day and night to that colloricated (heated), detained,
occupied, and useless, having lost (it) — inflamed and dried up, loving thee, sole elected to destroy my life — by that
which I manifestly see: that, the more I love thee, so much the more it seems that I, hardening thee, lapidise (turn thee
to stone). Ah, Polia — can it be that, in thee, would not be found one atom of piteous spirit, that a little gracious
audition, with internuncio (messenger) little epistles, I could find in thee — nor with pre-strepent sighs, nor with
affluent and frequent little tears, from my moist eyes vaporable, solicitous, irroring, which every hour weep —"

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Poliphilo sends the **third letter**, Polia unmoved "as Mount Olympus by the winds"; the letter
reproaches her cruelty (worse than the lion of Androcles, "of humanity naked, a spurner of Cytherea and of Nature"), and
makes the terrible observation: **"the more I love thee, the more I lapidise thee"** — his love hardens her to stone. All
secure; the third, most desperate plea.

- **"The more I love thee, the more I turn thee to stone."** Poliphilo's darkest insight — his love, instead of softening
  Polia, *hardens* her ("lapidise") — captures the tragedy of chs. XXVI from his side. His warmth met her stone and, far
  from melting it, seemed to harden it further. (The reader knows only the visions and Cupid's arrow, not love's pleas,
  finally melt her.) The stone-imagery, hers throughout, is here diagnosed by him.
- **the Agon persevered.** Twice-failed, Poliphilo writes a *third* time — "not leaving the begun Agon," testing "whether
  her heart were touchstone-stone or human." His perseverance is heroic and hopeless: he keeps writing into a heart of
  stone. The chapter's theme (perseverance, p. 436) at its most poignant — constancy that cannot succeed by its own
  efforts.
- **"a spurner of Nature."** He charges Polia with rebelling against "the divine Empire of shrewd Nature" (Venus
  Physizoa, generative nature) — the same charge the nurse made (p. 412): to refuse love is to offend Nature. His letter
  argues the book's creed, but arguments cannot move her. The letter continues on p. 450.

[p. 450]

"— its (my heart's) guilty condition and dolorous case? — (my eyes) which so easily believed, and, with mere faith,
judged, that thy incomparable beauty had allotted and associated itself with the inextricable congestion of some sweetness
of soul; which eyes, with prompt appetence and flagrant petulance, have been the cause and primary beginning of the ruin
and captivity of my life. Nor, for this, still, can I, with any temperament, bridle them, that they extremely desire not
those (thine) to re-behold — and that most-fulgent Sun which has made them to darken, and to relapse, precipitant, into
the pernicious harm. Whence, O celestial spirit, and venerable Idol of mine — if, propitiated to my writing, now thou
concede them not entry and audience, perhaps it is for my absence. But, amiable my Lady, if in sight, and presentially,
thou sawest me consume and languish, and all liquable in tears, together with re-increasing sighs — and me sweetly giving
heed to bend thy soul, and, supplicating, to mercy thee, and to placation, deprecate; and likewise, with every reverent
and ancillary meekness, narrate the incredible love that I bear thee, and the bitterness of heart that I sustain, and the
tedium of my already-odious life, and that which, for thee, continually, miserably, I suffer — alas me, illustrious Polia,
beauty of the Nymphs: I am certain that, to pity, thou wouldst commove thyself, and limpidly wouldst recognise that I merit
to obtain favour and prompt aid from thee.

"Which (aid) whenever, persisting pertinacious and impious, thou deniedst, reluctant — and so fervid and proterve a love
spurning — so much I can conjecture: that thou tellest me to burst and die for thee. Now, what convenient cause feelest
thou, to consent to so much evil? What praise, what prize, what victory, what content, canst thou ever, of this,
consequute? Nay, a most-vulgar, infamous mark of vituperable cruelty; and, perhaps, inexorable vengeance from the avenging
Gods (which, never stumbling, lets not the previous and criminal flee-er escape). Wish not, then, to assent to so much
vituperable evil; but rather, with thy supreme crown (glory), render thyself pious, mild, and pleasant — of which thing,
and (of) the ornament of thy commendable beauty, and long-life of our caducous life, and content, and quiescence, and
sweetest fruit, to sprout and grow up in a brief little point, not ungrateful thou shalt feel. Because what other treasure,
in the world, so precious could be esteemed, as two uniform lovers? Nor a more maledict, malign, and improbable thing, than
that thou be loved, and not love. For which thing, if, at present, a preserver of my love, and health-bringing to my ills,
thou present not thyself — what wilt thou that I do more of this sad life, henceforth, for thee so noxious and dolorous?
Being certain that, if, obdurate, obstinately unmitigable, thou shalt persevere, immense and stupid — of insupportable
passion, it will behove me, out of this life, to commeate (depart); and, by this way, finally, thy —"

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The third letter continues: Poliphilo's eyes, "the primary cause of my ruin," cannot stop
desiring Polia's; he pleads that, could she *see* him languishing, she would pity him; warns that her refusal earns only
"an infamous mark of cruelty and inexorable divine vengeance"; and asks "what treasure so precious as two united lovers?
what worse than to be loved and not love?" — threatening that, if she persists, he must die. All secure; the plea's dark
turn toward his death.

- **"To be loved, and not love."** The letter's central charge — the worst thing is "to be loved and not love." Polia's
  sin, named: she receives love and gives none. It is the imbalance Poliphilo asked the priestess to "equalise" (p. 430),
  and the "inequality" that is love's tragedy. The whole book's drama is the closing of this gap (her conversion).
- **the warning of vengeance — prophetic again.** He warns that her cruelty earns "inexorable divine vengeance… which lets
  not the criminal flee-er escape." This *exactly* foretells her punishment-visions (the fleeing damsels, the executioners,
  chs. XXVII) — Poliphilo's letter predicts, without knowing, the very torments she will suffer. The double narration
  makes his warning the plot's outline.
- **"two uniform lovers — the world's most precious treasure."** The letter's positive vision: mutual love is the
  supreme good, "no treasure so precious as two uniform lovers." This is the union the temple makes and the book
  celebrates — stated by Poliphilo as the thing Polia's cruelty denies them both. The value the whole work commends.
- **the threat of death.** He tells her plainly: if she persists, "it will behove me to depart this life" — the death
  that (chs. XXVI, XXIX) actually happens. His letter announces his own death-by-cruelty before it occurs. The letter
  concludes on p. 451.

[p. 451]

"— iniquitous will will cease, and the greatness of my grief. Farewell."

By this way, then, I gave heed, sedulous, to reduce and humanate, and her sweetly to blandish, and to mitigate — soliciting
the asperity received from the initiated arduous and perilous work. But neither she, nor the perfid Love, consented to my
suasive words, with high and sworn espousals, openly showing her the nod and semblance of my — of every sweetness sweetest —
flames; (that) she, in return, with requisite reciprocation, love me. And with every industrious art, and shrewd cogitation,
I forced myself to kindle her of that veracious, nude, simple, and excellent affect, and amorous fire, in which, without any
remedy, continually — like a *Pyraulus* (fire-fly/flame-moth) — I nourished myself, wretched. And, beyond this, with her,
infinite times, with the mind I feigned to have a charming colloquy; and, ratiocinating (with her), daringly — intermixed,
frequently, the tormentable wailings — I said: 'O my little Nymph, of inhuman and ferine heart — of nature a soft girl (yet)
more than solid Steel, and more than murex-stone hardest, more tenacious than a retaining Grapnel, more obstinate than a
hinged Beam; more mordant than a rapt Talon, and much more than the cruel and foul Harpies rapacious of my heart: how canst
thou persevere in so much hardness and impiety? — more impious than Mithridates, more savage than Alcmaeon, more ungrateful
of so much affection than Paris toward Oenone.' — To my prayers, remove, then, these iniquitous abjections from thy Nymphal
heart, and this vulgar mark; and assent thyself, propitiated, to my suppliant petitions; concede, my Lady, that I consequute
the desired quiet; permit to penetrate thy auditory, my tormentable little sighs; consent to my ardent loves.

And, many, and to these similar, complaints and instances performed — in the least I could not move such agitation from my
continual grief, which, in me pressed, was so much in all the viscera occupant, and had so high germinated in the heart its
most-bitter roots, that, by other art, nor way, nor mode — save by its chief hope (Polia herself) — ever, to extirpate, I
know not, nor can, nor avail. And less profitable, still, were the groaning voices, about her superb palace vainly dispersed
— (she) more deaf than Icarus to the paternal admonitions, and more displeasing than Caunus to the desperate Byblis;
abominatrix of sweet love, superseding to the false and habituated opinions, in the tender and virgin age wont to harden. And
an ardous thing it is to leave that which, some time, in the soul is impressed: enerve, not easily can one. Thence, then, was
the exordium and origin, that I, simply ensnared and implicated, in these enveloping nets, and fallacious decoy, and in
these subtle, caducous, uncertain, fugacious and momentary snares and sharpnesses of love, enslaved — that, under this
molesting Tyranny and condition, and miserable servitude, subjugated and enrolled, I found one sole pleasure and alluring
delightment: to love her extremely; nor did I repugn to the flying (arrows) —"

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** The **end of the third letter** ("by this way thy iniquitous will and my grief will cease.
Farewell"), and Poliphilo's continued **vain suit**: he pleads, imagines "charming colloquies" with her, catalogues her
hardness ("harder than steel, than murex-stone… more impious than Mithridates, more ungrateful than Paris to Oenone"),
haunts her palace — all fruitless, for love's roots are too deep in him to pull out except by "its chief hope, Polia
herself." All secure; the impasse of his unrequited love.

- **Love with no exit but the beloved.** Poliphilo's love is a "servitude" whose only "remedy" is Polia's own yielding —
  he cannot uproot it (its "roots germinated too high in the heart"), cannot flee it (the fish-trap, p. 447). His constancy
  is total and helpless: he can only keep loving and pleading, unto death. The perseverance the book praises is here shown
  as *inescapable devotion* — he perseveres because he cannot do otherwise.
- **the catalogue of her hardness.** "Harder than steel, than murex-stone; more impious than Mithridates; more ungrateful
  than Paris to Oenone" — Poliphilo's inventory of Polia's cruelty answers her own self-condemnation (she called herself
  worse than Anaxarete, Medea, p. 396). Both lovers, in their narrations, catalogue *her* cruelty — she confessing, he
  suffering it. The double account agrees on the crime.
- **the Pyraulus moth.** He "nourishes himself in love's fire like a Pyraulus" — the flame-moth that lives in fire (Pliny):
  the lover sustained by the very fire that consumes him, love as self-immolating sustenance. The sweet/bitter paradox
  (p. 279) in a single image.
- **love's one pleasure.** Even in this servitude he finds "one sole pleasure: to love her extremely." His love is its own
  reward, needing no return — the purest constancy. It is the love that will die for her and be revived by her. His death
  in the temple (the chapter's climax, from his side) follows on pp. 452+.

[p. 452]

— little arrows of blindfold Cupid. To whom, enticed, without delay, disposing myself, humbly I accepted, and all,
indefatigable, I dedicated myself an observer of his most-turbulent, sharp, investigatrix, cross, and unbridled little
laws — relying on the confidence of her angelic aspect, and that such were, still, her heart, and that the part with the
whole should agree, and the whole, mosaic-wise, accede to the part, and not, with desperate harmony (be), so beautiful, so
elegant, so comely and marvellous, and divine, a composite. Hoping reasonably that the arrow-shooting Cupid — who thus
tormentably had wounded, intimately, the sad heart in me — was, juridically, and to my adverse and pernicious love, a most-
safe presidium, and, to the blind errors incursant, an affable and remediable propulser, and a prompt and pious succour,
and, to the superfluous blight and ardour, a congruous temperament — expecting, however, salutary aid from nowhere else than
from him: that he, equally, should draw, in her, the hard and cruel bow, with which, in me, direly, he has drawn.

And, treating the gaping wound, the more it exacerbated in asperity, and the more re-doubled the wound-dealing and mortal
grief — but, the hope of re-healing the amplified wound ever having, in him, non-hesitant confidence (that, I being his most-
vowed subject and servant, and his opulent prey, bondman, captive, plunder, and spoil, and his copious Trophy), that same
medicament which his most-pious Mother, and my Lady (Venus), made to the wounded Aeneas, still to me, following the maternal
pity, would aid. And, again, being his most-devoted — that same patronage he should lend which holy Vesta lent to her
handmaid and subject Tuccia, benignly, by the miracle of the sieve (carrying water in a sieve), the perpetrated fault
occulted, freed (her) from public opprobrium and infamous supplice.

Whence — as, to lovers, is wont manifoldly to befall — thus, desperate, in grave litigation, without judge and adverse
party, I condemned both (Love and Fortune), conjured to my deadly harm, with querulous laments weeping, inculpating them as
guilty, and choice enemies of every pious humanity; (then) now, glad and festive, I revoked in me the sentence. Some time,
excited, like a rabid and impatient dog, biting at its retaining chain, I wished to avoid and flee the hard knot of the
amorous but molesting snare, and to un-armour myself. Then, vainly imagining, I feigned many and delectable solaces and
pleasures, false vengeances, temerarious insults, perturbing perils, and impavid death — I found myself, afterward, more
tightly knotted, and solidly armoured. By such altercation, and abortive appetites, consuming my tribulous life — and,
among sighs and bitter sobs, half-consumed — there remained no place that, by me, with solicitude, perennial care, and
scrutatory vigilance, was not indagated and lustrated, ratched, and re-searched; no way, and blind-alley, and almost even
through the porticoes, unattempted, omitted —

## Notes

**Confidence: medium.** Poliphilo's devotion to Cupid (hoping the god will "draw the same cruel bow in her" and heal his
wound as Venus healed Aeneas), his oscillation between cursing and blessing Love and Fortune, his straining against love's
"chain like a rabid dog," and his **searching everywhere** for Polia. All secure; the impasse before he finds her.

- **Hoping Cupid will wound her too.** Poliphilo prays that Cupid "draw the same bow in her" — that Polia be struck as he
  was, so their love be equal. This is the exact prayer he later makes to the priestess (p. 430), and — the reader knows —
  it is *granted* (Cupid strikes Polia, p. 419). His whole suffering is the petition the plot answers.
- **Venus healed Aeneas; Vesta saved Tuccia.** His learned hopes: as Venus cured her son Aeneas's wound, and Vesta saved
  the Vestal Tuccia (who carried water in a sieve to prove her chastity), so Love's "maternal pity" will aid him. Colonna's
  antiquarian consolation — the gods help their devotees. Poliphilo trusts the divine machinery that will, in fact, deliver
  the miracle (his revival).
- **love as a chain he cannot break.** He strains "like a rabid dog biting its chain," imagines fleeing, and finds himself
  "more tightly knotted" — the inescapable-captivity theme (pp. 447, 451) restated. His constancy is bondage; he cannot
  not-love. The search that follows leads him to the temple and his death (pp. 453–454).
- **the exhaustive search** — he ransacks every street and alley for Polia: the lover's obsessive pursuit (which Polia,
  from her side, felt as a "siege," p. 389). The double narration's two views of the same hunt — his desperation, her
  resentment — meet as he finds her.

[p. 453]

— only, exploring, most-vigilant and frequent, and minutely and corneredly investigating, if her I could find. It befell,
lastly, that Love and Fortune, in a benign ascension finding themselves, benignly most-pacate, unforeseenly conducted me
into the Sacramentary Temple — she inadvertent — into which she frequently went, but occult. And there, having found her
alone, swiftly — the heart shaken (of) every other appetence, like a spear-armed Lion (at) the insulting prey — thus, and
by no other mode, prompt to her, most-ferocious, invading, and, with the extreme virtues (strength) derived and joined,
and having accosted (her), of a sudden liquefied — like wax, by fire, adherent and near — lifeless I became, and
consternated; and, ignorant what to do or say, at length thus I began, with pained and inelegant speaking, humbly to say
(only, of all my forces, scarce remaining the tremulous voice, and a little of spirit, almost, in the afflicted jaws,
interdicted; and the soul mourning, stupefied the eloquent tongue, and, with all the body trembling, the torpid members),
lamentful:

"Alas me, Polia — golden and precious Column of my living, sole consolable hope of my afflictions — already several days
are transacted, that thee alone, most-fervidly, not so much have I loved, but, like a Goddess, venerating, honorificated,
and, with per-injury of the Gods, adored — with burning flame of love, my holocaust heart immolated (as the Priests did,
sacrificing to Bellona), and consigned to thee my living, voluntarily, to thy arbitrament and will. And thou art made
(alas, unhappy!), undeservedly, against me cruel, and a more irritable expultress of my every good — as if thou wast, by me,
noxiously hurt — like Juno, the Trojans, with great irascence, persecuting. More noxiously to me infest than the British
little stones to the mellificating Bee; and more pugnacious, contrary, and more different from my will than the infest
Thetis to Vulcan; and more molesting than the unstable tail to Lucius (the ass); more noxious than the *scandulacea*
(darnel) to the crops, and more than the sonorous hail to the most-tender little fronds; and more than the burning Phoebus
to the springing flowers and grassy meadows.

"Finally, wishing I, with every sweetness of heart, with alluring and meek speaking, to soothe, placate, propitiate,
enticing her, and to remove her from the unmild and obstinate purpose, and to divert and retrograde the dire and truculent
will, and to tranquillise so many her turbulences, and her soul unconsentaneous and indecent, and to reflect (it) to pity
and mercy, and her ferocity to moderate, and her morbid heart, of savagery, with tears and sighs to medicate, and, to the
charity and penury of affection, with fecund love to succour — blandishing, charming and sweetly, with profuse little tears
and —"
